children.translated_text:
The <s>Vakroktijīvita</s> (The Life of Oblique Expression) composed by the illustrious <s>Rājānaka Kuntaka</s>.
1. First Unfolding (<s>Prathamonmeṣa</s>).
The creator of the marvelous works that constitute the diversity of the three worlds —
we bow to <s>Śiva</s>, whose sole instrument is the vibration of <s>Śakti</s> (divine power). // VjivC_1.1 //
If the entities existing in the three worlds are discriminated as they truly are,

children.text: yadi tannādbhutaṃ nāma daivaraktā hi kiṃśukāḥ // VjivC_1.2 //
children.translated_text: then that is not wonderful — for the <s>kiṃśuka</s> flowers are naturally red. // VjivC_1.2 //
If, on the other hand, their true nature is established merely according to one's own intellect and inclination,

children.text: sthāpyate prauḍhimātraṃ tatparamārtho na tādṛśaḥ // VjivC_1.3 //
children.translated_text: that is mere boldness — the ultimate truth is not like that. // VjivC_1.3 //
Thus, disregarding even my own independence in the midst of invalid arguments,
I shall reveal the essence of the ocean of nectar that is literary meaning. // VjivC_1.4 //
By which both these [aspects] — characterized by the determination of true nature —
will produce in the knowledgeable a wonderment and amazement of marvelous fragrance. // VjivC_1.5 //

At the commencement of the work:
The salutation to one's chosen deity is customary; therefore, he begins with that very thing —
I salute the dancing girl in the theater of the beauty of the moon-like faces of the greatest poets,
the goddess resplendent with beautiful gestures that are the vibrations of excellent speech. // Vjiv_1.1 //

children.text:
iti /
devīṃ vande devatāṃ staumi /
kāmityāha---kavīndravaktrendulāsyamandiranartakīm /
kavīndrāḥ kavipravarāsteṣāṃ vaktrendurmukhacandraḥ sa eva lāsyamandiraṃ nāṭyaveśma tatra nartakī lāsikām /
kiṃviśiṣṭām---sūktiparispandasundarābhinayojjvalām /
sūktiparispandāḥ subhāṣitavilasitāni tānyeva sundarā abhinayāḥ sukumārāḥ sāttvikādayastairujjvalaṃ bhrājamānām /
yā kila satkavivaktre lāsyasadmanīva2 nartakī svavilāsā3 bhinayaviśiṣṭā nṛtyantī virājate tāṃ vande naumīti vākyārthaḥ /
tadidamatra tātparyam---yatkila prastutaṃ vastu kimapi kāvyālaṅkārakaraṇaṃ tadadhidaivatabhūtāmevaṃvidharāṇīyakahṛdayahāriṇīṃ vāgrūpāṃ sarasvatīṃ staumīti /
evaṃ namaskṛtyedānīṃ vaktavyavastuviṣayabhūtānyabhidhānābhidheyaprayojanānyāsūtrayati /
children.translated_text: Thus: 'I salute the goddess' means 'I praise the deity.' Why? — he says: 'the dancing girl in the theater of the beauty of the moon-like faces of the greatest poets.' The greatest poets (<s>kavīndra</s>) — the foremost among poets; their moon-like face (<s>vaktrendum</s>) — the moon that is their face; that itself is the theater of beauty (<s>lāsyamandira</s>) — the dance-hall; therein, the dancing girl (<s>nartakī</s>) — the danseuse. Of what kind? — 'resplendent with beautiful gestures that are the vibrations of excellent speech.' The vibrations of excellent speech (<s>sūktiparispanda</s>) — the displays of fine utterance; those very things are the beautiful gestures (<s>sundarābhinaya</s>) — the delicate enactments of the <s>sāttvika</s> and other kinds; by those, resplendent (<s>ujjvala</s>) — shining. She who indeed shines dancing in the face of a good poet as if in a dance-hall, distinguished by the gestures of her own charms — her I salute, I bow to — this is the meaning of the sentence. The purport here is this: whatever the subject at hand — which is some [system of] poetic ornamentation — I praise <s>Sarasvatī</s>, the form of speech, who captivates the heart, who is the presiding deity of that [subject], who is of such a nature as to be carried in the heart. Having thus made salutation, he now indicates the name, the content, and the purpose — which constitute the subject matter to be discussed —
In order to produce certainty regarding the scope of speech,
the name and so forth are stated in the opening verse, like the measuring cord of a building. // VjivC_1.6 //
This is an intermediate verse. (?)
For the accomplishment of a diversity that produces extraordinary wonder,
some unprecedented ornamentation of poetry is hereby established. // Vjiv_1.2 //

children.text:
alaṅkāro vidhīyate alaṅkāraṇaṃ kriyate /
kasya---kāvyasya /
kaveḥ karma kāvyaṃ tasya /
nanu ca santi cirantanāstadalaṅkārāstatkimarthamityāha---apūrvaḥ, tadvyatiriktārthābhidhāyī /
tadapūrvatvaṃ tadutkṛṣṭasya tannikṛṣṭasya ca dvayorapi saṃbhavatītyāha---ko 'pi, alaukikaḥ sātiśayaḥ /
so 'pi kimarthamityāha---lokottaramatkārakārivaicitryasiddhaye asāmānyāhlādavidhāyivicitrabhāvasampattaye /
yadyapi santi śataśaḥ kāvyālaṅkārāstathāpi na kutaścidapyevaṃvidhavaicitryasiddhaiḥ /
alaṅkāra-śabdaḥ śarīrasya śobhātiśayakāritvānmukhyatayā kaṭakādiṣu vartate, tatkāritvasāmānyādupacārādupamādiṣu, tadvadeva ca tatsadṛśeṣu guṇeṣu,4 tathaiva ca tadabhidhāyini granthe /
śabdārthayorekayogakṣematvādaikyena vyavahāraḥ,yathā gauriti śabdaḥ gaurityartha iti /
tadayamarthaḥ---granthasyā5 laṅkāra ityabhidhānam, upamādiprameyajātamabhidheyam, uktarūpavaicitryasiddhiḥ prayojanamiti /
evamalaṅkārasyāsya prayojanamastīti sthāpite 'pi tadalaṅkāryasya kāvyasya prayojanaṃ vinā sadapi tadapārthakamityāha---
children.translated_text: 'Ornamentation is established' means ornamentation is being made. Of what? — of poetry. Poetry is the work of a poet. Now, since there exist ancient ornamentations [of poetry by earlier writers], for what purpose [a new one]? — he says: 'unprecedented' — expressing a meaning different from those. That unprecedented quality is possible both for what is superior to those and for what is inferior to those — he says: 'some' (<s>ko'pi</s>) — extraordinary, surpassing. Even that, for what purpose? — he says: 'for the accomplishment of a diversity that produces extraordinary wonder' — for the attainment of a wealth of varied emotions that produces uncommon delight. Although there are hundreds of poetic ornamentations, none of them has accomplished diversity of this kind. The word 'ornamentation' (<s>alaṅkāra</s>) applies primarily to bangles and the like, because they cause a surpassing beauty of the body; by secondary usage based on the similarity of being a cause of that [beauty], it applies to simile and the like; likewise to qualities (<s>guṇa</s>) that resemble those; and also to the treatise that describes them. Since word and meaning have a single fortune, there is a unified usage — just as 'cow' is both the word and the meaning. The meaning is this: the name is 'ornamentation,' the content is the class of subjects such as simile and the like, and the purpose is the accomplishment of the kind of diversity described. Even though it is thus established that this ornamentation has a purpose, without the purpose of poetry — which is the thing to be ornamented — even though it exists, it would be pointless. He says —
A means for accomplishing <s>dharma</s> (righteousness) and the other [goals of life], set forth in a delicate manner —
the composition of poetry is a cause of delight to the hearts of the noble. // Vjiv_1.3 //

children.text:
hṛdayāhlādakārakaścittānandajanakaḥ kāvyabandhaḥ sargabandhādirbhavatīti saṃbandhaḥ /
kasyetyākāṅkṣāyāmāha---abhijātānām /
abhijātāḥ khalu rājaputrādayo dharmādyupeyārthino vijigīṣavaḥ kleśabhīravaśca, sukumārāśayatvātteṣām /
tathā satyapi tadāhlādakatve kāvyabandhasya krīḍanakādiprakhyatā prāpnotītyabhidhatte6---dharmādisāghanopāyaḥ /
dharmāderupeyasya7 caturvargasya sādhane saṃpādane tadupadekharūpatvādupāyastatprāptinimittam /
tathāvidha8 puruṣārthopadeśaparairaparairapi śāstraiḥ kimaparāddhamityabhidhīyate---sukumārakramoditaḥ /
sukumāraḥ sundaraḥ hṛdayahārī9 kramaḥ paripāṭīvinyāsastenoditaḥ kathitaḥ san /
abhijātānāmāhlādakatve sati pravartakatvātkāvyabandho dharmādiprāptyupāyātāṃ pratipadyate /
śāstreṣu punaḥ kaṭhorakramābhihītatvād dharmādyupadeśo duravagāhaḥ /
tathāvidhe viṣaye vidyamāno 'pyakiñcitkara eva /
rājaputrāḥ khalu samāsāditasvavibhavāḥ samastajagatīvyavasthākāritāṃ pratipadyamānāḥ ślāghyopadeśa10śūnyatayā svatantrāḥ santaḥ samucitasakalavyavahārocchedaṃ pravartayituṃ prabhavantītyetadarthameva11 tadvyutpattaye vyatītasaccaritarājacaritaṃ tannidarśanāya nibaghnanti kavayaḥ /
tadevaṃ śāstrātiriktamastyeva12 praguṇaṃ prayojanaṃ kāvyabandhasya /
mukhyaṃ puruṣārthasiddhilakṣaṇaṃ prayojanamāstāṃ tāvat anyadapi lokayātrāpravartananimittaṃ bhṛtyasuhṛtsvāmyādisamāvarjanamanena vinā samyaṅ na saṃbhavatītyāha---
children.translated_text: 'A cause of delight to the hearts' — a producer of joy in the mind — such is 'the composition of poetry,' meaning the composition of cantos (<s>sargabandha</s>) and the like. Of whom? In anticipation of this question, he says: 'of the noble.' The noble are indeed princes and the like, who seek the desirable objects beginning with <s>dharma</s>, who are ambitious, and who are averse to hardship, because of their refined disposition. Even though it is thus a cause of their delight, the composition of poetry would become comparable to a plaything and the like — therefore he declares: 'a means for accomplishing <s>dharma</s> and the other [goals of life].' It is a means, a cause for the attainment, because it takes the form of instruction in the accomplishment of the four goals of human life (<s>caturvarga</s>) beginning with <s>dharma</s>. What is lacking in other treatises that are devoted to instruction in such goals of human life? — he says: 'set forth in a delicate manner.' 'Delicate' means beautiful, captivating of the heart; 'manner' means orderly arrangement; 'set forth' in that [manner], i.e., narrated with that. When the composition of poetry causes delight to the noble, it attains the status of being a means for the attainment of <s>dharma</s> and the rest, because it motivates [them to action]. In treatises, however, because instruction in <s>dharma</s> and the rest is expressed in a harsh manner, it is difficult to penetrate. Even when present in such a domain, it is entirely ineffective. Princes indeed, having acquired their own resources, while undertaking the administration of the entire world, being independent through the absence of praiseworthy instruction, are capable of bringing about the destruction of all proper conduct — for this very purpose, poets compose accounts of the past conduct of good kings, to serve as examples. Thus, there is indeed a purpose of poetic composition that surpasses [that of] treatises. Setting aside the primary purpose characterized by the attainment of the goals of human life — there is another purpose too, [namely] the facilitation of worldly affairs: the winning over of servants, friends, masters, and the like cannot properly be accomplished without this [poetry]. He says —
The beauty of the activity of social conduct
is obtained by practitioners only from the study of good poetry — a fresh propriety is attained. // Vjiv_1.4 //

children.text:
vyavahāro lokavṛttaṃ tasya parispando vyāpāraḥ kriyākramalakṣaṇastasya saundaryaṃ rāmaṇīyakaṃ tadvyavahāribhirvyavahartṛbhiḥ satkāvyādhigamādeva kamanīyakāvyaparijñānādeva nānyasmād āpyate labhyata ityarthaḥ /
kīdṛśaṃ tatsaundaryam---nūtanaucityam /
nūtanamabhinavamalaukikamaucityamucitabhāvo yasya /
tadidamuktaṃ bhavati---mahatāṃ hi rājādīnāṃ vyavahāre varṇyamāne tadaṅgabhūtāḥ sarve mukhyamātyaprabhṛtayaḥ samucitaprātisvikakartavyavyavahāranipuṇatayā nibadhyamānāḥ sakalavyavahārivṛttopadeśatāmāpadyante /
tataḥ sarvaḥ kvacitkamanīyakāvye kṛtaśramaḥ samāsāditavyavahāraparispandasaundaryātiśayaḥ ślāghanīyaphalabhāg bhavatīti /
yo 'sau caturvargalakṣaṇaḥ puruṣārthastadupārjanaviṣayavyutpattikāraṇatayā kāvyasya pāraṃparyeṇa prayojanamityāmnātaḥ, so 'pi samayāntarabhāvitayā tadupabhogasya tatphalabhūtāhlādakāritvena tatkālameva paryavasyati /
tatastadatiriktaṃ kimapi sahṛdayahṛdayasaṃvādasubhagaṃ tadātvaramaṇīyaṃ prayojanāntaramabhidhātumāha---
children.translated_text: 'Social conduct' (<s>vyavahāra</s>) is worldly activity; its 'activity' (<s>parispanda</s>) is the operation characterized by the sequence of actions; its 'beauty' (<s>saundarya</s>) — that is obtained, i.e., acquired, by practitioners, i.e., those who engage in conduct, only from the study of good poetry, i.e., from the thorough knowledge of beautiful poetry, not from anything else. Of what kind is that beauty? — 'a fresh propriety' — one whose fitness is novel, new, extraordinary. This is what is being said: when the conduct of great kings and the like is being described, all those who are part of it, beginning with the chief minister, being represented with skill in their respective proper duties, come to serve as instruction in the conduct of all practitioners. Therefore, everyone who has exerted effort in some beautiful poetry, having attained the surpassing beauty of the activity of social conduct, becomes the enjoyer of praiseworthy fruit. The purpose of life (<s>puruṣārtha</s>) characterized by the four goals — [poetry's role in] producing competence in the earning of that has been traditionally cited as the indirect purpose of poetry. But even that, being experienced at another time, culminates in the delight that is its fruit only at the time [of reading]. Therefore, to express yet another purpose, one that is something beyond that, charming in its concordance with the hearts of the sensitive, and delightful at the present moment, he says —
Surpassing even the relishing of the fruit of the four goals of life, in the case of the knowledgeable,
by the nectar-essence of poetry, an inward wonderment is extended. // Vjiv_1.5 //

children.text:
camatkāro vitanyate camatkṛtirvistāryate, hlādaḥ punaḥ punaḥ kriyata ityarthaḥ /
kena---kāvyāmṛtarasena /
kāvyamevāmṛtaṃ tasya rasastadāsvādastadanubhavastena /
kvetyabhidadhāti---antaścetasi /
kasya---tadvidām /
taṃ vidanti jānantīti tadvidastajjñāsteṣām /
katham---caturvargaphalāsvādamapyatikramya /
caturvargasya dharmādeḥ phalaṃ tadupabhogastasyāsvādastadanubhavastamapi prasiddhātiśayamatikramya vijitya paspaśaprāyaṃ saṃpādya /
tadayamatrābhiprāyaḥ13---yo 'sau caturvargaphalāsvādaḥ prakṛṣṭapuruṣārthatayā sarvaśāstraprayojanatvena prasiddhaḥ so 'pyasyakāvyāmṛtacarvaṇacamatkārakalāmātrasyā14 pi na kāmapi sāmyakalanāṃ kartumarhatīti /
duḥśrava-durbhaṇa-duradhigamatvādidoṣaduṣṭa15 tvādadhyayanāvasare duḥsahaduḥkha16 dāyī śāstrasandarbhastatkālakalpitakamanīyacamatkṛteḥ kāvyasya na kathañcidapi spardhāmadhirohatītyetadapyarthato 'bhihitaṃ bhavati /
children.translated_text: 'Wonderment is extended' means the wonder-experience is expanded — the delight is produced again and again, this is the meaning. By what? — by the nectar-essence of poetry. Poetry itself is nectar; its essence is its taste, its experience — by that. Where? — he says: inwardly, i.e., in the mind. Of whom? — of the knowledgeable, i.e., those who know that, those who are experts in it. How? — 'surpassing even the relishing of the fruit of the four goals of life.' The fruit of the four goals beginning with <s>dharma</s> is their enjoyment; the relishing of that is the experience of it; even that, which is well-known in its surpassing excellence, having been surpassed, conquered, rendered insignificant. The purport here is this: the relishing of the fruit of the four goals of life, which is well-known as the purpose of all treatises by virtue of being the supreme goal of human life — even that is not capable of bearing any comparison with this art of wonder-experience that is the savoring of the nectar of poetry. The corpus of treatises, being unbearable, harsh to hear, difficult to utter, and difficult to understand — and thus vitiated by such defects — inflicts unbearable suffering at the time of study, and cannot in any way rival poetry, which produces charming wonder-experience at the moment. This too is implicitly stated.

Like a bitter medicine, a treatise destroys the disease of ignorance;
like delightful nectar, poetry removes the malady of non-discrimination. // VjivC_1.7 //
Both in the future and in the present, beautiful with the flow of <s>rasa</s> (aesthetic emotion) —

children.text: yena saṃpadyate kāvyaṃ taditānī vicāryate // VjivC_1.8 //
children.translated_text: that by which poetry is accomplished — that is now being examined. // VjivC_1.8 //
These are intermediate verses.
Ornamentation is analyzed by separating it from the thing to be ornamented;
[but] the truth is that poetry consists of the ornamented [whole], because [analysis] serves as a means to that. // Vjiv_1.6 //

children.text:
alaṅkṛtiralaṅkaraṇam alaṅkriyate yayeti vigṛhya /
sā vivecyate vicāryate /
yaccālaṅkāryamalaṅkaraṇīyaṃ vācakarūpaṃ vācyarūpaṃ ca tadapi vivecyate /
tayoḥ sāmānyaviśeṣalakṣaṇadvāreṇa svarūpanirūpaṇaṃ kriyate /
katham---apoddhṛtya /
niṣkṛṣya pṛthak pṛthagavasthāpya, yatra samudāyarūpe tayorantarbhāvastasmādvibhajya /
kena hetunā---tadupāyatayā /
taditi kāvyaṃ parāmṛśyate /
tasyopāyastadupāyastasya bhāvastadupāyatā tayā hetubhūtayā /
yasmādevaṃvidho18 vivekaḥ kāvyavyutpattyupāyatāṃ pratipadyate /
dṛśyate ca samudāyantaḥ pātināmastyabhūtānāmapi vyutpattinimittamapoddhṛtya vivecanam /
yathā---padāntarbhūtayoḥ prakṛtipratyayayorvākyāntarbhūtānāṃ padānāṃ ceti /
yadyevamasatyabhūto 'pyapoddhārastadupāyatā kriyate tat kiṃ punaḥ satyamityāha---tattvaṃ sālaṅkārasya kāvyatā /
tadayamatra19 paramārthaḥ---sālaṅkārasyālaṅkaraṇasahitasya sakalasya nirastāvayavasya sataḥ samudāyasya kāvyatā kavikarmatvam /
tenālaṅkṛtasya kāvyatvamiti sthitam,20 na punaḥ kāvyasyālaṅkārayoga iti /
sālaṅkārasya kāvyateti saṃmugdhatayā kiñcit kāvyasvarūpaṃ sūtritam21 nipuṇaṃ punarna niścitam /
kiṃlakṣaṇaṃ vastu kāvyavyapadeśabhāg bhavatītyāha---
children.translated_text: 'Ornamentation' (<s>alaṅkṛti</s>) means the act of ornamenting — analyzing by breaking it down as 'that by which something is ornamented.' That is analyzed, examined. And what is to be ornamented — the form of expression and the form of content — that too is analyzed. The determination of the essential nature of both is carried out through the characteristics of the general and the particular. How? — 'by separating.' By extracting, by establishing separately, by dividing out from the composite form in which both are included. For what reason? — 'because [analysis] serves as a means to that.' 'That' refers to poetry. Its means is the means to that; the state of being that means is 'that-means-ness,' by reason of which. Because such discrimination attains the status of being a means to the understanding of poetry. And it is observed that even for things that are included within a composite and do not really exist [separately], the analysis by separating them out serves as a cause of understanding — just as [the analysis of] the stem and the suffix that are included within a word, and of the words that are included within a sentence. If even such non-real separation serves as a means, then what about what is real? — he says: 'the truth is that poetry consists of the ornamented [whole].' The ultimate meaning here is this: the poeticality of the whole — the complete composite, free from parts — that is accompanied by ornamentation, i.e., inclusive of the act of ornamenting — that is poeticality, the quality of being a poet's creation. Therefore it is established that what is ornamented has the nature of poetry, not that poetry receives ornamentation. [The phrase] 'poetry consists of the ornamented [whole]' — the essential nature of poetry has been indicated in a condensed manner through this aphorism, but has not yet been precisely determined. What kind of entity deserves the designation 'poetry'? — he says —
Word and meaning together, established in a composition that is distinguished by the activity of the oblique poet —
that is poetry, which produces delight in the knowledgeable. // Vjiv_1.7 //

children.text:
22 śabdārthau kāvyaṃ vācako vācyaṃ ceti dvau saṃmilitau kāvyam /
dvāvekamiti vicitraivoktiḥ /
tena yatkeṣāñcinmataṃ kavikauśalakalpitakamanīyatātiśayaḥ śabda eva kevalaṃ kāvyamiti keṣāñcid vācyameva racanāvaicitryacamatkārakāri kāvyamiti, pakṣadvayamapi nirastaṃ bhavati /
yasmād23dvayorapi pratyekaṃ24 pratitilamiva tailaṃ tadvidāhlādakāritvaṃ vartate, na punarekasmin /
yathā---
children.translated_text: 22. 'Word and meaning together are poetry' — the speaker and the spoken, these two combined are poetry. 'Two are one' — this itself is a striking statement. Thereby, the view of some that 'it is word alone, distinguished by the charm created through poetic skill, that constitutes poetry,' and the view of others that 'it is the expressed content alone, producing wonder through the variety of composition, that constitutes poetry' — both positions are refuted. Because in both, taken individually, the capacity to delight connoisseurs exists like oil in sesame, but not in one alone. For example —
Speak, O young woman, O beautiful moon-faced one from whom joy overflows, going to the house of your lover —

children.text: yadi sallīlollāpini gacchasi tat kiṃ tvadīyaṃ me // VjivC_1.9 //
children.translated_text: if you are going, O playful conversationalist, then what is that of yours to me? // <s>Vjīv</s>C 1.9 //
The tinkling of the jeweled girdle, the unceasing jingling of lovely anklets, the walking about on rosy feet — it causes a trembling without reason. // <s>Vjīv</s>C 1.10 //

children.text:
pratibhādāridrayadainyādatisvalpasubhāṣitena kavinā varṇasāvarṇyaramyatāmātramatroditam, na punarvācyavaicitryakaṇikā kācidapyasti26 /
yatkila nūtanatāruṇyataraṅgitalāvaṇyalaṭabhakānteḥ27 kāntāyāḥ kāmayamānena kenacidevamu28cyate---yadi taruṇi tvaṃ29 ramaṇamandiraṃ vrajasi tatkiṃ tvadīyaṃ parisaraṇaṃ raṇaraṇakamakāraṇaṃ mama karotītyatigrāmyeyamuktiḥ /
kiñca, na akāraṇam, yatastasyāstadanādareṇa gamane30 tadanuraktāntaḥ karaṇasya virahavidhuratāśaṅkākātaratā kāraṇaṃ raṇaraṇakasya /
yadi vā parisaraṇasya mayā kimarāddhamityākaraṇatāsamarpakam, etadapyatigrāmyataram /
saṃbodhanāni ca bahūni munipraṇītastotrāmantraṇakalpāni na kāñcidapi tadvidāhlāda31 kāritāṃ puṣṇantīti yatkiñcidetat /
vastumātraṃ ca śabdaśobhā32 tiśayaśūnyaṃ na kāvyavyapadeśamarhati /
yathā---
children.translated_text: A poet impoverished in creative inspiration (<s>pratibhā</s>), out of the wretchedness [of that poverty], has here expressed only a slight beauty of speech consisting merely in the charm of alliteration of sounds, but there is not even a particle of variety in the expressed content. For when someone, desiring a beloved whose beauty ripples with the waves of fresh youth, says thus — 'If you, O young woman, are going to the house of your lover, then why does your walking about cause a trembling in me without reason?' — this is an exceedingly vulgar expression. Moreover, it is not without reason, since the agitation arising from the apprehension of the pain of separation on the part of one whose inner faculty is enamored of her — that is the reason for the trembling, when she departs with disregard for him. Or alternatively, if [the meaning is] 'what has been accomplished by me through [her] walking about?' — conveying the sense of futility — this too is even more vulgar. And the many vocatives, resembling invocations in hymns composed by sages, do not foster any delight in connoisseurs; hence all this amounts to nothing. And mere subject matter devoid of the excellence of verbal beauty does not deserve the designation of poetry. For example —

children.text: prakāśasvābhāvyaṃ vidadhati na bhāvāstamasi yattathā naite te syuryadi kila tathā yatra na katham /
children.translated_text: That darkness in which things do not manifest their nature of being luminous — if those [things] were thus [luminous by nature], then how could [darkness exist] where they are not?

children.text: guṇādhyāsābhāyāsavyasanadṛḍhadīkṣāguruguṇo ravivyāpāro 'yaṃ kimatha sadṛśaṃ tasya mahasaḥ // VjivC_1.11 //
children.translated_text: The activity of the sun, heavy with the quality of firm commitment to the enterprise of imposing the appearance of qualities — is it comparable to that radiance? // <s>Vjīv</s>C 1.11 //

children.text:
atra hi śuṣkatarkavākyavāsanādhivāsitacetasā pratibhāpratibhātamātrameva vastu vyasanitayā kavinā kevalamupanibaddham /
na puvarvācakavakratāvicchittilavo 'pi lakṣyate /
yasmāttarkavākyaśayyaiva śarīramasya ślokasya /
tathā ca---tamovyatiriktāḥ padārthā dharmiṇaḥ, prakāśasvabhāvā na bhavantīti sādhyam, tamasyatathābhūtatvāditi hetuḥ /
dṛṣṭāntastarhi kathaṃ na darśitaḥ, tarkanyāyasyaiva cetasi pratibhāsamānatvāt /
tathocyate---
children.translated_text: Here, a poet whose mind is perfumed by the impressions of dry logical discourse, out of his obsession, has merely set down bare subject matter that had barely flickered in his creative imagination. Not even a trace of the charm of oblique expression in the verbal medium is discernible. Because the very framework of logical discourse is the body of this verse. And thus — 'Things other than darkness, as substrates, are not of the nature of being luminous' — this is the thesis to be proved; 'because darkness is not of that nature' — this is the reason. 'Then why has no illustrative example been shown?' — because the logical form itself appears in the mind [without need for example]. Thus it is said —

children.text:
tadbhāvahetubhāvau hi dṛṣṭānte tadavedinaḥ /
khyāpyete33 viduṣāṃ vācyo hetureva hi kevalaḥ // VjivC_1.12 // 34 //
children.translated_text: The relation of essential connection between cause and effect is made known in the example; for the learned, only the reason itself needs to be stated. // <s>Vjīv</s>C 1.12 //

children.text:
iti /
vidadhatīti vipūrvo dadhātiḥ karotyarthe vartate /
sa ca karotyartho 'tra na suspaṣṭasamanvayaḥ, prakāśasvābhāvyaṃ na kurvantīti /
prakāśasvābhāvya-śabdo 'pi cintya eva /
prakāśaḥ svabhāvo yasyāsau prakāśasvabhāvaḥ, tasya bhāva iti bhāvapratyaye vihite pūrvapadasya vṛddhiḥ prāpnoti /
atha svabhāvasya bhāvaḥ svābhāvyamityatrāpi bhāvapratyayāntādbhāvapratyayo na pracuraprayogārhaḥ /
tathā ca prakāśaścāsau svābhāvyaṃ ceti viśeṣaṇasamāso 'pi na samīcīnaḥ /
tṛtīye ca pāde 'tyantāsamarpakasamāsabhūyastvavaiśasaṃ na tadvidāhlādakāritāmāvahati /
ravivyāpāra itiravi-śabdasya prādhānyenābhimatasya samāse guṇībhāvo na vikalpitaḥ, pāṭhāntarasya"raveḥ' iti saṃbhavāt /
nanu vastumātrasyāpyalaṅkāraśunyatayā kathaṃ tadvidāhlādakāritvamiti cettanna;yasmādalaṅkāreṇāprastutapraśaṃsālakṣaṇenānyāpadeśatayāsphur itameva kavicetasi prathamaṃ ca pratibhāpratibhāsamānamaghaṭitapāṣāṇaśakalakalpamaṇiprakhyameva vastu vidagdhakaviviracitavakravākyopārūḍhaṃ śaṇollīḍhamaṇimanoharatayā tadvidāhlādakārikāvyatvamadhirohati /
tathā caikasminneva vastunyavahitānavahitakavidvitayaviracitaṃ vākyadvayamidaṃ mahadantaramāvedayati---
children.translated_text: Thus — 'vidadhati' (they produce): the verb 'dadhāti' with the prefix 'vi-' is used in the sense of 'karoti' (to make). And this sense of 'making' here does not have a clearly evident syntactical connection — '[they] do not make [themselves] luminous by nature.' The compound 'prakāśasvābhāvya' too requires consideration. 'One whose nature is luminosity is prakāśasvabhāva'; in deriving the abstract noun with the suffix '-bhāva', <s>vṛddhi</s> [strengthening] of the first member is expected. If instead [the derivation is] 'the state of [one's own] nature is svābhāvya' — even here, applying an abstract suffix upon [a word already ending in] an abstract suffix is not worthy of frequent usage. And thus a determinative compound 'prakāśa and svābhāvya' is also not proper. And in the third quarter, the excessive prevalence of unintelligible compounds does not bring about delight in connoisseurs. '[The compound] ravivyāpāra' — the word 'ravi' (sun), which is intended as the principal [element], has been subordinated in the compound, which is not justified, since the alternative reading 'raveḥ' [as a genitive] is possible. Now, if [one objects:] 'How can mere subject matter devoid of <s>alaṅkāra</s> (ornament) delight connoisseurs?' — to that we say: no; because the subject matter, though it first flickers in the poet's consciousness through the figure called <s>aprastutapraśaṃsā</s> (praise of the irrelevant) in the guise of allegory, and though it resembles an unworked stone-fragment, when mounted upon the oblique expression crafted by a skilled poet, it ascends to the status of poetry that delights connoisseurs, like a gem polished on a grindstone becoming captivating. And thus, the following pair of verses composed by an attentive and an inattentive poet on the very same subject matter reveals a great difference —
Gracing [the sky] with glances of proud women's eyes followed by warm tears,

children.text: mandamandamuditaḥ priyayau khaṃ bhītabhīta iva śītamayūkhaḥ // VjivC_1.13 //
children.translated_text: slowly, slowly rising, the cool-rayed [moon] went to the sky as though frightened. // <s>Vjīv</s>C 1.13 //

children.text: kramādekadvitriprabhṛtiparipāṭīḥ prakaṭayan kalāḥ svairaṃ svairaṃ navakamalakandāṅkurarucaḥ /
children.translated_text: Gradually revealing its digits in the sequence of one, two, three and so on, each one beautiful as a sprout from a fresh lotus bulb,

children.text: purandhrīṇāṃ preyovirahadahanoddīpitadṛśāṃ kaṭākṣebhyo bibhyannibhṛta iva candro 'bhyudayate // VjivC_1.14 //
children.translated_text: as if timid before the sidelong glances of women whose eyes are inflamed by the fire of separation from their beloveds, the moon rises stealthily. // <s>Vjīv</s>C 1.14 //

children.text:
etayorantaraṃ sahṛdayasaṃvedya36 miti taireva vicāraṇīyam /
tasmāt sthitametat---na śabdasyaiva ramaṇīyatāviśiṣṭasya kevalasya kāvyatvam, nāpyarthasyeti /
tadidamuktam---
children.translated_text: The difference between these two is to be perceived and examined by connoisseurs (<s>sahṛdayas</s>) themselves. Therefore this stands established: neither word alone, distinguished by beauty, constitutes poetry, nor meaning alone. This has been stated —
Figures of speech (<s>alaṅkāra</s>) such as <s>rūpaka</s> (metaphor) and others have been declared of many kinds through its subdivisions;

children.text: na kāntamapi nirbhūṣaṃ vibhāti vanitāmukham38 // VjivC_1.15 //
children.translated_text: even a beautiful woman's face does not shine without ornament. // <s>Vjīv</s>C 1.15 //
Others call <s>rūpaka</s> and similar figures external ornament;

children.text: supāṃ tiṅāṃ ca vyutpattiṃ vācāṃ vāñchantyalaṅkṛtim // VjivC_1.16 //
children.translated_text: they desire the derivational formation of nominal and verbal stems to be the ornament of speech. // <s>Vjīv</s>C 1.16 //
This is called 'beauty of language' (<s>sauśabdya</s>), not this kind of derivation of meaning;
the two — word and referent — are what we consider, as indicated by the division of <s>alaṅkāra</s> (ornament). // <s>Vjīv</s>C 1.17 //

children.text:
tena śabdārthau dvau saṃmilitau kāvyamiti sthitam /
evamavasthāpite dvayoḥ kāvyatve kadācidekasya manāṅmātranyūnatāyāṃ satyāṃ kāvyavyavahāraḥ pravartetetyāha---sahitāviti /
sahitau sahitabhāvena sāhityenāvasthitau /
nanu ca vācyavācakasaṃbandhasya vidyamānatvādetayorna kathañcidapisāhityavirahaḥ, satyametat /
kintu viśiṣṭameveha sāhityamabhipretam /
kīdṛśam ?---vakratāvicitraguṇālaṅkārasaṃpadāṃ parasparaspardhādhirohaḥ /
tena
children.translated_text: Therefore it is established that word and meaning, the two combined, are poetry. Having thus determined the poeticality of both, [the author] states that sometimes, when one of the two is slightly deficient, the designation 'poetry' may still apply — [he says] 'sahitau' (together). 'Sahitau' — established in togetherness, that is, in <s>sāhitya</s> (literary composition). Now, since the relation of signifier and signified always exists, there can never be any absence of their togetherness — this is true. But what is intended here is a special kind of togetherness. Of what kind? — The mutual competitive ascent of the riches of <s>vakratā</s> (obliqueness), variety, qualities, and <s>alaṅkāras</s> (ornaments). Thus —
Being equal in all qualities, united like two friends,

children.text: parasparasya śobhāyai śabdārthau bhavato yathā // VjivC_1.18 //
children.translated_text: word and meaning exist for the enhancement of each other's beauty. // <s>Vjīv</s>C 1.18 //
Then the moon, its body made faint by the reddish trembling [of dawn],
assumed the pallor of the cheek of a woman emaciated by love. // <s>Vjīv</s>C 1.19 //

children.text:
atrāruṇaparispandamandīkṛtavapuṣaḥ śaśinaḥ kāmaparikṣāmavṛtteḥ kāminīkapolaphalakasya ca pāṇḍutvasāmyasamarthanādarthālaṅkāraparipoṣaḥ śobhātiśayamāvahati /
vakṣyamāṇavarṇavinyāsavakratālakṣaṇaḥ śabdālaṅkāro 'pyatitarāṃ ramaṇīyaḥ /
varṇavinyāsavicchittivihitā lāvaṇyalakṣaṇaguṇa40saṃpadastyeva /
yathā ca
children.translated_text: Here, the establishment of the similarity in pallor between the moon — whose form has been diminished by the reddish trembling [of dawn] — and the cheek-surface of a woman emaciated by love's torment, fosters the figure of meaning (<s>arthālaṅkāra</s>) and brings about a superabundance of beauty. The figure of sound (<s>śabdālaṅkāra</s>), characterized by the obliqueness of phonetic arrangement to be discussed later, is also exceedingly beautiful. The richness of the quality characterized as gracefulness (<s>lāvaṇya</s>), produced by the charm of phonetic arrangement, is indeed present. And as —

children.text:
līlāe kuvalaaṃ kuvalaaṃ va sīse samuvvahanteṇa /
seseṇa sesapurisāṇaṃ purisaāro samuvyasio // VjivC_1.20 //41 //
children.translated_text: Playfully a blue lotus, [or rather] a blue lotus indeed on the head — carried by him; by the rest, the manliness of the rest of men has been surpassed. // <s>Vjīv</s>C 1.20 // (Prākrit)
Playfully a blue lotus — indeed a blue lotus — on the head being carried;
by the rest [of him], the manliness of the rest of men has been surpassed.

children.text:
atrāpyaprastutapraśaṃsopamālakṣaṇavācyālaṅkāravaicitryavihitā helāmātraviracitayamakānuprāsahāriṇī samarpakatvasubhagā kāpi kāvyacchāyā sahṛdayahṛdayamāhlādayati /
dvivacanenātra vācyavācakajātidvitvamabhidhīyate /
vyaktidvitvābhidhāne punarekapadavyavasthitayorapi kāvyatvaṃ syādityāha---bandhe vyavasthitau /
bandho vākyavinyāsaḥ tatra vyavasthitau viśeṣeṇa lāvaṇyādiguṇālaṅkāraśobhināṃ saṃniveśena kṛtāvasthānau /
sahitāvityatrāpi yathāyukti sajātīyā42 pakṣayā śabdasya śabdāntareṇa vācyasya vācyāntareṇa ca sāhityaṃ parasparaspardhitvalakṣaṇameva vivakṣitam /
anyathā tadvidāhlādakāritvahāniḥ prasajyate /
yathā
children.translated_text: Here too, the charm of variety in the expressed figure, characterized by <s>aprastutapraśaṃsā</s> (praise of the irrelevant) and <s>upamā</s> (simile), together with the captivating <s>yamaka</s> (chiming) and <s>anuprāsa</s> (alliteration) fashioned with mere ease, and a certain ineffable poetic lustre (<s>kāvyacchāyā</s>) — felicitous in its suggestiveness — delights the hearts of connoisseurs. By the dual number here, the duality of the genus of signifier and signified is expressed. In the case of expressing duality of individual instances, [the author] states that even when two [elements] are established in a single sentence, poeticality may obtain — [he says] 'bandhe vyavasthitau' (established in composition). 'Bandha' means the arrangement of sentences; 'established therein' means having taken their position through a special disposition of gracefulness and other qualities and ornamental beauties. In 'sahitau' too, as appropriate, what is intended is the togetherness of word with [another] word of the same kind, and of expressed content with other expressed content, characterized precisely by mutual rivalry. Otherwise, the loss of the capacity to delight connoisseurs would follow. For example —

children.text: asāraṃ saṃsāraṃ parimuṣitaratnaṃ traibhuvanaṃ nirālokaṃ lokaṃ maraṇaśaraṇaṃ bāndhavajanam /
children.translated_text: Worthless is <s>saṃsāra</s>; the three worlds are robbed of their jewel; the world is without light; kinsmen are a refuge of death;

children.text: adarpaṃ kandarpaṃ jananayananirmāṇamaphalaṃ jagajjīrṇāraṇyaṃ kathamasi vidhātuṃ vyavasitaḥ43 // VjivC_1.21 //
children.translated_text: <s>Kandarpa</s> (the god of love) is without pride; the creation of eyes is fruitless; the world is like a withered forest — how are you resolved to arrange [all] this? // <s>Vjīv</s>C 1.21 //

children.text:
atra kila kutracitprabandhe kaścitkāpālikaḥ kāmapi kāminī44 vyāpādayitumadhyavasito sanneva45 mabhidhīyate---yadapagatasāraḥ saṃsāraḥ, hṛtaratnasarvasvaṃ trailokyam, ālokanīyakamanīyavastuvarjito jīvalokaḥ, sakalalokalocananirmāṇaṃ niṣphalaprayam, tribhuvanavijayitvadarpavihīnaḥ46 kandarpaḥ, jagajjīrṇāraṇyakalpamanayā bhavatīti kiṃ tvamevaṃvidhamakaraṇīyaṃ kartuṃ vyavasita iti /
etasmin śloke mahāvākyakalpe vākyāntaraṇyavāntaravākyasadṛśāni tasyāḥ sakalalokalobhanīyalāvaṇyasaṃpatpratipādanaparāṇi parasparaspardhonyatiramaṇīyānyupanibaddhāni kamapi kāvyacchāyātiśayaṃ puṣṇanti /
maraṇaśaraṇaṃ bāndhavajanamiti punareteṣāṃ na kalāmātramapi spardhitumarhatīti na tadvidāhlādakāri /
bahuṣu ca ramaṇīyeṣvekavākyopayogiṣu yugapat pratibhāsapadavīmavataratsu vākyārthaparipūraṇārthaṃ tatpratimaṃ prāptumaparaṃ prayatnena pratibhā prasādyate /
tathā cāsminneva prastutavastusabrahmacārivastvantaramapi suprāpameva---"vidhimapi vipannādbhutavidhim" iti /
prathamapratibhātapadārthapratinidhipadārthāntarāsaṃbhave sukumāratarāpūrvasamarpaṇena kāmapi kāvyacchāyāmunmīlayanti kavayaḥ /
yathā
children.translated_text: Here, in a certain narrative, a certain <s>Kāpālika</s> ascetic, having resolved to kill a certain beautiful woman, is being addressed thus: 'Since <s>saṃsāra</s> has lost its essence [with her death]; since the three worlds have been robbed of all their jewel-wealth; since the living world is devoid of anything worth seeing or beautiful; since the creation of the eyes of all the world is fruitless; since <s>Kandarpa</s> is devoid of the pride of conquering the three worlds; since the world would become like a withered forest by this [deed] of yours — how are you resolved to do such an unconscionable thing?' In this verse, which is like a great utterance, the intermediate clauses resembling sub-sentences, devoted to establishing the richness of her beauty that captivates the entire world, are composed in mutual rivalry and foster an ineffable excess of poetic lustre. But 'maraṇaśaraṇaṃ bāndhavajanam' (kinsmen are a refuge of death) — this cannot rival the others even to the slightest degree, and hence does not delight connoisseurs. And when many beautiful components serving a single sentence simultaneously descend upon the path of creative imagination, the creative faculty must be propitiated with effort to find another [component] worthy of matching them for the completion of the sentence-meaning. And thus, in this very context, a companion-subject to the subject at hand is easily attainable — 'vidhimapi vipannādbhutavidhim' (even the Creator, whose wondrous powers have failed). When a substitute matching the originally imagined content is not available, poets unveil an ineffable poetic lustre through an unprecedented and delicate offering. For example —

children.text: rudrādrestulanaṃ svakaṇṭhavipinacchedo47 harervāsanaṃ kārāveśmani puṣpakāpaharaṇam // VjivC_1.22 //
children.translated_text: Equaling [Mount] <s>Rudra</s>, the cutting down of the forest of one's own throat, the imprisonment of <s>Hari</s>, the seizure of the aerial car <s>Puṣpaka</s> — // <s>Vjīv</s>C 1.22 //

children.text:
ityupanibaddhya pūrvopanibaddhapadārthānurūpavastvantarāsaṃbhavādapūrvameva "yasyedṛśāḥ kalayaḥ" iti vinyastam,48 yenāneye 'pi kāmapi kamanīyatāmanīyanta /
yathā ca
children.translated_text: Having composed thus, since a comparable subject matter matching the previously composed content was not available, the unprecedented [expression] 'yasyedṛśāḥ kalayaḥ' ('whose such exploits are these') was employed, whereby even the other [elements] were made to assume a certain beauty. And as —

children.text: tadvaktrenduvilokanena divaso nītaḥ pradoṣastathā tadgoṣṭhyaiva niśāpi manmathakṛtotsāhaistadaṅgārpaṇaiḥ /
children.translated_text: With the sight of her moon-like face the day was spent, the evening likewise with conversation about her alone, the night too with the eagerness born of passion and with the dedication of those limbs;

children.text: tāṃ saṃpratyapi mārgadattanayanāṃ draṣṭuṃ pravṛttasya me baddhotkaṇṭhamidaṃ manaḥ kim // VjivC_1.23 //
children.translated_text: and even now, as I set out to see that same woman — the one to whom my eyes were given on the road — what is this mind of mine, bound with longing? // <s>Vjīv</s>C 1.23 //

children.text:
iti saṃpratyapi tāmevaṃvidhāṃ vīkṣituṃ pravṛttasya mama manaḥ kimiti baddhotkaṇṭhamiti parasamāpte 'pi tathāvidho vastu49 vinyāso vihitaḥ---"athavā premāsamāptotsavam" iti,yena pūrveṣāṃ jīvitamivārpitam /
yadyapi dvayorapyetayostatprādhānyenaiva vākyārthopanibandhaḥ,50 tathāpi kavipratibhāprauḍhireva prādhānyenāvitaṣṭhate /
śabdasyāpi śabdāntareṇa sāhityavirahodāharaṇaṃ yathā
children.translated_text: Thus, 'even now, for me who sets out to see her of such qualities, what is my mind that is bound with longing?' — even though the [verse] is syntactically complete, a similar arrangement of content has been fashioned [in the continuation]: 'athavā premāsamāptotsavam' (or rather, a festival whose love is incomplete) — whereby life, as it were, has been breathed into the preceding [elements]. Although in both of these [cases] the sentence-meaning is composed with the predominance of that [content], nevertheless it is the maturity of the poet's creative imagination that principally stands firm. An example of the absence of togetherness of word with [another] word [of the same kind] is as follows —
The beauty adorned their bodies, and the conjunction of ever-new youth [adorned] that [beauty],
and the splendor of <s>Makaraketana</s> (the god of love) [adorned] that [youth], and intoxication adorned by the union with the beloved [adorned] that [splendor]. // VjivC_1.24 //

children.text:
dayitasaṅgamastāmabhūṣayaditi vaktavye kīdṛśo madaḥ, dayatasaḍgamo bhūṣā yasyeti dayitasaṅgamaśabdasya prādhānyenābhimatasya samāsavṛttāvantarbhūtatvād guṇībhāvo na tadvidāhlādakārī /
dīpakālaṅkārasya ca kāvyaśobhākāritvenopanibaddhasya nirvahaṇāvasare truṭitaprāyatvāt prakramabhaṅgavihitaṃ sahasahṛdayavairasyamanivāryam /
"dayitasaṅgatirenam' iti pāṭhāntaraṃ sulabhameva /
dvayorapyetayorudāharaṇayoḥ prādhānyena pratyekamekatarasya sāhityaviraho vyākhyātaḥ /
paramārthataḥ punarubhayorapyekatarasya sāhityaviraho 'nyatarasyāpi paryavasyati /
tathā cārthaḥ samarthavācakāsadbhāve svātmanā sphurannapi mṛtakalpa evāvatiṣṭhate /
śabdo 'pi vākyopayogivācyāsaṃbhavevācyāntaravācakaḥ san vākyasya vyādhibhūtaḥ pratibhātītyalamatiprasaṅgena /
prakṛtaṃ tu /
kīdṛśai bandhe---vakrakavivyāpāraśālini /
vakro yo 'sau śāstrādiprasiddhaśabdārthopanibandhavyatirekī ṣaṭprakāravakratāviśiṣṭaḥ kavivyāpārastatkriyākramastena śālate ślāghate yastasmin /
evamapi kaṣṭakalpanopahate 'pi prasiddhavyatirekitvamastītyāha---tadvadāhlādikāriṇi /
taditi kāvyaparāmarśaḥ tadvidantīti tadvidastajjñāsteṣāmāhlādamānandaṃ karoti yasyasmin tadvidāhlādakāriṇi bandhe vyavasthitau /
vakratā52 prakārāṃstadvidāhlādakāritvaṃ ca pratyekaṃ yathāvasaramevodāhariṣyati53 /
evaṃ kāvyasya sāmānyalakṣaṇe vihite viśeṣalakṣaṇamupakramate /
tatra śabdārthayostāvatsvarūpaṃ nirūpayati---
children.translated_text: Instead of saying 'the union with the beloved adorned that,' what kind of intoxication [is it]? — 'the union with the beloved is the ornament of which' — since the word 'union with the beloved' (<s>dayitasaṅgama</s>), which is primarily intended, is subordinated through being absorbed into the compound construction, this subordination [of the principal element] does not produce delight in the connoisseurs. And since the figure of speech <s>dīpaka</s> (<s>dīpakālaṅkāra</s>), which is employed for its contribution to poetic beauty, is mostly broken at the point of conclusion, the dissonance produced by the breach of sequence inevitably strikes the heart of the connoisseur. The variant reading 'dayitasaṅgatirenam' is quite obvious. In both these examples, the absence of poetic harmony (<s>sāhityaviraha</s>) of one of the two [elements — word or meaning] has been principally explained with respect to each individually. In ultimate truth, however, the absence of harmony of one of the two entails [a deficiency] in the other as well. Thus, meaning, in the absence of a capable expression, even while manifesting by itself, remains as if dead. And the word too, when the expressible content appropriate to the sentence is impossible, being the expression of some other expressible, appears as a disease of the sentence — but enough of this digression. To return to the subject: What kind of composition? — One that is distinguished by the activity of the poet in the mode of obliquity (<s>vakra kavivyāpāra</s>). The oblique [expression] is that which deviates from the well-known modes of binding words and meanings as established in grammar and other [sciences], and is distinguished by six types of obliquity; [it is] the activity of the poet, and by its procedural method the [composition] is adorned — in such [composition]. Even so, though marred by forced interpretation, there is still deviation from the well-known — he says: 'delighting the connoisseurs' (<s>tadvadāhlādikāriṇi</s>). 'That' (<s>tad</s>) refers back to poetry; 'those who know it' (<s>tadvid</s>) are the connoisseurs — [the composition] that produces delight, joy, for them — in such a composition that delights the connoisseurs. The types of obliquity and [its] capacity to delight the connoisseurs will be illustrated individually as occasion arises. Thus, having formulated the general definition of poetry, he begins the specific definition. Therein, he first determines the nature of word and meaning:
Though it is well known that meaning is the expressed (<s>vācya</s>) and word is the expressor (<s>vācaka</s>),
nevertheless, on this path of poetry, this is the ultimate truth (<s>paramārtha</s>) regarding these two. // Vjiv_1.8 //

children.text:
iti evaṃvidhaṃ vastu prasiddhaṃ pratītam---yo vācakaḥ pratyāyakaḥ54 sa śabdaḥ, yo vācyaścābhidheyaḥ sor'tha iti /
nanu ca dyotakavyañjakāvapi śabdau saṃbhavataḥ, tadasaṃgrahānnāvyāptiḥ, yasmādarthapratītikāritvasāmānyādupacārāttāvapi vācakāveva /
evaṃ dyotyavyaṅgyayorapyarthayoḥ55 pratyeyatvasāmānyādupacārādvācyatvameva /
tasmād vācakatvaṃ vācyatvaṃ ca śabdārthayorloke suprasiddhaṃ yadyapi lakṣaṇam, tathāpyasmin alaukike kāvyamārge kavikarmavartmani ayametayorvakṣyamāṇaḥ56 paramārthaḥ kimapyapūrvaṃ tattvamityarthaḥ /
kīdṛśamityāha---
children.translated_text: Thus, the well-known, established matter is this: that which is the expressor, the conveyor (<s>pratyāyaka</s>), is the word; and that which is the expressed, the denotable (<s>abhidheya</s>), is the meaning. Now, words that are indicators (<s>dyotaka</s>) and suggestors (<s>vyañjaka</s>) are also possible — is there not under-extension through their non-inclusion? No, because through figurative usage based on the common property of being causes of the cognition of meaning, those too are indeed expressors. Similarly, regarding the indicated (<s>dyotya</s>) and suggested (<s>vyaṅgya</s>) meanings too, through figurative usage based on the common property of being cognizable, they are indeed expressed. Therefore, though 'being an expressor' and 'being expressed' are the well-known characterizations of word and meaning in the world, nevertheless, on this extraordinary path of poetry, on the road of the poet's craft, 'this ultimate truth regarding these two' — some unprecedented essence — is about to be stated. What kind? He says:
A word, even when others exist, is the sole expressor of the meaning intended by the speaker;
meaning is that which is beautiful through its own vibration (<s>svaspanda</s>) that causes delight in the connoisseurs (<s>sahṛdaya</s>). // Vjiv_1.9 //

children.text:
sa śabdaḥ kāvye yastatsamucitasamastasāmagrīkaḥ /
kīdṛk----vivakṣitārthaikavācakaḥ /
vivakṣito yo 'sau vaktumiṣṭor'thastadekavācakaḥ tasyaikaḥ kevala eva vācakaḥ /
katham---anyeṣu satsvapi /
apareṣu tadvācakeṣu bahuṣvapi vidyamāneṣu /
tathā ca---sāmānyātmanā vaktumabhipreto yor /
āthastasya viśeṣābhidhāyī śabdaḥ samyag vācakatāṃ na pratipadyate /
yathā
children.translated_text: That word in poetry is one that possesses all the appropriate resources. Of what kind? — 'The sole expressor of the intended meaning' (<s>vivakṣitārthaikavācaka</s>): the meaning that is desired to be spoken — of that, the sole, the only expressor. How? — 'Even when others exist': even when many other expressions for that [meaning] are available. And thus — the meaning that is intended to be expressed in its general aspect, the word that denotes its particular [aspect] does not properly attain the status of expressor. For example:
O ocean (<s>makarākara</s>), do not despise these gems, struck by the blows of the angry glances of waves,

children.text: kiṃ kaustubhena bhavato vihito na nāma yācñāprasāritakaraḥ puruṣottamo 'pi57 // VjivC_1.25 //
children.translated_text: for was not <s>Puruṣottama</s> (Viṣṇu) himself, with hand extended in supplication, created by you for the sake of the <s>Kaustubha</s> [gem]? // VjivC_1.25 //

children.text:
atra ratnasāmānyotkarṣābhidhānamupakrāntam /
kaustubheneti ratnaviśeṣābhidhāyī śabdastadviśeṣotkarṣābhidhānamupasaṃharatīti prakramopasaṃhāravaiṣamyaṃ na śobhātiśayamāvahati /
na caitadvaktuṃ śakyate---yaḥ kaścidviśeṣe guṇagrāmagarimā vidyate sa sarvasāmānye 'pi saṃbhavatyeveti /
yasmāt
children.translated_text: Here, a statement of the general excellence of gems was begun. The word '<s>Kaustubha</s>,' which denotes a particular gem, concludes with a statement of the excellence of that particular — thus the discrepancy between the commencement and conclusion does not bring about a superabundance of beauty. Nor can it be said that whatever abundance of qualities exists in a particular also obtains in the universal, because:
Among horses, elephants, and metals, among wood, stones, and garments,
among women, men, and waters — the difference is a great difference. // VjivC_1.26 //

children.text:
tasmādevaṃvidhe viṣaye sāmānyābhidhāyyeva śabdaḥ sahṛdayahṛdayahāritāṃ pratipadyate /
tathā cāsmin prakṛte pāṭhāntaraṃ sulabhameva---"ekena kiṃ na vihito bhavataḥ sa nāma" iti /
yatra ca59 viśeṣātmanā vastu pratipādayitumabhimataṃ tatra viśeṣābhidhāyakamevābhidhānaṃ nibadhnanti kavayaḥ /
yathā
children.translated_text: Therefore, in a subject of this kind, only the word denoting the universal captures the hearts of the connoisseurs. And thus in this context, a variant reading is quite obvious: 'Was not that one created by you for the sake of a single [gem]?' And where it is intended to present a thing in its particular aspect, there poets employ only the expression that denotes the particular. For example:

children.text: dvayaṃ gataṃ saṃprati śocanīyatāṃ samāgamaprārthanayā kapālinaḥ /
children.translated_text: Two things have now become pitiable through the desire for union with the Skull-Bearer (<s>Kapālin</s>, i.e. <s>Śiva</s>):

children.text: kalā ca sā kāntimatī kalāvata- satvamasya lokasya ca netrakaumudī60 // VjivC_1.27 //
children.translated_text: that lustrous digit (<s>kalā</s>) of the Moon (<s>kalāvat</s>), and the beauty of this world which is like moonlight to the eyes. // VjivC_1.27 //

children.text:
atra parameśvaravācakaśabdasahastrasaṃbhave 'pi kapālina iti bībhatsarasālambanavibhāvavācakaḥ śabdo jugupsāspadatvena prayujyamānaḥ kāmapi vācakavakratāṃ vidadhāti /
"saṃprati' "dvayaṃ' cetyatīva ramaṇīyam---yat kila pūrvamekā saiva durvyasanadūṣitatvena śocanīyā jātā,61 saṃprati punastvayā tasyāstathāvidhaduradhyavasāyasāhāyakamivārabdhamityupahasyate /
"prārthanā'-śabdo 'pyatitarāṃ ramaṇīyaḥ, yasmāt kākatālīyayogena tatsamāgamaḥ kadācinna vācyatāvahaḥ /
prārthanā punaratrātyantaṃ kaulīnakalaṅkakāriṇī /
"sā ca' "tvaṃ ca' iti dvayorapyanubhūyamānaparasparaspardhilāvaṇyātiśayapratipādanaparatvenopāttam /
"kalāvataḥ ' kāntimatī' iti ca matup62 pratyayena dvayorapi praśaṃsā pratīyata ityeṣāṃ pratyekaṃ kaścidapyarthaḥ śabdāntarābhidheyatāṃ notsahate /
kavivivakṣitaviśeṣābhidhānakṣamatvameva vācarakatvalakṣaṇam /
yasmātpratibhāyāṃ tatkālollikhitena kenacitparispandena parisphurantaḥ padārthāḥ prakṛtaprastāvasamucitena kenacidutkarṣeṇa vā samācchāditasvabhāvāḥ santo vivakṣāvidheyatvenābhidheyatāpadavīmavatarantastathāvidhaviśeṣapratipādanasamarthenābhidhānenābhidhīyamānāścetaścamatkāri63 tāmāpadyante /
yathā
children.translated_text: Here, though a thousand words denoting the Supreme Lord (<s>Parameśvara</s>) are available, the word '<s>Kapālin</s>' (Skull-Bearer), which is an expressor of the <s>vibhāva</s> (determinant) that supports the <s>bībhatsa rasa</s> (sentiment of disgust), being employed with the sense of being an object of revulsion, produces a certain obliquity of expression (<s>vācakavakratā</s>). 'Now' and 'two things' are exceedingly charming — for previously, she alone had become pitiable through being tainted by [his] vile addiction; but now [the poet] mocks [the moon] by suggesting that you have begun what amounts to assisting his such deplorable resolve. The word 'desire' (<s>prārthanā</s>) too is exceedingly charming, since by a mere coincidence his union [with the moon] never admits of being properly spoken of, while the desire here is utterly staining to [the moon's] noble lineage. 'She and you' — taken up with the purpose of conveying the superabundance of beauty that vies with each other as experienced by both. The praise of both is suggested through the possessive suffix <s>-matup</s> in 'of the one possessing digits' (<s>kalāvataḥ</s>) and 'lustrous' (<s>kāntimatī</s>). Each of these has a certain meaning that does not tolerate being expressed by another word. The very capacity to denote the particular intended by the poet is the defining characteristic of being an expressor. For the entities that flash forth through some vibration sketched at the very moment of poetic intuition (<s>pratibhā</s>), having their nature concealed by some excellence appropriate to the context at hand, enter the domain of the expressible as subject to the poet's intention, and when expressed by an expression capable of conveying such a particular, they attain the quality of producing wonder (<s>camatkāra</s>) in the mind. For example:

children.text: saṃrambhaḥ karikīṭameghaśakaloddeśena siṃhasya yaḥ sarvasyaiva sa jātimātravihito hevākaleśaḥ kila /
children.translated_text: The fury of a lion toward elephants, insects, and cloud-fragments is said to be merely a trifling agitation born of his species-nature, applicable to anything whatsoever.

children.text: ityāśādviradakṣayāmbhudaghaṭābandhe 'pyasaṃrabdhavān yo 'sau kutra camatkṛteratiśayaṃ yātvamvikākesarī // VjivC_1.28 //
children.translated_text: With this expectation, even when the assemblage of elephants and clouds is arrayed, he who remains unperturbed — where can the wonder at the lion among animals (<s>Amvikā-kesarin</s>) possibly go? // VjivC_1.28 //

children.text:
atra kariṇāṃ "kīṭa'- vyavapadeśena tiraskāraḥ, toyadānāṃ ca "śakala'- śabdābhidhānenānādaraḥ, "sarvasya' iti yasya kasyacittucchataraprāyastetyavahelā, jāteśca "mātra'- śabdaviśiṣṭatvenāvalepaḥ, hevākasya "leśa'- śabdābhidhānenālpatāpratipattirityete vivakṣitārthaikavācakatvaṃ dyotayanti /
"ghaṭābandha' - śabdaśca prastutamahattvapratipādanaparatvenopāttastannibandhanatāṃ pratipadyate /
viṃśeṣābhidhānākāṅkṣiṇaḥ punaḥ padārthasvarūpasya tatpratipādanaparaviśeṣāṇaśūnyatayā śobhāparihāṇirutpa64dyate /
tathā
children.translated_text: Here, the contempt for elephants through the designation 'insects' (<s>kīṭa</s>), the disregard for clouds through the expression 'fragments' (<s>śakala</s>), the disdain [expressed] by 'of anything whatsoever' (<s>sarvasya</s>) implying [even] the most trifling [creatures], the arrogance through the word 'species' qualified by 'mere' (<s>mātra</s>), and the notion of insignificance of agitation through the expression 'trifle' (<s>leśa</s>) for <s>hevāka</s> — these illustrate the [principle of] being the sole expressor of the intended meaning. The word 'assemblage' (<s>ghaṭābandha</s>) too, taken up with the purpose of conveying the greatness of the subject, attains its binding function. When, however, the entity-nature desires a particular expression and is devoid of particulars that would convey it, a diminution of beauty results. Thus:
Where the entire creation of such a maker has a name that is unimaginable, where even the fabrication of a rival to [his] excellence is the supreme limit of humiliation,
where the prosperity surpasses the very aspirations of living beings — for that [gem], among stones that have been turned into imitation gems, stone-hood itself is fitting. // VjivC_1.29 //

children.text:
atra "ābhāsa'- śabdaḥ svayameva mātrādiviśiṣṭatvamabhilaṣaṃllakṣyate /
pāṭhāntaram---"chāyāmātramaṇīkṛtāśmasu maṇestasyāśmataivocitā' iti /
etacca vācakavakratāprakārasvarūpanirūpaṇāvasare pratipadaṃ prakaṭībhaviṣyatītyalamatiprasaṅgena /
arthaśca vācyalakṣaṇaḥ kīdṛśaḥ---kāvye yaḥ sahṛdayāhlādakārisvaspandasundaraḥ /
sahṛdayāḥ kāvyārthavidasteṣāmāhlādamānandaṃ karoti yastena svaspandenātmīyena svabhāvena sundaraḥ sukumāraḥ /
tadetaduktaṃ bhavati---yadyapi padārthasya nānāvidhadharmakhacitatvaṃ saṃbhavati tathāpi tathāvidhena dharmeṇa saṃbandhaḥ samākhyāyate ya), sahṛdayahṛdayāhlādamādhātuṃ kṣamate /
tasya ca tadāhlādasāmarthyaṃ saṃbhāvyate yena kācideva svabhāvamahattā rasaparipoṣāṅgatvaṃ vā vyaktimāsādayati /
yathā
children.translated_text: Here the word 'imitation' (<s>ābhāsa</s>) is observed to itself desire qualification by 'mere' (<s>mātra</s>) and similar [terms]. The variant reading is: 'for that [gem], among stones turned into mere-imitation-gems, stone-hood itself is fitting.' This will become clear word by word at the occasion of examining the nature of the type of expressive obliquity (<s>vācakavakratā</s>) — enough of this digression. And meaning, characterized as the expressed — of what kind? In poetry, it is that which is beautiful through its own vibration (<s>svaspanda</s>) that causes delight in the connoisseurs (<s>sahṛdaya</s>). The connoisseurs are those who know poetic meaning — [meaning] that produces delight, joy, for them — [is] beautiful, delicate, through its own vibration, its own nature. What is being said is this: although it is possible for an entity to be studded with manifold properties, nevertheless, the relation is proclaimed with that property which is capable of producing delight in the hearts of the connoisseurs. And its capacity for that delight is conceived as that through which a certain greatness of nature or the quality of being an element that nourishes <s>rasa</s> (aesthetic sentiment) comes to manifestation. For example:

children.text: daṃṣṭrāpiṣṭeṣu sadyaḥ śikhariṣu na kṛtaḥ skandhakaṇḍūvinodaḥ sindhuṣvaṅgāvagāhaḥ khurakuharagalattucchatoyeṣu nāptaḥ /
children.translated_text: No scratching of shoulder-itch was done on the mountain peaks freshly crushed by the tusks, no bodily immersion was attained in the oceans whose trivial waters drip from the hollows of the hooves,

children.text: labdhāḥ pātālapaṅke na luṭhanaratayaḥ potramātropayukte yenoddhāre dharitryāḥ sa jayati vibhutāvighnitecchovarāhaḥ // VjivC_1.30 //
children.translated_text: no rolling pleasures were obtained in the mud of the netherworld that served merely as a snout-bath — yet he who thus [restrained himself] in the rescue of the Earth is victorious: the <s>Varāha</s> (Boar) of unobstructed power and desire! // VjivC_1.30 //

children.text:
atra ca tathāvidhaḥ padārthaparispandamahimā nibaddho yaḥ67 svabhāvasaṃbhavinastatparispandāntarasya saṃrodhasaṃpādanena svabhāvamahattāṃ samullāsayan sahṛdayahṛdayāhlāda68 kāritāmāpannaḥ69 /
yathā ca
children.translated_text: Here, such a greatness of the vibration of the entity's meaning is composed: by producing the restraint of other vibrations naturally possible for it, [the poet] causes its natural greatness to shine forth, and thus it attains the quality of producing delight in the hearts of the connoisseurs. And for example:
<s>Vālmīki</s>, the sage who had gone to gather <s>kuśa</s> grass and firewood, approached her, following the sound of weeping —
he whose grief, arising from the sight of the bird struck by the <s>Niṣāda</s> (hunter), became poetry (<s>śloka</s>). // VjivC_1.31 //

children.text:
atra ko 'sau munirvālmīkiriti paryāyapadamātre vaktavye paramakāruṇikasya niṣādanirbhinnaśakunisaṃdarśanamātralasamutthitaḥ śokaḥ ślokatvamabhajata yasyeti tasya tadavasthajanakarājaputrīdaśādarśana71 vivaśavṛtterantaḥ karaṇaparispandaḥ karuṇarasaparipoṣāṅgatayā sahṛdayahṛdayāhlādakārī kaverabhipretaḥ /
yathā ca
children.translated_text: Here, where merely a synonymous word 'who was that sage? <s>Vālmīki</s>' could have been said, [instead the poet says]: the grief of that supremely compassionate one, arising merely from the sight of the bird pierced by the hunter, became poetry — for him whose inner faculty vibrated involuntarily at the sight of the condition of the prince's daughter in that state, the vibration of the inner organ, as an element that nourishes the <s>karuṇa rasa</s> (sentiment of pathos), is intended by the poet to produce delight in the hearts of the connoisseurs. And for example:

children.text: bharturmitraṃ priyamavidhave viddhi māmambuvāhaṃ tatsaṃdeśāddhṛdayanihitādāgataṃ tvatsamīpam /
children.translated_text: Know me, O faithful one, to be the dear friend of your husband — a cloud who has come to your presence from his message deposited in [my] heart,

children.text: yo vṛndāni tvarayati pathi śrāmyatāṃ proṣitānāṃ mandrasnigdhairdhvanibhirabalāveṇimokṣotsukāni // VjivC_1. 32 //
children.translated_text: who, on the road, hastens the groups of traveling women separated [from their husbands], eager to loosen their braids, with deep and tender sounds. // VjivC_1.32 //

children.text:
atra prathamamāntraṇapadārthastadāśvāsakāriparispandanibandhanaḥ bharturmitraṃ māṃ viddhītyupādeyatāmā72 tmanaḥ prathayati /
tacca na sāmānyam, priyamiti viśrambhapātratām73 /
iti tāmāśvāsyonmukhīkṛtya ca tatsaṃdeśāttvatsamīpamāgamanamiti prakṛtaṃ prastauti /
hṛdayanihitāditi suhṛttvavihitaṃ74 sāvadhānatvaṃ dyotyate /
nanu cānyaḥ kaścidevaṃvidhavyavahāravidagdhabuddhiḥ kathaṃ na niyukta ityāha---mamaivātra kauśalaṃ kimapi75 vijṛmbhate /
ambuvāhamityātmanastatkāritābhidhānaṃ dyotayati /
yaḥ proṣitānāṃ vṛndāni tvarayati, saṃjātatvarāṇi karoti /
kīdṛśānām---śrāmyatāṃ tvarāyāmasamarthānāmapi /
vṛndānīti bāhulyāttatkāritābhyāsaṃ kathayati /
kena---mandrasnigdhairdhvanibhiḥ, mādhuryaramaṇīyaiḥ śabdairvidagdhadūtaprarocanāvacanaprayairityarthaḥ /
kva---pathi mārge /
yadṛcchayā yathākathañcidahametadācarāmīti kiṃ punaḥ prayatnena suhṛtpremanimittiṃ saṃrambhabuddhiṃ76 na karomīti /
kīdṛśāni vṛndāni---abalāveṇimokṣotsukāni /
abalā-śabdenātratatpreyasīvirahavaidhuryāsahatvaṃ bhaṇyate, tadveṇimokṣotsukānīti teṣāṃ tadanuraktacittavṛttatvam /
tadayamatra vākyārthaḥ---vidhivihitavirahavaidhuryasya parasparānuraktacittavṛtteryasya kasyacitkāmijanasya samāgamasaukhyasaṃpādanasauhārde sadaiva gṛhītavrato 'smīti /
atra yaḥ padārthaparispandaḥ kavinopanibaddhaḥ prabandhasya meghadūtatve paramārthataḥ sa eva jīvitamiti sutarāṃ sahṛdayāhlādakārī77 /
na punarevaṃ vidho yathā
children.translated_text: Here, the meaning of the first word of address, which is the ground for the reassuring gesture of the [messenger], establishes the acceptability of oneself [by saying] 'Know me as a friend of your husband.' And that is not ordinary—[the word] 'priya' (dear) indicates [his status as] a vessel of confidence. Thus, having reassured her and made her attentive, he introduces the subject matter—namely, that he has come to her presence on account of that [husband's] message. By 'placed in the heart' (hṛdayanihita), the attentiveness established through friendship is indicated. But then, why was not someone else of such worldly skill and shrewd intellect appointed? To this he says—'some special skill of mine alone shines forth here.' By 'cloud' (ambuvāha), it indicates the declaration of his own agency in that [task]. He who urges on the throngs of those whose husbands are abroad, making them eager to hasten—of what kind?—even those who are weary and unable to hurry. 'Throngs' (vṛndāni) indicates, through its plural form, the habitual nature of his agency. By what means?—by deep, smooth sounds, by words lovely in their sweetness, having the character of the enticing speech of a skilled messenger—this is the meaning. Where?—on the path, on the road. 'By chance' (yadṛcchayā)—if I do this much casually, then how much more would I not do it with deliberate effort, motivated by the affection of a friend? Of what kind are those throngs?—eager for the loosening of the braids of young women. By the word 'abalā' (young woman), the inability to endure the anguish of separation from their beloved is expressed; 'eager for the loosening of their braids' indicates their state of mind devoted to their beloved. Thus the sentence-meaning here is: 'I am one who has always taken the vow of bringing about the happiness of reunion for any passionate person whose mutually devoted heart endures the anguish of separation ordained by fate.' Here, the movement of word-meanings composed by the poet—which in reality constitutes the very life of the work as a <s>Meghadūta</s> (Cloud Messenger)—is supremely delightful to the sensitive reader. But not of this kind, as [in the following verse]—

children.text: sadyaḥ purīparisare 'pi śirīṣamṛdvī gatvā78 javāttricaturāṇi padāni sītā79 /
children.translated_text: Having gone just three or four steps quickly, even in the vicinity of the city, <s>Sītā</s>, tender as a <s>śirīṣa</s> (silk-cotton) flower,

children.text: gantavyamadya kiyadityasakṛd bruvāṇā rāmāśruṇaḥ kṛtavatī prathamāvatāram80 // VjivC_1.33 //
children.translated_text: repeatedly saying 'how far must we go today?', shed the first descent of tears for <s>Rāma</s>. (Vjiv 1.33)

children.text:
atrāsakṛtpratikṣaṇaṃ kiyadadya gantavyamityabhidhānalakṣaṇaḥ parispando na svabhāvamahattāmunmīlayati, na ca rasaparipoṣāṅgatāṃ pratipadyate /
yasmātsītāyāḥ sahajena kenāpyaucityena gantumadhyavasitāyāḥ saukumāryādevaṃvidhaṃ vastu hṛdaye parisphuradapi vacanamārohatīti sahṛdayaiḥ saṃbhāvayituṃna pāryate /
na ca pratikṣaṇamabhidhīyamānamapi rāghavāśruprathamāvatārasya samyak saṅgatiṃ bhajate, sakṛdākarṇanādeva tasyopapatteḥ /
etaccātyantaramaṇīyamapi manāṅmātracalitāvadhānatvena kaveḥ kadarthitam /
tasmād "avaśam' ityatra pāṭhaḥ kartavyaḥ /
tadevaṃvidhaṃ viśiṣṭameva śabdārthayorlakṣaṇamupādeyam /
tena neyārthāpārthādayo dūrotsāritatvātpṛthaṅna vaktavyāḥ /
evaṃ śabdārthayoḥ prasiddhasvarūpātiriktamanyadeva rūpāntaramabhidhāya na tāvanmātrameva kāvyopayogi, kintu vaicitryāntaraviśiṣṭamityāha---
children.translated_text: Here, the movement characterized by the repeated, moment-by-moment utterance 'how far must we go today?' does not reveal natural greatness, nor does it attain the status of contributing to the fullness of <s>rasa</s> (aesthetic sentiment). For sensitive readers cannot even conceive that <s>Sītā</s>, who has resolved to go, with her innate propriety, would—out of mere delicacy—allow such a matter, even as it flashes in her heart, to rise to utterance. Nor does the statement, even though repeated moment by moment, properly harmonize with the 'first descent of <s>Rāghava</s>'s tears,' since that is established by a single hearing alone. This [verse], though extremely beautiful, is marred by the poet's slightly wavering attention. Therefore the reading 'avaśam' (involuntarily) should be adopted [instead]. Thus it is a distinctive quality of word and meaning of precisely this kind that should be accepted. Therefore, <s>neyārtha</s> (suggested meaning), <s>apārtha</s> (non-meaning) and the like, being far removed, need not be discussed separately. Having thus stated that beyond the well-known nature of word and meaning there exists another form altogether, [the author says] that not merely that much is useful for poetry, but rather [it must be] distinguished by yet another kind of strikingness—
These two [word and meaning] are to be ornamented; their ornamentation, again,
is <s>vakrokti</s> (oblique expression) alone—this is called the mode of expression characterized by poetic skill. (Vjiv 1.10)

children.text:
ubhau dvāvapyetau śabdārthāvalaṅkāryāvalaṅkaraṇīyau kenāpi śobhātiśayakāriṇālaṅkaraṇena yojanīyau /
kiṃ tattayoralaṅkaraṇamityabhidhīyate---tayoḥ punaralaṅkṛtiḥ /
tayordvitvasaṃkhyāviśiṣṭayorapyalaṅkṛtiḥ punarekaiva, yayā dvāvapyalaṅkriyate /
kāsau---vakroktireva /
vakroktiḥ prasiddhābhidhānavyatirekiṇī vicitraivābhidhā /
kīdṛśī---vaidagdhyabhaṅgībhaṇitiḥ /
vaidagdhyaṃ vidagdhabhāvaḥ kavikarmakauśalaṃ tasya bhaṅgī vicchittiḥ, tayā bhaṇitiḥ vicitraivābhidhā vakroktirityucyate /
tadidamatra tātparyam---yat śabdārthau pṛthagavasthitau na81 kenāpi vyatiriktenālaṅkaraṇena yojyete, kintu vakratāvaicitryayogitayābhidhānamātra82 mavānayoralaṅkāraḥ, tasyaiva śobhātiśayakāritvāt /
etacca vakratāvyākhyānāvasara evodāhariṣyate /
nanu ca kimidaṃ prasiddhārthaviruddhaṃ pratijñāyate yadvakroktirevālaṅkāro nānyaḥ kaściditi, yataścirantanairaparaṃ svabhāvoktilakṣaṇamalaṅkaraṇamāmnātaṃ taccātīvaramaṇīyamityasahamānastadeva nirākartumāha---
children.translated_text: Both these two—word and meaning—are to be ornamented, that is, they should be joined with some ornamentation that produces an excess of beauty. What is their ornamentation? This is stated: 'their ornamentation, again'—the ornamentation of both these two, though distinguished by the number two, is nevertheless a single one, by which both are ornamented. What is it?—<s>vakrokti</s> (oblique expression) alone. <s>Vakrokti</s> is a mode of expression that differs from ordinary denotation—a striking expression indeed. Of what kind?—characterized by the mode of poetic skill. Skill (<s>vaidagdhya</s>) is the state of being accomplished, the expertise in the poet's craft; its mode (<s>bhaṅgī</s>) is its distinctive manner; expression through that is called <s>vakrokti</s>, the striking mode of speech. The purport here is: word and meaning, standing separately, are not to be joined by any extraneous ornamentation; rather, by virtue of being endowed with the charm of obliquity, the very mode of expression alone constitutes their ornamentation, since it alone produces the excess of beauty. This will indeed be illustrated on the occasion of explaining obliquity. But now, is not something contrary to established meaning being asserted—namely that <s>vakrokti</s> alone is the ornament and nothing else? For the ancients have taught another ornamentation characterized by <s>svabhāvokti</s> (natural description), and it is extremely beautiful—unable to tolerate [its exclusion], he proceeds to refute it—
For those whose ornamentation consists of <s>svabhāvokti</s> (natural description),
made by the makers of ornaments—what else remains for them as the thing to be ornamented? (Vjiv 1.11)

children.text:
yeṣāmalaṅkārakṛtāmalaṅkārakārāṇāṃ svabhāvoktiralaṅkṛtiḥ, yā svabhāvasya padārthadharmalakṣaṇasya parispandasya uktirabhidhā saivālaṅkṛtiralaṅkaraṇamiti pratibhāti, te sukumāramānasatvād vivekakleśadveṣiṇaḥ /
yasmāt svabhāvoktiriti kor'thaḥ ? svabhāva evocyamānaḥ sa eva yadyalaṅkārastatkimanyattadvyatiriktaṃ kāvyaśarīrakalpaṃ vastu vidyate yattoṣāmalaṅkāryatayā vibhūṣyatvenāvatiṣṭhate pṛthagavasthitimāsādayati, na kiñcidityarthaḥ /
nanu ca pūrvamavasthāpitam---yadvākyasyaivāvibhāgasya sālaṅkārasya kāvyatvamiti (1 /
6) tatkimarthametadabhidhīyate ? satyam, kintu tatrāsatyabhūto 'pyapoddhārabuddhivihito vibhāgaḥ kartuṃ śakyate varṇapadanyāyena vākyapadanyāyena cetyuktameva /
etadeva prakārāntareṇa vikalpayitumāha---
children.translated_text: For those who are makers of ornaments (<s>alaṅkārakṛt</s>) and for whom <s>svabhāvokti</s> (natural description) is the ornamentation—namely, the expression of the natural quality, the characteristic movement of the object expressed—if that itself appears to be the ornamentation, they are [merely] averse to the labor of discrimination, due to their delicate sensibility. For what is the meaning of '<s>svabhāvokti</s>'? If nature itself, as being expressed, is the ornament, then what other thing, distinct from it and constituting the body of poetry, exists that stands as the thing to be ornamented? Nothing at all—this is the meaning. But was it not earlier established that 'it is the undivided sentence itself, together with ornament, that constitutes poeticity' (1.6)? Then what purpose does this statement serve? True, but there it was said that though unreal, a division produced by abstractive cognition can be made, following the principle of phonemes and words, or the principle of words and sentences. He now puts forth this same [argument] from another angle—
Without the nature [of a thing], it is simply not possible to express
a thing, since devoid of it, [the thing] would become nameless. (Vjiv 1.12)

children.text:
svabhāvavyatirekeṇa svaparispandaṃ vinā niḥsvabhāvaṃ vaktumabhidhātumeva na yujyate na śakyate /
vastu vācyalakṣaṇam /
kutaḥ---tadrahitaṃ tena svabhāvena rahitaṃ varjitaṃ yasmānnirupākhyaṃ prasajyate /
upākhyāyā niṣkrāntaṃ nirupākhyam /
upākhyā śabdaḥ, tasyāgocarabhūtamabhidhānāyogyameva saṃpadyate /
yasmāt svabhāvaśabdasyedṛśī vyutpattiḥ---bhavato 'smādabhidhānapratyayāviti bhāvaḥ, svasyātmano bhāvaḥ svabhāvaḥ /
tena sa eva yasya kasyacitpadārthasya prakhyopākhyāvatāranibandhanam, tena varjitamasatkalpaṃ vastu śaśaviṣāṇaprāyaṃ śabdajñānāgocaratāṃ pratipadyate /
svabhāvayuktameva sarvathābhidheyapadavīmavataratīti śākaṭikavākyānāmapi sālaṅkāratā prāpnoti, svabhāvoktiyuktatvena /
etadeva yuktyantareṇa vikalpayati---
children.translated_text: Without the nature—that is, without its own movement, without its inherent character—it is simply not possible, not feasible, to express a thing whose character is the expressible. Why?—because devoid of that, devoid of nature, deprived of it, it would become <s>nirupākhya</s> (nameless). <s>Nirupākhya</s> means 'gone beyond designation'; <s>upākhyā</s> means 'word,' and what lies beyond its scope becomes unfit for designation. Since the etymological derivation of the word <s>svabhāva</s> (nature) is: 'the basis from which the cognition and designation arise'—<s>svabhāva</s> is the being of the self. Therefore, that [nature] alone is the ground for any object's entry into manifestation and designation; a thing devoid of it, being like the unreal, like a hare's horn, reaches the state of being beyond the scope of word and cognition. [But if one says] whatever is endowed with nature enters the domain of the expressible in all ways—then even the statements of cart-drivers would attain the status of being ornamented, by virtue of possessing <s>svabhāvokti</s>. He now puts forth the same [point] by yet another reasoning—
If the nature itself is the ornament, what else does it adorn?
The self never mounts upon its own shoulders, not anywhere. (Vjiv 1.13)

children.text:
yasya kasyacidvarṇyamānasya vastuno varṇanīyatvena svabhāva eva varṇyaśarīram /
sa eva cedalaṅkāro yadi vibhūṣaṇaṃ tatkimaparaṃ tadvyatiriktaṃ vidyate yadalaṅkurute vibhūṣayati /
svātmānamevālaṅkarotīti cettadayuktam anupapatteḥ /
yasmādātmaiva nātmanaḥ skandhaṃ kvacidapyadhirohati, śarīrameva śarīrasya na kutracidapyasamadhirohatītyarthaḥ, svatmani kriyāvirodhāt /
anyaccābhyupagamyāpi brūmaḥ---
children.translated_text: For whatever object being described, its very nature is the body of the thing to be described, by virtue of being describable. If that very [nature] is the ornament, the embellishment, then what other thing distinct from it exists that it adorns? And if [one says] it adorns itself—that is improper, since it is impossible. For the self never mounts upon its own shoulders, not anywhere—meaning the body itself never climbs upon the body anywhere, due to the contradiction of action upon oneself. Furthermore, even granting [the opponent's position], we say—
When the nature has been designated as an ornament, and another ornament [is posited],
the distinction between the two is either manifest or not manifest. (Vjiv 1.14)
Where it is clear, there is always combination; where unclear, there is confusion;
and the domain of other ornaments ceases to remain. (Vjiv 1.15)

children.text:
bhūṣaṇatve svabhāvasya alaṅkāratve parispandasya83 yadā bhūṣaṇāntaramalaṅkārāntaraṃ vidhīyate tadā vihite kṛte, tasmin sati, dvayī gatiḥ saṃbhavati /
kāsau---tayoḥ svabhāvoktyalaṅkārāntarayoḥ bhedāvabodho bhinnatvapratibhāsaḥ prakaṭaḥ suspaṣṭaḥ kadācidaprakaṭaścāparisphuṭo veti /
tadā spaṣṭe prakaṭe tasmin sarvatra sarvasmin kavivākye saṃsṛṣṭirevaikālaṅkṛtiḥ prāpnoti /
aspaṣṭe tasminnaprakaṭe sarvatraivaikaḥ saṃkaro 'laṅkāraḥ prāpnoti /
tataḥ ko doṣaḥ syādityāha---alaṅkārāntarāṇāṃ ca viṣayo nāvaśiṣyate /
anyeṣāmalaṅkārāṇāmupamādīnāṃ viṣayo gocaro na kaścidapyavaśiṣyate, nirviṣayatvamevāyātītyarthaḥ /
tatasteṣāṃ lakṣaṇakaraṇavaiyarthyaprasaṅgaḥ /
yadi ca84 tāveva saṃsṛṣṭisaṃkarau teṣāṃ viṣayatvena kalpyete tadapi na kiñcit, tairevālaṅkārakārai85 stasyārthasyānaṅgīkṛtatvāt /
ityanenākāśacarvaṇapratimenālamalīkanibandhanena /
prakṛtamanusarāmaḥ /
sarvathā yasya kasyacit padārthajātasya kavivyāpāriviṣayatvena varṇanāpadavīmavatarataḥ svabhāva eva sahṛdayāhlādakārī kāvyaśarīratvena varṇanīyatāṃ pratipadyate /
sa eva ca yathāyogaṃ śobhātiśayakāriṇā yena kenacidalaṅkāreṇa yojayitavyaḥ /
tadidamuktam---"arthaḥ sahṛdayāhlādakārisvaspandasundaraḥ' (1 /9) iti /
"ubhāvetāvalaṅkāryau' (1 /10) iti ca /
evaṃ śabdārthayoḥ paramārthamabhidhāya "śabdārthau' iti (1 /7) kāvyalakṣaṇavākye padamekaṃ vyākhyātam /
idānī "sahitau' iti (1 /7) vyākhyātuṃ sāhityametayoḥ paryālocyate---
children.translated_text: When the nature—that is, the movement [of expression]—has been designated as an ornament, and when another ornament, a different figure, is prescribed—when that is done, two possibilities arise. What are they?—the distinction between the two, between <s>svabhāvokti</s> and the other figure, the appearance of their being different, is either manifest, clearly evident, or sometimes not manifest, not clearly apparent. Then, when [the distinction is] clear—manifest—in all cases, in every poetic utterance, only <s>saṃsṛṣṭi</s> (combination of figures) results as the sole ornament. When unclear—not manifest—everywhere only <s>saṃkara</s> (confusion of figures) results as the sole ornament. What fault follows from this?—he says: 'and the domain of other ornaments ceases to remain'—the domain, the scope of other ornaments such as <s>upamā</s> (simile) and the rest, does not remain at all; it simply becomes devoid of scope—this is the meaning. Hence the absurd consequence of the purposelessness of defining them. And if those very <s>saṃsṛṣṭi</s> and <s>saṃkara</s> are posited as their domain, that too amounts to nothing, since that position has not been accepted by those very makers of ornamental figures. Enough then with this fictitious disputation that merely chews the void. Let us return to the main subject. In every case, the very nature of whatever class of objects enters the domain of poetic description by virtue of being the subject of the poet's activity—that nature itself, being delightful to the sensitive reader, attains the status of being the body of poetry. And that [nature] itself is to be joined, as appropriate, with whatever ornament produces an excess of beauty. This is what was stated: 'The meaning, beautiful through its own delightful movement to the sensitive reader' (1.9), and 'Both these two are to be ornamented' (1.10).
