Thus, having stated the ultimate truth about word and meaning, [the author] has explained one word—'<s>śabdārthau</s>' (word and meaning)—in the definition of poetry stated [in verse] 1.7. Now, to explain '<s>sahitau</s>' (united) from that same [verse], the <s>sāhitya</s> (togetherness/literature) of these two is considered—
Word and meaning, being united, always flash forth as cognized;
that they are 'united'—this is first prescribed with the prefix 'sam'. (Vjiv 1.16)

children.text:
śabdārthāvabhidhānābhidheyau sahitāvaviyuktāveva sadā sarvakālaṃ pratītau sphurataḥ jñāne pratibhāsete /
tatastāveva sahitāvaviyuktāviti punaḥ kimapūrvaṃ vidhīyate na kiñcidapūrvaṃ niṣpādyate, siddhaṃ sādhyata ityarthaḥ /
tadevaṃ śabdārthayoḥ svabhāvasiddhaṃ sāhityaṃ kaḥ sacetāḥ punastadabhidhānena niṣprayojanamātmānamāyāsayati ? satyametat, kintu na vācyavācakalakṣaṇaśāśvatasaṃbandhanibandhanaṃ vastutaḥ sāhitāmityucyate /
yasmādetasmin sāhitayaśabdenābhidhīyamāne kaṣṭakalpanoparacitāni gāṅkuṭādivākyānyasaṃbaddhāni śākaṭikādivākyāni ca sarvāṇi sāhityaśabdenābhidhīyeran /
tena padavākyapramāṇavyatiriktaṃ kimapi tattvāntaraṃ sāhityamiti vibhāgo 'pi na syāt /
nanu ca padādivyatiriktaṃ yatkimapi sāhityaṃ nāma tadapi suprasiddhameva, punastadabhidhāne 'pi kathaṃ na paunaruktyaprasaṅgaḥ ? ata evaitaducyate---yadidaṃ sāhityaṃ nāma tadetāvati niḥsīmani samayādhvani sāhityaśabdamātreṇaiva prasiddham /
na punaretasya kavikarmakauśalakāṣṭhādhirūḍharamaṇī yasyādyāpi kaścidapi vipaścidayamasya paramārtha iti manāṅmātramapi vicārapadavīmavatīrṇaḥ /
tadadya sarasvatīhṛdayāravindamakarandabindusandohasundarāṇāṃ satkavivacasāmantarāmodamanoharatvena parisphuradetat sahṛdayaṣaṭcaraṇagocaratāṃ nīyate /
children.translated_text: Word and meaning — the expression and the expressed — always at all times, being together, inseparable, appear in cognition, shine forth in knowledge. Therefore, since they are thus together and inseparable, what new thing is being established by [saying] again [that they are] 'together'? Nothing new is being produced; what is already established is being [restated as] established — this is the meaning. This being so, since the togetherness (<s>sāhitya</s>) of word and meaning is established by their own nature, what person with sense would pointlessly trouble himself by stating it again? This is true; however, the togetherness spoken of here is not essentially based on the permanent relation characterized by the signifier-signified connection. Because if the word 'togetherness' (<s>sāhitya</s>) were understood in that sense, then sentences such as those beginning with 'gāṅkuṭa' — manufactured through forced construction and incoherent — as well as all sentences of the <s>Śākaṭika</s> type, would all be designated by the word 'togetherness.' Consequently, there would be no distinction of togetherness as some further reality beyond word, sentence, and valid cognition. But surely, whatever that thing called togetherness is, which is distinct from word and the like — that too is quite well known; then how, even in restating it, would there be no occasion for redundancy? It is precisely for this reason that the following is said: what is called togetherness has been known throughout this boundless extent of time merely by the word 'togetherness' alone. But no wise person has ever descended even in the slightest degree into the path of inquiry [to determine] 'this is its ultimate truth' — the beauty that has ascended to the pinnacle of the poet's artistic skill. Therefore, today, by the internal fragrance-captivation of the words of good poets, which are beautiful with the mass of nectar-drops from the lotus-heart of <s>Sarasvatī</s>, this [togetherness] is being brought within the range of the bee-like sensitive readers.
The togetherness of these two is, with regard to their beauty and splendor, a certain
disposition that is charming through being neither deficient nor excessive. // Vjiv_1.17 //

children.text:
sahītayorbhāvaḥ sāhityam /
anayoḥ śabdārthayoryā kāpyalaukikī cetanacamatkārakāritāyāḥ kāraṇam avasthitirvicitraiva vinyāsabhaṅgī /
kīdṛśī---anyūnānatiriktatvamanohāriṇī, parasparaspardhitvaramaṇīyā /
yasyāṃ dvayorekatarasyāpi nyūnatvaṃ nikarṣo na vidyate nāpyatiriktatvamutkarṣo vāstītyarthaḥ /
nanu ca tathāvidhaṃ sāmyaṃ dvayorupahatayorapi saṃbhavatītyāha---śobhāśālitāṃ prati /
śobhā saundaryamucyate /
tayā śālate ślāghate yaḥ sa śobhāśālī, tasya bhāvaḥ śobhāśālitā, tāṃ prati saundaryaślāghitāṃ pratītyaryaḥ /
saiva ca sahṛdayāhlādakāritā /
tasyāṃ spardhitvena yāsāvavasthitiḥ parasparasāmyasubhagamavasthānaṃ sā sāhityamucyate /
atra ca vācakasya vācakāntareṇa vācyasya vācyāntareṇa sāhityamabhipretam, vākye kāvyalakṣaṇasya parisamāptatvāditi pratipāditameva ( 1 /
7) /
nanu ca vācakasya vācyāntareṇa vācyasya vācakāntareṇa kathaṃ na sāhityamiti cettanna, kramavyutkrame prayojanābhāvādasamanvayācca /
tasmādetayoḥ śabdārthayoryathāsvaṃ yasyāṃ svasampatsāmagrīsamudayaḥ sahṛdayāhlādakārī parasparaspardhayā parisphurati, sā kācideva vākyavinyāsasampatsāhityavyapadeśabhāg bhavati /
children.translated_text: The state of being together (<s>sahitau</s>) is togetherness (<s>sāhitya</s>). Of these two — word and meaning — the disposition, the particular mode of arrangement, which is some extraordinary cause of the wonder-experience of the sentient, [is their togetherness]. Of what kind? — 'charming through being neither deficient nor excessive' — delightful through mutual rivalry. In which neither deficiency, i.e., inferiority, of either one of the two exists, nor excess, i.e., superiority — this is the meaning. But surely such equality is possible even between two that are defective — he says: 'with regard to their beauty and splendor.' Beauty refers to loveliness. One who is distinguished by that is 'beautiful and splendid'; the state of being that is 'beauty and splendor'; 'with regard to that' means with regard to what is distinguished by loveliness — this is the meaning. And that itself is what produces delight in the sensitive. The disposition, the state of being situated in the felicity of mutual equality, that is the rivalry with respect to that [beauty] — that is called togetherness. And here the togetherness intended is that of the expression with another expression, and of the expressed with another expressed, since the definition of poetry is completed in the sentence — as has been established (1.7). But if one asks: why not the togetherness of the expression with another expressed, and of the expressed with another expression? — [the answer is:] No, because there would be no purpose in transposing the order, and because of the lack of syntactic connection. Therefore, of these two — word and meaning — the totality of the wealth of their respective excellences, which produces delight in the sensitive by shining forth through mutual rivalry — some particular felicity of sentence-arrangement alone deserves the designation of togetherness.
The arising of qualities such as sweetness (<s>mādhurya</s>), in harmony with the literary style (<s>mārga</s>);
the arrangement of ornamentation endowed with a surpassing degree of obliqueness; // VjivC_1.34 //
the nourishment of <s>rasas</s> (aesthetic emotions), charming through propriety of style (<s>vṛtti</s>) —
where [all this] exists in rivalry, in each of the two respectively — // VjivC_1.35 //
that certain disposition, the sole foundation of delight for the knowledgeable,
the essence of the activity of words, sentences, and so forth — that is called togetherness (<s>sāhitya</s>). // VjivC_1.36 //

children.text:
eteṣāṃ ca padavākyapramāṇasāhityānāṃ caturṇāmapi prativākyamupayogaḥ /
tathā caitatpadamevaṃsvarūpaṃ gakāraukāravisarjanīyātmakametasya cārthasya pratipadikārthapañcakalakṣaṇasyākhyātapadārthaṣaṭkalakṣaṇasya vā vācakamiti padasaṃskāralakṣaṇasya vyāpāraḥ /
padānāṃ ca parasparānvayalakṣaṇasaṃbandhanibandhanametadvākyārthatātparyam iti vākyavicāralakṣaṇasyopayogaḥ /
pramāṇena pratyakṣādinaitadupapannamiti yuktiyuktatvaṃ nāma pramāṇalakṣaṇasya prayojanam /
idameva parispandamāhātmyātsahṛdayahāritāṃ pratipannamiti sāhityasyopayujyamānatā /
eteṣāṃ yadyapi pratyekaṃ svaviṣaye prādhānyamanyeṣāṃ guṇībhāvastathāpi sakalavākya parispandajīvitāyamānasyāsya sāhityalakṣaṇasyaiva kavivyāpārasya vastutaḥ sarvā tiśāyitvam /
yasmādetadamukhyatayāpi yatra vākyasandarbhāntare svaparimalamātreṇaiva saṃskāramārabhave tasyaitadadhivāsanāśūnya tāmātreṇaiva rāmaṇīyakavirahaḥ paryavasyati /
tasmādupādeyatāyāḥ parihāṇirutpadyate /
tathā ca svapravṛttivaiyarthyaprasaṅgaḥ /
śāstrātiriktaprayojanatvaṃ śāstrābhidheyacaturvargādhikaphalatvaṃ cāsya pūrvameva pratipāditam (1 /3,5) /
children.translated_text: And of these four — word, sentence, valid cognition, and togetherness — each has application in every sentence. Thus, this particular word of such a form, consisting of the sounds 'ga,' 'au,' and the <s>visarjanīya</s>, is the signifier of this meaning — characterized by the five aspects of the nominal base meaning or the six aspects of the verbal base meaning — this is the operation characterized by word-analysis. And the mutual syntactic connection of words, characterized by their interrelation, [namely] 'this is the purport of the sentence-meaning' — this is the application of what is characterized by sentence-analysis. [The judgment] 'this is well-established by means of valid cognition such as direct perception' — this fitness for reason is the purpose of what is characterized by valid cognition. [The recognition] 'this very thing, through the greatness of its activity, has attained the capacity to captivate the sensitive' — this is the applicability of togetherness. Although each of these has primacy in its own domain and the others become subordinate, nevertheless, of this [quality of] togetherness — which is being animated as the life-force of all sentence-activity — the poet's creative activity characterized by togetherness is in reality the most surpassing of all. Because even where this is not primary, within some other literary composition, through the mere fragrance of its presence it initiates a refinement — and merely through the absence of its permeation, the result is a lack of beauty. Therefore, there arises a loss of desirability. And consequently, there would be the occasion of the futility of its own operation. That [togetherness] has a purpose surpassing that of treatises, and a fruit exceeding the four goals of life that are the subject matter of treatises — this has already been established (1.3, 1.5).
Even when the content has not been thoroughly examined, through the splendor of the beauty of composition,
it produces delight in the hearts of the knowledgeable, like a song. // VjivC_1.37 //
When the understanding of the expressed content is complete, it imparts some life-force of word-and-sentence meaning
that is inwardly experienced, like the flavor of a drink. // VjivC_1.38 //
Just as a body without life, or life without manifestation —

children.text: vinā nirjovatāṃ yena yāti kāvyaṃ vipaścitām // VjivC_1.39 //
children.translated_text: without which poetry attains lifelessness in the eyes of the wise — // VjivC_1.39 //
Because some felicity, accessible only to the knowledgeable,
enters <s>Sarasvatī</s> (the goddess of speech) — that is now being examined. // VjivC_1.40 //

children.text:
ityantaraślokāḥ /
evaṃ sahitāviti vyākhyāya kavivyāpāravakratvaṃ vyācaṣṭe
children.translated_text: These are intermediate verses. Having thus commented on 'together,' he now explains the obliqueness of the poet's creative activity —
The kinds of obliqueness in the poet's creative activity are six;
each has many subdivisions, shining with distinctive charm. // Vjiv_1.18 //

children.text:
kavīnāṃ vyāpāraḥ kavivyāpāraḥ kāvyakriyālakṣaṇastasya vakratvaṃ vakrabhāvaḥ prasiddhaprasthānavyatireki vaicitryaṃ tasya prakārāḥ prabhedāḥ ṣaṭ saṃbhavanti /
mukhyatayā tāvanta eva santītyarthaḥ /
teṣāṃ pratyekaṃ prakārāḥ bahavo bhedaviśeṣāḥ /
kīdṛśāḥ---vicchittiśobhinaḥ vaicitryabhaṅgībhrājiṣṇavaḥ /
saṃbhavantīti saṃbandhaḥ /
tadeva darśayati--
children.translated_text: The activity of poets is the poet's creative activity — characterized by the act of poetic creation; its obliqueness is its oblique nature — the diversity that departs from the common course; its kinds are its varieties — six. They exist as primary [types] — only that many, this is the meaning. The varieties of each — the many subdivisions. Of what kind? — 'shining with distinctive charm' — resplendent with modes of variety. 'They exist' — this is the syntactic connection. He shows that very thing —
The obliqueness of phonemic arrangement, the obliqueness of the first half of a word —
there is also another kind of obliqueness, based on the suffix. // Vjiv_1.19 //

children.text: varṇānāṃ vinyāso varṇavinyasāḥ lakṣarāṇāṃ viśiṣṭanyasanaṃ tasya vakratvaṃ vakrabhāvaḥ prasiddhaprasthānavyatirekiṇā vaicitryeṇopanibandhaḥ saṃniveśaviśeṣavihitastadvidāhlādakārī śabdaśobhātiśayaḥ /
children.translated_text: The arrangement of phonemes (<s>varṇa</s>) is phonemic arrangement — the specific placing of sounds; its obliqueness is its oblique nature — the surpassing beauty of sound, constituted by variety that departs from the common course, effected by a particular mode of configuration, producing delight in the knowledgeable.
For example: 'At first of a rosy hue, then of a golden radiance, thereafter of the complexion of the cheek of a slender maiden fainting in separation,

children.text: prasarati tato dhvāntadhvaṃsakṣamaḥ kṣaṇadāmukhe sarasabisinīkandacchavirmṛgalāñchanaḥ // VjivC_1.41 //
children.translated_text: then spreading forth, capable of destroying darkness, at the face of night — the moon-marked one, with the lustre of the fresh lotus stalk.' // VjivC_1.41 //

children.text:
atra varṇavinyāsavakratāmātravihitaḥ śabdaśobhātiśayaḥ sutarāṃ samunmīlitaḥ /
etadeva varṇavinyāsavakratvaṃ cirantaneṣvanuprāsa iti prasiddham /
asya ca prabhedasvarūpanirūpaṇaṃ svalakṣaṇā vasare kariṣyate (2 /1) /
padapūrvārdhavakratā---padasya subantasya tiṅantasya vā yatpūrvārdhaṃ prātipadikalakṣaṇaṃ dhātulakṣaṇaṃ vā tasya vakratā vakrabhāvo vinyāsavaicitryam /
children.translated_text: The obliqueness of the first half of a word — of a word, whether a nominal form (<s>subanta</s>) or a verbal form (<s>tiṅanta</s>), its first half, characterized by the nominal stem (<s>prātipadika</s>) or the verbal root (<s>dhātu</s>), its obliqueness is its oblique nature — the variety of arrangement.
And therein many varieties are possible.

children.text: yatra rūḍhiśabdasyaiva prastāvasamucitatvena vācyaprasiddhadharmāntarādhyāropagarbhatvena nibandhaḥ sa padapūrvārdhavakratāyāḥ prathamaḥ prakāraḥ /
children.translated_text: Where a conventional word (<s>rūḍhiśabda</s>) is employed because of its suitability for the occasion, with the pregnancy of the superimposition of some property other than the well-known property of the expressed [meaning] — that is the first variety of obliqueness of the first half of a word.
For example: '<s>Rāma</s> am I — I endure everything.' // VjivC_1.42 //

Here, the surpassing beauty of sound, effected solely by the obliqueness of phonemic arrangement, is exceedingly manifest. This very obliqueness of phonemic arrangement is well-known among the ancients as <s>anuprāsa</s> (alliteration). The determination of its essential nature and subdivisions will be made at the appropriate place (2.1).

children.text: dvitīyaḥ---yatra saṃjñāśabdasya vācyaprasiddhasya dharmasya lokottarātiśayādhyāropaṃ garbhokṛtyopanibandhaḥ /
children.translated_text: The second: where a proper name (<s>saṃjñāśabda</s>) is employed with the pregnancy of the superimposition of an extraordinary surpassing quality upon the well-known property of the expressed [meaning].

children.text: yathā rāmo 'sau bhuvaneṣu vikramaguṇaiḥ prāptaḥ prasiddhiṃ parā- masmadbhāgyaviparyayādyadi paraṃ devo na jānāti tam /
children.translated_text: For example: 'That <s>Rāma</s>, who in the worlds has attained supreme fame through the qualities of his valor — if, through the reversal of our fortune, God does not know him,

children.text: vandīvaiṣa yaśāṃsi gāyati marudyasyaikabāṇāhati- śreṇībhūtaviśālatālavivarodgīrṇaiḥ svaraiḥ saptabhiḥ // VjivC_1.43 //
children.translated_text: this panegyrist sings his glories with seven notes poured forth from the hollows of broad palm trees, aligned in a row, struck by his single arrow that is the wind.' // VjivC_1.43 //

children.text:
atra rāma-śabdo lokottaraśauryādidharmātiśayādhyāropaparatvenopātto vakratāṃ prathayati /
paryāyavakratvaṃ nāma prakārāntaraṃ padapūrvārdhavakratāyāḥ---yatrānekaśabdābhidheyatve vastunaḥ kimapi paryāyapadaṃ prastutānuguṇatvena prayujyate /
tathā---
children.translated_text: Here, the word '<s>Rāma</s>' — employed with the intent of superimposing the surpassing quality of extraordinary valor and the like — displays obliqueness. Another variety of the obliqueness of the first half of a word is the obliqueness of synonyms — where, when a thing can be expressed by many words, some particular synonym is employed because of its suitability to the context. Thus —

children.text: vāmaṃ kajjalavadvilocanamuro rohadvisāristanaṃ madhyaṃ kṣāmamakāṇḍa eva vipulābhogā nitambasthalī /
children.translated_text: 'The left eye like collyrium, the breast with a swelling mark of love, the waist slender, the hip-region ample quite without reason —

children.text: sadyaḥ prodgatavismayairiti gaṇairālokyamānaṃ muhuḥ pāyādvaḥ prathamaṃ vapuḥ smararipormiśrībhavatkāntayā // VjivC_1.44 //
children.translated_text: may that first body of the enemy of <s>Smara</s> (the God of Love), mixed with its beloved, protect you — being gazed upon again and again with suddenly arisen astonishment by the <s>gaṇas</s> (attendants).' // VjivC_1.44 //

children.text:
atra "smararipoḥ' iti paryāyaḥ kāmapi vakratāmunmīlayati /
yasmātkāmaśatroḥ kāntayā saha miśrībhāvaḥ śarīrasya na kathañcidapi saṃbhāvyata iti gaṇānāṃ sadyaḥ prodgatavismayatvamupapannam /
so 'pi punaḥ punaḥ pariśīlanenāścaryakārīti "prathama'--śabdasya jīvitam /
etacca paryāyavakratvaṃ vācyāṃsabhavidharmāntaragarbhokareṇāpi paridṛśyate /
yathā
children.translated_text: Here, the synonym 'enemy of <s>Smara</s>' (<s>smararipu</s>) reveals a certain obliqueness. Because the mixing of the body of the foe of <s>Kāma</s> with a beloved cannot in any way be expected — therefore the suddenly arisen astonishment of the <s>gaṇas</s> is justified. And that [astonishment], being wonder-producing even upon repeated contemplation — therein lies the life of the word 'first' (<s>prathama</s>). This obliqueness of synonyms is also observed with the pregnancy of some other property belonging to the expressed [meaning]. For example —

children.text: aṅgarāja senāpate rājavallabha rakṣainaṃ bhīmādduḥśāsanam iti // VjivC_1.45 //
children.translated_text: 'O king of <s>Aṅga</s>! O commander! O king's favorite! Protect him from <s>Bhīma</s> — [protect] <s>Duḥśāsana</s>!' // VjivC_1.45 //

children.text:
atra trayāṇāmapi paryāyāṇāmasaṃbhāvyamānatatparitrāṇapātratvalakṣaṇamakiñcitkaratvaṃ garbhokṛtyopahasyate---rakṣainamiti /
padapūrvārdhavakratāyā upacāravakratvaṃ nāma prakārāntaraṃ vidyate---yatrāmūrtasya vastuno mūrtadravyābhidhāyinā śabdenābhidhānamupacārāt /
yathā---niṣkāraṇaṃ nikārakaṇikāpi manasvināṃ mānasamāyāsayati /
yathā---hastāvaceyaṃ yaśaḥ iti /
"kaṇikā'---śabdo mūrtavastustokārthābhidhāyī stokatvasāmānyopacārādamūrtasyāpi nikārasya stokābhidhānaparatvena prayuktastadvidāhlādakāritvādvakratāṃ puṣṇāti /
"hastāvaceyam' iti mūrtapuṣpādivastusabhavisaṃhatatvasāmānyopacārādamūrtasyāpi yaśaso hastāvaceyamityabhidhānaṃ vakratvamāvahati /
dravarūpasya vastuno vācakaśabdastaraṅgitatvādidharmanibandhanaḥ kimapi sādṛśyamātramavalambya saṃhatasyāpi vācakatvena prayujyamānaḥ kavipravāhe prasiddhaḥ /
yathā
children.translated_text: Here, of all three synonyms [for <s>Karṇa</s>], the quality of ineffectuality — characterized by the impossibility of his being a vessel for that protection — is mocked with pregnancy: 'protect him!' Another variety of the obliqueness of the first half of a word is the obliqueness of figurative usage (<s>upacāra</s>) — where an immaterial thing is designated by a word that denotes a material substance, through figurative extension. For example: 'Even a mere particle (<s>kaṇikā</s>) of insult without cause troubles the mind of the proud.' Or: 'Fame that can be gathered by hand.' The word 'particle' (<s>kaṇikā</s>), which denotes a small material substance, is employed through figurative extension based on the commonality of smallness to express also the smallness of the immaterial insult — and because it produces delight in the knowledgeable, it fosters obliqueness. '[Fame that can be] gathered by hand' — through figurative extension based on the commonality with the collectability of material things like flowers, the expression 'gathered by hand' applied to the immaterial fame constitutes obliqueness. A word that signifies a liquid substance, depending on some mere similarity based on the property of waving and the like, being employed also as signifier of what is solid, is well-known in the stream of poetic usage. For example —
'On the slope of the breast, rippling with the tremors of breath' // VjivC_1.46 //
Sometimes, even a word denoting a liquid-form meaning is employed as signifier of something immaterial. For example —

children.text: ekāṃ kāmapi kālavipruṣamamī śauryoṣmakaṇḍūvyaya- vyagrāḥ syuściravismṛtāmaracamūḍimbāhavā bāhavaḥ // VjivC_1.47 //
children.translated_text: These arms, once busy spending the itch of martial heat, the combatants of the long-forgotten celestial hosts, might [now] become [eager for] even a single droplet of time [to fight]. // <s>Vjīv</s>C 1.47 //

children.text:
etayostaraṅgiṇīti vipruṣamiti ca kāmapi vakratāmāvahataḥ /
viśeṣaṇavakratvaṃ nāma padapūrvārdhavakratāyāḥ prakāro saṃbhavati---yatra viśeṣaṇamāhātmyādeva tadvidāhlādakāritvalakṣaṇaṃ vakratvamabhivyajyate /
yathā---
children.translated_text: In these two [verses], 'taraṅgiṇī' (river) and 'vipruṣam' (droplet) each introduce a certain obliqueness. A type of obliqueness of the first half of a word-unit called 'qualifier-obliqueness' (<s>viśeṣaṇavakratva</s>) can occur — where, by the very power of the qualifier, the obliqueness characterized as the capacity to delight connoisseurs is manifested. For example —

children.text: dāho 'mbhaḥ prasṛtiṃpacaḥ pracayavān bāṣpaḥ praṇālocitaḥ śvāsāḥ preṅkhitadīpradīpalatikāḥ pāṇḍimni magnaṃ vapuḥ /
children.translated_text: A burning that cooks the flow of tears; a copious steam of sighs that has been carefully observed; breaths that make the creeper-like lamp-flame swing; a body submerged in pallor —

children.text: kiñcānyatkathayāmi rātrimakhilāṃ tvadvartma vātāyane hastacchattravirudvacandramahasastasyāḥ sthitirvartate // VjivC_1.48 //
children.translated_text: what more shall I say? Throughout the entire night, at the window on the path [where you pass], there stands that woman, her hand an umbrella rivaling the moon's radiance. // <s>Vjīv</s>C 1.48 //

children.text:
atra dāho bāṣpaḥ śvāsā vapuriti na kiñcidvaicitryamunmīlitam /
pratyekaṃ ca viśeṣaṇamāhātmyāt kācideva vakratāpratītiḥ /
yathā ca
children.translated_text: Here, 'burning, tears, sighs, body' — no variety at all has been unfolded in these. But in each case, by the power of the qualifier, a certain perception of obliqueness [arises]. And as —
With face bowed due to the bond of modesty, in the presence of elders, with the pot-like breast heaving, restraining [her] anger,

children.text: tiṣṭhetyuktaṃ kimiva na tayā yatsamutsṛjya bāṣpaṃ mayyāsaktaścakitahariṇīhārinetratribhāgaḥ // VjivC_1. 49 //
children.translated_text: 'Stay!' — was there anything she did not say by that word? — releasing her tears, the three-quarter portion of her eyes, beautiful like those of a startled doe, resting upon me. // <s>Vjīv</s>C 1.49 //

children.text:
atra cakitahariṇīhārīti kriyāviśeṣaṇaṃ netratribhāgāsaṅgasya gurusaṃnidhānavihitāpragalbhatvaramaṇīyasya kāmapi kāma nīyatāmāvahati cakitahariṇīhārivilokana sāmyena /
ayamaparaḥ padapūrvārdhavakratāyāḥ prakāro yadidaṃ saṃvṛtivakratvaṃ nāma---yatra padārthasvarūpaṃ prastāvānuguṇyena kenāpi nikarṣeṇotkarṣeṇa vā yuktaṃ vyaktatayā sākṣādabhidhātumaśakyaṃ saṃvṛtisāmarthyopayoginā śabdenābhidhīyate /
yathā
children.translated_text: Here, 'beautiful like a startled doe' is an adverbial qualifier of the resting of the three-quarter portion of the eyes, which is made lovely by the timidity produced in the presence of elders, and it introduces a certain charm through the comparison with the gaze of a startled doe. This is another type of first-half-of-word obliqueness called 'concealment-obliqueness' (<s>saṃvṛtivakratva</s>) — where the true nature of the content, being impossible to express openly and directly due to some deficiency or excess appropriate to the occasion, is expressed by a word that serves the power of concealment. For example —

children.text: so 'yaṃ dambhadhṛtavrataḥ priyatame kartuṃ kimapyudyataḥ // VjivC_1.50 //
children.translated_text: This man, whose vows are maintained through hypocrisy, is about to do something unspeakable to [his] beloved. // <s>Vjīv</s>C 1.50 //

children.text:
atra vatsarāje vāsavadattāvipattividhurahṛdayastatprāpnipralobhanavaśena padmāvatīṃ pariṇetumīhamānastadevākaraṇīyamityavagacchan tasya vastuno mahāpatākasyevākīrtanīyatāṃ khyāpayati kimapītyanena saṃvaraṇasamarthena sarvanāmapadena /
yathā ca
children.translated_text: Here, regarding King <s>Vatsarāja</s>, whose heart is distressed by the calamity of <s>Vāsavadattā</s>, and who, through the allurement of obtaining her, strives to marry <s>Padmāvatī</s>, and who understands that this very thing is improper — [the poet] conveys the unspeakability of that deed, as though it were a great sin, by the indefinite pronoun 'kimapi' (something), which has the power of concealment. And as —

children.text: nidrānimīlatadṛśo madamantharāyā nāpyarthavanti na ca yāni nirthakāni /
children.translated_text: Of her, slow with intoxication, her eyes closed with drowsiness — [those words] that are neither meaningful nor meaningless,

children.text: adyāpi me varatanormadhurāṇi tasyā- stānyakṣarāṇi hṛdaye kimapi dhvananti // VjivC_1.51 //
children.translated_text: even now, those sweet syllables of that beautiful-bodied woman somehow resonate in my heart. // <s>Vjīv</s>C 1.51 //

children.text:
atra kimapīti tadākarṇanavihitāyāścittacamatkṛteranubhavaikagocaratvalakṣaṇamavyapadeśyatvaṃ pratipādyate /
tānīti tathāvidhānubhavaviśiṣṭatayā smaryamāṇāni /
nāpyarthavantīti svasaṃvedyatvena vyapadeśāviṣayatvaṃ prakāśyate /
teṣāṃ ca na ca yāni nirarthakānītyalaukikacamatkārakāritvādapārthakatvaṃ nivāryate /
triṣvapyeteṣu viśeṣaṇavakratvaṃ pratīyate /
idamaparaṃ padapūrvārdhavakratāyāḥ prakārāntaraṃ saṃbhavati vṛttivaicitryavakratvaṃ nāma---yatra samāsādivṛttīnāṃ kāsāṃcid vicitrāṇāmeva kavibhiḥ parigrahaḥ kriyate /
yathā
children.translated_text: Here, 'kimapi' (somehow) conveys the inexpressibility — characterized by the fact that the wonder of consciousness produced by hearing those [syllables] can only be grasped through direct experience — [of what she said]. 'Tāni' (those) likewise —
In the middle, a sprout; the leaves — // <s>Vjīv</s>C 1.52 //
And as —
A body submerged in pallor — // <s>Vjīv</s>C 1.53 //
Or as — 'producing the effusion of the flow of nectar,'

children.text: himadhāmani khaṇḍe 'pi na jano nonmanāyate // VjivC_1.54 //
children.translated_text: Even when the cool-rayed moon is waning, people are not undelighted. // <s>Vjīv</s>C 1.54 //

children.text:
aparaṃ liṅgavaicitryavakratvaṃ nāma padapūrvārdhavakratāyāḥ prakārāntaraṃ dṛśyate---yatra bhinnaliṅgānāmapi śabdānāṃ vaicitryāya sāmānādhikaraṇyopanibandhaḥ /
yathā
children.translated_text: Another type of first-half-of-word obliqueness can be seen, called 'gender-variety-obliqueness' (<s>liṅgavaicitryavakratva</s>) — where, even for words of different genders, through [poetic] variety —

children.text: itthaṃ jaḍe jagati ko nu bṛhatpramāṇakarṇaḥ karī nanu bhaved dhvanitasya pātram // VjivC_1.55 //
children.translated_text: Thus, in this dull world, who indeed with large ears — surely the elephant — could be a vessel for that which has been sounded? // <s>Vjīv</s>C 1.55 //
And as —
<s>Maithilī</s> is his wife. // <s>Vjīv</s>C 1.56 //
Thus.

children.text:
anyadapi liṅgavaicitryavakratvam---yatrānekaliṅgasaṃbhave 'pi saukumāryāt kavibhiḥ strīliṅgameva prayujyate, "nāmaiva strīti peśalam' (2 /
22) iti kṛtvā /
yathā
children.translated_text: There is yet another gender-variety-obliqueness — where, even when multiple genders are possible, poets employ the feminine gender out of delicacy — 'the name itself being feminine' —
'Behold this river-bank before [you]!' — thus. // <s>Vjīv</s>C 1.57 //

children.text:
padapūrvārdhasya dhātauḥ kriyāvaicitryavakratvaṃ nāma vakratā prakārāntaraṃ vidyate---yatra kriyāvaicitryapratipādanaparatvena vaidagdhyabhaṅgībhaṇitiramaṇīyān prayogān nibadhnanti kavayaḥ /
tatra kriyāvaicitryaṃ bahuvidhaṃ vicchattivitatavyavahāraṃ dṛśyate /
yathā
children.translated_text: Another type of obliqueness of the first half of the word-unit, pertaining to the verbal root, is called 'action-variety-obliqueness' (<s>kriyāvaicitryavakratva</s>) — where the [poetic expression] is devoted to conveying variety of action —
Of him whose pair of eyes is covered by the lotus-shoot-like hand [of her] removing the garment in love-play — (Prākrit)
the third eye of the captive, kissed by [his wife], is victorious! (Prākrit) // <s>Vjīv</s>C 1.58 //
Of him whose pair of eyes is covered by the lotus-shoot-like hand of [her] removing the garment in love-play —
the third eye of <s>Rudra</s>, kissed by <s>Pārvatī</s>, is victorious!
Thus the <s>chāyā</s> (Sanskrit rendering).

children.text:
atra samāne 'pi hi sthaganaprayojane sādhye sāmānye ca locanatve, devyāḥ paricumbanena yasya nirodhaḥ saṃpādyate tadbhagavatastṛtīyanayanaṃ jayati sarvotkarṣeṇa vartata iti vākyārthaḥ /
atra jayatīti kriyāpadasya kimapi sahṛdayahṛdayasaṃvedyaṃ vaicitryaṃ parisphuradeva lakṣyate /
yathā ca
children.translated_text: Here, although the purpose of covering and the commonality of being an eye are the same, the action-variety whereby the covering of the goddess is accomplished through kissing — this introduces a unique charm belonging to <s>Bhagavān</s> [Śiva] —

Self-willed lions, dark moons with their own pure reflections, may the nails of <s>Madhusūdana</s> (<s>Viṣṇu</s>), which cut the suffering of those who take refuge, protect you! // <s>Vjīv</s>C 1.59 //

children.text: trāyantāṃ vo madhuripoḥ prapannārticchido nakhāḥ // VjivC_1.59 //
children.translated_text: Here, contrary to the well-known action of cutting that universally pertains to nails, a certain unprecedented action-variety characterized by the cutting of the suffering of the refuge-seekers has been presented by the poet —

children.text:
atra nakhānāṃ sakalalokaprasiddhacchedanavyāpāravyatireki kimapyapūrvameva prapannārticchedanalakṣaṇaṃ kriyāvaicitryamupanibaddham /
yathā ca
children.translated_text: here, of the nails, contrary to the universally known cutting function, a certain unprecedented action-variety characterized as cutting the suffering of refuge-seekers is presented.

children.text: sa dahatu duritaṃ śāmbhavo vaḥ śarāgniḥ // VjivC_1.60 //
children.translated_text: May the fire of <s>Śambhu</s>'s (<s>Śiva</s>'s) arrow burn away your sins! // <s>Vjīv</s>C 1.60 //

children.text:
atra ca pūrvavadeva kriyāvaicitryapratītiḥ /
yathā ca
children.translated_text: Here too, as before, the perception of action-variety [is present]. And as —
With eyes merged with the ear-lotus petals, with playfully rolling and proud glances — (Prākrit)

children.text: līlai līlāvarihi ṇiruddhāo siḍhiliacāo jaai maaraddhao // VjivC_1.61 //
children.translated_text: playfully, by the playful women, [he is] restrained, [his] bow made slack — victorious is the banner-of-Makara! (Prākrit) // <s>Vjīv</s>C 1.61 //
With eyes merged with the ear-lotus petals, by [women] with playfully rolling and proud glances —
playfully, by the playful women (<s>Līlāvatīs</s>), restrained, his bow made slack, victorious is <s>Makaradhvaja</s> (the god of love)!

children.text:
atra locanairlolayā līlāvatībhirniruddhaḥ svavyāpāraparāṅmukhīkṛtaḥ san śithilīkṛtacāpaḥ kandarpo jayati sarvotkarṣeṇa vartata iti kimucyate, yatastāstathāvidhavijayāvāptau satyāṃ jayantīti vaktavyam /
tadayamatrābhiprāyaḥ---yadelallo canavilāsānāmevaṃvidhaṃ jaitratāprauḍhibhāvaṃ paryālocya cetanatvena sa svacāpādhiropa ṇāyāsamupasaṃhṛtavān /
yatastenaiva tribhuvanavijayāvāptiḥ parisamāpyate /
mameti manyamānasya tasya sahāyatvotkarṣātiśayo jayatīti kriyāpadena kartṛtāyāḥ kāraṇatvena kaveścetasi parisphuritaḥ /
tena kimapi kriyāvaicitryamatra tadvidāhlādakāri pratīyate /
yathā ca
children.translated_text: Here, restrained by the glances of the playful women — that is, turned away from his own function — <s>Kandarpa</s> (the god of love) with his bow made slack is victorious with supreme excellence —
those syllables somehow resonate in [my] heart. // <s>Vjīv</s>C 1.62 //

children.text:
atra jalpanti vadantītyādi na prayuktam, yasmāttāni kayāpi vicchittyā kimapyanākhyeyaṃ samarpayantīti kaverabhipretam /
vakratāyāḥ paro 'pyasti prakāraḥ pratyayāśrayaḥ iti /
vakrabhāvasyānyo 'pi prabhedo vidyate /
kīdṛśaḥ---pratyayāśrayaḥ /
pratyayaḥ suptiṅ ca yasyāśrayaḥ sthānaṃ sa tathoktaḥ /
tasyāpi bahavaḥ prakārāḥ saṃbhavanti---saṃkhyāvaicitryavihitaḥ, kārakavaicitryavihitaḥ, puruṣavaicirtyavihitaśca /
tatra saṃkhyāvaicitryavihitaḥ---yasmin vacanavaicitryaṃ kāvyaśobhopanibandhanāya nibadhnanti /
yathā vā
children.translated_text: Here, rather than employing 'they speak' or 'they say,' [the poet says 'they resonate'], since the poet intends that those [syllables], with a certain charm, convey something inexpressible.
<s>Maithilī</s> is his wife. // <s>Vjīv</s>C 1.63 //
Thus.

children.text: yathā vā phullendīvarakānanāni nayane pāṇī sarojākarāḥ // VjivC_1.64 //
children.translated_text: Or as — 'the eyes are gardens of blooming blue lotuses; the hands are lotus-pools.' // <s>Vjīv</s>C 1.64 //

children.text:
atra dvivacanabahuvacanayoḥ sāmānādhikaraṇyamatīva camatkārakāri /
kārakavaicitryavihitaḥ---yatrācetanasyāpi padārthasya cetanatvādhyāropeṇa cetanasyaiva kriyāsamāveśalakṣaṇaṃ rasādiparipoṣaṇārthaṃ kartṛtvādikārakatvaṃ nibadhyate /
yathā
children.translated_text: Here, the co-referentiality of dual and plural numbers is exceedingly wonder-producing. [Now,] obliqueness produced through case-variety (<s>kārakavaicitryavihita</s>) — where even an inanimate object —

children.text: stanadvandvaṃ mandaṃ snapayati balādvāṣpanivaho haṭhādantaḥ kaṇṭhaṃ luṭhati sarasaḥ pañcamaravaḥ /
children.translated_text: The flood of tears slowly bathes the pair of breasts; forcibly, the sweet fifth note of passion rolls within the throat;

children.text: śarajjyotsnāpāṇḍuḥ patati ca kapolaḥ karatale na jānīmastasyā ka iva hi vikāravyatikaraḥ // VjivC_1.65 //
children.translated_text: the cheek, pale as autumn moonlight, falls into the palm of the hand — we do not know what indeed is the confusion of transformations in her. // <s>Vjīv</s>C 1.65 //

children.text:
atra bāṣpanivahādīnāmacetavānāmapi cetanatvādhyāropeṇa kavinā kartṛtvamupanibaddham---yattasyā vivaśāyāḥ satyāsteṣāmevaṃvidho vyavahāraḥ, sā punaḥ svayaṃ na kiñcidapyācarituṃ samarthetyabhiprāyaḥ /
anyacca kapolādīnāṃ tadavayavānāmetadavasthatvaṃ pratyakṣatayāsmadādigocaratāmāpadyate, tasyāḥ punaryo 'sāvantarvikāravyatikarastaṃ tadanubhavaikaviṣayatvādvayaṃ na janīmaḥ /
yathā ca
children.translated_text: Here, the poet has attributed agency to the flood of tears and other inanimate things through the superimposition of consciousness upon them — because, as she is helpless, their acting thus [of their own accord] —

children.text: cāpācāryastripuravijayī kārtikeyo vijeyaḥ bāṇavyastaḥ sadanamudadhirbhūriyaṃ hantakāraḥ /
children.translated_text: The conqueror of <s>Tripura</s> is the archery-master; <s>Kārtikeya</s> the one to be conquered; the arrow is <s>Bāṇa</s> (the demon); the ocean is the abode; this earth is the slaying-ground —

children.text: astyevaitat kimu kṛtavatā reṇukākaṇṭhabādhāṃ baddhaspardhastava paraśunā lajjate candrahāsaḥ // VjivC_1.66 //
children.translated_text: all this is so; but what — does your <s>Candrahāsa</s> (moonlight-sword), having rivaled the axe of him who committed the offense of cutting <s>Reṇukā</s>'s throat, feel ashamed? // <s>Vjīv</s>C 1.66 //

children.text:
atra candrahāso lajjata iti pūrvavat kārakavaicitryapratītiḥ /
puruṣavaicitryavihitaṃ vakratvaṃ vidyate---yatra pratyaktāparabhāvaviparyāsaṃ prayuñjate kavayaḥ, kāvyavaicitryārthaṃ yuṣmadyasmadi vā prayoktavye prātipadikamātraṃ nibadhnanti /
yathā
children.translated_text: Here, '<s>Candrahāsa</s> feels ashamed' — as before, this is the perception of case-variety obliqueness. There exists obliqueness produced through person-variety (<s>puruṣavaicitryavihita</s>) — where the first person [is replaced by another] —

children.text: asmadbhāgayaviparyayādyadi paraṃ devo na jānāti tam // VjivC_1.67 //
children.translated_text: Due to the reversal of our fortune, if the supreme god does not know that — // <s>Vjīv</s>C 1.67 //

children.text:
atra tvaṃ na jānāsīti vaktavye vaicitryāya devo na jānātītyuktam /
evaṃ yuṣmadādivaparyāsaḥ kriyāpadaṃ vinā prātipadikamātre 'pi dṛśyate /
yathā
children.translated_text: Here, instead of saying 'you do not know,' for the sake of variety, 'the god does not know' is said. Similarly, the transposition of 'you' and other [persons], even without a verbal form, as a nominal stem —

children.text: ayaṃ janaḥ praṣṭumanāstapodhane na cedrahasyaṃ prativaktumarhasi // VjivC_1.68 //
children.translated_text: This person wishes to ask, O ascetic woman — if it is not a secret, please deign to answer. // <s>Vjīv</s>C 1.68 //

children.text:
atrāhaṃ praṣṭukāma iti vaktavye tāṭasthyapratītyarthamayaṃ jana ityuktam /
yathā vā /
children.translated_text: Here, instead of saying 'I wish to ask,' for the purpose of conveying detachment, 'this person' is said. Or as —
'This man, whose vows are maintained through hypocrisy' — thus. // <s>Vjīv</s>C 1.69 //

children.text:
atra so 'hamiti vaktavye pūrvavad "ayam' iti vaicitryapratītiḥ /
ete ca mukhyatayā vakratāprakārāḥ katicinnadarśanārthaṃ pradarśitāḥ /
śiṣṭāśca sahastraśaḥ saṃbhavantīti mahākavipravāhe sahṛdayaiḥ svayamevotprekṣaṇīyāḥ /
evaṃ vākyāvayavānāṃ padānāṃ pratyekaṃ varṇādyavayavadvāreṇa yathāsaṃbhava vakrabhāvaṃ vyākhyāyedānīṃ padasamūhabhūtasya vākyasya vakratā vyākhyāyate---
children.translated_text: Here, instead of saying 'I myself,' as before, the perception of variety [arises from] 'this one' (ayam). These primary types of obliqueness — a few have been shown for the purpose of illustration —
The oblique nature of the sentence is another [category], which is divided a thousandfold,
wherein that entire class of <s>alaṅkāras</s> (figures of speech) will be subsumed. // <s>Vjīv</s> 1.20 //

children.text:
vākyasya vakrabhāvo 'nyaḥ /
vākyasya padasamūhabhūtasya /
ākhyātaṃ sāvyayakārakaviśeṣaṇaṃ vākyamiti yasya pratītistasya ślokādervakrabhāvo bhaṅgībhaṇitivaicitryam anyaḥ pūrvoktavakratāvyatirekī samudāyavaicitryanibandhanaḥ ko 'pi saṃbhavati /
yathā
children.translated_text: The obliquity of a sentence is something different. Of a sentence, which is a collection of words—a sentence being understood as a verb together with indeclinable particles, case-relations, and qualifiers—of such a verse and so forth, the obliquity, the strikingness of the mode of expression, is something different from the previously stated obliquity, arising from some charm based on collective strikingness. For example:

children.text: upasthitāṃ pūrvamapāsya lakṣmīṃ vanaṃ mayā sārdhamasi prapannaḥ /
children.translated_text: Having formerly cast aside <s>Lakṣmī</s> (prosperity) who had presented herself, you entered the forest together with me;

children.text: tvamāśrayaṃ prāpya tayā nu kopā- tsoḍhāsmi na tvadbhavane vasantī // VjivC_1.70 //
children.translated_text: now that you have obtained a refuge, I cannot endure, out of her anger, to dwell in your house. (Vjiv 1.70)

children.text:
etatsītayā tathāvidhakaruṇākrāntāntaḥ karaṇayā vallabhaṃ prati saṃdiśyate ---yadupasthitāṃ sevāsamāpannāṃ lakṣmīmapāsya śriyaṃ parityajya pūrvaṃ yastvaṃ mayā sārdhaṃ prapanno vipinaṃ prāptastasya tava svapne 'pyetanna sabhāvyate /
tayā punastasmādeva kopāt strīsvabhāvasamucitasapatnīvidveṣāttvadgṛhe vasantī na soḍhāsmi /
tadidamuktaṃ bhavati--- yattasmin vidhuradaśāvisaṃṣṭhule 'pi samaye tathāvidhaprasādāspadatā /
madhyāropya yadidānīṃ sāmrājye niṣkāraṇaparityāgatiraskārapātratā /
nītāsmītyetaducitamanucitaṃ vā viditavyavahāraparaṃpareṇa bhavatasvayameva vicāryatāmiti /
sa ca vakrabhāvastathāvidho yaḥ sahastradhā bhidyate bahuprakāraṃ bhedamāsādayati /
sahastra-śabdo 'tra saṃkhyābhūyastvamātravācī, na niyatārthavṛttiḥ, yathā---sahastramavadhyamiti /
yasmāt kavipratibhānāmānantyānniyatatvaṃ na saṃbhavati /
yo 'sau vākyasya vakrabhāvo bahuprakāraḥ, na jānīmaḥ kīdṛśa ityāha---yatrālaṅkāravargo 'sau sarvo 'pyantarbhaviṣyati /
children.translated_text: That manifold obliquity of the sentence—we do not know of what kind it is—to this he says: 'wherein that entire class of ornaments will be subsumed.'

children.text: yatra yasminnasāvalaṅkāravargaḥ kavipravāhaprasiddhapratītirupamādiralaṅkaraṇakalāpaḥ sarvaḥ sakalo 'pyantarbhaviṣyati antarbhāvaṃ gamiṣyati pṛthakatvena nāvasthāpyate /
children.translated_text: Wherein—in which—that class of ornaments, the collection of ornamental arts such as <s>upamā</s> (simile) and the rest, well-known through the tradition of poetic discourse, will be entirely subsumed, will undergo absorption, and will not be established separately.
Rather, it will attain designation precisely as a variety of the types [of obliquity]—this is the meaning.
And that class of ornaments will be illustrated word by word at the occasion of their respective definitions.

This is spoken by <s>Sītā</s>, whose inner faculty is overwhelmed by such compassion, addressed to her beloved—'You who formerly cast aside <s>Lakṣmī</s> (prosperity) who had come to serve you, abandoning royal glory, and entered the forest together with me—such a thing cannot even be imagined in your dreams. But again, out of her anger—out of the jealousy toward a co-wife that is natural to feminine nature—I cannot endure to dwell in your house.' What is being said is this: that in such a desperate and tumultuous time, there was such grace and favor [from you]; having been placed in the midst [of royal power], now in sovereignty, that there is groundless abandonment and disrespect—'I have been brought to this'—whether this is proper or improper, let it be deliberated by you yourself, who are familiar with the succession of proper conduct. And that obliquity is of such a kind that it splits into a thousand forms, attaining manifold varieties. The word 'thousand' here denotes merely a great quantity, not a fixed number—as in 'a thousand are inviolable.' Since the infinitude of poetic inspirations precludes any fixed [number].

children.text: evaṃ vākyavakratāṃ vyākhyāya vākyasamūharūpasya prakaraṇasya tatsamudāyātmakasya ca prabandhasya vakratā vyākhyāyate---
children.translated_text: Having thus explained sentence-level obliquity, the obliquity of the section (<s>prakaraṇa</s>), which has the form of a group of sentences, and of the work (<s>prabandha</s>), which consists of the aggregate of those [sections], is now explained—
The obliquity that exists in a section and also in a work—
of what kind—is now stated, [being] charming through delicacy both innate and cultivated. (Vjiv 1.21)

children.text:
vakrabhāvo vinyāsavaicitryaṃ prabandhaikadeśabhūte prakaraṇe yādṛśo 'sti yādṛg vidyate prabandhe vā nāṭakādau so 'pyucyate kathyate /
kīdṛśaḥ---sahajāhāryasaukumāryamanoharaḥ /
sahajaṃsvābhāvikamāhāryaṃ vyutpattyupārjitaṃ yatsaukumāryaṃ rāmaṇīyakaṃ tena manoharo hṛdayahārī yaḥ sa tathoktaḥ /
tatra prakaraṇe vakrabhāvo yathā---rāmāyaṇe mārīcamāyāmayamāṇikyamṛgānusāriṇo rāmasya karuṇākrandākarṇanakātarantaḥ- karaṇayā janakarājaputryā vtatprāṇaparitrāṇāya svajīvitaparirakṣānirapekṣayā lakṣmaṇo nirbhartsya preṣitaḥ /
tadetadatyantamanaucityayuktam, yasmādanucarasaṃnidhāne pradhānasya tathāvidhavyāpārakaraṇamasaṃbhāvanīyam /
tasya ca sarvātiśāyicarita yuktatvena varṇyamānasya tena kanīyasā prāṇakaritrāṇasaṃbhāvanetyedatyantamasamīcīnamiti paryālocya udāttarāghave kavinā vaidagdhyavaśena mārīcamṛgamāraṇāya prayātasya paritrāṇārthaṃ lakṣmaṇasya sītayā kātaratvenarāmaḥ preritaḥ ityupanibaddham /
atra ca tadvidāhlādakāritvameva vakratvam /
yathā vā kirātārjunīye kirātapuruṣoktiṣu vācyatvena svamārgaṇamārgaṇamātramevopakrāntam /
vastutaḥ punararjunena saha tātparyārthaparyālocanayā vigraho vākyārthatāmupanītaḥ /
tathā ca tatraivocyate---
children.translated_text: The obliquity—the strikingness of arrangement—that exists in a section, which is a part of a work, of what kind—and that which exists in a work such as a drama and so forth—that too is now stated, described. Of what kind?—charming through delicacy both innate and cultivated. The innate, natural; the cultivated, acquired through learning; the delicacy, the beauty—that which is captivating to the heart through that [delicacy] is so described. In a section, the obliquity is exemplified as follows: in the <s>Rāmāyaṇa</s>, when <s>Rāma</s> is pursuing the illusory jewel-deer created by <s>Mārīca</s>'s magic, <s>Lakṣmaṇa</s> is rebuked and sent by <s>Sītā</s>, daughter of King <s>Janaka</s>, whose inner faculty is terrorized by hearing the piteous cry, for the protection of [<s>Rāma</s>'s] life, without regard for her own self-preservation. Now this is extremely inappropriate, since the performance of such an action by the principal [character] in the presence of his attendant is inconceivable. And since he [<s>Rāma</s>] is described as one of supremely surpassing conduct, the expectation that his younger [brother] would protect his life is utterly improper. Having considered this, in the <s>Udāttarāghava</s>, the poet, through his skill, composed [the episode] such that when [<s>Rāma</s>] set out to kill the <s>Mārīca</s>-deer, <s>Rāma</s> was dispatched by <s>Sītā</s> in her distress to go for <s>Lakṣmaṇa</s>'s protection. And here, the very quality of being delightful to the knowledgeable constitutes the obliquity. Or, as in the <s>Kirātārjunīya</s>, in the speeches of the <s>Kirāta</s> (hunter, i.e. <s>Śiva</s> in disguise) and <s>Puruṣa</s> (man, i.e. <s>Arjuna</s>), only the tracing of his own arrows is introduced as the ostensible topic. In reality, however, the conflict with <s>Arjuna</s>, when considered in terms of its ultimate purport, is brought to the level of sentence-meaning. And thus it is said there—

children.text: prayujya sāmācaritaṃ vilobhanaṃ bhayaṃ vibhedāya dhiyaḥ pradarśitam /
children.translated_text: Having first employed the customary enticement, then displaying fear to break [the opponent's] resolve,
so adeptly was it employed by the one seeking arrows that it appears as though the other [course of action] were the proper one. (Vjiv 1.71)

children.text:
prabandhe vakrabhāvo yathā---kutracinmahākaviviracite rāmakathopanibandhe nāṭakādau pañcavidhavakratāsāmagrīsamudayasundaraṃ sahṛdayahṛdayahāri mahāpuruṣavarṇanamupakrame pratibhāsate /
paramārthatastu vidhiniṣedhātmakadharmopadeśaḥ paryavasyati, rāmavadvartivyaṃ na rāvaṇavaditi /
yathā ca tāpasavatsarāje kusumasukumāracetasaḥ sarasavinodaikarasikasya nāyakasya caritavarṇanamupakrāntam /
vastutastu vyasanārṇave nimajjannijo rājā tathāvidhanayavyavahāranipuṇairamātyaistaistairupāyairuttāraṇīya ityupadiṣṭam /
etacca svalakṣaṇavyākhyānāvasare vyaktimāyā syati /
evaṃ kavivyāpāravakratāṣaṭkamuddeśamātreṇa vyākhyātam /
vistureṇa tu svalakṣaṇāvasare vyākhyāsyate /
kramaprāptatvena bandho 'dhunā vyākhyāsyate---
children.translated_text: In a work, the obliquity is exemplified as follows: in some composition of a narrative about <s>Rāma</s> composed by a great poet—in a drama and such—in the beginning appears the description of a great personage, beautiful through the aggregate of all five types of obliquity, captivating to the hearts of connoisseurs. But in ultimate reality, it culminates in a moral instruction of the nature of injunction and prohibition: 'one should conduct oneself like <s>Rāma</s>, not like <s>Rāvaṇa</s>.' And similarly, in the <s>Tāpasavatsarāja</s> (The Ascetic and the Prince), the description of the conduct of the hero, whose mind is delicate as a flower, uniquely devoted to the relish of refined amusement, is begun. In reality, however, the instruction is: 'a king drowning in the ocean of calamity should be rescued by his ministers, skilled in such diplomatic conduct, through various expedients.' This will become manifest at the occasion of explaining the individual characteristics. Thus the sixfold obliquity of the poet's activity has been explained in summary form. It will be explained in detail at the occasion of [treating] the individual characteristics. Next, composition (<s>bandha</s>) is explained, as it comes in due order—
That which nourishes the elegance and charm of the expressed and the expressor,

children.text: vyāpāraśālī vākyasya vinyāso bandha ucyate // Vjiv_1.22 //
children.translated_text: an arrangement endowed with efficacy—that is called <s>bandha</s> (composition) of a sentence. (Vjiv 1.22)

children.text:
vinyāso viśiṣṭaṃ nyasanaṃ yaḥ sanniveśaḥ sa eva vyāpāraśālī bandha ucyate /
vyāpāro 'tra prastutatvāt kāvya kriyālakṣaṇaḥ /
tena śālate ślāghate yaḥ sa tathoktaḥ /
kasya---vākyasya ślokādeḥ /
kīdṛśaḥ---vācyavācakasaubhāgyalāvaṇyaparipoṣakaḥ /
vācyavācakayordvayorapi vācyasyābhidheyasya vācakasya ca śabdasya vakṣyamāṇaṃ saubhāgyalāvaṇyalakṣaṇaṃ yadguṇadvayaṃ tasya paripoṣakaḥ puṣṭatātiśayakārī /
saubhāgyaṃ pratibhāsaṃrambhaphalabhūtaṃ cetanacamatkāritvalakṣaṇam, lāvaṇyaṃ saṃniveśasaundaryam, tayoḥ paripoṣakaḥ /
yathā
children.translated_text: Arrangement—a distinctive placing, a configuration—that very thing, endowed with efficacy, is called <s>bandha</s> (composition). 'Efficacy' here, since the topic is poetry, refers to what characterizes poetic activity. That which is distinguished by it is so described. Of what?—of a sentence, a verse, and so forth. Of what kind?—that which nourishes the elegance and charm of the expressed and the expressor. Of both—of the expressed, the signified content, and of the expressor, the word—the quality-pair of elegance (<s>saubhāgya</s>) and charm (<s>lāvaṇya</s>), which will be explained, is nourished, brought to superabundance [by this arrangement]. Elegance is the quality of producing wonder (<s>camatkāra</s>) in consciousness, which is the fruit of the impulse of poetic inspiration; charm is the beauty of arrangement. The [composition] nourishes both of these. For example:

children.text: dattvā vāmakaraṃ nitambaphalake līlāvalanmadhyayā prottuṅgastanamaṃsacumbicibukaṃ kṛtvā tayā māṃ prati /
children.translated_text: Having placed her left hand on her hip, she of playfully bending waist, pressing her chin against the flesh of her high breasts, turning toward me—

children.text: prāntaprotanavendranīlamaṇimanmuktāvalīvibhramāḥ sāsūyaṃ prahitāḥ smarajvaramuco dvitrāḥ kaṭākṣacchaṭāḥ // VjivC_1.72 //
children.translated_text: two or three salvos of sidelong glances, vying with the tips of shoots on the tusks of tender young she-elephants, their play resembling pearl necklaces threaded with emeralds at their edges—[those glances] releasing the fever of love were cast with jealousy. (Vjiv 1.72)

children.text:
atra samagrakavikauśalasaṃpādyasya cetanacamatkāritvalakṣaṇasya saubhāgyasya kiyanmātravarṇavinyāsavicchittivihitasya padasaṃdhānasampadupārjitasya ca lāvaṇyasya paraḥ paripoṣo vidyate /
evaṃ ca svarūpamabhidhāya tadvidāhlādakāritvamabhidhatte---
children.translated_text: Here there is the supreme nourishment of elegance—characterized by the wonder in consciousness that is produced by the totality of the poet's skill—and of charm, which is fashioned by the strikingness of a certain minimal arrangement of syllables and acquired through the felicity of word-conjunction. Having thus stated the essential nature [of bandha], he now states its quality of being delightful to the knowledgeable—
Transcending the excellence of the triad of expressed, expressor, and <s>vakrokti</s>,
the quality of being delightful to the knowledgeable is somehow beautiful in its fragrance. (Vjiv 1.23)

children.text:
tadvidāhlādakāritvaṃ kāvyavidānandavidhāyitvam /
kīdṛśam--- vācyavācakavakroktitritayātiśayottaram /
vācyamabhidheyaṃ vācakaḥ śabdo vakroktiralaṅkaraṇam, etasya tritayasya yo 'tiśayaḥ ko 'pyutkarṣastasmāduttaramatiriktam /
svarūpeṇātiśayena ca svarūpeṇānyat kimapi tattvāntarametadatiśayenaitasmāttritayādapi lokottaramityarthaḥ /
anyacca kīdṛśam---kimapyāmodasundaram /
kimapyavyapadeśyaṃ sahṛdayahṛdayasaṃvedyam āmodaḥ sukumāravastudharmo rañjakatvaṃ nāma, tena sundaraṃ rañjakatvaramaṇīyam /
yathā
children.translated_text: The quality of being delightful to the knowledgeable—the capacity to produce bliss in those who know poetry. Of what kind?—transcending the excellence of the triad of expressed, expressor, and <s>vakrokti</s>. The expressed is the signified, the expressor is the word, <s>vakrokti</s> is the ornamentation—of this triad, the excellence is some extraordinary eminence, and [the delight] transcends that, surpasses it. In its own nature, and through its excellence—in its own nature it is something else, a different principle; through its excellence, it is beyond even this triad, transcending the worldly—this is the meaning. And what else characterizes it?—it is 'somehow beautiful in its fragrance.' 'Somehow' means indescribable, knowable only to the hearts of connoisseurs; <s>āmoda</s> (fragrance) is the delicate quality of objects, namely their capacity to produce aesthetic pleasure; 'beautiful' through that means delightful through the beauty of that capacity for aesthetic pleasure. For example:

children.text: haṃsānāṃ ninadeṣu yaiḥ kavalitairāsajyate kūjatā- manyaḥ ko 'pi kaṣāyakaṇṭhaluṭhanādāghargharo vibhramaḥ /
children.translated_text: Those [lotus stalks] by which, when swallowed by the honking geese, some other charming warbling arises from the harsh rolling in their throats—
those knots at the tips of lotus-stalk tubers, now rivaling the tusk-shoots of tender young she-elephants, have emerged in the lotus-ponds. (Vjiv 1.73)

children.text:
atra tritaye 'pi vācyavācakavakroktilakṣaṇe prādhānyena na kaścidapi kaveḥ saṃrambho vibhāvyate /
kintu pratibhāvaicitryavaśena kimapi tadvidāhlādakāritvamunmīlitam /
yadyapi sarveṣāmudāharaṇānāmavikalakāvyalakṣaṇaparisamāptiḥ saṃbhavati tathāpi yatprādhānyenābhidhīyate sa evāṃśaḥ pratyekamudriktatayā teṣāṃ parisphuratīti sahṛdayaiḥ svayamevotprekṣaṇīyam /
evaṃ kāvyasāmānyalakṣaṇamabhidhāya tadviśeṣalakṣaṇaviṣayapradarśanārthaṃ mārgabhedanibandhanaṃ traividhyamabhidhatte---
children.translated_text: Here, regarding the triad characterized by expressed, expressor, and <s>vakrokti</s>—no deliberate effort of the poet is predominantly perceived. Rather, through the power of the strikingness of poetic inspiration, a certain quality of being delightful to the knowledgeable has been brought to light. Although the complete fulfillment of the full poetic definition is possible for all examples, nevertheless, the aspect that is predominantly stated shines forth in each [example] with prominence—this should be inferred by the connoisseurs themselves. Having thus stated the general definition of poetry, in order to indicate the subject of its particular definitions, he states a threefold classification based on the distinction of poetic paths (<s>mārga</s>)—
There are three paths (<s>mārgas</s>) therein, the causes of poetic traditions;
the delicate (<s>sukumāra</s>), the elaborate (<s>vicitra</s>), and the intermediate (<s>madhyama</s>), which partakes of both natures. (Vjiv 1.24)

children.text:
tatra tasmin kāvye mārgāḥ panthanastrayaḥ santi saṃbhavanti /
na dvau na catvāraḥ svarādisaṃkhyāvattāvatāmeva vastutastajjñairupalambhāt /
te ca kīdṛśāḥ---kaviprasthānahetavaḥ /
kavīnāṃ prasthānaṃ vartanaṃ tasya hetavaḥ, kāvyakaraṇasya kāraṇabhūtāḥ /
kimabhidhānāḥ--- sukumāro vicitraśca madhyamaśceti /
kīdṛśo madhyamaḥ---ubhayātmakaḥ /
ubhayamanantaroktaṃ mārgadvayamātmā yasyeti vigṛhya chāyādvayopajīvītyuktaṃ bhavati /
teṣāṃ ca svalakṣaṇāvasare svarūpamākhyāsyate /
atra bahuvidhā vipratipattayaḥ saṃbhavanti /
yasmāccirantanairvidarbhādideśaviśeṣasamāśrayaṇena vaidarbhoprabhṛtayo rītayastistraḥ samāmnātāḥ /
tāsāṃ cottamādhamamadhyamatvena traividhyam /
anyaiśca vaidarbhagauḍīyalakṣaṇaṃ mārgadvitayamākhyātam /
etaccobhayamapyayuktiyuktam /
yasmāddeśabhedanibandhanatve rītibhedānāṃ deśānāmānantyādasaṃkhyātvaṃ prasajyate /
na ca viśiṣṭarītiyuktatvena kāvyakaraṇaṃ mātuleyabhaginīvivāhavad deśadharmatayā vyavasthāpayituṃ śakyam /
deśadharmo hi vṛddhavyavahāraparaṃparāmātraśaraṇaḥ śakyānuṣṭhānatāṃ nātivartate /
tathāvidhakāvyakaraṇaṃ punaḥ śaktyādikaraṇakalāpasākalyamapekṣyamāṇaṃ na śakyate yathākathañcidanuṣṭhātum /
na ca dākṣiṇātyagītaviṣayasusvaratvādi dhvanirāmaṇīyakavattasya svābhāvikaṃ kiñcid vaktuṃ pāryate /
tasmin sati tathāvidhakāvyakaraṇaṃ sarvasya syāt /
kiñca śaktau vidyamānāyāmapi vyutpattyādirāhāryakāraṇasampatpratiniyatadeśaviṣayatayā na vyatiṣṭhate, niyamanibandhanābhāvāt tatrādarśanād anyatra ca darśanāt /
na ca rītīnāmuttamamadhyamādhamatvabhedena traividhyaṃ vyavasthāpayituṃ nyāyyam /
yasmāt sahṛdayahṛdayā hlādakārikāvyalakṣaṇaprastāve vaidarbhosadṛśasaundaryāsaṃbhavānmadhyamādhamayorupadeśavaiyarthyamāyāti /
parihāryatvenāpyupadeśo na yuktatāmālambate, tairevānabhyupagatatvāt /
na cāgatikagatinyāyena yathāśakti daridradānavat kāvyaṃ karaṇīyatā marhati /
tadevaṃ nirvacanasamākhyāmātrakaraṇakāraṇatve deśaviśeṣāśrayaṇasya vayaṃ na vivadāmahe /
mārgadvitayavādināmapyetānyeva dūṣaṇān /
tidalamanena niḥsāravastuparimalanavyasanena /
kavisvabhāvabhedanibandhanatvena kāvyaprasthānabhedaḥ samañjasatāṃ gāhate /
sukumārasvabhāvasya hi kavestathāvidhaiva sahajā śaktiḥ samudbhavati, śaktiśaktimatorabhedāt /
tayā ca tathāvidhasaukumāryaramaṇīyāṃ vyutpattimābadhnāti /
tābhyāṃ ca sukumāravartmanābhyāsatatparaḥ kriyate /
tathaivai tasmād vicitraḥ svabhāvo yasya kavestadvidāhlādakārikāvyalakṣaṇaprastā vāt saukumāryavyatirekiṇā vaicitryeṇa ramaṇīya eva, tasya kācidvicitraiva tadanurūpā śaktiḥ samullasati /
tayā ca tathāvidhavaidagdhyabandhurāṃ vyutpattimābadhnāti /
tābhyāṃ ca vaicitryavāsanādhivāsitamānaso vicitravartmanābhyāsabhāg bhavati /
evametadubhayakavinibandhanasaṃvalitasvabhāvasya kavestaducitaiva śabalaśobhātiśayaśālinī śaktiḥ samudeti /
tayā ca tadubhayaparispandasundaraṃ vyutpattyupārjanamācarati /
tatastacchāyādvitayaparipoṣapeśalābhyāsaparavaśaḥ saṃpadyate /
tadevamete kavayaḥ kāvya karaṇakalāpakāṣṭhādhirūḍhiramaṇīyaṃ kimapi kāvyamārabhante, sukumāraṃ vicitramubhayātmakaṃ ca /
ta eva tatpravartananimittabhūtā mārgā ityucyante /
yadyapi kavisvabhāvabhedanibandhanatvādanantabhedabhinnatvamanivāryaṃ, tathāpi parisaṃkhyātumaśakyatvāt sāmānyena traividhyamevopapadyate /
tathā ca ramaṇīyakāvyaparigrahaprastāve svabhāvasukumārastāvadeko rāśiḥ, tadvyatiriktasyāramaṇīyasyānupādeyatvāt /
tadvyatirekī rāmaṇīyakaviśiṣṭo vicitra ityucyate /
tadetayordvayorapi ramaṇīyatvādetadīyacchāyādvitayopajīvino 'sya ramaṇīyatvameva nyāyopapannaṃ paryavasyati /
tasmādeteṣāṃ pratyekamaskhalitasvaparispandamahimnā tadvidāhlādakāritvaparisamāpterna kasyacinnyūnatā /
nanu ca śaktyorāntaratamyāt svābhāvikatvaṃ vaktuṃ yujyate, vyutpattyabhyāsayoḥ punarāhāryayoḥ kathametad ghaṭate ? naiṣa doṣaḥ, yasmādāstāṃ tāvat kāvyakaraṇam, viṣayāntare 'pi sarvasya kasyacidanādivāsanābhyāsādhivāsitacetasaḥ svabhāvānusāriṇāveva vyutpattyabhyāsau pravartate /
tau ca svabhāvābhivyañjanenaiva sāphalyaṃ bhajataḥ /
svabhāvasya tayośca parasparamupakāryopakārakabhāvenāvasthānāt svabhāvastāvadārabhate, tau ca tatparipoṣamātanutaḥ /
tathā cācetanānāmapi padārthānāṃ svabhāvaḥ svabhāvasaṃvādibhāvāntarasaṃnidhānamāhātmyādabhivyaktimāsādayati, yathā candrakāntamaṇayaścandramasaḥ kiraṇaparā marśavaśena spandamānasahajarasaprasarāḥ saṃpadyante /
tadevaṃ mārgānuddiśya tāneva krameṇa lakṣayati---
children.translated_text: Therein, in that poetry, three paths (<s>mārga</s>) exist — not two, not four — because exactly that many are in reality apprehended by experts, just as with the syllables <s>svar</s> and so forth. And of what kind are they? — 'The causes of the poet's progression' (<s>kaviprasthānahetavaḥ</s>): the progression, the movement, of poets — their causes, being the reasons for poetic composition. What are their names? — The delicate (<s>sukumāra</s>), the elaborate (<s>vicitra</s>), and the middle (<s>madhyama</s>). Of what kind is the middle? — 'Of the nature of both' (<s>ubhayātmaka</s>): analyzing it as 'that whose nature is the pair of paths just mentioned,' it means 'subsisting on the flavor of both.' Their essential nature will be described at the occasion of their individual characteristics. Here many divergent views are possible. For the ancients, taking recourse to specific regions such as <s>Vidarbha</s> and so forth, transmitted three styles (<s>rīti</s>) beginning with the <s>Vaidarbhī</s>. And of those, a threefold division into superior, inferior, and middle. Others again described a pair of paths characterized as <s>Vaidarbhī</s> and <s>Gauḍīyā</s>. Both of these are fraught with logical faults. For if the differences of style are bound to regional differences, then because of the infinity of regions, an innumerable [number of styles] would follow. Nor can the composition of poetry be established as a regional custom, like marriage with a maternal uncle's daughter or a sister, on the basis of being endowed with a particular style. For regional custom, resting merely on the succession of the practices of elders, does not extend beyond what can be practiced. Such poetic composition, however, requiring the totality of all instruments beginning with creative power (<s>śakti</s>), cannot be practiced in just any manner. Nor can something natural be attributed to it as with the charm of sound such as the melodiousness of the singing of Southerners — if that were the case, everyone would produce such poetry. Moreover, even when creative power is present, it does not remain confined to a specific region due to the wealth of acquirable causes such as learning, for there is no basis for such restriction — it is not seen there, and is seen elsewhere. Nor is it proper to establish a threefold division of styles into superior, middle, and inferior, for when the definition of poetry as that which delights the hearts of the connoisseurs is proposed, since beauty equal to the <s>Vaidarbhī</s> is impossible [for the other two], instruction in the middle and inferior becomes futile. And instruction for the purpose of avoidance is also unjustified, since even they [the proponents] do not accept that [position]. Nor does it deserve to be said that poetry should be composed to the best of one's ability, like the giving of alms by a pauper, as a last resort. Thus, we do not dispute the reliance on specific regions when it serves merely as an etymology or designation. For the proponents of the twofold path also, these very faults [apply] — enough of this devotion to examining empty matters. The difference in poetic approaches being grounded in the difference of the poet's nature is the fitting [explanation]. For the poet of delicate nature, a creative power (<s>śakti</s>) of just that kind arises spontaneously, since there is no difference between the power and the one possessing it. By that power, he acquires a training beautiful with such delicacy. By those two, he is made devoted to practice on the delicate path. Just so, the poet whose nature is elaborate — since, in the context of the definition of poetry as delighting the connoisseurs, it is charming through an elaborateness that differs from delicacy — for him too some elaborate creative power appropriate to it shines forth. By that he acquires a training rich in such artfulness. By those two, with a mind perfumed by the disposition toward elaborateness, he partakes in practice on the elaborate path. Thus, for the poet whose nature is intertwined with both, a creative power endowed with a superabundance of variegated beauty fitting to both arises. By that he cultivates a learning beautiful through the vibrations of both. Then he becomes devoted to practice nourished by the flavor of both. Thus these poets, having ascended the summit of the art of poetic composition, begin some charming poetry — delicate, elaborate, or of both natures. Those very [natures], being the causes of their proceeding [in composition], are called paths (<s>mārga</s>). Although, because they are grounded in the difference of poets' natures, an infinity of differences is unavoidable, still, since they cannot be enumerated [individually], a threefold division alone is established in general terms. And thus, in the context of apprehending charming poetry, the naturally delicate [poet] is one category — since what differs from that and is not charming is not to be accepted. That which differs [from the delicate] yet is endowed with charm is called the elaborate. Since both of these are charming, the charm of the [middle path] that subsists on the flavor of both is logically established. Therefore, since through the unfaltering greatness of each one's own vibration, their capacity to delight the connoisseurs is fully achieved, there is no inferiority in any of them. Now, one might object: due to the gradation between the creative powers, it is appropriate to speak of their being natural; but how does this apply to learning and practice, which are acquirable? This is no fault, for — leaving aside poetic composition — even in other domains, for anyone whose mind has been perfumed by beginningless dispositions through practice, both learning and practice proceed in conformity with one's nature. And those two attain fulfillment only through the manifestation of [one's] nature. Since nature and those two exist in a relationship of mutual assistance — nature initiates, and those two nourish it. And even of inanimate objects, their nature reaches manifestation through the power of the proximity of states concordant with that nature — just as moonstone gems, through contact with the rays of the moon, become coursed through with spontaneous liquid flow. Thus, having indicated the paths, he characterizes them in sequence:
Beautiful through fresh words and meanings that burst forth from unfading poetic intuition (<s>pratibhā</s>),
with a small amount of charming ornamentation produced effortlessly, // Vjiv_1.25 //
predominantly characterized by natural emotional expression, with subdued artful skill,
beautiful through accordance with the mind of one who knows the ultimate truth of <s>rasa</s> and the like, // Vjiv_1.26 //
charming through an unstudied, natural arrangement of beauty,
comparable to the superb creation produced by the skillful application of [artistic] rules, // Vjiv_1.27 //
whatever variety [there may be], all of it born of poetic intuition,
flowing with the vibration of delicacy — where it shines forth, // Vjiv_1.28 //
that [path] called the delicate (<s>sukumāra</s>) — by which excellent poets have traveled,
by that path, like bees through a grove of blossoming flowers. // Vjiv_1.29 //

children.text:
sukumārābhidhaḥ so 'yam, so 'yaṃ pūrvophalakṣaṇaḥ sukumāraśabdābhidhānaḥ /
yena mārgeṇa satkavayaḥ kālidāsaprabhṛtayo gatāḥ priyātāḥ, tadāśrayeṇa kāvyāni kṛtavantaḥ /
katham---utphullakusumakānanaiva ṣaṭpadāḥ /
utphullāni vikasitāni kusumāni puṣpāṇi yasmin kānane vane tena ṣaṭpadā iva bhramarā yathā /
vikasitakusumakānanasāmyena tasya kusumasaukumārya sadṛśamābhaijātyaṃ dyotyate /
teṣāṃ ca bhramarasādṛśyena kusumamakarandakalpasārasaṃgrahavyasanitā /
sa ca kīdṛśaḥ---yatra yasmin kiñcanāpi kiyanmātramapi vaicitryaṃ vicitrabhāvo vakroktiyuktatvam /
tatsarvamalaṅkārādi pratibhodbhavaṃ kaviśaktisamullasitameva, na punarāhāryaṃ yathākathañcitprayatnena niṣpādyam /
kīdṛśam---saukumāryaparispandasyandi /
saukumāryamābhijātyaṃ tasya parispandastadvidāhlādakāritvalakṣaṇaṃ rāmaṇīyakaṃ tena syandate rasamayaṃ saṃpadyate yattathoktam /
yatra virājate śobhātiśayaṃ puṣṇātīti saṃbandhaḥ /
yathā
children.translated_text: 'That [path] called the delicate' — this, characterized by the foregoing descriptions, is designated by the word 'delicate.' The path by which excellent poets such as <s>Kālidāsa</s> and others have gone, have been attracted — relying on it, they composed their poems. How? — 'Like bees through a grove of blossoming flowers': just as bees through a grove in which the flowers, the blossoms, have opened and bloomed. By the comparison with a grove of blossoming flowers, its noble birth resembling the delicacy of flowers is indicated. And by the similarity with bees, their addiction to extracting the nectar-like essence [of poetry] [is indicated]. And of what kind is it? — 'Wherein' (<s>yatra</s>), in which, 'whatever variety' (<s>kiñcanāpi vaicitryam</s>), however small the amount of elaborate quality, the possession of <s>vakrokti</s> (oblique expression) — 'all of that' is born of poetic intuition, shining forth through the poet's creative power alone, and not acquirable, not produced somehow through [mere] effort. Of what kind? — 'Flowing with the vibration of delicacy' (<s>saukumāryaparispandasyandi</s>): delicacy is noble birth; its vibration is the charm characterized by its capacity to delight the connoisseurs; by that it flows, becomes suffused with <s>rasa</s> — thus it is stated. 'Where it shines forth' — it nourishes a superabundance of beauty — this is the connection. For example:

children.text: pravṛddhatāpo divaso 'timātra- matyarthameva kṣaṇadā ca tanvī /
children.translated_text: The day, with heat intensely increased, has grown exceedingly [long], and the night [has become] exceedingly slender;

children.text: ubhau virodhakriyayā vibhinnau jāyāpatī sānuśayāvivāstām // VjivC_1.74 //
children.translated_text: both, divided by the action of opposition, were like a husband and wife filled with remorse. // VjivC_1.74 //

children.text:
atra śleṣacchāyācchuritaṃ kaviśaktimātrasamullasitamalaṅkaraṇamanāhāryaṃ kāmapi kamanīyatāṃ puṣṇāti /
tathā ca "pravṛddhatāpaḥ' tanvī' iti vācakau sundarasvabhāvamātrasamarpaṇaparatvena vartamānāvarthāntarapratītyanurodhaparatvena pravṛttiṃ na saṃmanyete, kavivyaktakauśalasamullasitasya punaḥ prakārāntirasya pratītāvānuguṇyamātreṇa tadvidāhlādakāritāṃ pratipadyete /
kiṃ tatprakārāntaraṃ nāma ?---virodhavibhinnayoḥ śabdayorarthāntarapratītikāriṇorupanibandhaḥ /
tathā copameyayoḥ sahānavasthānalakṣaṇo virodhaḥ, svabhāvabhedalakṣaṇaṃ ca vibhinnatvam /
upamānayoḥ punarīrṣyākalahalakṣaṇo virodhaḥ, kopāt pṛthagavasthānalakṣaṇaṃ vibhinnatvam /
"atimātram' "atyarthaṃ' ceti viśeṣaṇadvitayaṃ pakṣadvaye 'pi sātiśayatāpratītikāritvenātitarāṃ ramaṇīyam /
śleṣacchāyā kleśa saṃpādyāpyayatnaghaṭitatvenātra manohāriṇī /
punaśca kīdṛśaḥ---amlānapratibhodbhinnanavaśabdārthabandhuraḥ /
amlānā yāsāvadoṣopahatā prāktanādyatanasaṃskāraparipākaprauḍhā pratibhā kācideva kaviśaktiḥ, tata udbhinnau natanāṅkuranyāyena svayameva samullasitau, na punaḥ kadarthanākṛṣṭau navau pratyagrau tadvidāhlādakāritvasāmarthyayuktau śabdārthāvabhidhānābhidheyau tābhyāṃ bandhuro hṛdayahārī /
anyacca kīdṛśaḥ---ayatnavihitasvalpamanohārivibhūṣaṇaḥ /
ayatnenākleśena vihitaṃ kṛtaṃ yat svalpaṃ manāṅmātraṃ manohāri hṛdayāhlādakaṃ vibhūṣaṇamalaṅkaraṇaṃ yatra sa tathoktaḥ /
"svalpa'- śabdo 'tra prakaraṇādyapekṣaḥ, na vākyamātraparaḥ /
udāharaṇaṃ yathā---
children.translated_text: Here, the ornamentation tinged with the flavor of <s>śleṣa</s> (paronomasia), shining forth through the poet's creative power alone, is not artfully contrived — it nourishes a certain loveliness. And thus the expressions 'with heat intensely increased' (<s>pravṛddhatāpaḥ</s>) and 'slender' (<s>tanvī</s>), functioning with the sole purpose of conveying their own beautiful nature, do not consent to being directed toward the cognition of another meaning; yet, through mere congruity in the cognition of the other sense manifested by the poet's skill, they attain the quality of delighting the connoisseurs. What is that other sense? — The yoking together of two words that, through opposition, cause the cognition of another meaning. Thus, in the case of the objects compared, the opposition is characterized by non-coexistence, and the distinctness is characterized by a difference of nature. For the objects of comparison, however, the opposition is characterized by a quarrel of jealousy, and the distinctness is characterized by separate dwelling due to anger. The pair of qualifiers 'exceedingly' (<s>atimātram</s>) and 'intensely' (<s>atyartham</s>) are exceedingly charming by producing the cognition of superlativeness in both senses. The flavor of <s>śleṣa</s>, though laboriously achieved, is captivating here by appearing effortlessly produced. And further, of what kind [is the delicate path]? — 'Beautiful through fresh words and meanings burst forth from unfading poetic intuition' (<s>amlānapratibhodbhinnanavaśabdārthabandhura</s>): 'unfading' — that is, unimpaired by faults, ripened through the maturation of both old and new impressions (<s>saṃskāra</s>) — is a certain unique poetic power (<s>kaviśakti</s>), and from it 'burst forth,' shining forth spontaneously like fresh sprouts, and not extracted by force — fresh, recent, possessing the capacity to delight the connoisseurs — words and meanings, expressions and expressibles — by those, 'beautiful,' captivating to the heart. And what else [characterizes it]? — 'With a small amount of charming ornamentation produced effortlessly' (<s>ayatnavihitasvalpamanohārivibhūṣaṇa</s>): ornamentation, figuration, that is produced without effort, without strain; that is small, just a little, [yet] charming, delighting the heart — in which [path] that is [found], it is so called. The word 'small' (<s>svalpa</s>) here is dependent on context, not confined to the sentence alone. An example:
The <s>palāśa</s> (flame-of-the-forest) leaves, curved like a crescent moon, were exceedingly red due to their not having bloomed,

children.text: sadyo vasantena samāgatānāṃ nakhakṣatānīva vanasthalīnām // VjivC_1.75 //
children.translated_text: [appearing] like nail-marks on the forest-grounds that had just been united with spring. // VjivC_1.75 //

children.text:
atra "bālenduvakrāṇi' "atilohitāni' "sadyo vasantena samāgatānām' iti padāni saukumāryāt svabhāvavarṇanāmātraparatvenopāttānyapi "nakhakṣatānīva' ityalakaraṇasya manohāriṇaḥ kleśaṃ vinā svabhāvodbhannatvena yojanāṃ bhajamānāni camatkārakāritā māpadyante /
yaścānyacca kīdṛśaḥ--- bhāvasvabhāvapradhānyanyakkṛtāhāryakauśalaḥ /
bhāvāḥ padārthasteṣāṃ svabhāvastattvaṃ tasya prādhānyaṃ mukhyabhāvastena nyakkṛtaṃ tiraskṛtamāhārthaṃ vyutpattivihitaṃ kauśalaṃ naipuṇyaṃ yatra sa tathoktaḥ /
tadayamatrābhiprāyaḥ---padārthaparamārthamahimaiva kaviśaktisamunmīlitaḥ, tathāvidho tatra vijṛmbhate /
yena vividhamapi vyutpattivilasitaṃ kāvyāntaragataṃ tiraskārāspadaṃ saṃpadyate /
atrodāharaṇaṃ raghuvaṃśe mṛgayāvarṇanaparaṃ prakaraṇam, yathā
children.translated_text: Here, the words 'crescent-moon-curved,' 'deeply red,' and 'of those who have just met the spring' — though employed merely for the purpose of natural description owing to their delicacy — when entering into connection with the ornamentation 'as if nail-marks,' charming and arising naturally without effort, they attain the quality of producing wonder. And yet another [kind] — of what sort? — 'one in whom the primacy of the true nature of things has eclipsed the skill of artifice.' The nature (<s>svabhāva</s>) of things (<s>bhāva</s>), i.e., of objects, is their truth; the primacy of that is its predominance; by that, the artificial skill (<s>āhāryakauśala</s>), i.e., the dexterity fashioned by learning, has been eclipsed, surpassed — one who is so is thus described. The purport here is this: the very grandeur of the ultimate truth of objects, revealed by the poet's power, manifests itself in such a way that even manifold displays of learning found in other poetry are rendered an object of contempt. The example here is the passage in the <s>Raghuvaṃśa</s> devoted to the description of the hunt, such as —
'Before him appeared a herd of deer, their progress impeded repeatedly by fawns clinging to their mothers' teats for milk,

children.text: āvirbabhūva kuśagarbhamukhaṃ mṛgāṇāṃ yūthaṃ tadagrasaragarvitakṛṣṇasāram // VjivC_1.76 //
children.translated_text: their mouths filled with blades of <s>kuśa</s> grass, led proudly at the front by a black antelope.' // VjivC_1.76 //
And so forth. And as in the <s>Kumārasambhava</s> —
'The couples expressed their feelings through their actions.' // VjivC_1.77 //
And so on. Beyond that, [there is] the description of the nature of living beings —

children.text: śṛṅgeṇa ca sparśanimīlitākṣīṃ mṛgīmakaṇḍūyata kṛṣṇasāraḥ // VjivC_1.78 //
children.translated_text: 'The black antelope scratched the doe whose eyes closed at the touch of his horn.' // VjivC_1.78 //

children.text:
anyacca kīdṛśaḥ---rasādiparamārthajñamanaḥ saṃvādasundaraḥ /
rasāḥ śṛṅgārādayaḥ /
tadādigrahaṇena ratyādayo 'pi gṛhyante /
teṣāṃ paramārthaḥ para rahasyaṃ tajjānantīti tajjñāstadvidasteṣāṃ manaḥ saṃvādo hṛdayasaṃvedanaṃ svānubhavagocaratayā pratibhāsaḥ, tena sundaraḥ sukumāraḥ sahṛdayahṛdayāhlādakārī vākyasyopanibandha ityarthaḥ /
atrodāharaṇāni raghau rāvaṇaṃ nihatya puṣpakeṇāgacchato rāmasya sītāyāstadvirahavidhurahṛdayena mayāsminnasmin samuddeśe kimapyevaṃvidhaṃ vaiśasamanubhūtamiti varṇayataḥ sarvāṇyeva vākyāni /
tathā
children.translated_text: And yet another [kind] — of what sort? — 'beautiful through concordance with the minds of those who know the ultimate truth of <s>rasa</s> (aesthetic emotion) and the like.' The <s>rasas</s> are <s>śṛṅgāra</s> (the erotic) and so forth. By the word 'and the like,' <s>rati</s> (love) and such [permanent emotions] are also included. Their ultimate truth is their innermost secret; those who know that are experts in it; their mind's concordance is the resonance of their hearts, the appearance [of the emotion] as falling within their own experience; 'beautiful' through that means delicate, producing delight in the hearts of the sensitive — such is the construction of the sentence, this is the meaning. The examples here are all the sentences in the <s>Raghuvaṃśa</s> where <s>Rāma</s>, returning by the <s>Puṣpaka</s> [aerial chariot] after slaying <s>Rāvaṇa</s>, describes to <s>Sītā</s>, with a heart distressed by her absence, 'In this and that place, such and such distress was experienced by me.' Thus —

children.text: pūrvānubhūtaṃ smaratā ca rātrau kampottaraṃ bhīru tavopagūḍham /
children.translated_text: 'Remembering at night what was experienced before — your embrace, O timid one, trembling all over,
the thunderings of the clouds were somehow endured by me, blown into the cave.' // VjivC_1.79 //

children.text:
atra rāśidvayakaraṇasyāyamabhiprāyo yad vibhāvādirūpeṇa rasāṅgabhūtāḥ śakunirutatarusalilakusumasamayaprabhṛtayaḥ padārthāḥ sātiśayasvabhāvavarṇanaprādhānyenaiva rasāṅgatāṃ pratipadyante /
tadvyatiriktāḥ suragandharvaprabhṛtayaḥ sotkarṣacetanāyoginaḥ śṛṅgārādirasanirbharatayā varṇyamānāḥ sarasahṛdayāhlādakāritāmāyāntīti kavibhirabhyupagatam /
tathāvidhameva lakṣye dṛśyate /
anyacca kīdṛśaḥ---avibhāvitasaṃsthānarāmaṇīyakarañjakaḥ /
avibhāvitamanālocitaṃ saṃsthānaṃ saṃsthitiryatra tena rāmaṇīyakena ramaṇīyatvena rañjakaḥ sahṛdayāhlādakaḥ /
