tenāyamarthaḥ---yadi tathā vidhaṃ kavikauśalamatra saṃbhavati tad vyapadeṣṭumiyattayā na kathañcidapi pāryate, kevalaṃ sarvātiśāyitayā cetasi parisphurati /
anyacca kīdṛśaḥ---vidhivaidagdhayaniṣpannanirmāṇātiśayopamaḥ /
vidhirvidhātā tasya vaidagdhyaṃ kauśalaṃ tena niṣpannaḥ parisamāpto yo 'sau nirmaṇātiśayaḥ sundaraḥ sargollekho ramaṇīyalāvaṇyādiḥ sa upamā nidarśanaṃ tasya sa tathoktaḥ /
tena vidhāturiva kaveḥ kauśalaṃ yatra vivektumaśakyam /
yathā
children.translated_text: Here, the purport of treating these as a pair is this: objects that are constituents of <s>rasa</s> — such as bird-songs, trees, waters, flowers, seasons, and so forth — which are in the form of <s>vibhāvas</s> (determinants) and the like, attain their status as components of <s>rasa</s> primarily through the excellence of their natural description. Others, such as gods, <s>gandharvas</s>, and the like, who are endowed with surpassing consciousness — being described as imbued with <s>śṛṅgāra</s> and other <s>rasas</s> — they come to produce delight in the sensitive reader: this is accepted by poets. And such is indeed observed in literary works. And yet another [kind] — of what sort? — 'one that delights with a loveliness whose configuration has not been [previously] conceived.' Whose configuration, i.e., arrangement, has not been conceived, i.e., not previously imagined — one that, through such loveliness, delights the sensitive reader. The meaning then is: if such poetic skill is possible here, it cannot in any way be designated in its extent — it merely shines forth in the mind as surpassing everything. And yet another [kind] — of what sort? — 'comparable to the surpassing creation accomplished by the skill of the Creator.' The Creator (<s>Vidhi</s>, i.e., <s>Brahmā</s>); his skill; accomplished by that — the beautiful outline of creation, charming with loveliness and grace — that is the example, the illustration. Therefore, the skill of the poet is, as it were, like that of the Creator — indiscernible [from it]. For example —
'By him, the ten-faced <s>Rāvaṇa</s>, who had conquered <s>Indra</s>, whose arm was immobile from the binding of the bowstring,
through whose succession of exhaling faces — in prison, [he remained] until [<s>Indra's</s>] grace.' // VjivC_1.80 //

children.text:
atra vyapadeśaprakārāntaranirapekṣaḥ kaviśaktipariṇāmaḥ paraṃ paripākamadhirūḍhaḥ /
etasmin kulake---prathamaśloke prādhānyena śabdālaṅkārayoḥ saundaryaṃ pratipāditam /
dvitīye varṇanīyasya vastunaḥ saukumāryam /
tṛtīye prakārāntaranirapekṣasya saṃniveśasya saukumāryam /
caturthe vaicitryamapi saukumāryāvisaṃvādi vidheyamityuktam /
pañcamo viṣayaviṣayisaukumāryapratipādanaraparaḥ /
evaṃ sukumārābhidhānasya mārgasya lakṣaṇaṃ vidhāya tasyaiva guṇān lakṣayati---
children.translated_text: Here, the maturation of the poet's power, independent of any other mode of description, has attained its supreme ripeness. In this group [of verses]: in the first verse, the beauty of verbal ornamentation has been primarily demonstrated. In the second, the delicacy of the object being described. In the third, the delicacy of arrangement that is independent of any other mode. In the fourth, it is stated that even variety should be consistent with delicacy. The fifth is devoted to demonstrating the delicacy of both object and subject. Having thus established the definition of the delicate (<s>sukumāra</s>) style, he now defines its qualities —
The life of which is the arrangement of words that are entirely captivating —

children.text: mādhuryaṃ sukumārasya mārgasya prathamo guṇaḥ // Vjiv_1.30 //
children.translated_text: <s>mādhurya</s> (sweetness) is the first quality of the delicate style. // Vjiv_1.30 //

children.text:
asamastāni samāsavarjitāni manohārīṇi hṛdayāhlādakāni śrutiramyatvenārtharamaṇīyatvena ca yāni padāni suptiṅantāni teṣāṃ vinyāsaḥ saṃniveśavaicitryaṃ jīvitaṃ sarvasvaṃ yasya tattathoktaṃ mādhṛryaṃ nāma sukumāralakṣaṇasya mārgasya prathamaḥ pradhānabhūto guṇaḥ /
asamastaśabdo 'tra prācuryārthaḥ, na samāsābhāvaniyamārthaḥ /
udāharaṇaṃ yathā
children.translated_text: 'Entirely' (<s>asamasta</s>) means free from compounds; 'captivating' means delighting the heart — through their beauty to the ear and through the beauty of their meaning — such words, both nominal and verbal; their 'arrangement' is the variety of their configuration; that which has that as its life-force, its very essence — such a thing called <s>mādhurya</s> (sweetness) is the first, i.e., primary, quality of the style characterized as delicate. The word 'asamasta' here means 'predominantly [free from compounds],' not 'absolutely devoid of compounds.' An example —

children.text: krīḍārasena rahasi smatapūrvamindor lekhāṃ vikṛṣya vinibad ca mūrdhni gauryā /
children.translated_text: 'Having playfully drawn the crescent moon from the head of <s>Gaurī</s>, remembered in private with the <s>rasa</s> of sport,

children.text: kiṃ śobhitāhamanayota śaśāṅkamauleḥ pṛṣṭasya pātu paricumbhanamuttaravaḥ // VjivC_1.81 //
children.translated_text: 'Am I beautified by this?' — when [<s>Śiva</s>] of the moon-crested was asked thus, may his kiss be the reply that protects [you].' // VjivC_1.81 //

children.text:
atra padānāmasamastatvaṃ śabdārtharamaṇīyatā vinyāsavaicitryaṃ ca tritayamapi cakāsti /
tadevaṃ mādhuryamabhidhāya prasādamabhidhatte---
children.translated_text: Here, all three — the predominantly non-compound nature of the words, the beauty of sound and meaning, and the variety of arrangement — shine forth. Having thus described <s>mādhurya</s>, he describes <s>prasāda</s> (clarity) —
The yielding of meaning instantly, with the intent revealed without difficulty,
that which has the domain of <s>rasa</s> and <s>vakrokti</s> (oblique expression) — that is called <s>prasāda</s> (clarity). // Vjiv_1.31 //

children.text:
jhagiti prathamataramevārthasamarpaṇaṃ vastupratipādanam /
kīdṛśam--- akleśavyañjitākūtam akadarthanāprakaṭitābhiprāyam /
kiṃviṣayam---rasavakroktiviṣayam /
rasāḥ śṛṅgārādayaḥ, vakroktiḥ sakalālaṅkārasāmānyaṃ viṣayo yasya tattathoktam /
sa eva prasādākhyo guṇaḥ kathyate bhaṇyate /
atra padānāmasamastatvaṃ prasiddhābhidhānatvam avyavahitasaṃbandhatvaṃ samāsasadbhāve 'pi gamakasamāsayuktatā ca paramārthaḥ /
"ākūta'- śabdastātparye vicchittau ca vartate /
udāharaṇaṃ yathā
children.translated_text: 'Instantly' means at the very first [hearing]; 'the yielding of meaning' is the presentation of the subject matter. Of what kind? — 'with the intent revealed without difficulty' — with the purpose made manifest without harsh effort. In what domain? — 'that which has the domain of <s>rasa</s> and <s>vakrokti</s>.' The <s>rasas</s> are <s>śṛṅgāra</s> and so forth; <s>vakrokti</s> is the generality of all ornamentation — one whose domain is that is thus described. That itself, the quality called <s>prasāda</s>, is declared. Here, the ultimate meaning involves: the predominantly non-compound nature of words, the use of well-known expressions, unmediated syntactic connection, and even when compounds exist, the use of transparent compounds. The word '<s>ākūta</s>' (intent) applies both to purport and to distinctive charm. An example —
'Of the <s>kiṃpuruṣa</s> women, whose lips became clear after the departure of the cold season and whose facial lustre grew pallid,

children.text: svedodgamaḥ kiṃpuruṣāṅganānāṃ cakre padaṃ patraviśeṣakeṣu // VjivC_1.82 //
children.translated_text: the perspiration took its place among the decorative leaf-patterns.' // VjivC_1.82 //

children.text:
atrāsamastatvādisāmagrī vidyate /
yadapi vividhapatraviśeṣakavaicitryavihitaṃ kimapi vadanasaundaryaṃ muktākaṇākārasvedalavopabṛṃhitaṃ tadapi suvyaktameva /
yathā vā
children.translated_text: Here the complete set [of qualities] including non-compound nature and the rest is present. And the certain beauty of the face, produced by the variety of diverse decorative leaf-patterns, augmented by drops of perspiration resembling pearls — that too is quite manifest. Or for example —
'Sport with him on the shores of the ocean, in the rustling palm groves,
with the breezes that have dispelled the drops of perspiration, bearing clove-blossoms brought from other islands.' // VjivC_1.83 //
An example of ornamentation [combined with <s>prasāda</s>] —
'Crescent-moon-curved' and so forth. // VjivC_1.84 //
Having thus described <s>prasāda</s>, he defines <s>lāvaṇya</s> (gracefulness) —
Through a small [measure of] the charm of phonemic arrangement and the excellence of word-conjunction,
the beauty of composition — that is called <s>lāvaṇya</s> (gracefulness). // Vjiv_1.32 //

children.text:
bandho vākyavinyāsastasya saundaryaṃ rāmaṇīyakaṃ lāvaṇyamabhidhīyate lāvaṇyamityucyate /
kīdṛśam---varṇānāmakṣarāṇāṃ vinyāso vicitraṃ nyasanaṃ tasya vicchittiḥ śobhā vaidagdhyabhaṅgī tayā lakṣitaṃ padānāṃ suptiṅantānāṃ saṃdhānaṃ saṃyojanaṃ tasya sampat, sāpi śobhaiva, tayā lakṣitam /
kīdṛśyā---ubhayarūpayāpi svalpayā manāṅmātrayā nātinirbandhanirmitayā /
tadayamatrārthaḥ---śabdārthasaukumāryasubhagaḥ saṃniveśamahimā lāvaṇyarūpo guṇaḥ kathyate /
yathā
children.translated_text: 'Composition' (<s>bandha</s>) is the arrangement of sentences; its 'beauty' is its loveliness — that is called <s>lāvaṇya</s>. Of what kind? — the arrangement of phonemes, i.e., syllables, is their varied placement; its charm is its beauty, its mode of deftness; characterized by that — and the conjunction of words, both nominal and verbal, their joining together; its excellence, which is also beauty — characterized by that. Of what sort? — 'small,' i.e., slight, not produced by excessive insistence — in both forms. The meaning then is: the quality called <s>lāvaṇya</s>, in the form of the grandeur of arrangement, charming with the delicacy of sound and meaning, is being described. For example —
'In tresses released moist from bathing, receiving the fragrance of after-incense, into which evening jasmine blossoms have been woven,

children.text: kāmo vasantātyayamandavīryaḥ keśeṣu lebhe balamaṅganānām // VjivC_1.85 //
children.translated_text: <s>Kāma</s> (the god of love), whose power was languid after the passing of spring, gained strength in the hair of women.' // VjivC_1.85 //

children.text:
atra saṃniveśasaundaryamahimā sahṛdayasaṃvedyo na vyapadeṣṭuṃ pāryate /
yathā vā
children.translated_text: Here, the grandeur of the beauty of arrangement, perceptible to the sensitive, cannot be put into words. Or for example —
'[He] made with arrows the cheek-surfaces of the <s>asura</s> women bereft of their ornamental leaf-patterns, like those whose husbands have departed.' // VjivC_1.86 //

children.text:
atrāpi varṇavinyāsavicchittiḥ padasaṃdhānasampacca saṃniveśasaundaryanibandhanā sphuṭāvabhāsaiva /
evaṃ lāvaṇyamabhidhāya ābhijātyamabhidhatte---
children.translated_text: Here too, the charm of phonemic arrangement and the excellence of word-conjunction, both founded on the beauty of arrangement, are quite manifest. Having thus described <s>lāvaṇya</s>, he states <s>ābhijātya</s> (nobility) —
Endowed with the delicacy of what is pleasing to the ear, as if softly touchable by the mind,
naturally smooth in lustre — that they call <s>ābhijātya</s> (nobility). // Vjiv_1.33 //

children.text:
evaṃ vidhaṃ vastu ābhijātyaṃ pracakṣate ābhijātyābhidhānaṃ guṇaṃ varṇayanti /
śrutiḥ śravaṇendriyaṃ tatra peśalatā rāmaṇīyakaṃ tena śālate ślāghate yattathoktam /
suraparśamiva cetasā manasā susparśamiva /
sukhena spṛśyata ivetyatiśayoktiriyam /
yasmādubhayamapi sparśayogyatve sati saukumāryāt kimapi cetasi sparśasukhamarpayatīva /
yataḥ svabhāvamasṛṇacchāyam ahāryaślakṣṇakānti yattad ābhijātyaṃ kathayantītyarthaḥ /
yathā
children.translated_text: Such a thing they call <s>ābhijātya</s> — they describe the quality designated by the name 'nobility.' The ear (<s>śruti</s>) is the organ of hearing; delicacy therein is its beauty; 'endowed with that' means distinguished by that. 'As if softly touchable by the mind (<s>cetasā</s>)' — as if touchable softly, i.e., pleasantly — this is hyperbole. Because both [word and meaning], being eligible for touch owing to their delicacy, seem to impart some pleasure of touch to the mind. Because: 'naturally smooth in lustre' — with a non-artificial, sleek radiance — what possesses that, that they call <s>ābhijātya</s>, this is the meaning. For example —

children.text: jyotirlekhāvalayi galitaṃ yasya barhaṃ bhavānī putraprītyā kuvalayadalaprāpi karṇe karoti // VjivC_1.87 //
children.translated_text: 'The peacock feather, encircled by a ring of light-streaks, which has fallen — <s>Bhavānī</s>, out of love for her son, places it on her ear, resembling a blue-lotus petal.' // VjivC_1.87 //

children.text:
atra śrutipeśalatādi svabhāvamasṛṇacchāyatvaṃ kimapi sahṛdayasaṃvedyaṃ parisphurati /
nanu ca lāvaṇyamābhijātyaṃ ca lokottarataruṇīrūpalakṣaṇavastudharmatayā yat prasiddhaṃ tat kathaṃ kāvyasya bhavitumarhatīti cettanna /
yasmādanena nyāyena pūrvaprasiddhayorapi mādhuryaprasādayoḥ kāvyadharmatvaṃ vighaṭate /
mādhuryaṃ hi guḍādimadhuradravyadharmatayā prasiddhaṃ tathāvidhāhlādakāritvasāmānyopacārāt kāvye vyapadiśyate /
tathaiva ca prasādaḥ svacchasalilasphaṭikādidharmatayā prasiddhaḥ sphuṭāvabhāsitvasāmānyopacārāj jhagitipratītikāriṇi kāvye pravartitavyahārastadevaṃvidhavaidagdhyavihitavicitravinyāsaramaṇīrāmaṇīyakaṃ yathā lāvaṇyaśabdābhidheyatayā pratītipeśalatāṃpratipadyate /
tadvadeva ca kāvye kaviśaktikauśalollikhitakāntikamanīyaṃ bandhasaundaryaṃ cetanacamatkārakāritvasāmānyopacārāllavaṇyaśabdavyatirekeṇa śabdāntarābhidheyatāṃ notsahate /
tathaiva ca kāvye svabhāvamasṛṇacchāyatvamābhijātyaśabdenābhidhīyate /
nanu ca kaiścitpratīyamānaṃ vastu lalanālāvaṇyasāmyāllāvaṇyamityutpāditapratīti---
children.translated_text: Here, the delicacy of what is pleasing to the ear and the rest, the natural smoothness of lustre — some quality perceptible to the sensitive shines forth. Now, <s>lāvaṇya</s> and <s>ābhijātya</s> are well-known as properties of the form of an extraordinary young woman — how can they be properties of poetry? To this [objection] — no, that is not so. Because by this same reasoning, the poeticness of <s>mādhurya</s> (sweetness) and <s>prasāda</s> (clarity), which were also previously established, would also be undermined. For <s>mādhurya</s> is well-known as a property of sweet substances like molasses; through figurative usage based on the commonality of producing similar delight, it is applied to poetry. Likewise, <s>prasāda</s> is well-known as a property of clear water, crystal, and the like; through figurative usage based on the commonality of manifest appearance, it comes to be used of poetry that produces immediate comprehension. In exactly the same way, the beauty of arrangement — charming with the loveliness of a varied configuration fashioned by such deftness — just as it attains a delicacy of comprehension by being the referent of the word <s>lāvaṇya</s>. And likewise in poetry, the beauty of composition that is charming, with radiance inscribed by the skill of the poet's power, does not consent to being designated by any word other than <s>lāvaṇya</s>, through figurative usage based on the commonality of producing wonder in the sentient. And likewise, the natural smoothness of lustre in poetry is designated by the word <s>ābhijātya</s>. Now, some have, on the basis of the similarity with the <s>lāvaṇya</s> of women, produced the notion that the thing perceived is called <s>lāvaṇya</s> —
'There is indeed some other thing perceived in the speech of great poets,
which, being beyond the well-known constituent parts, shines forth like the <s>lāvaṇya</s> (grace) of women.' // VjivC_1.88 //

children.text:
tatkathaṃ bandhasaundaryamātraṃ lāvaṇyamityabhidhīyate ? naiṣa doṣaḥ, yasmādanena dṛṣṭāntena vācyavācakalakṣaṇaprasiddhāvayavavyatiriktatvenāstitvamātraṃ sādhyate pratīyamānasya, na punaḥ sakalalokalocanasavedyasya lalanālāvaṇyasya /
sahṛdayahṛdayānāmeva saṃvedyaṃ sat pratīyamānaṃ samīkartuṃ pāryate /
tasya bandhasaundaryamevāvyutpannapadapadārthānāmapi śravaṇamātreṇaiva hṛdayahāritvaspardhayā vyapadiśyate /
pratīyamānaṃ punaḥ kāvyaparamārthajñānāmevānubhavagocaratāṃ pratipadyate /
yathā kāminīnāṃ kimapi saubhāgyaṃ tadupabhogocitānāṃ nāyakānāmeva saṃvedyatāmarhati, lāvaṇyaṃ punastāsāmeva satkavigirāmiva saundaryaṃ sakalalokagocaratāmāyātītyuktamevetyalamatiprasaṅgena /
evaṃ sukumārasya lakṣaṇamabhidhāya vicitraṃ pratipādayati---
children.translated_text:
Then how can mere beauty of composition be called <s>lāvaṇya</s> (charm/grace)? This is not a defect, because by this illustration only the mere existence of the <s>pratīyamāna</s> (suggested meaning) is established as being distinct from the well-known components characterized by <s>vācya</s> (expressed meaning) and <s>vācaka</s> (expressive word), not that [the suggested meaning is identical to] the charm of a woman which is perceptible to the eyes of the entire world.
Being perceptible only to the hearts of <s>sahṛdayas</s> (connoisseurs), the <s>pratīyamāna</s> (suggested meaning) can be compared [to charm]. Its beauty of composition is designated [as charm] because of its power to captivate the heart even of those unlearned in words and their meanings, merely upon hearing, as if competing [with feminine charm].
The <s>pratīyamāna</s> (suggested meaning), however, comes within the range of experience only of those who know the ultimate truth of poetry.
Just as the ineffable <s>saubhāgya</s> (good fortune/attractiveness) of beautiful women is worthy of being perceived only by the heroes suited to enjoy them, while their <s>lāvaṇya</s> (charm), like the beauty of the speech of good poets, comes within the perception of the entire world — thus it has already been stated. Enough of this digression.
Having thus described the characteristics of the <s>sukumāra</s> (delicate) type, he now explains the <s>vicitra</s> (variegated) type —
Where, at the moment of the first emergence of <s>pratibhā</s> (creative intuition), the obliqueness
within word and meaning is perceived as if flashing forth — Vjiv_1.34
Where poets, unsatisfied with one <s>alaṅkāra</s> (ornament),
compose yet another ornamentation upon the ornament, like setting gems upon a necklace — Vjiv_1.35
Just as a beloved's body, covered over by ornaments
resplendent with the effulgence of rays of jewels, is adorned for the sake of beauty — Vjiv_1.36
where, in the same manner, by ornaments shining in their own nature,
the <s>alaṅkārya</s> (that which is to be ornamented) is revealed as contained within the surpassing splendor of its own beauty — Vjiv_1.37
Where even a subject matter that has been depicted without novelty is, by the mere
variegation of expression, brought to some extraordinary pinnacle — Vjiv_1.38
Where everything that was one way becomes entirely otherwise, as one pleases,
by the greatness of the creative intuition's delineation of the great poet — Vjiv_1.39
Where the suggestedness of the sentence-meaning is composed
as something distinct from the functions of <s>vācya</s> (expressed) and <s>vācaka</s> (expressive word) — Vjiv_1.40
Where the nature of emotions, full of charming intent, is bound
enriched by some ineffable and beautiful variegation — Vjiv_1.41
The <s>vicitra</s> (variegated) — where the variegation of <s>vakrokti</s> (oblique expression) becomes the life-force,
and within which shines forth a certain indescribable surpassing expression — that is it. Vjiv_1.42
That path, most difficult to traverse, by which accomplished poets have gone,
is like the path along a sword's edge for the aspirations of great warriors — Vjiv_1.43

children.text:
sa vicitrābhidhānaḥ panthāḥ kīdṛśaḥ---atiduḥsaṃcaraḥ, yatrātiduḥkhena saṃcarante /
kiṃ bahunā, yena vidagdhakavayaḥ kecideva vyutpannāḥ kevalaṃ gatāḥ prayātāḥ, tadāśrayeṇa kāvyāni cakrurityarthaḥ /
katham---kaṅgadhārāpatheneva subhaṭānāṃ manorathāḥ /
nistraiṃśadhārāmārgeṇa yathā subhaṭānāṃmahāvīrāṇāṃ manorathāḥ /
nistriṃśadhārāmārgeṇa yathā subhaṭānāṃ mahāvīrāṇāṃ manorathāḥ saṃkalpaviśeṣāḥ /
tadayamatrābhiprāyaḥ---yadasidhārāmārgagamane manorathānāmaucityānusāreṇa yathāruci pravartamānānāṃ manāṅmātramapi mlānatā na saṃbhāvyate /
sākṣātsamarasaṃmardana samācaraṇe punaḥ kadācit kimapi mlānatvamapi saṃbhāvyeta /
tadanena mārgasya durgamatvaṃ tatprasthitānāṃ ca viharaṇaprauḍhiḥ pratipādyate /
kīdṛśaḥ sā mārgaḥ---yatra yasmin śabdābhidheyayorabhidhānābhidhīyamānayorantaḥ svarūpānupraveśinī vakratā bhaṇitivicchittiḥ sphuratīva praspandamāneva vibhāvyate lakṣyate /
kadā---pratibhāprathamodbhedasamaye /
pratibhāyāḥ kaviśakteracaramollekhāvasare /
tadayamatra paramārthaḥ---yat kaviprayatnanirapekṣayoreva śabdārthayoḥ svābhāvikaḥ ko 'pi vakratāprakāraḥ parisphuran paridṛśyate /
yathā
children.translated_text:
That path called <s>vicitra</s> (variegated) — what is it like? It is <s>atiduḥsaṃcara</s> (most difficult to traverse), where one proceeds only with the greatest difficulty.
In short, only certain accomplished poets, those who are learned, have merely gone along it — meaning they have composed poetry taking recourse to it.
How? — "Like the aspirations of great warriors along the path of a sword's edge." Just as the aspirations — the particular resolves — of <s>subhaṭas</s> (great warriors), the mighty heroes, [proceed] along the path of a sword's edge.
Here the intended meaning is this: in traversing the path of a sword's edge, not even the slightest wilting can be imagined in the aspirations that proceed as they please, following the course of propriety. In actual engagement in the crush of battle, however, some wilting might occasionally be possible.
Thus by this, the difficulty of traversing the path and the boldness of movement of those who have set out upon it are both established.
What kind of path is it? — Where, within word and meaning — that is, within expression and what is expressed — an obliqueness, a charm of utterance, entering into their very essence, is perceived as if flashing forth, as if vibrating.
When? — At the moment of the first emergence of <s>pratibhā</s> (creative intuition), at the occasion of the ultimate delineation of the poet's creative power.
Here the ultimate truth is this: that some natural mode of obliqueness, independent of the poet's deliberate effort, is seen shining forth and manifest in both word and meaning.
For example —

children.text: ko 'yaṃ bhāti prakārastava pavana padaṃ lokapādāhatīnāṃ tejasvivrātasevye nabhasi nayasi yatpāṃsupūraṃ pratiṣṭhām /
children.translated_text: "What is this manner of yours, O wind? You carry loads of dust to an established place in the sky — that gathering-place of the luminous, that path trodden by the feet of the world's people —

children.text: yasminnutthāpyamāne jananayanapathopadravastāvadāstāṃ kenāpāyena sahyo vapuṣi kaluṣatādoṣa eva tvayaiva // VjivC_1.89 //
children.translated_text: When you raise it up, let the affliction to the path of people's eyes be set aside for now; by what means is the defect of turbidity in your own body tolerable, [caused] by none other than yourself?" VjivC_1.89

children.text:
atrāprastutapraśaṃsālakṣaṇo 'laṅkāraḥ prādhānyena vākyārthaḥ, pratīyamānapadārthāntaratvena prayuktatvāt tatra ca vicitrakaviśaktisamullikhitavakraśabdārthopanibandhamāhātmyāt pratīyamānamapyabhidheyatāmiva prāpitam /
prakrama eva pratibhāsamānatvānna cārthāntarapratītikāritvena padānāṃ śleṣavyapadeśaḥ śakyate kartum, vācyasya samapradhānabhāvenānavasthānāt /
arthāntarapratītikāritvaṃ ca padānāṃ pratīyamānārthasphuṭatāva bhāsanārthamupanibadhyamānamatīva camatkārakāritāṃ pratipadyate /
tameva vicitraṃ prakārāntareṇa lakṣayati---alaṅkārasyetyādi /
yatra yasminmārge kavayo nibadhnanti viracayanti, alaṅkārasya vibhūṣaṇasyālaṅkāraṇāntaraṃ bhūṣaṇāntaram asaṃtuṣṭāḥ santaḥ /
katham---hārādermaṇibandhavat /
muktākalāpaprabhṛteryathā padakādimaṇibandhaṃ ratnaviśeṣavinyāsaṃ vaikaṭikāḥ /
yathā
children.translated_text:
Here the <s>alaṅkāra</s> (figure) characterized as <s>aprastutapraśaṃsā</s> (praise of the irrelevant) is principally the sentence-meaning, because it is employed with a suggested secondary subject matter; and there, due to the greatness of the composition of oblique word and meaning delineated by the <s>vicitra</s> (variegated) poetic power, even the <s>pratīyamāna</s> (suggested meaning) has been brought to the status of the expressed, as it were.
Since it appears as such from the very outset, the words cannot be designated as <s>śleṣa</s> (double entendre) on account of conveying an alternative meaning, because the expressed meaning does not remain in equal prominence.
And the capacity of words to convey an alternative meaning, being employed for the purpose of making the suggested meaning vivid, attains an exceedingly high degree of <s>camatkāra</s> (aesthetic wonder).
He characterizes the same <s>vicitra</s> (variegated) type in another manner — "<s>alaṅkārasya</s>" and so forth. Where, on which path, poets compose — that is, fashion — yet another ornamentation upon an ornament, being unsatisfied.
How? — "Like the setting of gems upon a necklace and so on." Just as craftsmen [set] a particular arrangement of special gems — such as the <s>padaka</s> ornament — upon a string of pearls and the like.
For example —

children.text: he helājitabodhisattva vacasāṃ kiṃ vistaraistoyadhe nāsti tvatsadṛśaḥ paraḥ parahitādhāne gṛhītavrataḥ /
children.translated_text: "O cloud, you who effortlessly surpass a <s>Bodhisattva</s> — what need of elaborate words? There is no other like you who has taken a vow for the welfare of others.

children.text: tṛṣyatpānthajanopakāraghaṭanāvaimukhyalabdhāyaśo bhāraprodvahane karoṣi kṛpayā sāhāyyakaṃ yanmaroḥ // VjivC_1.90 //
children.translated_text: You who have gained ill-repute through your aversion to helping thirsty travelers on the road — out of compassion, you render assistance to <s>Maru</s> (the desert/the wind-god) in bearing his burden!" VjivC_1.90

children.text:
atrātyantagarhaṇīyacaritaṃ padārthāntaraṃ pratīyamānatayā cetasi nidhāya tathāvidhavilasitaḥ salilanidhirvācyatayopakrāntaḥ /
tadetāvadevālaṅkṛteraprastutapraśaṃsāyāḥ svarūpam---garhaṇīyapratīyamānapadārthāntaraparyavasānamapi vākyaṃ śrutyupakramaramaṇīyatayopanibadhyamānaṃ tadvidāhlādakāritāmāyāti /
tadetad vyājastutipratirūpakaprāyamalaṅkaraṇāntaramaprastutapraśaṃsāyā bhūṣaṇatvenopāttam /
na cātra saṃkarālaṅkāravyavahāro bhavitumarhati, pṛthagatiparisphuṭatvenāvabhāsanāt /
na cāpi saṃsṛṣṭisaṃbhavaḥ samapradhānabhāvenānavasthiteḥ /
na ca dvayorapi vācyālaṅkāratvam, vibhinnaviṣayatvāt /
yathā vā
children.translated_text:
Here, keeping in mind the suggested secondary subject matter whose conduct is utterly reprehensible, the ocean is taken up as the expressed subject, one whose play is of that very kind.
This alone, then, is the nature of the ornament of <s>aprastutapraśaṃsā</s> (praise of the irrelevant) — that even a statement culminating in a suggested secondary meaning that is reprehensible, when composed so as to be charming to hear from the very beginning, brings delight to the discerning.
This secondary ornamentation, resembling <s>vyājastuti</s> (ironic praise) and <s>pratirūpaka</s> (counter-metaphor), has been adopted as an embellishment of <s>aprastutapraśaṃsā</s>.
Nor can the designation of <s>saṃkara</s> (confusion of figures) apply here, since each appears separately and distinctly.
Nor is <s>saṃsṛṣṭi</s> (combination of figures) possible, since they do not remain in equal prominence.
Nor are both expressed ornaments, since they have different domains.
Or, for example —

children.text: nāmāpyanyatarornimīlitamabhūttattāvadunmīlitaṃ prasthāne skhalataḥ svartmani vidheranyad gṛhītaḥ karaḥ /
children.translated_text: "Even one eye of the other one was closed; that much then was opened. When he stumbles on his own path, Fate seizes his hand, providing another.

children.text: lokaścāyamadṛṣṭadarśanakṛtā dṛgvaiśasāduddhṛto yuktaṃ kāṣṭhika lūnavān yadasi tāmāmrālimākālikīm // VjivC_1.91 //
children.translated_text: And this world has been rescued from the cruelty to the eyes caused by seeing the unseen — it is fitting, O woodcutter, that you cut down that mango grove — the <s>Ākālikī</s>." VjivC_1.91

Here the same principle should be understood.
And for example —

children.text: kiṃ tāruṇyataroriyaṃ rasabharodbhinnā navā mañjarī līlāprocchalitasya kiṃ laharikā lāvaṇyavārāṃnidheḥ /
children.translated_text: "Is this a fresh cluster of blossoms bursting forth from the tree of youth, heavy with <s>rasa</s> (aesthetic juice/sap)? Or is this a wave of the ocean of <s>lāvaṇya</s> (grace), playfully surging?

children.text: udgāḍhotkalikāvatāṃ svasamayopanyāsaviśrambhiṇaḥ kiṃ sākṣādupadeśayaṣṭirathavā devasya śṛṅgāriṇaḥ // VjivC_1.92 //
children.translated_text: Or is this the very teaching-staff of the god <s>Śṛṅgārin</s> (the amorous one / the god of love), who displays his own season with confidence, replete with fully blossomed buds?" VjivC_1.92

children.text:
atra rūpakalakṣaṇo yo 'yaṃ kāvyālaṅkāraḥ tasya sandehoktiriyaṃ chāyāntarātiśayotpadānāyopanibaddhā cetanacamatkārakāritā māvahita /
śiṣṭaṃ pūrvodāharaṇadvayoktamanusartavyam /
anyacca kīdṛk---ratnetyādi /
yugalakam /
yatra yasminnalaṅkārairbhrājamānairnijātmanā svajīvitena bhāsamānairbhūṣāyai parikalpyate śobhāyai bhūṣyate /
katham---yathā bhūṣaṇaiḥ, kaṅkaṇādibhiḥ /
kīdṛśaiḥ---ratnaraśmicchaṭotsekabhāsuraiḥ maṇimayūkhollāsabhrājiṣṇubhiḥ /
kiṃ kṛtvā---kāntāśarīramācchādya kāminīvapuḥ svaprabhāprasaratirohitaṃ vidhāya /
bhūṣāyai kalpanam---yadetaiḥ svaśobhātiśayāntaḥ sthaṃ nijakāntikamanīyāntargatamalaṅkāryamalaṅkāraṇīyaṃ prakāśyate dyotyate /
tadidamatra tātparyam---tadalaṅkāramahimaiva tathāvidho 'tra bhrājate tasyātyantodriktavṛtteḥ svaśobhātiśayāntargatamalaṅkāryaṃ prakāśyate /
yathā
children.translated_text:
Here, this expression of doubt — which is the poetic figure characterized as <s>rūpaka</s> (metaphor) — has been composed for the purpose of generating a surpassing splendor of suggestive overtones, so that it may produce <s>camatkāra</s> (aesthetic wonder) in the conscious mind.
The rest should be understood as stated in the two preceding illustrations.
Further, what else [characterizes the <s>vicitra</s>]? — "<s>ratna</s>" and so forth. This is a pair of verses.
Where, by ornaments shining in their own nature — appearing resplendent through their own life — it is adorned for the sake of beauty, that is, beautified for splendor.
How? — Just as by ornaments, such as bracelets and the like.
Of what kind? — Resplendent with the effulgence of rays of jewels — shining with the radiance of gem-luster.
Having done what? — Having covered the body of the beloved — having made the woman's body hidden by the spread of their own radiance.
The adornment for beauty means: that by these [ornaments], the <s>alaṅkārya</s> (that which is to be ornamented), contained within the surpassing splendor of its own beauty, having an interior made beautiful by its own radiance, is revealed — that is, illuminated.
Here the purport is this: the very greatness of those ornaments shines forth in such a manner, and because of their exceedingly exuberant functioning, the <s>alaṅkārya</s>, contained within the surpassing splendor of its own beauty, is revealed.
For example —

children.text: āryasyājimahotsavavyatikare nāsaṃvibhakto 'tra vaḥ kaścit kāpyavaśiṣyate tyajata re naktañcarāḥ saṃbhramam /
children.translated_text: "In the great festival that is the master's battle, no one among you remains unshared — abandon, O night-roaming demons, your agitation!

children.text: bhūyiṣṭheṣvapi kā bhavatsu gaṇanātyarthaṃ kimuttāmyate tasyodārabhujoṣmaṇo 'navasitā nārāca saṃpattayaḥ // VjivC_1.93 //
children.translated_text: Even if you are numerous, what does counting matter? Why do you exert yourselves in vain? The wealth of arrows from his mighty arm's valor is inexhaustible!" VjivC_1.93

children.text:
atrājermahotsavavyatikaratvena tathāvidhaṃ rūpaṇaṃ vihitaṃ yatrālaṅkāryam "āryaḥ svaśauryeṇa yuṣmān sarvāneva mārayati" ityalaṅkāraśobhātiśayāntargatatvena bhrājate /
tathā ca kaścit sāmānyo 'pi kvāpi davīyasyapi deśe nāsaṃvibhakto yuṣmākamavaśiṣyate /
tasmāt samaramahotsavasavibhāgalampaṭatayā pratyekaṃ yūyaṃ saṃbhramaṃ tyajata /
gaṇanayā vayaṃ bhūyiṣṭhā ityaśakyānuṣṭhānatāṃ yadi manyadhve tadapyayuktam /
yasmādasaṃkhyasaṃvibhāgāśakyatā kadācidasaṃpattyā kārpaṇyena vā saṃbhāvyate /
tadetadubhayamapi nāstītyuktam---tasyodārabhujoṣmaṇo 'navasitā nārāca saṃpattayaḥ (iti) /
yathā ca
children.translated_text:
Here, by the depiction of the battle as a great festival, such a <s>rūpaṇa</s> (metaphorical portrayal) has been fashioned wherein the <s>alaṅkārya</s> (the thing to be ornamented) — namely, "the master slays all of you by his own valor" — shines forth as contained within the surpassing beauty of the ornament.
And thus not a single ordinary one, even in the most distant region, remains without receiving his share among you.
Therefore, being eager for the distribution of shares in the great festival of battle, each of you — abandon your agitation!
If you think, "We are numerous by count, so it cannot be accomplished" — that too is wrong.
For the impossibility of distributing among innumerable [foes] might be imagined either through lack of capacity or through poverty.
That both of these are absent has been stated: "The wealth of arrows from his mighty arm's valor is inexhaustible."
And for example —

children.text: katamaḥ pravijṛmbhitavirahavyathaḥ śanyatāṃ nīto deśaḥ // VjivC_1.94 //
children.translated_text: "Which region has been emptied, with the anguish of separation fully manifested?" VjivC_1.94
Thus.

children.text: yathā ca kāni ca puṇyabhāñji bhajantyabhikhyāmakṣarāṇi // VjivC_1.95 //
children.translated_text: "And what meritorious syllables attain fame?" VjivC_1.95
Thus.

children.text:
atra kasmādāgatāḥ stha, kiṃ cāsya nāma ityalaṅkāryamaprasutapraśaṃsālakṣaṇālaṅkāracchāyācchuritatvenaitadīyaśobhāntargatatvena sahṛdayahṛdayāhlādakāritāṃ prāpitam /
etaccavyājastutiparyāyoktaprabhṛtīnāṃ bhūyasā vibhāvyate /
nanu ca rūpakādīnāṃ svalakṣaṇāvasara eva svarūpaṃ nirṇeṣyate tat kiṃ prayojanameteṣāmihodāharaṇasya ? satyametat, kintvetadeva vicitrasya vaicitryaṃ nāma yadalaukikacchāyātiśayayogitvena bhūṣaṇopanibandhaḥ kāmapi vākyavakratāmunmīlayati /
vicitrameva rūpāntareṇa lakṣaṇayati---yadapītyādi /
yadapi vastu vācyamanūtanollekhamanabhinavatvenollikhitaṃ tadapi yatra yasminnalaṃ kāmapi kāṣṭhāṃ nīyate lokottarātiśayakoṭimadhiroṣyate /
katham---uktivaicitryamātreṇa, bhaṇitivaidagdhyenaivetyarthaḥ /
yathā
children.translated_text:
Here, the <s>alaṅkārya</s> (that which is to be ornamented) — namely "From where have you come?" and "What is his name?" — has been brought to produce delight in the hearts of <s>sahṛdayas</s> (connoisseurs) by being tinged with the suggestive shade of the ornament characterized as <s>aprastutapraśaṃsā</s> (praise of the irrelevant), its beauty being contained within that [ornament's beauty].
This is extensively observed in <s>vyājastuti</s> (ironic praise), <s>paryāyokta</s> (circumlocution), and other such figures.
Now, since the essential nature of <s>rūpaka</s> (metaphor) and other figures will be determined at the proper occasion of their own definitions, what is the purpose of illustrating them here? True, but the very distinctiveness of the <s>vicitra</s> (variegated) type is this: that the composition of an ornament, being endowed with a surpassing tinge of extraordinary suggestive overtones, reveals some ineffable obliqueness of the sentence.
He characterizes the <s>vicitra</s> itself in yet another form — "<s>yadapi</s>" and so forth.
Even a subject matter that has been depicted without novelty — delineated as not new — that too, where it is brought to some extraordinary pinnacle — that is, it ascends the summit of a transcendent excellence.
How? — By the mere variegation of expression; the meaning is: by the skillfulness of utterance alone.
For example —

children.text: aṇṇaṃ laḍahattaṇaaṃ aṇṇa ccia kāvi vattaṇacchāā /
children.translated_text: [Prakrit:] The mischievousness is one thing, and the manner of conduct is yet another;

children.text: sāmā sāmaṇṇāpaāvaiṇo reha ccia ṇa hoi // VjivC_1.96 //
children.translated_text: [Prakrit:] O dark-complexioned one, of the lord of common folk, the line itself does not exist. VjivC_1.96
[Sanskrit <s>chāyā</s> (translation):] The mischievousness is one thing, and a certain manner of conduct is yet another;

children.text: śyāmā sāmānyaprajāpate rekhaiva ca na bhavati //
children.translated_text: O <s>Śyāmā</s> (dark-complexioned one), of the lord of common people, even the line does not exist.
Thus the <s>chāyā</s> (Sanskrit rendering of the Prakrit verse).

children.text: yathā vā uddeśo 'yaṃ saṃrasaviṭapi śreṇiśobhātiśāyī kuñjotkarṣāṅkuritahariṇīvibhramo narmadāyāḥ /
children.translated_text: Or, for example: "This is the region of the <s>Narmadā</s>, surpassing the beauty of rows of trees full of ripe fruits, with the playful wandering of deer generated by the excellence of its bowers —"

children.text: kiṃ caitasmin suratasuhṛdastanvi te vānti vātā yeṣāmagre sarati kalitākāṇḍakopo manobhūḥ // VjivC_1.97 //
children.translated_text: Moreover, in this [separation], O slender one, the winds that blow — those friends of love-making — before which the love-god rushes with sudden, unprovoked anger — // <s>Vjīv</s>C 1.97 //

children.text:
bhaṇitivaicitryamātramevātra kāvyārthaḥ, na tu nūtanollekhaśāli vācyavijṛmbhitam /
etacca bhaṇitivaicitryaṃ sahastraprakāraṃ saṃbhavatīti svayamevotprekṣaṇīyam /
punarvicitrameva prakārāntareṇa lakṣayati---yatrānyathetyādi /
yatra yasminnanyathābhavadanyena prakāreṇa sat sarvameva padārthajātam anyathaiva prakārāntareṇaiva bhāvyate /
katham---yathāruci /
svapratibhāsānurūpeṇotpādyate /
kena---pratibhollekhamahattvena mahākaveḥ, pratibhāsonmeṣā tiśayatvena satkaveḥ /
yatkila varṇyamānasya vastunaḥ prastāvamucitaṃ kimapi sahṛdayahṛdayahāri rūpāntaraṃ nirmimīte kaviḥ /
yathā
children.translated_text: Here the poetic import is merely the variety of expression (<s>bhaṇitivaicitrya</s>), not a novel flourish of expressed content. And this variety of expression, being possible in a thousand forms, should be imagined by oneself. [The author] now characterizes yet another type of variety in a different manner — 'yatrānyathā' and so on. Where — in which — the entire class of objects, being otherwise, having existed in one form, is to be conceived otherwise, in another form entirely. How? — As one pleases, produced in accordance with one's own creative vision. By whom? — By a great poet, through the greatness of creative inspiration's impulse; by a good poet, through the excellence of the flowering of creative inspiration. For indeed, the poet creates a certain form, different from the subject being described, suitable to the occasion and captivating to the hearts of connoisseurs. For example —

children.text: tāpaḥ svātmani saṃśritadrumalatāśoṣo 'dhyavagairvarjanaṃ sakhyaṃ duḥśamayā tṛṣā tava maro ko 'sāvanartho na yaḥ /
children.translated_text: Heat belongs to yourself; the drying of trees and creepers that have taken refuge [in you] is the travelers' avoidance; friendship with the unquenchable thirst is yours, O desert — what calamity is not associated with you?

children.text: ekor'thastu mahānayaṃ jalalavasvāmyasmayodgarjinaḥ saṃnahyanti na yattavopakṛtaye dhārādharāḥ prākṛtāḥ // VjivC_1.98 //
children.translated_text: But this one thing is great — that the ordinary rain-clouds, thundering with the pride of their sovereignty over drops of water, do not gird themselves for your assistance. // <s>Vjīv</s>C 1.98 //
Or as —

children.text: viśati yadi no kañcitkālaṃ kilāmbunidhaṃ vidheḥ kṛtiṣu sakalāsveko loke prakāśakatāṃ gataḥ /
children.translated_text: If the Sun, who alone in the world has attained the capacity to illuminate, among all the creations of <s>Vidhātṛ</s> (the Creator), does not enter the ocean for some time,

children.text: kathamitarathā dhāmnāṃ dhātā tamāṃsi niśākaraṃ sphuradidamiyattārācakraṃ prakāśayati sphuṭam // VjivC_1.99 //
children.translated_text: then how otherwise does the Bestower of Light clearly illuminate the darkness, the moon, and this twinkling multitude of stars? // <s>Vjīv</s>C 1.99 //

children.text:
atra jagadgarhitasyāpi maroḥ kavipratibhollikhitena lokottaraudāryadhurādhiropaṇena tādṛk svarūpāntaramunmīlitaṃ yatpratīyamānatvenodāracaritasya kasyāpi satsvapyucitaparispandasundareṣu padārthasahastreṣu tadeva vyapadeśapātratāmarhatīti tātparyam /
avayavārthastu---duḥśamayet "tṛḍ'viśeṣaṇena pratīyamānasya trailokyarājyenāpyaparitoṣaḥ paryavasyati /
adhvagairvarjanamityaudārye 'pi tasya samucitasaṃvibhāgāsaṃbhavādarthibhirlajjamānairapi svayamevānabhisaraṇaṃ pratīyate /
saṃśritadrumalatāśoṣa iti tadāśritānāṃ tathāvidhe 'pi saṅkaṭe tadekaniṣṭhatāpratipattiḥ /
tasya ca pūrvoktasvaparikaraparipo ṣākṣamatayā tāpaḥ svātmani na bhogalavalaulyeneti pratipādyate /
uttarārdhena---tādṛśe durvilasite 'pi paropakārāviṣayatvena ślāghāspadatvamunmīlitam /
aparatrāpi vidhivihitasamucitasamayasaṃbhavaṃ salilanidhinimajjanaṃ nijodayanyakkṛtanikhilasvaparapakṣaḥ prajāpatipraṇītasakalapadārthaprakāśanavratābhyupagamanirvahaṇāya vivasvāna svayameva samācaratītyanyathā kadācidapi śaśāṅkatamastārāprabhṛtī nāmabhivyaktirmanāgapi na saṃbhavatīti kavinā nūtanatvena yadullikhitaṃ tadatīva pratīyamānamahattvavyaktiparatvena camatkāritāmāpadyate /
vicitrameva prakārāntareṇonmīlayāta---pratīyamānatetyādi /
yatra yasmin pratīyamānatā gamyamānatā vākyārthasya mukhyatayā vivakṣitasya vastunaḥ kasyacidanākhyeyasya nibadhyate /
kayā yuktyā---vācyavācakavṛttibhyāṃ śabdārthaśaktibhyām /
vyatiriktasya tadatiriktavṛtteranyasya vyaṅgyabhūtasyābhivyaktiḥ kriyate /
"vṛtti'--śabdo 'tra śabdārthayostatprakāśanasāmarthyamabhidhatte /
eṣa ca "pratīyamāna'--vyavahāro vākyavakratāvyākhyāvasare sutarāṃ samunmīlyate /
anantaroktamudāharaṇadvayamatra yojanīyam /
yathā vā
children.translated_text: Here, even though the desert is universally condemned, through the poet's creative delineation, an extraordinary magnanimity is superimposed upon it, thereby unveiling a transformed nature such that — since it is perceived [in this new light] — even though there are thousands of objects with appropriate and beautiful functions belonging to one of noble conduct, that [desert] alone deserves to be the recipient of the designation. This is the purport. As for the component meanings — 'duḥśamayā tṛṣā' (unquenchable thirst): the qualifier conveys through suggestion an insatiability that cannot be appeased even by the sovereignty of the three worlds. 'Adhvagairvarjanam' (avoidance by travelers): despite its generosity, since equitable distribution [of its resources] is impossible, it is suggested that even the supplicants, though ashamed, do not approach it of their own accord. 'Saṃśritadrumalatāśoṣa' (drying of trees and creepers that have taken refuge): the perception that those who have taken shelter remain devoted to it alone even in such dire straits. And since it cannot nourish its own retinue as described, its heat belongs to itself, not from any greed for the slightest enjoyment — this is established. By the second half — even in such an unfortunate situation, the fact that it is not an object of others' assistance unfolds as a ground for praise. In the other [verse] too — the Sun's submersion in the ocean at the appropriate time ordained by <s>Vidhātṛ</s> — he himself performs this for the sake of fulfilling the vow of illuminating all objects established by <s>Prajāpati</s>, having by his own rising eclipsed all others of his own and the opposing side. Otherwise, the manifestation of the moon, darkness, stars, and so forth would never be possible even in the slightest — this is what the poet has delineated as novel, and it becomes exceedingly wonder-producing through its predominant orientation toward manifesting the perceived greatness. [The author] unfolds yet another type of variety in a different manner — 'pratīyamānatā' and so on. Where — in which — the suggestedness, the to-be-inferred nature, of the expressed content that is principally intended as the sentence-meaning, of some inexpressible subject, is composed. By what means? — By the functions of the expressed and the expressor, by the powers of word and meaning. The manifestation of something different, beyond these, having a function beyond theirs, something that is the suggested (<s>vyaṅgya</s>), is accomplished. The word 'vṛtti' (function) here denotes the capacity of word and meaning to illuminate that [suggested content]. And this usage of 'pratīyamāna' (the suggested) will be more fully unfolded at the occasion of explaining sentence-obliqueness. The two examples just cited should be applied here. Or as —

children.text: vaktrendorna haranti bāṣpapayasāṃ dhārā manojñāṃ śriyaṃ niśvāsā na kadarthayanti madhurāṃ bimbādharasya dyatim /
children.translated_text: The streams of tears do not carry away the lovely beauty of the moon-like face; the sighs do not spoil the sweet radiance of the <s>bimba</s>-fruit-like lower lip;

children.text: tasyāstvadvirahe vipakvalavalīlāvaṇyasaṃvādinī chāyā kāpi kapolayoranudinaṃ tanvyāḥ paraṃ puṣyati // VjivC_1.100 //
children.translated_text: but in her, in your absence, a certain lustre of the cheeks, O slender one, harmonizing with the charm of ripened beauty, daily grows ever more. // <s>Vjīv</s>C 1.100 //

children.text:
atratvadvirahavaidhuryasaṃvaraṇakadarthanāmanubhavantyāstasyāstathāvi dhe mahati gurusaṅkaṭe vartamānāyāḥ---kiṃ bahunā---bāṣpaniśvāsamokṣāvasaro 'pi na saṃbhavatīti /
kevalaṃ pariṇatalavalīlāvaṇyasaṃvādasubhagā kāpi kapolayoḥ kāntiraśakyasaṃvaraṇā pratidinaṃ paraṃ paripoṣamāsādayatīti vācyavyatiriktavṛtti dūtyuktitātparyaṃ pratīyate /
uktaprakārakāntimattvakathanaṃ ca kāntakautukotkalikākāraṇatāṃ pratipadyate /
vicitrameva rūpāntareṇa pratipādayati---svabhāva ityādi /
yatra yasmin bhāvānāṃ svabhāvaḥ parispandaḥ sarasākūto rasanirbharābhiprāyaḥ padārthānāṃ nibadhyate niveśyate /
kīdṛśaḥ---kenāpi kamanīyena vaicitryeṇopabṛṃhitaḥ, lokottareṇa hṛdayahāriṇā vaidagdhyenottejitaḥ /
"bhāva'- śabdenātra sarvapadārtho 'bhidhīyate, na ratyādireva /
udāharaṇam
children.translated_text: Here, of that woman, enduring the concealment and the thwarting of the distress of separation from you, even in such a great and dire predicament — in short — there is not even an opportunity for the release of tears and sighs. Only a certain beauty of the cheeks, felicitous in its harmony with the charm of mature beauty, and impossible to conceal, daily reaches ever greater fullness — thus, the purport of the messenger-woman's speech, whose function exceeds the expressed content, is suggested. And the narration of that kind of beauty becomes the cause of awakening the lover's curiosity and longing. [The author] expounds yet another type of variety in a different form — 'svabhāva' and so on. Where — in which — the natural disposition (<s>svabhāva</s>), the activity, of things — the passionate intention, the sentiment-laden purpose — is composed, is set down. Of what kind? — Enhanced by a certain lovely variety, stimulated by an extraordinary, heart-captivating ingenuity. The word '<s>bhāva</s>' here denotes every object, not merely the <s>ratis</s> (erotic sentiments) and so forth. The example —

children.text: krīḍāsu bālakusumāyudhasaṃgatāyā yattat smitaṃ na khalu tat smitamātrameva /
children.translated_text: That smile of hers, when united with the young flower-armed [god of love] in amorous play, is surely not merely a smile;

children.text: ālokyate smitapaṭāntaritaṃ mṛgākṣyās tasyāḥ parisphuradivāparameva kiñcit // VjivC_1.101 //
children.translated_text: something else is seen shimmering, concealed behind the veil of that smile of the doe-eyed one. // <s>Vjīv</s>C 1.101 //

children.text:
atra na khalu tat smitamātrameveti prathamārdhe 'bhilāṣasubhagaṃ sarasābhiprāyatvamuktam /
aparārdhe tu---hasitāṃśukatirohitamanyadeva kimapi parisphuradālokyata iti kamanīyavaicitryavicchittiḥ /
idānīṃ vicitramevopasaṃharati---vicitro yatretyādi /
evaṃvidho vicitro mārgo yatra yasmin vakroktivaicitryam alaṅkāravicitrabhāvo jīvitāyate jīvatavadācarati /
vaicitryādeva vicitre "vicitra' śabdaḥ pravartate /
tasmāttadeva tasya jīvitam /
kiṃ tadvaicitryaṃ nāmetyāha---parisphurati yasyāntaḥ sā kāpyatiśayābhidhā /
yasyāntaḥ svarūpānupraveśena sā kāpyalaukikātiśayoktiḥ parisphurati bhrājate /
yathā---
children.translated_text: Here, 'it is surely not merely a smile' — in the first half, the passionate purpose, felicitous with desire, is stated. In the second half — 'something else, some other [thing], is seen shimmering, concealed behind the rays of laughter' — this is the charm of a lovely variety. Now [the author] concludes [the discussion of] variety itself — 'vicitro yatra' and so on. The variety of such a kind — the path that is 'varied' — wherein the variety of <s>vakrokti</s> (oblique expression), the variegated nature of ornamentation, is made to live, acts as though alive. It is 'varied' precisely because of its variety — the word 'vicitra' applies [to it for that reason]. Therefore that [variety] alone is its life. 'What is that variety?' he says: 'there shines forth within it a certain extraordinary expression.' 'Within it' — by penetrating its essential nature — 'a certain extraordinary, other-worldly utterance' shines forth, radiates. For example —

children.text: yatsenārajasāmudañcati yade dvābhyāṃ davīyo 'ntarān pāṇibhyāṃ yugapadvilocanapuṭānaṣṭākṣamo rakṣitum /
children.translated_text: When the dust of his army rises, unable with [only] two hands to simultaneously protect the pair of eye-lids from what is far away,

children.text: ekaikaṃ dalamunnamayya gamayan vāsāmbujaṃ kośatāṃ dhātā saṃvaraṇākulaściramabhūtsvādhyāyavandhyānanaḥ // VjivC_1.102 //
children.translated_text: <s>Dhātṛ</s> (the Creator), raising each petal one by one, causing the day-lotus to close into a bud, long remained troubled by the task of concealment, his face rendered barren of self-recitation. // <s>Vjīv</s>C 1.102 //

children.text:
evaṃ vaicitryaṃ saṃbhāvanānumānapravṛttāyāḥ pratīyamānatvamutprekṣāyāḥ /
tacca dhārādhiroharaṇaramaṇīyatayātiśayoktiparispandasyandi saṃdṛśyate /
tadevaṃ vaicitryaṃ vyākhyāya tasyaiva guṇān vyācaṣṭe---
children.translated_text: Thus, the variety that consists in the suggestedness of <s>utprekṣā</s> (poetic fancy), which proceeds from probable inference — and that is seen flowing with the pulsation of <s>atiśayokti</s> (hyperbole), beautified by the escalation of streams [of meaning]. Having thus explained the variety, [the author] now sets forth the qualities of that very [variety] —
<s>Mādhurya</s> (sweetness), emanating from poetic ingenuity, is woven into the words here,
which, having shed their looseness, attain the grace of compositional elegance. // <s>Vjīv</s> 1.44 //

children.text:
atrāsmin mādhuryaṃ vaidagdhyasyāndi vaicitryasamarpakaṃ padānāṃ badhyate vākyaikadeśānāṃ niveśyate /
yattyaktaśaithilyamujjhitakomalabhāvaṃ bhavadvandhabandhuratāṅgatāṃ yāti saṃniveśasaundaryopakaraṇatāṃ gacchati /
yathā
children.translated_text: Here, in this [vicitra path], <s>mādhurya</s> (sweetness) — emanating from poetic ingenuity (<s>vaidagdhya</s>), conveying variety — is woven into, is established in, the words, the components of the sentence. [That sweetness] which, having shed its looseness — having discarded the quality of softness — attains the grace of compositional elegance, arrives at the status of being an instrument of beauty of arrangement. For example —
'kiṃ tāruṇyataroḥ' — here, the first half — // <s>Vjīv</s>C 1.103 //
Having thus described <s>mādhurya</s> (sweetness), [the author] describes <s>prasāda</s> (lucidity) —
The arrangement of non-compound words, well-known on the path of poets,

children.text: kiñcidojaḥ spṛśan prāyaḥ prasādo 'pyatra dṛśyate // Vjiv_1.45 //
children.translated_text: touching slightly upon <s>ojas</s> (energy), is seen here generally as <s>prasāda</s> (lucidity). // <s>Vjīv</s> 1.45 //

children.text:
asamastānāṃ samāsarahitānāṃ padānāṃ nyāso nibandhaḥ kavivartmani vipaścinmārgeyaḥ prasiddhaḥ prakhyātaḥ so 'pyasmin vicitrākhye prasādābhidhāno guṇaḥ kiñcit kiyanmātramojaḥ spṛśannuttānatayā vyavasthitaḥ prāyo dṛśyate prācuryeṇa lakṣyate /
bandhasaundaryanibandhanatvāt /
tathāvidhasyaujasaḥ samāsavatī vṛttiḥ-"ojaḥ'-śabdena cirantanairucyate /
tadayamatra paramārthaḥ---pūrvasmin prasādalakṣaṇe satyojaḥ saṃsparśamātramiha vidhīyate /
yathā
children.translated_text: The arrangement, the composition, of non-compound — that is, free from compounds — words, on the path of poets, on the way of the learned, is well-known, is celebrated. That too, in this [path] called 'vicitra,' is the quality designated <s>prasāda</s> (lucidity), touching — that is, contacting to a small degree — <s>ojas</s> (energy), established as predominant through directness; it is 'generally seen,' that is, frequently observed. Because it is the basis of the beauty of composition. Of that kind of <s>ojas</s>, the compound-bearing style is what the ancients call by the word 'ojas.' This then is the ultimate purport here — when the previously described quality of <s>prasāda</s> is present, only a touch of <s>ojas</s> is prescribed here. For example —
With stars gone to the corners of the eyes, borne by the still eyelashes, radiant with sparkling lovely beauty, illumined by the rise of smiles,
languid with the burden of coquetry, with a single eyebrow arched in flickering play — victorious are the glances of intoxicated beauties, directed at their lovers! // <s>Vjīv</s>C 1.104 //
[The author] reveals <s>prasāda</s> in yet another manner —
Even other sentences that are suggestive are composed within a sentence
as though they were [merely] words — this is some other mode of <s>prasāda</s> (lucidity). // <s>Vjīv</s> 1.46 //

children.text:
atrāsmin vicitre yadvākyaṃ padasamudāyastasmin gamakāni samarpakāṇyanyāni vākyāntarāpi nibadhyante niveśyante /
katham---padānīva padavat, parasparānvitānītyarthaḥ /
eṣa ko 'pyapūrvaḥ prasādasyāparaḥ kramaḥ bandhacchāyāprakāraḥ /
yathā
children.translated_text: Here, in this 'vicitra' [path], within the sentence — the collection of words — other sentences too that are suggestive, that convey [meaning], are composed, are set down. How? — As though they were words — like words, mutually connected in syntax. This is some unprecedented, other mode of <s>prasāda</s>, a type of compositional lustre. For example —
'nāmāpyantaroḥ' — thus. // <s>Vjīv</s>C 1.105 //
Now, having described <s>prasāda</s>, [the author] characterizes <s>lāvaṇya</s> (gracefulness) —
Here, with words ending in unelided <s>visarga</s>, interwoven with one another,
short and preceded by conjunct consonants, <s>lāvaṇya</s> (gracefulness) is intensified. // <s>Vjīv</s> 1.47 //

children.text:
atrāsminnevaṃvidhaiḥ padairlāvaṇyamatiricyate paripoṣaṃ prāpnoti /
kīdṛśaiḥ---parasparamanyonyaṃ protaiḥ saṃśleṣaṃ nītaiḥ /
anyacca kīdṛśaiḥ---aluptavisargāntaiḥ, aluptavisargāḥ śrūyamāṇavisarjanīyā antā yeṣāṃ tāni tathoktāni taiḥ /
hrasvaiśca laghubhiḥ /
saṃyogebhyaḥ pūrvaiḥ /
atiricyate iti saṃbandhaḥ /
tadidamatra tātparyam---pūrvoktalakṣaṇaṃ lāvaṇyaṃ vidyamānamanenātiriktatāṃ nīyate /
yathā
children.translated_text: Here, in this [vicitra path], by words of such a kind, <s>lāvaṇya</s> (gracefulness) is intensified, brought to fullness. Of what kind? — Interwoven with one another, brought into conjunction. And again, of what kind? — Ending in unelided <s>visarga</s>: those whose finals are audible <s>visargas</s> — such are those [words], and by those. And short — that is, light [in syllabic quantity]. And preceded by conjunct consonants — 'is intensified' is the syntactic connection. This then is the purport here — the previously described quality of <s>lāvaṇya</s>, being already present, is brought to superabundance by these [features]. For example —

children.text: śvāsotkampataraṅgiṇi stanataṭe dhautāñjanaśyāmalāḥ kīryante kaṇaśaḥ kṛśāṅgi kimamī bāṣpāmbhasāṃ bindavaḥ /
children.translated_text: On the breast-slope, rippling with the waves of heaving sighs, are these drops of tears shed, O slender one — dark as washed collyrium, falling grain by grain?

children.text: kiñcākuñcitakaṇṭharodhakuṭilāḥ karṇāmṛtasyandino hūṅkārāḥ kalapañcamapraṇayinastrucyantiniryānti ca // VjivC_1.106 //
children.translated_text: And further, those <s>hūṅkāras</s> (moans), curving with the obstruction of a slightly constricted throat, flowing as nectar to the ears, intimate with the fifth note of the cuckoo — are they being shed, or are they issuing forth? // <s>Vjīv</s>C 1.106 //
Or as —
This [pair of breasts], dark-bellied as a faintly ripened <s>tinduka</s> fruit, with pale edges — alas, worthy of the touch of the beautiful hand of a <s>Pulinda</s> — is observed.

children.text: tat pallīpatiputri kuñjarakulaṃ kumbhābhayābhyarthanā- dīnaṃ tvāmanunāthate kucayugaṃ patrāṃśukairmā pidhāḥ // VjivC_1.107 //
children.translated_text: Therefore, O daughter of the village chief, the elephant herd, pitiable with its entreaties born of the fear of [your] pot-like [breasts] — follows you; do not cover [your] pair of breasts with leaf-garments! // <s>Vjīv</s>C 1.107 //
Or as —
'haṃsānāṃ ninadeṣu' — thus. // <s>Vjīv</s>C 1.108 //
Having thus described <s>lāvaṇya</s>, [the author] describes <s>ābhijātya</s> (nobility of style) —
That which is neither of an excessively soft hue nor bearing excessive harshness,
<s>ābhijātya</s> (nobility of style), captivating to the mind, is here fashioned by maturity [of skill]. // <s>Vjīv</s> 1.48 //

children.text:
atrāsmin tadābhijātyaṃ yannātikomalacchāyaṃ nātyantamasṛṇakānti nātikāṭhinyamudvahannātikaṭhoratāṃ dhārayat tat prauḍhinirmitaṃ sakalakavikauśalasaṃpāditaṃ sanmanohāri hṛdayarañjakaṃ bhavatītyarthaḥ /
yathā
children.translated_text: Here, in this [vicitra path], that <s>ābhijātya</s> (nobility of style) which is neither of an excessively soft hue — not of an overly smooth beauty — nor bearing excessive harshness — not sustaining an overly rigid quality — that, fashioned by maturity of skill — produced by the complete poetic mastery — is truly captivating to the mind, delightful to the heart. This is the meaning. For example —
Upon the superior flat surface of the couch, [her] cheek-line has grown pale from the closing [of her eyes] caused by the fragrance of the playfully contrived pretense of sleep;

children.text: sutanu kathaya kasya vyañjayatyañjasaiva smaranarapatikelīyauvarājyābhiṣekam // VjivC_1.109 //
children.translated_text: O slender one, tell me—whose coronation into the regency of the amorous sport of <s>Smara</s> (the god of love) does it reveal so directly? (Vjiv 1.109)

children.text: evaṃ sukumāravihitānāmeva guṇānāṃ vicitre kaścidatiśayaḥ saṃpādyata iti boddhavyam /
children.translated_text: Thus it should be understood that a certain excellence is achieved in the elaborate [path] with respect to the very qualities established in the delicate [path].
The qualities beginning with nobility (<s>ābhijātya</s>), which were stated in the first path,
attain here an excellence, having generated a cultivated richness. (Vjiv 1.110)
Thus ends the intervening verse. Having thus described the elaborate [path], he commences the middle [path]—

children.text: vaicitryaṃ saukumāryaṃ ca yatra saṃkīrṇatāṃ gate /
children.translated_text: Where elaborateness and delicacy, having entered into a state of intermixture,
shine forth, endowed with an excess of beauty both innate and cultivated, (Vjiv 1.49)
where the cluster of qualities beginning with <s>mādhurya</s> (sweetness), resorting to the middle style,
nourishes some unprecedented excellence surpassing the beauty of composition, (Vjiv 1.50)
that is called the middle path (<s>madhyama mārga</s>), captivating through its manifold flavors,
where the excellences of the two [other] paths coexist in mutual rivalry. (Vjiv 1.51)

children.text:
mārgo 'sau madhyamo nāma madhyamābhidhāno 'sau panthāḥ /
kīdṛśaḥ---nānārucimanoharaḥ /
nānāvidhā rucayaḥ pratibhāsā yeṣāṃ te tathoktāsteṣāṃ sukumāravicitramadhyamavyasanināṃ sarveṣāmeva manoharo hṛdayahārī /
yasmin spardhayā mārgadvitayasaṃpadaḥ sukumāravicitraśobhāḥ sāmyena vartante vyavatiṣṭhante, na nyūnātiriktatvena /
yatra vaicitryaṃ vicitratvaṃ saukumāryaṃ sukumāratvaṃ saṃkīrṇatāṃ gate tasmin miśratāṃ prāpte satī bhrājete śobhete /
kīdṛśe---sahajāhāryaśobhātiśayaśālinī, śaktivyutpattisaṃbhavo yaḥ śobhātiśayaḥ kāntyutkarṣastena śālete ślāghet ye te tathokte /
mādhuryetyādi /
yatra ca mādhuryādiguṇagrāmo mādhuryaprabhṛtiguṇasamūho madhyamāmubhayacchāyācchuritāṃ vṛttiṃ svaspandagatimāśritya kāmapyapūrvāṃ bandhacchāyātiriktatāṃ saṃniveśakāntyadhikatāṃ puṣṇāti puṣyatītyarthaḥ /
guṇā nāmudāharaṇāni /
tatra mādhuryasya yathā---
children.translated_text: That path called the middle (<s>madhyama</s>)—that is the path designated as 'middle.' Of what kind?—captivating through its manifold flavors. Those having manifold, varied flavors and appearances—for all of those devoted to the delicate, the elaborate, and the middle [paths]—it is captivating, stealing the heart. In which the excellences of the two paths, the beauties of the delicate and the elaborate, exist in rivalry, in equality—not in deficiency or excess. Where elaborateness, the quality of being elaborate, and delicacy, the quality of being delicate, having entered into a state of intermixture—when they have attained a mixed state—they shine forth, they are beautiful. In what kind [of state]?—endowed with an excess of beauty both innate and cultivated: that excess of beauty, that superabundance of brilliance, which arises from creative power and learning—that which is adorned by it is so described. Regarding '<s>mādhurya</s>' and so forth: where the cluster of qualities beginning with <s>mādhurya</s> (sweetness), the collection of qualities beginning with sweetness, resorting to the middle style (<s>vṛtti</s>)—a movement tinged with the flavor of both—nourishes, cultivates some unprecedented excellence surpassing the beauty of composition, an abundance of the beauty of arrangement—this is the meaning. The qualities are exemplified as follows. Of <s>mādhurya</s> (sweetness), for example—
Those women of the western shore, with tresses disheveled by gentle sea-breezes, sing his deeds,

children.text: līlānatāḥ samavalambya latāstarūṇāṃ hintālamāliṣu taṭeṣu mahārṇavasya // VjivC_1.111 //
children.translated_text: gracefully leaning upon the vine-creepers of trees, on the shores by the palm-groves of the great ocean. (Vjiv 1.111)
Of <s>prasāda</s> (clarity), for example: 'By the sight of her face like the moon' and so forth. (Vjiv 1.112)
Of <s>lāvaṇya</s> (charm), for example:
Her cheek rests on [her] hand, its fingers' joints revealing the sleep of [her] hand, her eyes turbid from freely shed tears, her lower lip stretched out by her sighs,

children.text: baddhodbhedavisaṃṣṭhulālakalatā nirvedaśūnyaṃ manaḥ kaṣṭaṃ durnayavedibhiḥ kusacivairvatsā dṛḍhaṃ khedyate // VjivC_1.113 //
children.translated_text: the vine-creeper of her tangled locks in disheveled disorder, her mind void of dejection—alas! The princess is sorely tormented by wicked ministers who know improper conduct. (Vjiv 1.113)
Of <s>ābhijātya</s> (nobility), for example:

children.text: ālambya lambāḥ sarasāgravallīḥ pibanti yatra stanabhāranamrāḥ /
children.translated_text: Where, stooping under the weight of their breasts, they lean upon hanging, sappy vine-tips and drink,
with eyes squinting from the spray, the waterfall of the <s>Mandākinī</s>—the excellent mares [of heaven]. (Vjiv 1.114)
Here, some who are devoted [to this path],
delighted by the variety of its flavors, are attentive to the art of refined poetic attire, like connoisseur-serpents. (Vjiv 1.52)

children.text:
evaṃ madhyamaṃ vyākhyāya tamevopasaṃharati---atreti /
atraitasmin kecit katipaye sādarāstadāśrayeṇa kāvyāni kurvanti /
yasmāt arocakinaḥ kamanīyavastuvyasaninaḥ /
kīdṛśe cāsmin---chāyāvaicitryarañjake kāntivicitrabhāvāhlādake /
katham---vidagdhanepathyavidhau bhujaṅgā iva, agrāmyākalpakalpane nāgarā yathā /
so 'pi chāyāvaicitryarañjaka eva /
atra guṇodāharaṇāni parimitatvātpradarśitāni, pratipadaṃ punaśchāyāvaicitryaṃ sahṛdayaiḥ svayamevānusartavyam /
anusaraṇadikpradarśanaṃ punaḥ kriyate /
yathā---mātṛguptamāyurājamañjīraprabhṛtīnāṃ saukumāryavaicitryasaṃvalitaparispandasyandīni kāvyāni saṃbhavanti /
tatra madhyamamārgasaṃvalitaṃ svarūpaṃ vicāraṇīyam /
evaṃ sahajasaukumāryasubhagāni kālidāsasarvasenādīnāṃ kāvyāni dṛśyante /
tatra sukumāramārgasvarūpaṃ carcanīyam /
tathaiva ca vicitravakratvavijṛmbhitaṃ harṣacarite prācuryeṇa bhaṭṭabāṇasya vibhāvyate, bhavabhūtirājaśekharaviraciteṣu bandhasaundaryasubhageṣumuktakeṣu paridṛśyate /
tasmāt sahṛdayaiḥ sarvatra sarvamanusartavyam /
evaṃ mārgatritayalakṣaṇaṃ diṅmātrameva pradarśitam, na punaḥ sākalyena satkavikauśalaprākārāṇāṃ kenacidapi svarūpamabhidhātuṃ pāryate /
mārgeṣu guṇānāṃ samudāyadharmatā /
yathā na kevalaṃ śabdādidharmatvaṃ tathā tallakṣaṇavyākhyāvasara eva pratipāditam /
evaṃ pratyekaṃ pratiniyataguṇagrāmaramaṇīyaṃ mārgatritayaṃ vyākhyāya sādhāraṇaguṇasvarūpavyākhyānārthamāha---
children.translated_text: Having thus explained the middle [path], he now summarizes it—'here' (atra). Here, in this [path], some, a few, are attentive—they compose poems with reliance upon it. Because they are connoisseurs of beautiful objects (<s>arocakin</s>). And in what kind of [path]?—one that delights through the variety of its flavors, that which gives pleasure through the diversity of charming appearances. How?—like connoisseur-serpents in the art of refined, un-rustic poetic attire; like urbane [people] in a non-rustic arrangement of adornment. That [path] too is one that delights through the variety of its flavors. Here, the examples of qualities have been shown because of their limited [number]; but the variety of flavor in every detail should be followed by the connoisseurs themselves. An indication of the direction for following [this path] is now given. For example—the poems of <s>Mātṛgupta</s>, <s>Māyurāja</s>, <s>Mañjīra</s> and others flow with the vibration intertwined with delicacy and elaborateness. In those, the form intertwined with the middle path should be examined. Similarly, the poems of <s>Kālidāsa</s>, <s>Sarvasena</s> and others are seen to be blessed with natural delicacy. In those, the essential nature of the delicate path should be investigated. And likewise, the exuberance of elaborate obliquity is abundantly perceived in <s>Bāṇa</s>'s <s>Harṣacarita</s>, and is seen in the stray verses (<s>muktaka</s>) composed by <s>Bhavabhūti</s> and <s>Rājaśekhara</s>, blessed with the beauty of composition. Therefore, the connoisseurs should follow everything everywhere. Thus the characteristics of the three paths have been shown merely in outline; the full essential nature of the ramparts of true poetic skill cannot be stated by anyone in its entirety. The fact that qualities are collective properties of the paths—and not merely properties of words and so forth—was established at the very occasion of explaining their definitions. Having thus explained the threefold path, each beautiful through its own particular cluster of qualities, he now speaks for the purpose of explaining the nature of the common quality—
That by which the greatness of a thing's nature is nourished
through a direct mode—that <s>aucitya</s> (propriety) is the life of fitting expression. (Vjiv 1.53)

children.text:
tadaucityaṃ nāma guṇaḥ /
kīdṛk---āñjasena suspaṣṭena svabhāvasya padārthasya mahattvamutkarṣo yena poṣyate paripoṣaṃ prāpyate /
prakāreṇeti prastutatvādabhidhāvaicitryamatra "prakāra'---śabdenocyate /
kīdṛśam---ucitākhyānamudārābhidhānaṃ jīvitaṃ paramārtho yasya tattathoktam /
etadānuguṇyenaiva vibhūṣaṇavinyāso vicchattimāvahati /
yathā
children.translated_text: That <s>aucitya</s> (propriety) is indeed a quality. Of what kind?—through a direct, perspicuous mode, the greatness, the excellence of the nature, of the object, is nourished, brought to full growth. 'Mode' (<s>prakāra</s>) here, since the topic is relevant, denotes the variety of expression. Of what kind?—that whose life, whose ultimate purport, is fitting expression (<s>ucitākhyāna</s>), noble denotation. In conformity with this [propriety] alone does the arrangement of ornaments produce strikingness. For example:
Of the two lords [<s>Rāma</s> and <s>Lakṣmaṇa</s>], holding rosaries in the palms of their hands, their hands stiffened with the onset of trepidation,
who had fashioned beautiful arrangements of matted locks—their meeting [with <s>Bharata</s>] was as though of two different [<s>Rāmas</s>]. (Vjiv 1.115)
Or for example:

O lord of the mountain, this is the encampment of <s>Puruhūta</s>'s (<s>Indra</s>'s) army at the base of the mountain; let the other, immeasurable ridge of the mountain be the resting place of your forces;

children.text: dhruvamiha kariṇaste durdharāḥ saṃnikarṣe suragajamadalekhāsaurabhaṃ na kṣamante // VjivC_1.116 //
children.translated_text: surely your elephants here, being irresistible when nearby, would not tolerate the fragrance of the rut-marks of the divine elephant. (Vjiv 1.116)
And for example:

children.text: he nāgarāja bahudhāsya nitambabhāgaṃ bhogena gāḍhamabhiveṣṭaya mandarādreḥ /
children.translated_text: O lord of serpents, entwine tightly with your coils the slope-region of this Mount <s>Mandara</s>;
for you who have endured the unbearable sport of yoking with the Bull-Rider [<s>Śiva</s>] as a couch-strap, what great burden could this be? (Vjiv 1.117)

children.text:
atra pūrvatrodāharaṇayorbhūṣaṇaguṇenaiva tadguṇaparipoṣaḥ, itaratra ca svabhāvaudāryābhidhānena /
aucityasyaiva chāyāntareṇa svarūpamunmīlayati---
children.translated_text: Here, in the first two examples, the nourishment of that quality [aucitya] is [achieved] through the quality of ornamentation itself; in the other [example], through the noble expression of natural grandeur. He now reveals the nature [of aucitya] through another shade—
Where the expressible is concealed by a nature that excels in beauty,
whether of the speaker or the experiencer—that too is called <s>aucitya</s> (propriety). (Vjiv 1.54)

children.text: yatra yasmin vakturabhidhātuḥ pramāturanubhaviturvā svabāvena svaparispandena vcyamabhidheyaṃ vastu śobhātiśāyinā rāmaṇīyakamanohareṇa ācchādyate saṃvriyate tadapyaucityamevocyate /

children.translated_text: For example:
O king, standing with your body alone, you do not appear as one whose wealth has been given away at holy sites;
[rather you appear] like a <s>nīvāra</s> (wild rice) stalk remaining from a tree whose fruit was produced by wild cultivation, with its stump [alone]. (Vjiv 1.118)

Where—in which case—the expressible, the denotable object, is concealed, veiled, by the nature, the own vibration, of the speaker, the one who expresses, or of the experiencer, the one who perceives—by a [nature] excelling in beauty, captivating in its loveliness—that too is called propriety (<s>aucitya</s>).

children.text:
atra ślāghyatayā tathāvidhamahārājaparispande varṇyamāne muninā svānubhavasiddhavyavahārānusāreṇālaṅkaraṇayojanamaucityaparipoṣamāvahati /
atra vaktuḥ svabhāvena ca vācyaparispandaḥ saṃvṛtaprāyo lakṣyate /
pramāturyathā /
children.translated_text: Here, when such a great king's vibration [of condition] is being described in a laudatory manner by the sage, the yoking of ornamentation following the course of conduct validated by his own experience brings about the nourishment of propriety. Here the vibration of the expressible is observed as mostly concealed by the nature of the speaker. Of the experiencer, for example:
The <s>aśoka</s> branch, its flower-clusters being sucked by bees, its tender young shoots trembling,
was seen to mimic the shaking of hands and biting of lips of young brides that is not at all mild. (Vjiv 1.119)

children.text:
atra vadhūjanairnijānubhavavāsanānusāreṇa tathāvidhaśobhābhirāmatānubhūtiraucitya māvahati /
yathā vā
children.translated_text: Here, the perception of such a beauty-full loveliness by the young brides, following the course of impressions from their own experience, produces propriety. Or for example:

children.text: vāpītaḍe kuḍuṅgā piasahi hnāuṃ gaehiṃ dīsaṃti /
children.translated_text: [In Prakrit:] At the edge of the pond, the bowers—having gone to bathe, they are seen;

children.text: ṇa dharanti kareṇa bhaṇanti ṇa tti valiuṃ puṇa ṇar deti // VjivC_1.120 //
children.translated_text: they do not restrain [themselves] by hand, they do not say anything, yet they do not allow [him] to turn back, nor do they give [permission] again. (Vjiv 1.120)
[In Sanskrit:] At the edge of the pond, the bowers—having gone to bathe, they are seen;

children.text: na dharanti kareṇa bhajanti na kimapi valituṃ punarna dadati //
children.translated_text: they do not restrain by hand, they do not say anything, yet they do not permit turning back, nor do they give [permission] again.

children.text:
iti chāyā /
atra kasyāścitpramātṛbhūtāyāḥ sātiśayamaugdhyaparispandasundareṇa svabhāvena vācyamācchāditamaucityaparipoṣamāvahati /
evamaucityamabhidhāya saubhāgyamabhidhatte---
children.translated_text: Thus is the <s>chāyā</s> (Sanskrit rendering). Here, the expressible is concealed by the nature of a certain woman who is the experiencer, [that nature being] beautiful through the charm of an exceedingly artless vibration—and this produces the nourishment of propriety. Having thus described <s>aucitya</s> (propriety), he describes <s>saubhāgya</s> (elegance)—
In this excellent assemblage [of word and meaning], that for the sake of which the poet's creative power (<s>pratibhā</s>)

children.text: samyak saṃrabhate tasya guṇaḥ saubhāgyamucyate // Vjiv_1.55 //
children.translated_text: properly exerts itself—the quality of that [object] is called <s>saubhāgya</s> (elegance). (Vjiv 1.55)

children.text: ityevaṃvidhe 'sminnupādeyavarge śabdādyupeyasamūhe yadarthaṃ yannimittaṃ kaveḥ saṃbandhinī pratibhā śaktiḥ samyak sāvadhānatayā saṃrabhate vyavasyati tasya vastunaḥ prastutatvāt kāvyābhidhānasya yo guṇaḥ sa saubhāgyamityucyate bhaṇyate //
children.translated_text: In this excellent assemblage of such a kind—the group of what is to be employed, the collection of words and such—for the sake of which, on account of which, the creative power, the faculty belonging to the poet, properly, with full attention, exerts itself, resolves—of that object, since it is the subject under discussion, the quality that pertains to poetic expression is called <s>saubhāgya</s> (elegance).
And that [elegance] is not achieved merely through the impulse of creative inspiration, but rather through the totality of instruments arranged by it—thus he says:
Produced by the vibration of total perfection, for those of refined sensibility,
[it is] the producer of extraordinary wonder—the sole life of poetry. (Vjiv 1.56)

children.text:
sarvasaṃpatparispandasaṃpādyaṃ sarvasyopādeyarāśeryā saṃpattiranavadyatākāṣṭhā tasyāḥ parispandaḥ sphuritatvaṃ tena saṃpādyaṃ niṣpādanīyam /
anyacca kīdṛśam---sarasātmanāmārdracetasāmalaukikacamatkārakāri lokottarāhlādavidhāyi /
kiṃ bahunā, tacca kāvyaikajīvitaṃ kāvyasya paraḥ paramārtha ityarthaḥ /
yathā
children.translated_text: 'Produced by the vibration of total perfection'—of the entire assemblage of what is to be employed, the perfection is the summit of faultlessness; its vibration is its shining forth; by that it is to be produced, to be accomplished. And what else characterizes it?—for those of refined sensibility, of tender heart, it produces extraordinary wonder, wonder that transcends the worldly. In a word, it is the sole life of poetry—the supreme ultimate meaning of poetry—this is the meaning. For example:

children.text: dormūlāvadhisūtritastanamuraḥ snihyatkaṭākṣe daśau kiñcittāṇḍavapaṇḍite smitasudhāsiktoktiṣa bhrūlate /
children.translated_text: In the glance that is affectionate, threaded from the root of the arm to the breast, in the two eyes that are somewhat skilled in dance, in the brow-creeper whose speech is sprinkled with the nectar of smiles,

children.text: cetaḥ kandalitaṃ smaravyatikarairlāvyamaṅgairvṛtaṃ tanvaṅgyāstaruṇimnisarpatiśanairanyaiva kāciddyutiḥ // VjivC_1.121 //
children.translated_text: the mind is germinated by the encounters of love, enveloped by limbs possessing charm—in the slender-bodied maiden, as fresh youthfulness gradually pervades, some other radiance altogether [appears]. (Vjiv 1.121)

children.text:
tanvyāḥ prathamataratāruṇye 'vatīrṇe, ākārasya cetasaśceṣṭāyāścavaicitryamatra varṇitam /
tatra sūtritastanamuro lāvaṇyamaṅgairvṛtamityākārasya, smaravyatikaraiḥ kandalitamiti cetasaḥ, snihyatkaṭākṣe dṛśāviti kiñcittāṇḍavapaṇḍite smitasudhāsiktoktiṣu bhrūlate iti ceṣṭāyāśca /
sūtrita-sikta-tāṇḍava-paṇḍita-kandalitānāmupacāravakratvaṃ lakṣyate, snihyadityetasya kālaviśeṣāvedakaḥ pratyayavakrabhāvaḥ, anyaiva kācidavarṇanīyeti saṃvṛtivakratāvicchittiḥ, aṅgairvṛtamiti kārakavakratvam /
vicitramārgaviṣayo lāvaṇyaguṇātirekaḥ /
tadevametasmin pratibhāsaṃrambhajanitasakalasāmagrīsamunmīlitaṃ sarasahṛdayāhlādakāri kimapi saubhāgyaṃ samudbhāsate /
anantaroktasya guṇadvayasya viṣayaṃ pradarśayati---
children.translated_text: When the maiden's earliest youthful bloom has descended, the variety of her form, her mind, and her behavior is here described. There: 'threaded from breast to arm' pertains to form; 'enveloped by limbs' [pertains to form]; 'germinated by the encounters of love' pertains to mind; 'the glance that is affectionate in the two eyes,' 'somewhat skilled in dance,' 'the brow-creeper whose speech is sprinkled with the nectar of smiles' pertain to behavior. The figurative obliquity (<s>upacāravakratva</s>) of 'threaded,' 'sprinkled,' 'skilled in dance,' 'germinated' is observed; the oblique nature of the suffix in 'affectionate' (<s>snihyat</s>) indicates a particular time; 'some other altogether, not to be described' shows the strikingness of concealment-obliquity (<s>saṃvṛtivakratā</s>); 'enveloped by limbs' shows case-obliquity (<s>kārakavakratva</s>). The excess of the quality of charm (<s>lāvaṇya</s>) is within the domain of the elaborate path. Thus, in this [example], born from the impulse of creative inspiration, [with] the full complement of all instruments brought to light—some certain elegance (<s>saubhāgya</s>) that delights the refined connoisseur shines forth. He now shows the domain of the pair of qualities just stated—
This radiant pair of qualities pervades
words, sentences, and works alike, in all three paths. (Vjiv 1.57)

children.text:
etadguṇadvaya maucityasaubhāgyābhidhānam ujjvalamatīva bhrājiṣṇu padavākyaprabandhānāṃ trayāṇāmapi vyāpakatvena vartate sakalāvayavavyāptyāvatiṣṭhate /
kvetyāha---triṣvapi mārgeṣu sukumāravicitramadhyamākhyeṣu /
tatra padasya tāvadaucityaṃ bahuvidhabhedabhinnovakrabhāvaḥ /
svabhāvasyāñjasena prakāreṇa paripoṣaṇameva vakratāyāḥ paraṃ rahasyam /
ucitābhidhānajīvitātvād vākyasyāpyekadeśe 'pyaucityavirahāttadvidāhlādakāritvahāniḥ /
yathā
children.translated_text: This pair of qualities, designated as propriety (<s>aucitya</s>) and charm (<s>saubhāgya</s>), exceedingly radiant, operates pervading all three — word, sentence, and composition — and remains through pervading all constituents. Where? He says — in all three paths named the delicate (<s>sukumāra</s>), the elaborate (<s>vicitra</s>), and the middle (<s>madhyama</s>). Therein, the propriety of the word is an oblique character diversified by manifold distinctions. The nourishment of [the word's] nature in a straightforward manner is indeed the supreme secret of obliquity. Since the sentence lives through appropriate expression, even in a single portion of a sentence, when propriety is absent, the capacity to delight the connoisseurs is lost. For example:

children.text: raghuvaṃśe puraṃ niṣādādhipatestadeta- dyasminmayā maulimaṇiṃ vihāya /
