children.translated_text: In the <s>Raghuvaṃśa</s>, [<s>Rāma</s> says:] 'At the town of the lord of the <s>Niṣādas</s>, having removed the crest-jewel,

children.text: jaṭāsu baddhāsvarudatsumantraḥ kaikeyi kāmāḥ phalītāstaveti // VjivC_1.122 //
children.translated_text: with matted locks bound and weeping together with his ministers — O <s>Kaikeyī</s>, your desires have borne fruit.' // VjivC_1.122 //

children.text:
atra raghupateranarghamahāpuruṣasaṃpadupetatvena varṇyamānasya "kaikeyi kāmāḥ phalitāstava' ityevaṃvidhatucchatarapadārthasaṃsmaraṇaṃ tadabhidhānaṃ cātyantamanaucityamāvahati /
prabandhasyāpi kvacitprakaraṇaikadeśe 'pyaucityavirahādekadeśadāhadūṣitadagdhapaṭaprāyatā prasajyate /
yathā---raghuvaṃśe eva dilīpa-siṃha-saṃvādāvasare
children.translated_text: Here, when the lord of the <s>Raghus</s> is being described as endowed with invaluable greatness of character, the recollection of such a trifling matter as 'O <s>Kaikeyī</s>, your desires have borne fruit' and its expression brings about an extreme impropriety (<s>anaucitya</s>). Even in a composition, if in any single portion of a section propriety is absent, the result is like a cloth ruined by being scorched in one spot. For example — in the <s>Raghuvaṃśa</s> itself, on the occasion of the dialogue between <s>Dilīpa</s> and the lion:
If you fear the preceptor [<s>Vasiṣṭha</s>], furious at the offense against his single cow, like a fire,

children.text: śakyo 'sya manyurbhavatāpi netuṃ gāḥ koṭiśaḥ sparśayatā ghaṭodhnīḥ // VjivC_1.123 //
children.translated_text: his anger can be appeased even by you — by making him touch millions of cows with full udders. // VjivC_1.123 //

children.text:
iti siṃhasyābhidhātumucitameva, rājopahāsaparatvenābhaidhīyamānatvāt /
rājñaḥ punarasya nijayaśaḥ parirakṣaṇaparatvena tṛṇavallaghuvṛttayaḥ prāṇāḥ pratibhāsante /
tasyaitatpūrvapakṣottaratvena
children.translated_text: This is indeed appropriate for the lion to say, since it is uttered with the purpose of mocking the king. For the king, however, whose purpose is to protect his own glory, his life appears as light as a blade of grass. As a reply to this objection:
How can the great sage be conciliated by the gift of other milch cows?

children.text: imāmanūnāṃ surabheravehi rudraujasā tu prahṛtaṃ tvayāsyām // VjivC_1.124 //
children.translated_text: Know that among [all] cows this one, <s>Surabhī</s>'s [descendant], is unequaled; it is by the power of <s>Rudra</s> that you have attacked her. // VjivC_1.124 //

children.text:
ityanyāsāṃ gavāṃ tatprativastupradānayogyatā yadi kadācitsaṃbhavati tatastasya munermama cobhayorapyetajjīvitaparirakṣaṇanairapekṣyamupapannamiti tātparyaparyavasānādatyantamanaucityayukteyamuktiḥ /
yathā ca kumārasaṃbhave trailokyākrāntipravaṇaparākramasya tārakākhyasya riporjigīṣāvasare surapatirmanmathenābhidhīyate---
children.translated_text: If the suitability of offering other cows as substitute were ever possible, then for both the sage and me the indifference to preserving this life would be justified — since the purport concludes thus, this utterance is fraught with extreme impropriety. And as in the <s>Kumārasaṃbhava</s>, on the occasion of the desire to conquer the enemy named <s>Tāraka</s>, whose valor is inclined toward conquering the three worlds, the lord of the gods (<s>Indra</s>) addresses <s>Manmatha</s> (the god of love):
'Do you desire her — the one devoted to the vow of having a single husband, of austere and painful conduct, whose fickle mind has entered [<s>Śiva</s>] through his beauty,
the broad-hipped one who has abandoned modesty, with arms clinging to [his] neck like a self-winding garland?' // VjivC_1.125 //

children.text:
ityavinayānuṣṭhānaniṣṭhaṃ triviṣṭapādhipatyapratiṣṭhitasyāpi tathāvidhābhiprāyānuvartanaparatvenābhidhīyamānamanaucityamāvahati /
etaccaitasyaiva kaveḥ sahajasaukumāryamudritasūktiparaspandasaundaryasya paryālocyate, na punaranyeṣāmāhāryamātrakāvyakaraṇakauśalaślāghinām /
saubhāgyamapi padavākyaprakaraṇaprabandhānāṃ pratyekamanekākārakamanīyakāraṇakalāpakalitarāmaṇīyakānāṃ kimapi sahṛdayahṛdayasaṃvedyaṃ kāvyaikajīvitamalaukikacamatkārakāri saṃvalitānekarasāsvādasundaraṃ sakalāvayavavyāpakatvena kāvyasya guṇāntaraṃ parisphuratītyalamatiprasaṅgena /
idānīmetadupasaṃhṛtyānyadavatārayati---
children.translated_text: This, being uttered with the intent of pursuing such a purpose even by one established in the lordship of heaven, who is devoted to the practice of impudence, brings about impropriety. And this is being considered specifically with regard to this very poet [<s>Kālidāsa</s>], whose beauty of utterance is stamped with innate delicacy of vibration, and not with regard to others who pride themselves on poetic skill that is merely acquired. Charm (<s>saubhāgya</s>) too — of words, sentences, passages, and compositions — each adorned by manifold forms of lovely causal clusters, it is some extraordinary quality of poetry that is cognizable by the hearts of connoisseurs, that produces supramundane wonder, beautiful through the relish of multiple <s>rasas</s> combined, and shines forth as another poetic virtue pervading all constituents — but enough of this digression. Now, having concluded this, he introduces another [topic]:

children.text: mārgāṇāṃ tritayaṃ tadetadasakṛtprāptavyaparyutsukaiḥ kṣuṇṇaṃ kairapi yatra kāmapi bhuvaṃ prāpya prasiddhiṃ gatāḥ /
children.translated_text: This triad of paths has been trodden repeatedly by certain [poets] eager for attainment, who, having reached a certain ground, became renowned.

children.text: sarve svairavihārahāri kavayo yāsyanti yenādhunā tasmin ko 'pi sa sādhusundarapadānyāsakramaḥ kathyate // Vjiv_1.58 //
children.translated_text: All poets will now travel on that [path] which is charming through spontaneous play — therein, a certain beautiful sequence of placing well-formed words is being described. // VjivC_1.126 //

children.text:
mārgāṇāṃ sukumārādīnāmetattritayaṃ kairapi mahākavibhireva, na sāmānyaiḥ, prāptavyaparyutsukaiḥ prāpyotkaṇṭhitairasakṛt bahuvāramabhyāsena kṣuṇṇaṃ parigamitam /
yatra yasmin mārgatraye kāmapi bhuvaṃ prāpya prasiddhiṃ gatāḥ lokottarāṃ bhūmimāsādya pratītiṃ prāptāḥ /
idānīṃ sarve kavayastasminmārgatritaye yena yāsyanti gamiṣyanti svairavihārahāri svecchāviharaṇaramaṇīyaṃ sa ko 'pi alaukikaḥ sādhuśobhanaṃ kṛtvā sundarapadanyāsakramaḥ kathyate subhagasuptiṅantasamarpaṇaparipāṭīvinyāso varṇyate /
mārga-svairavihāra-pada-prabhṛtayaḥ śabdāḥ śleṣacchāyāviśiṣṭatvena vyākhyeyāḥ /
children.translated_text: This triad of paths — delicate and so forth — has been trodden by certain great poets only, not by ordinary ones, who, eager for attainment, have traversed them repeatedly through practice. 'Where' — in which triad of paths, 'having reached a certain ground,' having attained an extraordinary level, they 'became renowned,' gained recognition. Now, all poets will travel that [triad of paths] — 'which is charming through spontaneous play,' delightful through freely roaming at will — in that [triad], a certain extraordinary, beautiful sequence of placing words is being described, the procedure for deploying well-formed noun and verb forms. Words such as 'path,' 'spontaneous play,' 'placing,' and so forth should be interpreted as qualified by the flavor of <s>śleṣa</s> (paronomasia).

children.text: iti śrīrājānakakuntakaviracite vakroktijīvite kāvyālaṅkāre prathama unmeṣaḥ /
children.translated_text: Thus [ends] the first <s>unmeṣa</s> (chapter) of the <s>Vakroktijīvita</s>, a work on poetic ornamentation, composed by the illustrious <s>Rājānaka Kuntaka</s>.
<s>Vakroktijīvita</s>, Second <s>Unmeṣa</s> (Chapter)

children.text:
sarvatraiva sāmānyalakṣaṇe vihite viśeṣalakṣaṇaṃ vidhātavyamiti kāvyasya "śabdārthau sahitau" ityādi (1 /7) sāmānyalakṣaṇaṃ vidhāya tadavayavabhūtayoḥ śabdārthayoḥ sāhityasya prathamonmeṣa eva viśeṣalakṣaṇaṃ vihitam /
idānīṃ prathamoddiṣṭasya varṇavinyāsavakratvasya viśeṣalakṣaṇamupakramate---
children.translated_text: Since everywhere, once a general definition has been formulated, a specific definition must be provided — having formulated the general definition of poetry as 'word and meaning conjoined' (1.7) and so forth, the specific definition of the conjunction of word and meaning, which are its constituents, was provided in the first chapter itself. Now he begins the specific definition of the obliquity in letter arrangement (<s>varṇavinyāsavakratā</s>), which was first mentioned:

children.text: eko dvau bahavo varṇā badhyamānāḥ punaḥ punaḥ /
children.translated_text: One, two, or many letters, being repeatedly bound together,
with small intervals, are said to constitute obliquity in letter arrangement, of three kinds. // Vjiv_2.1 //

children.text:
varṇaśabdo 'tra vyañjanavinyasanavicchittiḥ tridhā tribhiḥ prakārairuktāvarṇitā /
ke punaste trayaḥ prakārā ityucyate---ekaḥ kevala eva, kadācid dvau bahavo vā varṇāḥ punaḥ punarbadhyamānā yojyamānāḥ /
kīdṛśāḥ---svalpāntarāḥ /
svalpaṃ sutarāmalpaṃ stokamantaraṃ vyavadhānaṃ yeṣāṃ te tathoktāḥ /
ta eva trayaḥ prakārā ityucyante /
atra vīpsayā punaḥ punarityayogavyavacchedaparatvena niyamaḥ, nānyayogavyavacchedaparatvena /
tasmātpunaḥ punarbadhyamānā eva, na tu punaḥ punareva badhyamānā iti /
tatraikavyañjananibandhodāharaṇaṃ yathā
children.translated_text: The word 'letter' (<s>varṇa</s>) here [means] consonant. The arrangement-design (<s>vinyāsavicchitti</s>) is described (<s>uktā</s>) as threefold, in three ways. What then are those three ways? It is stated: one alone, sometimes two or many letters, being repeatedly bound together, conjoined. Of what kind? — 'With small intervals' (<s>svalpāntara</s>): 'small' means very small, slight; 'interval' means gap — those whose gap is such are so called. Those very [three kinds] are the three ways. Here, by the repetition 'repeatedly' (<s>punaḥ punaḥ</s>), the restriction pertains to the exclusion of non-conjunction, not to the exclusion of other [types of] conjunction. Therefore, 'being bound repeatedly' — not 'being bound only repeatedly.' Therein, an example of a single consonant arrangement:

children.text: dhammillo viniveśitālpakusumaḥ saundaryadhuryaṃ smitaṃ vinyāso vacasāṃ vidagdhamadhuraḥ kaṇṭhe kalaḥ pañcamaḥ /
children.translated_text: A coiffure with a few flowers placed in it, a smile that is the foremost ornament of beauty, an arrangement of words that is charmingly sweet, a melodious sound in the throat,

children.text: līlāmantharatārake ca nayane yātaṃ vilāsālasaṃ ko 'pyevaṃ hariṇīdṛśaḥ smaraśarāpātāvadātaḥ kramaḥ // VjivC_2.1 //
children.translated_text: and eyes with playfully slow pupils that have attained a languid grace — such is the sequence of the doe-eyed one, radiant like the fall of <s>Kāma's</s> (Love's) arrows. // VjivC_2.2 //
An example of one, two, and many [consonants]: as in

[A verse with elaborate repetition of consonant clusters:] the broken <s>elā</s>-creeper trunks, the trembling plantain-stalks, the betel, <s>jambū</s>, citron, the <s>tāla</s> palms, the <s>tālī</s>, the <s>sarala</s> trees — whose swaying dance [they performed];

children.text: vellatkallolahelā viśakala najaḍāḥ kūlakaccheṣu sindhoḥ senāsīmantinīnāmanavarataratābhyāsatāntiṃ samīrāḥ // VjivC_2.2 //
children.translated_text: the rolling surges of waves at the banks and shores of the ocean, like the untiring practice of the restlessness of army-leading women. // VjivC_2.1 (illustrative verse) //
He further distinguishes this very obliquity through another kind of design:
Stops conjoined with class-finals, doubled <s>ta</s>, <s>la</s>, <s>na</s> and the like,
and the remaining [consonants] combined with <s>ra</s> and so forth — [all] shining with propriety to the subject. // Vjiv_2.2 //

children.text:
iyamaparā varṇavinyāsavakratā tridhā tribhiḥ prakārairukteti "ca'-śabdenābhisambandhaḥ /
ke punarasyāstrayaḥ prakārā ityāha---vargāntayoginaḥ sparśāḥ /
sparśāḥ kādayo makāraparyantā vargāstadantaiḥ ṅakārādibhiryogaḥ saṃyogo yeṣāṃ te tathoktāḥ, punaḥ punarbadhyamānāḥ---prathamaḥ prakāraḥ /
ta-la-nādayaḥ takāra-lakāra-nakāra-prabhṛtayo dviruktā dviruccāritā dviguṇāḥ santaḥ, punaḥ punarbadhyamānāḥ---dvitīyaḥ /
tadvyatiriktāḥ śiṣṭāśca vyañjanasaṃjñā ye varṇāste rephaprabhṛtibhiḥ saṃyuktāḥ punaḥ punarbadhyamānāḥ---tṛtīyaḥ /
svalpāntarāḥ parimitavyavahitā iti sarveṣāmabhisabandhaḥ /
te ca kīdṛśāḥ---prastutaucityaśobhinaḥ /
prastutaṃ varṇyamānaṃ vastu tasya yadaucityamucitabhāvastena śobhante ye te yathoktāḥ /
na punarvarṇasāvarṇyavyasanitāmātreṇopanibaddhāḥ prastutaucityamlānatvakāriṇaḥ /
prastutaucityaśobhitvāt kutracitparuṣarasaprastāve tādṛśānevābhyanujānāti /
atha prathamaprākārodāharaṇaṃ yathā
children.translated_text: This is another obliquity in letter arrangement, said to be threefold, in three ways — connected by the word 'and' (<s>ca</s>). What then are its three ways? He says: 'Stops conjoined with class-finals' (<s>vargāntayoginaḥ sparśāḥ</s>): stops — the letters from <s>ka</s> to <s>ma</s> — those that have conjunction with their class-finals, the <s>ṅa</s>-syllable and so forth — being repeatedly bound together: this is the first kind. '<s>Ta</s>, <s>la</s>, <s>na</s> and the like doubled' — the letters <s>ta</s>, <s>la</s>, <s>na</s> and so forth, being doubled, pronounced twice, being repeatedly bound together: the second kind. 'And the remaining' — other consonants, combined with <s>ra</s> and so forth, being repeatedly bound together: the third kind. 'With small intervals' — with limited gaps — is connected with all [three]. And of what kind are they? — 'Shining with propriety to the subject' (<s>prastutaucityaśobhin</s>): the subject is the matter being described; the propriety to it — the state of being fitting — by that they shine; [letters] that are not merely employed out of a passion for consonantal alliteration, which would cause the fading of propriety to the subject. Because of their shining with propriety to the subject, in certain contexts where the <s>raudra</s> (fierce) or similar <s>rasa</s> is being presented, he approves of exactly such [harsh combinations]. Now, an example of the first kind:
The bees hum sweetly in the lotus-ponds, their bodies tinted tawny by the pollen of the awakened day-lotuses;
and this new orb of the sun, resting on the eastern mountain, shines like a fresh <s>bandhujīva</s> flower-petal. // VjivC_2.3 //
And for example:
'Plantain-stalks, betel, <s>jambū</s>, citron' — thus. // VjivC_2.4 //
Or for example:
'Of those beautiful with the clustering drops of nectar from the lotus of the heart of <s>Sarasvatī</s>.' // VjivC_2.5 //
Thus.
An example of the second kind: 'First the reddish hue' // VjivC_2.6 //

children.text:
ityasya dvitīyacaturtho pādau /
tṛtīyaprakārodāharaṇamasyaiva tṛtīyaḥ pādaḥ /
yathā vā
children.translated_text: — this is the second and fourth quarter-verse [of that example]. An example of the third kind is the third quarter-verse of this very [example]. Or for example:
'A smile that is the foremost ornament of beauty.' // VjivC_2.7 //

And as [an example of propriety], due to the proximity of the word '<s>kahlāra</s>' (white lotus), the non-use of the word '<s>hlāda</s>' (delight) [which would break the consonantal pattern]. An example of such conjuncts in the context of the fierce <s>rasa</s>:

children.text: uttāmyattālavaśca pratapati taraṇāvāṃśavī tāpatandrīmadridroṇīkuṭīre kuhariṇi hariṇārātayo yāpayanti // VjivC_2.8 //
children.translated_text: The languishing palm trees, the sun blazing with heat-weariness, in the hollowed mountain-valley caves the enemies of deer (i.e., lions) while away [the time]. // VjivC_2.8 //
He explains this very [obliquity] through another kind of variety:
Sometimes, even without interval, being the basis of charm,

children.text: sā svarāṇāmasārūpyāt parāṃ puṣṇāti vakratām // Vjiv_2.3 //
children.translated_text: it nourishes a supreme obliquity through the non-similarity of vowels. // Vjiv_2.3 //

children.text:
kvacidaniyataprāyavākyaikadeśe kasmiṃścidavyavadhāne 'pi vyavadhānābhāve 'pyekasya dvayoḥ samuditayośca bahūnāṃ vā punaḥ punarbadhyamānānāmeṣāṃ manoharinibandhanā hṛdayāvarjakavinyāsā bhavati /
kācidevaṃ saṃpadyata ityarthaḥ /
yamakavyavahāro 'tra na pravartate, tasya niyatasthānatayā vyavasthānāt /
svarairavyavadhānamatra na vivakṣitam, tasyānupapatteḥ /
tatraikasyāvyavadhānodāharaṇaṃ yathā
children.translated_text: Sometimes, in a portion of a sentence that is mostly unfixed, even without interval — that is, even in the absence of a gap — of one, of two combined, or even of many [consonants], being repeatedly bound, the charming arrangement, the heart-captivating design, comes about. A certain [obliquity] is thus produced — this is the meaning. The practice of <s>yamaka</s> (rhyming repetition) does not apply here, since that is established by being restricted to fixed positions. The non-interval of vowels is not intended here, since that is impossible. Therein, an example of a single [consonant] without interval:
'The eye is leftward, dark with collyrium; the breast [has] a spreading mark of [nail-]wound.' // VjivC_2.9 //
Of two, for example:
'In the spread of the charming areca-tree creepers intertwined with betel, with their attendant [vines], drinking repeatedly a cup made from a plantain leaf, with coconut fruit...' // VjivC_2.10 //

children.text: sevyantāṃ vyomayātrāśramajalajayinaḥ sainyasīmantinībhi- rdātyubavyūhakelīkalitakuhakuhārāvakāntā vanāntāḥ // VjivC_2.10 //
children.translated_text: 'Let the army-leading women attend upon [these groves], conquering the fatigue of journeys through the sky, charming with the cooing sounds arranged in the play of battle-array formations.' // VjivC_2.10 (cont.) //
Or for example:

children.text: ayi pibata cakorāḥ kṛtsanamunnamya kaṇṭhān kramukavalanacañcaccañcavaścandrikāmbhaḥ /
children.translated_text: O <s>cakora</s> birds, drink the moonlight-water fully, raising your necks, moving swiftly with mouthfuls of areca,

children.text: virahavidhuritānāṃ jīvitatrāṇahetor- bhavati hariṇalakṣmā yena tejodaridraḥ // VjivC_2.11 //
children.translated_text: for the sake of preserving the lives of those afflicted by separation — for that [moon] marked with a deer becomes poor in radiance. // VjivC_2.11 //
Of many, for example:
'The swaying dance of the <s>sarala</s> trees, the <s>tāla</s> palms, the <s>tālī</s>...' — thus. // VjivC_2.12 //
From the word 'even' (<s>api</s>), [we understand] sometimes even with interval.
Of two, with [interval], for example:

children.text: svasthāḥ santu vasanta te ratipateragresarā vāsarāḥ // VjivC_2.13 //
children.translated_text: 'May the days, the heralds of <s>Ratipati</s> (the god of love), remain at ease in your spring.' // VjivC_2.13 //
Of many, even with interval, for example:
'The startled <s>cātaka</s> bird, the darkened sky, at the end of the rainy season.' // VjivC_2.14 //

children.text:
sā svarāṇāmasārūpyāt seyamanantaroktā svarānāmakārādīnāmasārūpyādasādṛśyāt kvacitkasmiṃścidāvartamānasamudāyaikadeśe parāmanyāṃ vakratāṃ kāmapi puṣṇāti puṣyatītyarthaḥ /
yathā
children.translated_text: That [variety of alliteration], due to the dissimilarity of vowels — the one just mentioned, due to the dissimilarity, the non-identity, of vowels such as 'a' and the like — in some particular position within a recurring aggregate, fosters some other obliqueness, i.e., nourishes it — this is the meaning. For example —
'<s>rājīvajīvitaśvare</s>' (Lord of lotus-life) // VjivC_2.15 //
Or for example —
'<s>dhūsarasariti</s>' (in a grey river) // VjivC_2.16 //
Or for example —
'<s>svasthāḥ santu vasante</s>' (may they be well in spring) // VjivC_2.17 //
Or for example —
'<s>tālatālī</s>' (palm trees and <s>tālī</s> trees) // VjivC_2.18 //

children.text:
so 'yamubhayaprakāro 'pi varṇavinyāsavakratāviśiṣṭāvayavavinyāso yamakābhāsaḥ saṃniveśaviśeṣo muktākalāpamadhyaprotamaṇiyamayapadakabandhabandhuraḥ sutarāṃ sahṛdayahṛdayahāritāṃ pratipadyate /
tadidamuktam
children.translated_text: This [alliteration], of both kinds, being a specific component-arrangement distinguished by the obliqueness of phonemic arrangement — this semblance of <s>yamaka</s> (punning repetition), this particular configuration — resplendent like a composition of gem-studded words strung through the center of a pearl necklace — exceedingly attains the capacity to captivate the hearts of the sensitive. This is what was stated —
'Where poets, unsatisfied with the ornamentation of an ornament,
bind yet another ornamentation, like the setting of gems within a necklace.' // VjivC_2.19 //

children.text:
iti /
etāmeva vividhaprakārāṃ vakratāṃ viśinaṣṭi, yadevaṃvidhavakṣyamāṇaviśeṣaṇaviśiṣṭā vidhātavyeti---
children.translated_text: He now specifies this very obliqueness of various kinds — [saying] that it must be fashioned as distinguished by the following qualifications —
Not fashioned with excessive insistence, nor adorned with undelicate [sounds],
shining with the abandonment of what has been used before and the introduction of what is new. // Vjiv_2.4 //

children.text:
nātinirbandhavihitā---"nirbandha'-śabdo 'tra vyasanitāyāṃ vartate /
tenātinirbandhena punaḥ punarāvartanavyasanitayā na vihitā, aprayatnaviracitetyarthaḥ /
vyasanitayā prayatnaviracane hi prastutaucityaparihāṇervācyavācakayoḥ parasparaspardhitvalakṣaṇasāhityavirahaḥ paryavasyati /
yathā
children.translated_text: 'Not fashioned with excessive insistence' — the word 'insistence' (<s>nirbandha</s>) here applies to obsessive attachment. Therefore, 'not fashioned' through excessive insistence, through the obsessive attachment of repeated recurrence — meaning: fashioned without effort. For when fashioned with obsessive effort, the neglect of propriety to the subject matter results in the loss of the togetherness (<s>sāhitya</s>) characterized by the mutual rivalry of the expressed and the expression. For example —
'<s>bhaṇa taruṇi</s>' (speak, young woman) and so on // VjivC_2.20 //
'Nor adorned with undelicate [sounds]' — not ornamented with undelicate, non-refined syllables. For example —
'<s>śīrṇaghrāṇāṅghri</s>' (with shattered nose and feet) and so on // VjivC_2.21 //

children.text:
tadevaṃ kīdṛśī tarhi kartavyetyāha---pūrvāvṛttaparityāganūtanāvartanojjvalā pūrvamāvṛttānāṃ punaḥ punarviracitānāṃ parityāgena prahāṇena nūtanānāmabhinavānāṃ varṇānāmāvartanena punaḥ punaḥ parigraheṇa ca tadevamubhābhyāṃ prakārābhyāmujjvalā bhrājiṣṇuḥ /
yathā
children.translated_text: This being so, what kind should it then be? — he says: 'shining with the abandonment of what has been used before and the introduction of what is new' — by the abandonment, the discarding of those [phonemic patterns] that have been used before, fashioned again and again; and by the introduction, the repeated adoption of new, fresh phonemes — thus, shining through both methods, resplendent. For example —

children.text: etāṃ paśya purastaṭīmahi kila krīḍākirāto haraḥ kodaṇḍena kirīṭinā sarabhasaṃ cūḍāntare tāḍitaḥ /
children.translated_text: '"Behold this cliff-face before us! <s>Hara</s> was indeed a hunter in his sport, and was struck forcefully on the crest of his crown by the diademed one [<s>Arjuna</s>] with his bow" —

children.text: ityākarṇya kathādbhutaṃ himanīdhāvadrau subhadrāpater mandaṃ mandamakāri yena nijayorderdaṇḍayormaṇḍanam // VjivC_2.22 //
children.translated_text: hearing this astonishing tale on the snow-mountain, by <s>Subhadrā's</s> husband [<s>Arjuna</s>], slowly, slowly was made the adornment of his own two arms.' // VjivC_2.22 //
Or for example —
'In the calls of the swans' and so on // VjivC_2.23 //
And also —
'This, slightly ripened' and so forth, etc. // VjivC_2.24 //
Or for example —
[Prakrit:] '<s>ṇamaha dasāṇaṇasarahasakaratuliavalantaselabhaavihalaṃ</s> /
<s>vevatathorathaṇaharaharakaakaṇṭhaggahaṃ goriṃ</s>' // VjivC_2.25 //
[Sanskrit shadow:] 'Bow to <s>Gaurī</s>, trembling with fear of the mountain shaken by the force of <s>Daśānana's</s> (<s>Rāvaṇa's</s>) hand,
whose throat was clasped by <s>Hara</s> (<s>Śiva</s>) while trembling with her heavy breasts.'
This is the <s>chāyā</s> (Sanskrit rendering).
Having thus explained this obliqueness of phonemic arrangement, he now concludes it —
Following the lustre of phonemes, conforming to the qualities and styles,
endowed with the variety of <s>vṛttis</s> (compositional modes) — thus it has been spoken of by the ancients. // Vjiv_2.5 //

children.text:
varṇānāmakṣarāṇāṃ yā chāyā kāntiḥ śravyatādiguṇasaṃpattayā hetubhūtayā yadanusaraṇamanusāraḥ prāpyasvarūpānupraveśastena /
guṇamārgāṃśca sukumāraprabhṛtīnanuvartate yā sā tathoktā /
tatra guṇānāmāntaramyāt prathamamupanyasanam, guṇadvāreṇaiva mārgānusaraṇopapatteḥ /
tadayamatrārthaḥ---yadyaṣā varṇavinyāsavakratā vyañjanacchāyānusāreṇaiva, tathāpi pratiniyataguṇaviśiṣṭānāṃ mārgāṇāṃ guṇānuvartanadvāreṇa yathā svarūpānupraveśaṃ vidadhāti tathā vidhātavyeti /
tata eva ca tasyāstannibandhanāḥ pravitatāḥ prakārāḥ samullasanti /
cirantanaiḥ punaḥ saiva svātantryeṇa vṛttivaicitryayukteti proktā /
vṛttīnāmupanāgarikādīnāṃ yad vaicitryaṃ vicitrabhāvaḥ svaniṣṭhasaṃkhyābhedabhinnatvaṃ tena yuktā samanviteti cirantanaiḥ pūrvasūribhirabhihitā /
tadidamatra tātparyam---yadasyāḥ sakalāguṇa svarūpānusaraṇasamanvayena sukumārādimārgānuvartanāyattavṛtteḥ pāratantryamaparigaṇitaprakāratvaṃ caitadubhayamapyavaśyaṃbhāvi tasmādapāratantryaṃ parimitaprakāratvaṃ ceti nāticaturastram /
nanu ca prathamameko dvāvityādinā prakāreṇa parimitān prakārān svatantratvaṃ ca svayameva vyākhyāya kimetaduktamiti cennaiṣa doṣaḥ, yasmāllakṣaṇakārairyasya kasyācitpadārthasya samudāyaparāyattavṛtteḥ paravyutpattaye prathamamapoddhārabuddhyā svatantratayā svarūpamullikhyate, tataḥ samudāyāntarbhāvo bhaviṣyatītyalamatiprasaṅgena /
yeyaṃ varṇavinyāsavakratā nāma vācakālaṅkṛtiḥ sthānaniyamābhāvāt sakalavākyaviṣayatvena samāmnāt, saiva prakārāntaraviśiṣṭā niyatasthānatayopanibadhyamānā kimapi vaicitryāntaramābadhnātītyāha---
children.translated_text: The lustre (<s>chāyā</s>) of phonemes, i.e., of syllables — their radiance produced by the excellence of qualities such as euphoniousness — the 'following' of that, the entering into the attainable essential nature [of each style] through that [lustre]. And [this obliqueness] 'conforms to the qualities and styles' — to the delicate (<s>sukumāra</s>) style and so forth — one that does so is thus described. Therein, the qualities are mentioned first, since conformity to the styles is justified precisely through the qualities. The meaning here is: even though this obliqueness of phonemic arrangement [operates] through the mere following of the lustre of phonemes, still it should be fashioned so as to enter the essential nature of styles distinguished by specific qualities, through the medium of conforming to those qualities. And from that very [principle], the varieties founded upon that shine forth in profusion. By the ancients, however, this very thing was spoken of independently as 'endowed with the variety of <s>vṛttis</s>.' The variety of <s>vṛttis</s>, i.e., the <s>upanāgarikā</s> (urbane) and the other [modes], is their varied character — their differentiation based on their own inherent number of kinds; 'endowed with' that means joined with it — thus it was stated by the ancients, the earlier authorities. The purport here is this: since its dependence upon the complete conformity to all qualities and the variety of its types arising from its adherence to the delicate and other styles — both of these are inevitable — therefore, independence and a fixed number of types are not particularly clever [claims]. But surely, you yourself first explained its fixed types by saying 'first, two' and so forth, and its independence — so what is the point of this [observation]? This is not a fault, because when the makers of definitions first outline the essential nature of some entity — which in reality has an operation dependent upon a composite — independently, by way of abstractive cognition, for the purpose of the reader's understanding, thereafter its inclusion within the composite will follow. Enough with this over-elaboration. This obliqueness of phonemic arrangement, which is the ornamentation of the expression, being taught as pertaining to all sentences due to the absence of any restriction of position — this very thing, when distinguished by another variety and being bound to a fixed position, produces some further variety. He says —
That which has identical phonemes, a different meaning, is clear, is pleasing to the ear,
is endowed with propriety, and shines in fixed positions such as the beginning and so forth — // Vjiv_2.6 //
<s>yamaka</s> (punning repetition) by name — some variety of this [phonemic obliqueness] is observed.
But it is not extensively treated here, due to the absence of any [additional] beauty [beyond phonemic obliqueness]. // Vjiv_2.7 //

children.text:
ko 'pyasyāḥ prakāraḥ paridṛśyate, asyāḥ pūrvoktāyāḥ, ko 'pyapūrvaḥ prabhedo vibhāvyate /
ko 'sāvityāha---yamakaṃ nāma /
yamakamiti yasya prasiddhiḥ /
tacca kīdṛśam---samānavarṇam /
samānāḥ sarūpāḥ sadṛśaśrutayo varṇā yasmin tattathoktam /
evamekasya dvayorbahūnāṃ sadṛśaśrutīnāṃ vyavahitamavyavahitaṃ vā yadupanibandhanaṃ tadeva yamakamityucyate /
tadevamekarūpe saṃsthānadvaye satyapi---anyārthaṃ bhinnābhidheyam /
anyacca kīdṛśam---prasādi prasādaguṇayuktaṃ jhagiti vākyārthasamarpakam, akadarthanābodhyamiti yāvat /
śrutipeśalamityatadeva viśiṣyate---śrutiḥ śravaṇendriyaṃ tatra peśalaṃ rañjakam, akaṭhoraśabdaviracitam /
kīdṛśam---aucityayuktam /
aucityaṃ varṇyamānasya vastunaḥ svabhāvotkarṣastena saṃyuktaṃ samanvitam /
yatra yamakopanibandhanavyasanitvenāpyaucityamaparimlānamityarthaḥ /
tadeva viśeṣaṇāntareṇa viśinaṣṭi---ādyādiniyatasthānaśobhi yat /
ādirādiryeṣāṃ te tathoktāḥ prathamamadhyāntāstānyeva niyatāni sthānāni viśiṣṭāḥ saṃniveśāstaiḥ śobhate bhrājate yattathoktam /
atrādyādayaḥ saṃbandhiśabdāḥ pādādi bhirviśeṣaṇīyāḥ /
sa tu prakāraḥ proktalakṣaṇasaṃpadupeto 'pi bhavan iha nātipratanyate granthe 'sminnātivistāryate /
kutaḥ---śobhāntarābhāvāt /
sthānaniyamavyatiriktasyānyasya śobhāntarasya chāyāntarasyāsaṃbhavādityarthaḥ /
asya ca varṇavinyāsavaicitryavyatirekeṇānyatkiñcidapi jīvitāntaraṃ na paridṛśyate /
tenānantaroktālaṅkṛtiprakārataiva yuktā /
udāharaṇānyatraśiśupālavadhe caturthe sarge samarpakāṇi kānicideva yamakāni, raghuvaṃśe vā vasantavarṇane /
evaṃ padāvayavānāṃ varṇānāṃ vinyāsavakrabhāve vicārite varṇasamudāyātmakasya padasya ca vakrabhāvavicāraḥ prāptāvasaraḥ /
tatra padapūrvārdhasya tāvadvakratāprākārāḥ kiyantaḥ saṃbhavantīti prakramate---
children.translated_text: 'Some variety of this is observed' — 'of this,' i.e., of the previously mentioned [phonemic obliqueness]; 'some unprecedented variety is discerned.' What is it? — he says: '<s>yamaka</s> by name' — that which is well-known as <s>yamaka</s>. And what is it like? — 'having identical phonemes.' Those that are identical, i.e., of the same form, similar in sound, are its phonemes — it is thus described. In this way, the binding together of one, two, or many similar-sounding [phonemes], whether separated or contiguous — that itself is called <s>yamaka</s>. Even though the configuration is thus of identical form in both positions — 'of different meaning,' i.e., with different signifieds. And what else? — 'clear' (<s>prasādi</s>) — endowed with the quality of clarity, yielding the sentence-meaning instantly — meaning: comprehensible without difficulty. 'Pleasing to the ear' — this further qualifies it: the ear is the organ of hearing; 'pleasing' therein means delighting it — fashioned with non-harsh words. Of what kind? — 'endowed with propriety' (<s>aucityayukta</s>). The propriety is the natural excellence of the subject being described; endowed with, i.e., joined with that. Where even through the obsessive effort of constructing <s>yamaka</s>, the propriety remains unfaded — this is the meaning. He qualifies it with another attribute: 'shining in fixed positions such as the beginning and so forth.' Those whose beginning is the beginning — the beginning, middle, and end — those very [positions] are the fixed positions, the specific configurations; by those it shines, it gleams — it is thus described. Here, 'beginning and so forth' are relational words to be qualified by 'of the quarter-verse' and the like. That variety, even though possessing the full set of the stated characteristics, 'is not extensively treated here' — in this treatise it is not elaborated at length. Why? — 'due to the absence of any [additional] beauty.' Because apart from the restriction of position, no other additional beauty, no other lustre, is possible — this is the meaning. And apart from the variety of phonemic arrangement, no other life-force whatsoever is observed in it. Therefore, its [classification as] a variety of the previously stated kind of ornamentation is fitting. Examples here are: in the <s>Śiśupālavadha</s>, in the fourth canto, there are a few <s>yamakas</s> that are exemplary; or in the <s>Raghuvaṃśa</s>, in the description of spring. Having thus examined the oblique nature of the arrangement of phonemes — which are components of words — the examination of the oblique nature of the word itself, which is an aggregate of phonemes, has now become timely. Therein, he first undertakes [to determine] how many kinds of obliqueness of the first half of the word are possible —
Where the pregnancy of the superimposition of an inconceivable property upon the conventional [meaning],
or the pregnancy of the superimposition of a surpassing quality upon an actual property, is perceived — // Vjiv_2.8 //
with the intention of expressing an extraordinary superiority that is praiseworthy and that eclipses the mundane,
of the expressed meaning — there is declared a certain obliqueness of conventional variety. // Vjiv_2.9 //

children.text:
yatra rūḍherasaṃbhāvyadharmādhyāropagarbhatā pratīyate /
śabdasya niyatavṛttitā nāma dharmo rūḍhirucyate, rohaṇaṃ rūḍhiriti kṛtvā /
sā ca dviprakārā saṃbhavati--niyatasāmānyavṛttitā niyataviśeṣavṛttitā ca /
tena rūḍhiśabdenātra rūḍhipradhānaḥ śabdo 'bhidhīyate, dharmadharmiṇorabhedopacāradarśanāt /
yatra yasmin viṣaye rūḍhiśabdasya asaṃbhāvyaḥ saṃbhāvayitumaśakyo yo dharmaḥ kaścitparispandastasyādhyāropaḥ samarpaṇaṃ garbho 'bhiprāyo yasya sa tathoktastasya bhāvastattā sā pratīyate pratipādyate /
yatreti saṃbandhaḥ /
saddharmātiśayāropagarbhatvaṃ vā /
saṃścāsau dharmaśca saddharmaḥ vidyamānaḥ padārthasya parispandastasmin yasya kasyacidapūrvasyātiśayasyādbhutarūpasya mahimna āropaḥ samarpaṇaṃ garbho 'prāyo yasya sa tathoktasya bhāvastattvam /
tacca vā yasmin pratīyate /
kena hetunā---lokoktaratiraskāraślādhyotkarṣābhidhitsayā /
lokottaraḥ sarvātiśāyī yastiraskāraḥ khalīkaraṇaṃ ślādhyaśca spṛhaṇīyo ya utkarṣaḥ sātiśayatvaṃ tayorabhidhitsā abhidhātumicchā vaktukāmatā tayā /
kasya vācyasya /
rūḍhiśabdasya vācyo yo 'bhidheyor'thastasya /
socyate kathyate kāpyalaukikī rūḍhivaicitryavakratā /
rūḍhiśabdasyaivaṃvidhena vaicitryeṇavicitrabhāvena vakratā vakrabhāvaḥ /
tadidamatra tātparyam---yatsāmānyavicitrasaṃsparśināṃ śabdānāmanumānavanniyataviśeṣāliṅganaṃ yadyapi svabhāvādeva na kiñcidapi saṃbhavati, tathāpyanayā yuktyā kavivivakṣitaniyataviśeṣaniṣṭhatāṃ nīyamānāḥ kāmapi camatkārakāritāṃ pratipadyante /
yathā
children.translated_text: 'Where the pregnancy of the superimposition of an inconceivable property upon the conventional [meaning] is perceived.' The property of a word's fixed usage is called convention (<s>rūḍhi</s>) — from the root 'to grow.' And that is of two kinds: fixed usage in a general sense and fixed usage in a particular sense. Therefore, by the word 'convention,' what is meant here is a word that is primarily conventional, since figurative non-differentiation of property and property-bearer is observed. 'Where' — in which domain — the superimposition, i.e., the attribution, of a property that is inconceivable, i.e., impossible to conceive, of a conventional word — some activity — of which [word] the pregnancy, i.e., the implied intention, is that; the state of being that — that 'is perceived,' i.e., is demonstrated. 'Where' — this is the syntactic connection. 'Or the pregnancy of the superimposition of a surpassing quality upon an actual property.' An actual property (<s>saddharma</s>) — an existing activity of the object — upon that, the superimposition, i.e., the attribution of some unprecedented, extraordinary, wondrous greatness — of which [expression] the pregnancy, i.e., the implied intention, is that; the state of being that, that reality. And that too — 'where it is perceived.' For what reason? — 'with the intention of expressing an extraordinary superiority that is praiseworthy and that eclipses the mundane.' 'Extraordinary' means all-surpassing; 'eclipsing' means overcoming; 'praiseworthy' means desirable; 'superiority' means surpassing excellence — the intention to express, to declare, to want to state both of those. Of what? — of the expressed meaning — the referent that is the expressed meaning of the conventional word. 'There is declared' — there is spoken of — 'a certain extraordinary obliqueness of conventional variety.' The obliqueness, the oblique nature, through such variety, such varied character, of the conventional word. The purport here is this: although words that touch upon a general variety — like inference — cannot by their very nature grasp any fixed particular at all, nevertheless, when by this device they are brought to bear on a specific particular intended by the poet, they attain a certain capacity to produce wonder. For example —

children.text: tālā jāanti guṇā jālāte sahiaehi gheppanti /
children.translated_text: [Prakrit:] 'Then qualities arise — when they are grasped by the sensitive;
favored by the rays of the sun, lotuses become lotuses.' // VjivC_2.26 //

children.text: tadā jāyante guṇā yadā te sahṛdayairgṛhyante /
children.translated_text: [Sanskrit shadow:] 'Then qualities arise — when they are grasped by the sensitive;
favored by the rays of the sun, lotuses become lotuses.'
This is the <s>chāyā</s> (Sanskrit rendering).

children.text:
pratīyate iti kriyāpadavaicitryasyāyamabhiprāyo yadevaṃvidhe viṣaye śabdānāṃ vācakatvena na vyāpāraḥ, api tu vastvantaravatpratītikāritvamātreṇeti yuktiyuktamapyetadiha nātipratanyate /
yasyād dhvanikāreṇa vyaṅgyavyañjakabhāvo 'tra sutarāṃ samarthitastat kiṃ paunaruktyena /
sā ca rūḍhivaicitryavakratā mukyatayā dviprakārā saṃbhavati---yatra rūḍhivācyor'thaḥ svayameva ātmanyutkarṣaṃ nikarṣaṃ vā samāropayitukāmaḥ kavinopanibadhyate, tasyānyo vā kaścidvakteti /
yathā
children.translated_text: The purport of using the word 'is perceived' as the verbal form is this: in such a domain, the operation of words is not as signifiers [in the direct sense], but rather, as with another entity, merely as producers of cognition — this, though logically sound, is not extensively elaborated here. Since the <s>Dhvani</s> theorist [<s>Ānandavardhana</s>] has thoroughly established the relation of suggestor and suggested here — what then is the point of repetition? And this obliqueness of conventional variety is primarily of two kinds: where the expressed meaning of the conventional word, wishing to superimpose upon itself either superiority or inferiority, is represented by the poet as [doing so]; or someone else is the speaker. For example —

children.text: snigdhaśyāmalakāntiliptaviyato velladvalākā ghanā vātāḥ śīkariṇaḥ payodasuhṛdāmānandakekāḥ kalāḥ /
children.translated_text: The clouds with smooth dark beauty smearing the sky, the rolling <s>valākā</s> cranes, the moisture-laden winds, the joyful peacock-cries — songs of the rain-cloud's friends —

children.text: kāmaṃ santu dṛḍhaṃ kaṭhorahṛdayo rāmo 'smi sarvaṃ sahe vaidehī tu kathaṃ bhaviṣyati hahā hā devi dhīrā bhava // VjivC_2.27 //
children.translated_text: let them all be! I am <s>Rāma</s>, firmly hard-hearted; I endure everything. But what will become of <s>Vaidehī</s>? Alas! Alas, O <s>Devī</s>, be courageous! // <s>Vjīv</s>C 2.27 //

children.text:
atra "rāma'-śabdena "dṛḍhaṃ kaṭhorahṛdayaḥ' "sarvaṃ sahe' iti yadubhābhyāṃ pratipādayituṃ na pāryate, tadevaṃvidhavividhoddīpanavibhāvavibhavasahanasāmarthyakāraṇaṃ duḥsahajanakarājaputrīviraha vyathāvisaṃṣṭhule 'pi samaye nirapatrapaprāṇaparirakṣāvaicakṣaṇyalakṣaṇaṃ saṃjñāpadanibandhanaṃ kimapyasaṃbhāvyamasādhāraṇaṃ krauryaṃ pratīyate /
vaidehītyanena jaladharasamayasundarapadārthasaṃdarśanāsahatvasamarpakaṃ sahajasaukumāryasulabhaṃ kimapi kātaratvaṃ tasyāḥ samarthyate /
etadeva /
ca pūrvasmādviśeṣābhidhāyinaḥ "tu'-śabdasya jīvitam /
vidyamānadharmātiśayādhyāropagarbhatvaṃ yathā
children.translated_text: Here, through the word '<s>Rāma</s>' — what cannot be conveyed by both [statements] 'firmly hard-hearted' and 'I endure everything' — namely, a certain inconceivable, extraordinary cruelty that is the cause of the capacity to endure the splendor of such manifold stimulant-factors (<s>vibhāvas</s>) and excitants (<s>uddīpanas</s>), characterized by the shameless skill of preserving one's life even at a time overwhelmed by the unbearable pain of separation from the Princess born of the Earth — [and that cruelty is] based on the designation [Rāma, meaning 'one who delights'] — this is suggested. By [the word] '<s>Vaidehī</s>' (daughter of <s>Videha</s>), a certain timidity — easily arising from her innate delicacy, and conveying her inability to endure the sight of beautiful things in the rain-cloud season — is established for her. And this indeed is the life of the particle 'tu' (but), which conveys a distinction from what precedes. [Another type] whose essence contains the superimposition of an excess of existing attributes — for example:
Then, laughing, the son of the king of the earth spoke again to <s>Purandara</s> (<s>Indra</s>), his fear departed:

children.text: gṛhāṇa śastraṃ yadi sarga eṣa te na khalvanirjitya raghuṃ kṛtī bhavān // VjivC_2.28 //
children.translated_text: 'Take up your weapon, if this is your creation — for surely you will not succeed without conquering <s>Raghu</s>.' // <s>Vjīv</s>C 2.28 //

children.text:
"raghu'-śabdenātra sarvatrāpratihataprabhāvasyāpi surapatestathāvidhādhyavasāyavyaghātasāmarthyanibandhanaḥ ko 'pi svapauruṣātiśayaḥ pratīyate /
prahasyetyanenaitadevopabṛṃhitam /
anyo vaktā yatra tatrodāharaṇaṃ yathā
children.translated_text: By the word '<s>Raghu</s>' here, a certain extraordinary excess of personal valor is suggested, based on the capacity to thwart the determination of even the lord of the gods whose power is everywhere irresistible. By 'laughing' (prahasya), this very [suggestion] is reinforced. Where there is another speaker — an example of that is as follows:

children.text: ājñā śakraśikhāmaṇipraṇayinī śāstrāṇi cakṣurnavaṃ bhaktirbhūtapatau pinākini padaṃ laṅketi divyā purī /
children.translated_text: His command wins the affection of the crest-jewel of <s>Śakra</s> (<s>Indra</s>); the scriptures are his fresh eye; his devotion is to the Lord of Beings, the Trident-bearer (<s>Śiva</s>); his domain is <s>Laṅkā</s>, that divine city;

children.text: saṃbhūtirdruhiṇānvaye ca tadaho nedṛgvaro labhyate syāccedeṣa na rāvaṇaḥ kva nu punaḥ sarvatra sarve guṇāḥ // VjivC_2.29 //
children.translated_text: his birth is in the lineage of <s>Druhiṇa</s> (<s>Brahmā</s>) — alas, such a bridegroom cannot be obtained! If only this one were not <s>Rāvaṇa</s>! But alas, where are all virtues in all things? // <s>Vjīv</s>C 2.29 //

By the word '<s>Rāvaṇa</s>' here, there is suggested a certain incorrigibleness that is the cause of eclipsing the complete aggregate of all the choicest qualities — characterized by the wealth of good lineage, discrimination, virtuous conduct, power, enjoyment, and prosperity — distinct from the universally notorious misconduct of the ten-headed one,

children.text: atraiva vidhyamānaguṇātiśayāvyāropagarbhatvaṃ yathā--- rāmo 'sau bhuvaneṣu vikramaguṇaiḥ prāptaḥ prasiddhiṃ parām // VjivC_2.30 //
children.translated_text: and which is the basis of his undesirability. In this very [passage], an example of the essence containing the superimposition of an excess of existing attributes: '<s>Rāma</s> has attained supreme fame in the worlds through the virtues of valor.' // <s>Vjīv</s>C 2.30 //

children.text:
atra "rāma'-śabdena sakalatribhuvanātiśāyī rāvaṇānucaravismayāspadaṃ śauryātiśayaḥ pratīyate /
eṣā ca rūḍhivaicitryavakratā pratīyamānadharmabāhulyād bahuprakārā bhidyate /
tacca svayamevotprekṣaṇīyam /
yathā
children.translated_text: Here, by the word '<s>Rāma</s>', an excess of heroic valor is suggested — surpassing the entire three worlds, an object of astonishment even to <s>Rāvaṇa</s>'s attendants. And this <s>rūḍhivaicitryavakratā</s> (conventional-usage-variety obliqueness) divides into many types due to the multiplicity of suggested attributes. And that should be imagined by oneself. For example —
The one who saw across the ocean of learning, from <s>Raghu</s>'s presence, his purpose not yet fulfilled — [thinking] 'a wealth for a worthy purpose' —

children.text: gato vadānyāntaramityayaṃ me mā bhūtparīvādanavāvatāraḥ // VjivC_2.31 //
children.translated_text: 'He has gone to another generous patron' — may this thought of mine not become an occasion for reproach! // <s>Vjīv</s>C 2.31 //

children.text:
"raghu'-śabdenātra tribhuvanātiśāyyaudā ryātirekaḥ pratīyate /
etasyāṃ vakratāyāmayameva paramārtho yat sāmānyamātraniṣṭhatāmapākṛtya kavivivakṣitaviśeṣapratipādanasāmarthyalakṣaṇaḥ śobhātiśayaḥ samullāsyate /
saṃjñāśabdānāṃ niyatārthaniṣṭhatvāt sāmānyaviśeṣabhāvo na kaścit saṃbhavatīti na vaktavyam /
yasmātteṣāmapyavasthāsahastrasādhāraṇavṛttervācyasya niyatadaśāviśeṣavṛttiniṣṭhatā satkavivivakṣitā saṃbhavatyeva, svaraśrutinyāyena lagnāṃśukanyāyena ceti /
evaṃ rūḍhivakratāṃ vivecya kramaprāptasamanvayāṃ paryāyavakratāṃ vivinakti---
children.translated_text: By the word '<s>Raghu</s>' here, an extraordinary excess of generosity surpassing the three worlds is suggested. In this type of obliqueness, the essential purport is this: setting aside the mere generality [of meaning], the superabundance of beauty, characterized by the capacity to convey the particular [meaning] intended by the poet, is brought to efflorescence. One should not say that since proper names have a fixed referent, no general-particular distinction is possible — because even for those [proper names], since their function is common to a thousand states, a fixation of the expressed meaning upon a particular state can be intended by a good poet, according to the principle of 'accent and [Vedic] text' and the principle of 'the clinging garment.' Having thus analyzed <s>rūḍhivakratā</s> (conventional obliqueness), [the author] proceeds to analyze <s>paryāyavakratā</s> (synonym obliqueness), which comes in due order —
That [synonym] which is the closest to the expressed [meaning], which nourishes the excellence of that [meaning],
which, through the touch of another shade of lovely beauty, is capable of adorning it; // <s>Vjīv</s> 2.10 //
which, even by itself as a qualifier, is deft in elevating the beauty of its own lustre;
and which is uttered with the essence of being a vessel for an inconceivable sense; // <s>Vjīv</s> 2.11 //
and which is the basis of the captivating refinement of ornamental figures —
[such] a synonym, by that variety, constitutes the supreme synonym-obliqueness (<s>paryāyavakratā</s>). // <s>Vjīv</s> 2.12 //

children.text:
pūrvoktaviśeṣaṇaviśiṣṭaḥ kāvyaviṣaye paryāyastena hetunā yadvaicitryaṃ yo vicitrabhāvo vicchittiviśeṣaḥ sā parā prakṛṣṭā kācideva paryāyavakratetyucyate /
paryāyapradhānaḥ śabdaḥ paryāyo 'bhidhīyate /
tasya caitadeva paryāyaprādhānyaṃ yat sa kadācidvivakṣite vastuni vācakatayā pravartate, kadācidvācakāntaramiti /
tena pūrvoktayā nītyā bahuprakāraḥ paryāyo 'bhihitaḥ, tat kiyantastasya prakārāḥ santītyāha---abidheyāntaratamaḥ /
abidheyaṃ vācyaṃ vastu tasyāntaratamaḥ pratyāsannatamaḥ /
yasmāt paryāyaśabdatve satyapyantaraṅgatvāt sa yathā vivakṣitaṃ vastu vyanakti tathā nānyaḥ kaściditi /
yathā
children.translated_text: A synonym in the domain of poetry, distinguished by the above-stated qualifiers — the variety, the distinctive charm, the particular strikingness produced by it — that is called the supreme, the pre-eminent, synonym-obliqueness. A word whose primary function is as a synonym is called a 'paryāya' (synonym). And its being principally a synonym consists precisely in this: that it sometimes functions as the denoter of the intended subject, and sometimes [yields to] another denoter. Thus, by the previously stated method, the manifold synonym has been described. 'How many types does it have?' — to this [the author] says: 'abhidheyāntaratamaḥ' — the one closest to the expressed, the most proximate to the expressed subject. Because, even when [other words] have the status of synonyms, through its being the most intimate, it illuminates the intended subject in a way that no other [word] can. For example —
'You are not fit to be assailed with falsehood — what regard is there for the arrows of ascetics?'

children.text: santi bhūbhṛti hi naḥ śarāḥ pare ye pākramavasūni vajriṇaḥ // VjivC_2.32 //
children.translated_text: 'We have other arrows in our king's possession — the riches of valor of <s>Vajrin</s> (<s>Indra</s>, the thunderbolt-wielder).' // <s>Vjīv</s>C 2.32 //

children.text:
atra mahendravācakeṣvasaṃkhyeṣu saṃbhavatsu paryāyaśabdeṣu "vajriṇaḥ' iti prayuktaḥ paryāyavakratāṃ puṣṇāti /
yasmāt satasaṃnihitavajrasyāpi surapaterye parākramavasūni vikramadhanānīti sāyakānāṃ lokottaratvapratītiḥ /
"tapasvi'-śabdo 'pyatitarāṃ ramaṇīyaḥ /
yasmāt subhaṭasāyakānāmādaro bahumānaḥ kadācidupapadyate, tāpasamārgaṇeṣu punarakiñcitkareṣu kaḥ saṃrambha iti /
yathā vā
children.translated_text: Here, among the innumerable synonym-words that are available as denoters of <s>Mahendra</s>, the one employed — '<s>Vajrin</s>' (the thunderbolt-wielder) — fosters synonym-obliqueness. Because, even though the lord of the gods has the thunderbolt always at hand, what are his 'riches of valor,' his 'wealth of prowess' — [namely,] the arrows — thus arises the perception of their being extraordinary. The word '<s>tapasvin</s>' (ascetic) too is exceedingly beautiful — because regard, that is esteem, for the arrows of great warriors is sometimes justified; but regarding the arrows of the ascetic path, which are of no account, what intensity [of feeling] could arise? Or as —

children.text: kastavaṃ jñāsyasi māṃ smara smarasi māṃ diṣṭyā kimabhyāgatastvāmunmādayituṃ kathaṃ nanu balāt kiṃ te balaṃ paśya tat /
children.translated_text: 'Who are you? — You shall know me! — Remember! — You remember me? — Fortunately! — Why have you come? — To drive you mad. — How? — By force indeed! — What is your strength? — Behold it! —'

children.text: pasyāmītyabhidhāya pāvakamucā ye locanenaiva taṃ kāntākaṇṭhaniṣaktabāhumadahattasmai namaḥ śūline // VjivC_2.33 //
children.translated_text: 'I see!' — having said this, with his fire-emitting eye alone he who was embracing his beloved's neck burned that one — salutation to the Trident-bearer (<s>Śūlin</s>)! // <s>Vjīv</s>C 2.33 //

children.text:
atra parameśvare paryāyasahastreṣvapi saṃbhavatsu "śūline' iti yatprayuktaṃ tatrāyamabhiprāyo yattasmai bhagavate namaskāravyatirekeṇa kimanyadabhidhīyate /
yattathāvidhotsekaparityaktavinayavṛtteḥ smarasya kupitenāpi tadabhimatāvalokavyatirekeṇa tena satatasaṃnihitaśūlenāpi kopasamucitamāyudhagrahaṇaṃ nācaritam /
locanapātamātreṇaiva kopakāryakaraṇādbhagavataḥ prabhāvātiśayaḥ paripoṣitaḥ /
ataeva tasmai namo 'stviti yuktiyuktatāṃ pratipadyate /
ayamaparaḥ padapūrvārdhavakratāhetuḥ paryāyaḥ---yastasyātiśayapoṣakaḥ /
tasyābhidheyasyārthasyātiśayamutkarṣa puṣṇāti yaḥ sa tathoktaḥ /
yasmāt sahajasaukumāryasubhago 'pi padārthastena paripoṣitātiśayaḥ sutarāṃ sahṛdayahṛdayahāritāṃ pratipadyate /
yathā
children.translated_text: Here, though thousands of synonyms are available for the Supreme Lord, 'Śūlin' (Trident-bearer) is employed — the purport being this: what else is said to that Blessed One, other than salutation? Because, even though angered by the Love-god whose deportment of propriety had been abandoned through such arrogance, [<s>Śiva</s>] did not resort to the taking up of a weapon fitting for anger — not even with his trident, ever at hand — except for the glance of [<s>Śiva</s>'s beloved]. By accomplishing the work of anger through a mere glance of the eye, the Lord's superabundance of power is nourished. Therefore 'salutation to him' attains the quality of being well-reasoned. This is another type of synonym that is a cause of first-half-of-word obliqueness — 'that which nourishes the excellence of that [meaning].' 'Of that' — of the expressed subject — it nourishes the excellence, the eminence. Because even a subject naturally graced with beauty, when its excellence is nourished by such [a synonym], all the more attains the quality of captivating the hearts of connoisseurs. For example —

A kinsman of the <s>Raghu</s> kings; the preceptor in the initiation-rite of the Love-god's activity; accustomed to comparison with the face of the fair-limbed [woman]; the beloved of the star-maidens;

children.text: sadyomārjitadākṣiṇātyataruṇīdantāvadātadyuti- ścandraḥ sundari dṛśyatāmayamasau caṇḍī śacūḍāmaṇiḥ // VjivC_2.34 //
children.translated_text: his radiance the whiteness of the newly polished teeth of a southern girl — O beautiful one, behold this moon, that <s>Caṇḍī</s>'s crest-jewel! // <s>Vjīv</s>C 2.34 //

children.text:
atra paryāyāḥ sahajasaundaryasaṃpadupetasyāpi candramasaḥ sahṛdayahṛdayāhlādakāraṇaṃ kamapyatiśayamūllāsayantaḥ padapūrvārdhavakratāṃ pūṣṇanti /
tathā ca rāmeṇa rāvaṇaṃ nihatya puṣpakena gacchatā sītāyāḥ savistrambhaṃ svairakathāsvetadabhidhīyate yaccandraḥ sundari dṛśyatāmiti, rāmaṇīyakamanohāriṇi sakalalokalocanotsavaścandramā vicāryatāmiti /
yasmāttathāvidhānāmeva tādṛśaḥ samucito vicāragocaraḥ /
saṃbandhī raghubhūbhujāmityanena cāsmākaṃ nāpūrvo bandhurayamityavalokanena saṃmānyatāmiti prakārāntareṇāpi tadviṣayo bahumānaḥ pratīyate /
śiṣṭāśca tadatiśayādhānapravaṇatvamevātmanaḥprathayanti /
tata eva ca prastutamarthaṃ prati pratyekaṃ pṛthaktvenotkarṣaprakaṭanātparyāyāṇāṃ bahūnāmapyapaunaruktyam /
tṛtīye pāde viśeṣaṇavakratā vidyate, na paryāyavakratvam /
ayamaparaḥ paryāyaprakāraḥ padapūrvārdhavakratānibandhanaḥ---yastadalaṅkarttumīśvaraḥ /
tadabhidheyalakṣaṇaṃ vastu vibhūṣayituṃ yaḥ prabhavatītyarthaḥ /
kasmāt---ramyacchāyāntarasparśāt /
ramyaṃ ramaṇīyaṃ yacchāyāntaraṃ vicchittyantaraṃ śliṣṭatvādi tasya sparśāt,śobhāntarapratīterityarthaḥ /
katham---svayaṃ viśeṣaṇenāpi /
svayamātmanaiva, svaviśeṣaṇabhūtena padāntareṇa vā /
tatra svayaṃ yathā
children.translated_text: Here, the synonyms, even though the moon is endowed with the wealth of natural beauty, bring to efflorescence a certain extraordinary excess that is the cause of delighting the hearts of connoisseurs, and thus foster first-half-of-word obliqueness. And thus, by <s>Rāma</s>, having slain <s>Rāvaṇa</s> and traveling by the aerial car <s>Puṣpaka</s>, this is said to <s>Sītā</s> in intimate, playful conversation — 'O beautiful one, behold the moon,' meaning: O one whose beauty captivates the heart, let the moon, which is a festival for the eyes of all the world, be contemplated. Since such a subject is an appropriate object of contemplation for those of such a nature alone. And by 'kinsman of the <s>Raghu</s> kings,' the esteem regarding that [moon] is also suggested in another manner — 'this is no unfamiliar kinsman of ours' — [meaning] 'let him be honored by [our] beholding.' And the learned [synonyms] display their own inclination toward bestowing that excellence upon [the moon]. And precisely for that reason — because each synonym individually and separately manifests the excellence with respect to the subject at hand — there is no redundancy even among many synonyms. In the third quarter there is qualifier-obliqueness, not synonym-obliqueness. This is another type of synonym that is a basis of first-half-of-word obliqueness — 'that which is capable of adorning it.' [That synonym] which has the power to embellish the subject characterized as the expressed — this is the meaning. Why? — 'Through the touch of another shade of lovely beauty.' A 'lovely shade' — another shade of charm, such as sleekness of fit and so forth — through the contact, the perception, of that [beauty] — this is the meaning. How? — 'Even by itself as a qualifier.' By itself alone, or by another word that serves as its qualifier. Of the first [type], for example —

children.text: itthaṃ jaḍe jagati ko nu bṛhatpramāṇa- karṇaḥ karī nanu bhaved dhvanitasya pātram /
children.translated_text: 'Thus, in this dull world, who indeed — large-eared — an elephant surely — could be a vessel for what has been sounded?'

children.text: ityāgataṃ jhaṭiti yo 'linamunmamātha mātaṅga eva kimataḥ paramucyate 'sau // VjivC_2.35 //
children.translated_text: — this having occurred to him, he who instantly uprooted that bee-swarm — is it said to be anything other than an elephant (<s>mātaṅga</s>)? // <s>Vjīv</s>C 2.35 //

children.text:
atra "mātaṅga'-śabdaḥ prastute vāraṇamātre pravartate /
śliṣṭayā vṛttyā caṇḍālalakṣaṇasyāprastutasya vastunaḥ pratītimutpādayan rūpakālaṅkāracchāyāsaṃsparśād gaurvāhīka ityanena nyāyena sādṛśyanibandhanasyopacārasya saṃbhavāt prastutasya vastunastattvamadhyāropayan paryāyavakratāṃ puṣṇāti /
yasmādevaṃvidhe viṣaye prastutasyāprastutena saṃbandhopanibandho rūpakālaṅkāradvāreṇa kadācidupamāmukhena vā /
yathā sa evāyaṃ sa ivāyamiti vā /
eṣa eva ca śabdaśaktimūlānuraṇanarūpavyaṅgyasya padadhvanerviṣayaḥ, bahuṣu caivaṃvidheṣu satsu vākyadhvanervā /
yathā
children.translated_text: Here, the word '<s>mātaṅga</s>' functions in the context of a mere elephant at hand. But through a sleek secondary function, by producing the perception of a <s>caṇḍāla</s> (outcaste) — an irrelevant subject — through the touch of the shade of the <s>rūpaka</s> (metaphor) figure, since the possibility of figurative usage based on resemblance exists — as in the maxim 'a <s>gaur</s> is a <s>vāhīka</s>' — by superimposing the reality of the irrelevant subject upon the relevant one, it fosters synonym-obliqueness. Because in such a case, the relation between the relevant and irrelevant subjects is established either through the <s>rūpaka</s> (metaphor) figure, or sometimes through <s>upamā</s> (simile) — as 'he is this very one' or 'he is like this one.' And this indeed is the domain of <s>padadhvani</s> (word-suggestion), the type of suggested meaning that has the form of reverberating from the power of the word; and when many such [instances] are present, of <s>vākyadhvani</s> (sentence-suggestion) as well. For example —
Withdrawing the pair of flower-seasons, with a loud laugh white as a blooming <s>mallikā</s> jasmine, there yawned the great destroyer (<s>Mahākāla</s>) named Summer. // <s>Vjīv</s>C 2.36 //
For example —
'When this great dissolution has occurred, now for the support of the earth, you are <s>Śeṣa</s> (the cosmic serpent).' // <s>Vjīv</s>C 2.37 //
Thus.

children.text: atra yugādayaḥ śabdāḥ prastutābhidhānaparatvena prayujyamānāḥ santo 'pyaprastutavastupratītikāritayā kāmapi kāvyacchāyāṃ samunmīlayantaḥ pratīyamānālaṅkāravyapadeśabhājanaṃ bhavanti //
children.translated_text: Here, words like 'yuga' (pair/age) and so forth, even while being employed with the primary purpose of denoting the relevant subject, by causing the perception of an irrelevant subject, unveil a certain poetic lustre (<s>kāvyacchāyā</s>) and thereby become worthy of the designation of 'suggested figure' (<s>pratīyamānālaṅkāra</s>).
Through a qualifier, for example —
Having beheld it, very smooth and white as milk, beautiful — something sweet, artless, and anointed with coquetry —

children.text: bhasmīcakāra madanaṃ nanu kāṣṭhameva tannunamīśa iti vetti purandhrilokaḥ // VjivC_2.38 //
children.translated_text: 'He surely burned <s>Madana</s> (the Love-god) [when he was] nothing but a log of wood' — thus the world of women thinks: 'This is the Lord (<s>Īśa</s>).' // <s>Vjīv</s>C 2.38 //

children.text:
atra kāṣṭhamiti viśeṣaṇapadaṃ varṇyamānapadārthāpekṣayā manmathasya nīrasatāṃ pratipādayad ramyacchāyāntarasparśiśleṣacchāyāmanojñavinyāsamaparamasmin vastunyaprastute madanābhidhānapādapalakṣaṇe pratītimutpāpayad rūpakālaṅkāracchāyāsaṃsparśāt kāmapi paryāyavakratāmunmīlayati /
ayamaparaḥ paryāyaprakāraḥ padapūrvārdhavakratāyāḥ kāraṇam---yaḥ svacchāyotkarṣapeśalaḥ /
svasyātmanaśchāyā kāntiryā sukumāratā tadutkarṣeṇa tadatiśayena yaḥ peśalo hṛdayahārī /
tadidamatra tātparyam---yadyapi varṇyamānasya vastunaḥ prakārāntarollāsakatvena vyavasthitistathāpi parispandasaundaryasaṃpadeva sahṛdayahṛdayahāritāṃ pratipadyate /
yathā
children.translated_text: Here the qualifying word 'wood' (<s>kāṣṭha</s>), while establishing the passionlessness of <s>Manmatha</s> (the god of love) in relation to the object being described, through its producing a delightful arrangement by touching the shade of a <s>śleṣa</s> (paronomasia) that contacts another charming shade of meaning, and by generating a cognition of <s>rūpaka</s> (metaphor)-figure's shade in another unintended object marked by the word '<s>madana</s>' (love), reveals a certain synonym-obliquity. This is another type of synonym [obliquity] that is the cause of obliquity in the first half of a word-unit: 'which is charming through the excellence of its own splendor.' Of its own self, the splendor (<s>chāyā</s>), the beauty, the delicacy—through the excellence of that, through its superabundance, [the synonym] that is charming, captivating to the heart. The purport here is: although the object being described exists as the occasion for the shining forth of another aspect, nevertheless, it is the beauty of the vibration [of expression] alone that attains the quality of captivating the hearts of connoisseurs. For example:
Thus the fever of separation assails me with the rays of [the moon]—the patriarch of the crooked-ray clan—

children.text: utthitaṃ viṣamakāṇḍakuṭumba- syāṃśubhiḥ smaravatīviraho mām // VjivC_2.39 //
children.translated_text: rising with heavy steps, as though skillful in the sport of the <s>tāṇḍava</s> dance of the ocean waves. (Vjiv 2.39)

children.text:
atrenduparyāyo "viṣamakāṇḍakuṭumba'-śabdaḥ kavinopanibaddhaḥ /
yasmānmṛgāṅkodayadveṣiṇā virahavidhurahṛdayena kenacidetaducyate /
yadayamaprasiddho 'pyaparimlānasamanvayatayā prasiddhatamatāmupanītastena prathamatarollikhitatvena ca cetanacamatkārakāritāmavagāhate /
eṣa ca svacchāyotkarṣapeśalaḥsahajasaundaryasu bhagatvena nūtanollekhavilakṣaṇatvena ca kavibhiḥ paryāyāntaraparihārapūrvakamupavarṇyate /
yathā kṛṣṇakuṭilakeśīti vaktavye yamunākallolavakrālaketi /
yathā vā "gaurāṅgīvadanopamāparicita' ityatravanitādivācakasahastrasadbhāve 'pi gaurāṅgītyabhidhānamatīvaramaṇīyam /
ayamaparaḥ paryāyaprakāraḥ padapūrvārdhavakratābhidhāyī---alaṃbhāvyārthapātratvagarbhaṃ yaścābidhīyate /
varṇyamānasya saṃbhāvyaḥ saṃbhāvayitumaśakyo yor'thaḥ kaścitparispandastatra pātratvaṃ bhājanatvaṃ garbho 'bhiprāyo yatrābhidhāne tattathāvidhaṃ kṛtvā yaścābhidhīyate bhaṇyate /
yathā
children.translated_text: Here the word '<s>viṣamakāṇḍakuṭumba</s>' (patriarch of the crooked-ray clan) is composed by the poet as a synonym for the moon. Since this is spoken by someone whose heart is distressed by separation, hostile to the rising of the moon—even though this [expression] is unprecedented, it is brought to the highest familiarity through its unimpaired syntactic coherence, and because it is etched for the first time, it enters into the quality of producing wonder in consciousness. This [type of synonym], being charming through the excellence of its own splendor, through the quality of possessing innate beauty and through the uniqueness of a fresh coinage, is described by poets with the prior exclusion of other synonyms. As, for instance, instead of saying 'one with black, curly hair,' [one says] 'one with tresses wavy like the waves of the <s>Yamunā</s>.' Or, as in the expression 'familiar with comparison to the face of a fair-limbed woman'—even though a thousand words meaning 'woman' exist, the designation '<s>gaurāṅgī</s>' (fair-limbed one) is exceedingly beautiful. This is another type of synonym [obliquity] that expresses the obliquity in the first half of a word-unit: 'and that which is uttered as pregnant with the capacity to contain an inconceivable meaning.' Of the object being described, a meaning, a certain vibration, that is inconceivable, impossible to imagine—the capacity (<s>pātratva</s>), the fitness to contain that, is the inner purport in which expression—[the synonym] being constituted as such, 'and that which is uttered.' For example:

children.text: alaṃ mahīpāla tava śrameṇa prayuktamapyastramito vṛthā syāt /
children.translated_text: Enough, O protector of the earth, with your effort; even a weapon employed would be in vain here,

children.text: na pādaponmūlanaśakti raṃhaḥ śiloccaye mūrchati mārutasya // VjivC_2.40 //
children.translated_text: for the force of the wind does not gather strength against a rocky peak sufficient to uproot a tree. (Vjiv 2.40)

children.text:
atra mahīpāleti rājñaḥ sakalapṛthvīparirakṣaṇakṣamapauruṣasyāpi tathāvidhaprayatnaparipālanīyagurugorūpajīvamātraparitrāṇāsāmarthyaṃ svapne 'pyasaṃbhāvanīyaṃ yattatpātratvagarbhamāmantraṇamupanibaddham /
yathā vā
children.translated_text: Here, [the address] 'O protector of the earth' (<s>mahīpāla</s>) composes an address pregnant with the capacity [to contain an inconceivable meaning]—for one whose heroism is capable of protecting the entire earth, the inability to protect the life of even a venerable teacher's cow, which requires such effort to preserve, is something inconceivable even in a dream. Or for example:

children.text: bhūtānukampā tava cediyaṃ gau- rekā bhavet svastimatī tvadante /
children.translated_text: If this [intention of sacrificing your life] is your compassion for living beings, then at your death this one cow alone would be safe;

children.text: jīvan punaḥ śasvadupaplavebhyaḥ prajāḥ prajānātha piteva pāsi // VjivC_2.41 //
children.translated_text: but by living, you constantly protect your subjects from calamities, like a father, O lord of the people. (Vjiv 2.41)

children.text:
atra yadi prāṇikaruṇākāraṇaṃ nijaprāṇaparityāgamācarasi tadapyayuktam /
yasmāttvadante svastimatī bhavediyamekaiva gauriti tritayamapyanādarāspadam /
jivan punaḥ śaśvatsadaivopaplavebhyo 'narthebhyaḥ prajāḥ sakalabhūtadhātrīvalayavartinīḥ prajānātha pāsi rakṣasi /
pitevetyanādarātiśayaḥ prathate /
tadevaṃ yadyapi suspaṣṭasamanvayo 'yaṃ vākyārthastathāpi tātparyāntaramatra pratīyate /
yasmāt sarvasya kasyācitprajānāthatve sati sadaiva tatparirakṣaṇasyākaraṇamasaṃbhāvyam /
tatpātratvagarbhameva tadabhihitam /
yasmāt pratyakṣaprāṇimātrabhakṣmamāṇaguruhomadhenuprāṇaparirakṣaṇāpekṣānirapekṣasya sato jīvatastavānena nyāyena kadācidapi prijāparirakṣaṇaṃ manāgapi na saṃbhāvyata iti pramāṇopapannam /
tadidamuktam
children.translated_text: Here: if you practice the renunciation of your own life on account of compassion for creatures, even that is improper. For at your death, only this one cow alone would be safe—this triviality is a ground for disregard. But by living, constantly, at all times, you protect from calamities, from misfortunes, your subjects, those dwelling in the sphere of the entire earth, O lord of the people. By 'like a father,' the superabundance of disregard [for the trivial motive] is conveyed. Thus, although this sentence-meaning has a perfectly clear syntactic construction, nevertheless another purport is perceived here. For it is inconceivable that one who is lord of all subjects would ever fail to protect them. That [address] was uttered as pregnant with the capacity [to contain that inconceivable meaning]. Since the protection of the life of a guru's sacrificial cow—when creatures are being devoured right before one's eyes—cannot even slightly be conceived of for one who lives by such reasoning, this is established by valid reasoning. Thus it is said:
'A current that has arrived because it is well-grounded—by whom can it be blocked?' (Vjiv 2.42)
Thus.

children.text:
atrābhidhānapratītigocarīkṛtānāṃ padārthānāṃ parasparapratiyogitvamudāharaṇapratyudāharaṇanyāyenānusaṃdheyam /
ayamaparaḥ paryāyaprakāraḥ padapūrvārdhavakratāṃ vidadhāti---alaṅkāropasaṃskāramanohārinibandhanaḥ /
atra "alaṅkāropasaṃskāra' śabde tṛtīyāsamāsaḥ ṣaṣṭhīsamāsaśca karaṇīyaḥ /
tenārthadvayamabhihitaṃ bhavati /
alaṅkāreṇa rūpakādinopasaṃskāraḥ śobhāntarādhānaṃ yattena manohāri hṛdayarañjakaṃ nibandhanamupanibandho yasya sa tathoktaḥ /
alaṅkārasyotprekṣāderupasaṃskāraḥ śobhāntarādhānaṃ ceti vigṛhya /
tatra tṛtīyāsamāsapakṣodāharaṇaṃ yathā
children.translated_text: Here the mutual opposition of the word-meanings brought within the scope of direct and [implied] cognition should be followed through according to the principle of example and counter-example. This is another type of synonym [obliquity] that produces the obliquity in the first half of a word-unit: 'that whose ground is the charm produced by the embellishment of ornamentation.' Here in the expression '<s>alaṅkāropasaṃskāra</s>' (embellishment of/by ornamentation), both a third-case (instrumental) compound and a sixth-case (genitive) compound should be understood. Thereby two meanings are expressed. [First:] the embellishment, the imposition of additional beauty, effected by ornamentation such as <s>rūpaka</s> (metaphor) and the like—by that, [the synonym] whose ground, whose composition, is charming, captivating to the heart, is so described. [Second:] analyzing as 'the embellishment of ornamentation such as <s>utprekṣā</s> (poetic fancy) and the like, i.e. the imposition of additional beauty.' The example for the instrumental compound interpretation is as follows:

children.text: yo līlātālavṛnto rahasi nirupadhiryaśca kilīpradīpaḥ kopakrīḍāsu yo 'straṃ daśanakṛtarujo yo 'dharasyaikasekaḥ /
children.translated_text: He who is a playful fan in private, who is a sincere lamp at night, who is a weapon in the sports of anger, who is the sole balm for the bruised lower lip,

children.text: ākalpe darpaṇa yaḥ śramaśayanavidho yaśca gaṇḍopadhānaṃ devyāḥ sa vyāpadaṃ vo haratu harajaṭākandalīpuṣpaminduḥ // VjivC_2.43 //
children.translated_text: who is a mirror for [her] toilette, who is a pillow for the cheek in the manner of the couch of fatigue—that moon, the flower of the vine-creeper of <s>Hara</s>'s (<s>Śiva</s>'s) matted locks, may he remove your misfortune, O <s>Devī</s>! (Vjiv 2.43)

children.text:
atra tālavṛntādikāryasāmānyādabhedopacāranibandhano rūpakālaṅkāravinyāsaḥ sarveṣāmeva paryāyāṇāṃ śobhātiśayakāritvenopanibaddhaḥ /
ṣaṣṭhīsamāsapakṣodāharaṇaṃ yathā
children.translated_text: Here, the arrangement of <s>rūpaka</s> (metaphor) ornamentation, grounded in the figurative identification based on the generality of [being instruments for] actions such as fanning and so forth, is composed as producing a superabundance of beauty for all the synonyms. The example for the genitive compound interpretation is as follows:
O <s>Devī</s>, by the lotus of your face, which surpasses the beauty of the moon,

children.text: paśyābjāni vinirjitāni sahasā gacchanti vicchāyatām // VjivC_2.44 //
children.translated_text: look—the lotuses, suddenly defeated, are losing their luster. (Vjiv 2.44)

children.text:
atra svarasasaṃpravṛttasāyaṃsamayasamucitā saroruhāṇāṃ vicchāyatāpratipattirnāyakena nāgarakatayā vallabhopalālanāpravṛttena tannidarśanopakramaramaṇīyatvamukhena nirjitānīveti pratīyamānotprekṣālaṅkārakāritvena pratipādyate /
etadeva ca yuktiyuktam /
yasmātsarvasya kasyacitpaṅkajasya śaśāṅkaśobhātiraskārakāritā pratipadyate /
tvanmukhapaṅkajena punaḥ śaśinaḥ śobhātiraskāriṇā nyāyato nirjitāni santi vicchāyatāṃ gacchantīveti pratīyamānasyotprekṣālakṣaṇasyālaṅkārasya śobhātiśayaḥ samullāsyate /
evaṃ paryāyavakratāṃ vicārya kramasamucitāvasarāmupacāravakratāṃ vicārayati---
children.translated_text: Here, the lotuses' loss of luster, which naturally befits the evening time that has commenced of its own accord, is presented by the hero—who has initiated the flattering of his beloved with urbane gallantry—through the charming device of introducing an illustration for that [flattery], expressed through the function of producing the perceived figure of <s>utprekṣā</s> (poetic fancy) in 'as if defeated.' And this alone is proper. For of every lotus whatsoever, the capacity to eclipse the beauty of the moon is [ordinarily] acknowledged. But 'by the lotus of your face, which surpasses the beauty of the moon'—the lotuses are reasonably 'defeated' and 'lose their luster, as it were'—thus the superabundance of beauty of the ornament characterized as perceived <s>utprekṣā</s> is brought to light. Having thus examined synonym-obliquity, he examines figurative-transfer obliquity (<s>upacāravakratā</s>), which comes in due order—
Where a generality with something far distant is figuratively transferred,
existing even in the slightest degree, in order to express a certain extraordinary quality, (Vjiv 2.13)
that which is the basis for the lively figuration of <s>rūpaka</s> (metaphor) and the like—
this obliquity, in which figurative transfer predominates, is described as a certain [type]. (Vjiv 2.14)

children.text:
asau kācidapūrvā vakratocyate vakrabhāvo 'bhidhīyate /
kīdṛśī---upacārapradhānā /
upacaraṇamupacāraḥ sa eva pradhānaṃ yasyāḥ sā tathoktā /
kiṃsvarūpā---yatra yasyāmanyasmātpadārthāntarāt prastutatvādvarṇyamāne vastuni sāmānyamupacaryate sādhāraṇo dharmaḥ kaścidvaktumabhipretaḥ samāropyate /
kasmin varṇyamāne vastuni---dūrāntare /
dūramanalpamantaraṃ vyavadhānaṃ yasya tattathoktaṃ tasmin /
nanu ca vyavadhānamamūrtatvādvarṇyamānasya vastuno deśavihitaṃ tāvanna saṃbhavati /
kālavihitamapi nāstyeva, tasya kriyāviṣayatvāt /
kriyāsvarūpaṃ kārakasvarūpaṃ cetyubhayātmakaṃ yadyapi varṇyamānaṃ vastu, tathāpi deśakālavyavadhānenātra na bhavitavyam /
yasmātpadārthānāmanumānavat sāmānyamātrameva śabdairviṣayīkartuṃ pāryate, na viśeṣaḥ /
tatkathaṃ dūrāntaratvamupapadyate ? satyametat, kintu "dūrāntara'-śabdo mukhyatayā deśakālaviṣaye viprakarṣe pratyāsattivirahe vartamāno 'pyupacārāt svabhāvaviprakarṣe vartate /
so 'yaṃ svabhāvaviprakarṣo viruddhadharmādhyāsalakṣaṇaḥ padārthānām /
yathā mūrtimattvamamūrtatvāpekṣayā, dravatvaṃ ca ghanatvāpekṣayā, cetanatvamacetanatvāpekṣayeti /
kīdṛk tatsāmānyam---leśenāpi bhavat /
manāṅmātreṇāpi sat /
kimartham ---kāñcidapūrvāmudriktavṛttitāṃ vaktuṃ sātiśayaparispandatāmabhidhātum /
yathā
children.translated_text: This is a certain unprecedented obliquity that is described, whose oblique nature is stated. Of what kind?—one in which figurative transfer predominates. The act of figurative transfer (<s>upacaraṇa</s>) is <s>upacāra</s>; that which has it as predominant is so described. Of what essential nature?—'where,' in which, upon the object being described—which, being the subject, is being portrayed—from another, from a different object, a generality, some common property intended to be expressed, is figuratively superimposed. Upon what kind of object being described?—'far distant.' Having a distance, a separation that is not small—upon that which is such. But then, since the object being described is incorporeal, spatial distance is not possible. Temporal distance too does not exist, since it [time] is the domain of action. Although the object being described is of a twofold nature—the nature of action and the nature of case-relation—still, spatial and temporal distance need not apply here. Since, like inference, only the generality of objects can be made the domain of words, not the particular. Then how is the 'far-distant' character justified? This is true, but the word 'far-distant,' though primarily applying to spatial and temporal remoteness, to the absence of proximity, applies by figurative usage to the remoteness of nature. This remoteness of nature consists in the superimposition of contradictory properties upon objects. For example, corporeality relative to incorporeality, fluidity relative to solidity, sentience relative to insentience, and so on. Of what kind is that generality?—'existing even in the slightest degree,' present even to the most minimal extent. For what purpose?—to express a certain unprecedented extraordinary quality, to denote a state of superabundant vibration. For example:
'Of the sky smeared with smooth, dark-blue radiance...' (Vjiv 2.45)

children.text:
atra yathā buddhipūrvakāriṇaḥ keciccetanavarṇacchāyātiśayotpādanecchayā kenacidvidyamānalepanaśaktinā mūrtena nīlādinā rañjanadravyaviśeṣeṇa kiñcideva lepanīyaṃ mūrtimadvastu vastraprāyaṃ limpanti, tadvadeva tatkāritvasāmānyaṃ manāṅmātreṇāpi vidyamānaṃ kāmapyudriktavṛttitāmabhidhātumupacārāt snigdhaśyāmalayā kāntyā liptaṃ viyad dyaurityupanibaddham /
"snigdha'-śabdo 'pyupacāravakra eva /
yathā mūrtaṃ vastu sparśasaṃvedyaṃ sneha naguṇayogāt snigdhamityucyate, tathaiva kāntiramūrtāpyupacārāt snigdhetyuktā /
yathā vā
children.translated_text: Here, just as certain agents acting deliberately, desiring to produce a superabundance of color-shade in some sentient being, smear some corporeal object to be smeared—such as a garment—with a particular coloring substance that is corporeal, like blue and so forth, possessing the capacity for smearing; just so, the generality of agency, existing even to the slightest degree, is figuratively transferred in order to express a certain extraordinary quality—thus it is composed: 'the sky, smeared with smooth, dark-blue radiance.' The word 'smooth' (<s>snigdha</s>) too is itself an instance of figurative-transfer obliquity. Just as a corporeal object, perceivable by touch, is called 'smooth' by virtue of possessing the quality of oiliness, just so, radiance, though incorporeal, is called 'smooth' by figurative usage. Or for example:

children.text: gacchantīnāṃ ramaṇavasatiṃ yoṣitāṃ tatra naktaṃ ruddhāloke narapatipathe sūcibhedyaistamobhiḥ /
children.translated_text: Of the women going to their lovers' dwellings at night, when the royal road is blocked with darkness impenetrable even by a needle—

children.text: saudāminyā kanakanikaṣasnigdhayā darśayorvoṃ toyotsargastanitamukharo māsma bhūrviklavāsatāḥ // VjivC_2.46 //
children.translated_text: O [cloud], do not, with your rain-discharge announced by thunder, show [them] your golden-touchstone-smooth lightning—lest they become distressed! (Vjiv 2.46)

children.text:
atrāmūrtānāmapi tamasāmatibāhulyād ghanatvānmūrtasamucitaṃ sūcibhedyatvamupacaritam /
yathā vā
children.translated_text: Here, even though darkness is incorporeal, because of its great abundance and density, the corporeal-appropriate quality of being 'impenetrable by a needle' is figuratively transferred [to it]. Or for example:

children.text: gaaṇaṃ ca mattamehaṃ dhārāluliajjuṇāiṃ a vaṇāiṃ /
children.translated_text: [In Prakrit:] The sky with its intoxicated clouds, the forests with their whiteness washed by rain-showers,

children.text: ṇirahaṅkāramiaṅkā haranti ṇīlāo a ṇisāo // VjivC_2.47 //
children.translated_text: and the dark nights with their prideless moon—they steal [my heart]. (Vjiv 2.47)

children.text: gaganaṃ ca mattameghaṃ dhārālulitārjunāni ca vanāni /
children.translated_text: [In Sanskrit:] The sky with its intoxicated clouds, the forests with their whiteness washed by rain-showers,
and the dark nights with their prideless moon—they steal [my heart].
Thus is the <s>chāyā</s> (Sanskrit rendering).

children.text:
atra mattatvaṃ nirahaṅkāratvaṃ ca cetanadharmasāmānyamupacaritam /
so 'yamupacāravakratāprakāraḥ satkavipravāhe sahastraśaḥ saṃbhavatīti sahṛdayaiḥ svayamevotprekṣaṇīyaḥ ataeva ca pratyāsannāntare 'sminnupacāre na vakratāvyavahāraḥ, yathā gaurvāhīka iti /
idamaparamupacāravakratāyāḥ svarūpam---yanmūlā sarasollekhā rūpakādiralaṅkṛtiḥ /
yā mūlaṃ yasyāḥ sā tathoktā /
rūpakamādiryasyāḥ sā tathoktā /
