kā sā---alaṅkṛtiralaṅkaraṇaṃ rūpakaprabhṛtiralaṅkāravicchittirityarthaḥ /
kīdṛśī---sarasollekhā /
sarasaḥ sāsvādaḥ sacamatkṛtirullekhaḥ samunmeṣoyasyāḥ sā tathoktā /
samānādhikaraṇayoratra hetuhetumadbhāvaḥ, yathā
children.translated_text: Here, the qualities of 'intoxication' and 'pridelessness,' being properties common to sentient beings, are figuratively transferred [to the clouds and moon]. This type of figurative-transfer obliquity is found a thousandfold in the tradition of true poets—the connoisseurs should infer this themselves. And therefore, in figurative transfer where [the objects are] close to each other, there is no application of the term 'obliquity'—as in '<s>gaurvāhīkaḥ</s>' (the ox is a <s>Vāhīka</s>). This is another aspect of figurative-transfer obliquity: 'that which is the basis for the lively figuration of <s>rūpaka</s> and the like.' 'That of which it is the basis'—it is so described. 'That of which <s>rūpaka</s> and the like are the beginning'—it is so described. What is it?—the figuration, the ornamentation, the strikingness of figures beginning with <s>rūpaka</s>—this is the meaning. Of what kind?—'lively in its delineation' (<s>sarasollekhā</s>); that which has a lively, relishable, wonder-producing delineation, efflorescence—it is so described. Here, between the co-referential [terms], there is a relation of cause and effect. For example:

children.text: atiguravo rājamāṣā na bhakṣyā iti // VjivC_2.48 //
children.translated_text: 'Black lentils (<s>rājamāṣa</s>) are exceedingly heavy and should not be eaten.' (Vjiv 2.48)

children.text:
yanmūlā satī rūpakādiralaṅkṛtiḥ sarasollekhā /
tena rūpakāderalaṅkaraṇakalāpasya sakalasyaivopacāravakratā jīvitamityarthaḥ /
nanu ca pūrvasmādupacāravakratāprakārādetasya ko bhedaḥ ? pūrvasmin svabhāvaviprakarṣāt sāmānyena manāṅmātrameva sāmyaṃ samāśritya sātiśayatvaṃ pratipādayituṃ taddharmamātrādhyāropaḥ pravartate, etasmin punaradūraviprakṛṣṭasādṛśyasamudbhavapratyāsattisamucitatvādabhedopacāranibandhanaṃ tattvamevādhyāropyate /
yathā
children.translated_text: That which, being the root, makes the ornamentation of <s>rūpaka</s> (metaphor) and so forth vivid — therefore, figurative obliquity (<s>upacāravakratā</s>) is the life-force of the entire complex of ornamentation such as <s>rūpaka</s> and so forth — this is the meaning. Now, what is the difference between this and the previous type of figurative obliquity? In the previous one, due to the great distance from the natural state, the superimposition of a property alone takes place, relying on a mere trace of similarity in a general way, in order to convey superlative quality. In this one, however, because of the appropriateness arising from a proximity born of not-too-distant similarity, the reality itself is superimposed, grounded in the figurative usage of non-difference. For example:
Among your assemblies — those with dark, ear-like [night-]lotuses, those with army-like rows of poison-sprouts,

children.text: gāmbhīryapātālaphaṇīśvareṣu saṅgeṣu ko vā bhavatāṃ murāriḥ // VjivC_2.49 //
children.translated_text: those with serpent-kings of the netherworld-like profundity — who indeed is your enemy, O <s>Murāri</s> (slayer of <s>Mura</s>)? // VjivC_2.49 //

children.text:
atra kālaśravaṇotpalādisādṛśyajanitapratyāsattivihatamabhedopacāranibandhanaṃ tattvamāropitam /
"ādi'-grahaṇādaprastutapraśasāprakārasya kasyacidanyāpadeśalakṣaṇasyopacāravakrataiva jīvitatvena lakṣyate /
tathā ca kimapi padārthāntaraṃ prādhānyena pratīyamānatayā cetasi nidhāya tathāvidhalakṣaṇasāmyasamanvayaṃ samāśritya padārthāntaramabhidhīyamānatāṃ prāpayantaḥ prāyaśaḥ kavayo dṛśyante /
yathā
children.translated_text: Here, the reality, grounded in the figurative usage of non-difference, is superimposed through the proximity generated by the similarity to dark night-lotuses at the ears and so forth. From the word 'and so forth' (<s>ādi</s>), the type called <s>aprastutapraśaṃsā</s> (indirect praise), a certain kind whose characteristic is allegory (<s>anyāpadeśa</s>), is recognized as having figurative obliquity as its life-force. Thus, having placed in mind some other referent as being cognized with predominance, and relying upon the correlation of similarity of such a kind, poets are generally observed to bring another referent into the domain of expression. For example:

children.text: anardhaḥ ko 'pyantasvava hariṇa hevākamahimā sphuratyekasyaiva tribhuvanacamatkārajanakaḥ /
children.translated_text: Some inexpressible, priceless, trifling-in-agitation greatness shines forth, producing wonder in the three worlds, of one alone —

children.text: yadindormūrtiste divi viharaṇāraṇyavasudhā sudhāsārasyandī kiraṇanikaraḥ śaṣpakavalaḥ // VjivC_2.50 //
children.translated_text: for the body of your moon in heaven is a forest ground for roaming, the mass of rays streaming with nectar-essence is a mouthful of grass, O deer! // VjivC_2.50 //

children.text:
atra lokottaratvalakṣaṇamubhayānuyāyi sāmānyaṃ samāśritya prādhānyena vivakṣitasya vastunaḥ pratīyamānavṛtterabhedopacāranibandhanaṃ tattvamadhyāropitam /
tathā caitayordūyorapyalaṅkārayostulye 'pyupacāravakratājīvitattve vācyatvamekatra pratīyamānatvamaparasmin svarūpabhedasya nibandhanam /
etaccobhayorapi svalakṣaṇavyākhyānāvasare sutarāṃ samunmīlyate /
evamupacāravakratāṃ vivecya samānantaraprāptāvakāśāṃ viśeṣaṇavakratāṃ vivinakti /
children.translated_text: Here, relying on the common property of extraordinary nature that applies to both, the reality is superimposed, grounded in the figurative usage of non-difference, upon the primarily intended object whose character is being suggested. And thus, in both of these two figures, even though figurative obliquity is equally their life-force, the basis of the difference in essential nature is that in one the content is expressed directly, while in the other it is suggested. This will be fully revealed at the occasion of explaining the individual characteristics of both. Having thus examined figurative obliquity, he distinguishes qualificative obliquity (<s>viśeṣaṇavakratā</s>), whose occasion has presented itself in sequence:
Where beauty shines forth through the greatness of the qualifier,
whether of the action or of the agent — that is qualificative obliquity (<s>viśeṣaṇavakratā</s>). // Vjiv_2.15 //

children.text:
sā viśeṣaṇavakratā viśeṣaṇavakratvavicchittirabhidhīyate /
kīdṛśī---yatra yasyāṃ lāvaṇyamullasati rāmaṇīyakamudbhidyate /
kasya---kriyāyāḥ kārakasya vā /
kriyālakṣaṇasya vastunaḥ kārakalakṣaṇasya vā /
kasmāt---viśeṣaṇasya māhātmyāt /
etayoḥ pratyekaṃ yadviśeṣaṇaṃ bhedakaṃ padārthāntaraṃ tasya sātiśayatvāt /
bhāvasvabhāva saukumāryasamullāsakatvamalaṅkāracchāyātiśayaparipoṣakatvam ca /
yathā
children.translated_text: That 'qualificative obliquity' — the design of qualificative obliqueness — is being described. Of what kind? — 'Where' — in which [expression] — 'beauty shines forth,' charm arises. Of what? — 'Of the action or of the agent': of the entity characterized as action, or of the entity characterized as agent. From what [cause]? — 'Through the greatness of the qualifier': the qualifier, the differentiating element, some other referent, of each of these respectively — through its superlative quality. [The qualifier has] the character of causing the natural beauty of the emotional state to shine forth, and of nourishing the superabundance of the flavor of figuration. For example:

Dazed by the burning sensation at the spots of nail-marks freshly traced by the sprinkling of exertion-sweat, half-concealed by the mass of charming ringlet-circles disheveled in the beloved's eager embrace,

languid with the bashful fragrance of the sequence of love-making variously performed in the passion of love — victorious is the glance of the young woman at dawn's end, faintly rosy-red with the delicate intoxication of spring-honey! // VjivC_2.51 //
Or for example:
With her cheek-surface nestled in the hollow of her hand, her painted brow-line crinkled by surging tears,

children.text: śrotrāntare piṇḍitacittavṛttiḥ śṛṇoti gītadhvanimatra tanvī // VjivC_2.52 //
children.translated_text: her mental activity concentrated at the opening of her ear — the slender one listens here to the sound of a song. // VjivC_2.52 //
Or for example:
The directions, bathed in pure, cool moonlight, charming in their long silence —

children.text: praśamasya manobhavasya vā hṛdi kasyā pyatha hetutāṃ yayuḥ // VjivC_2.53 //
children.translated_text: did they then become the cause in someone's heart of tranquility, or of the god of love? // VjivC_2.53 //
An example of obliqueness of the action-qualifier:
The lord of elephants remembered, with eyes half-closed, the great festivals of dwelling in forests of free-roaming pleasure. // VjivC_2.54 //
Here, in every case, the qualifiers cause the natural beauty to shine forth. An example of the qualifier nourishing the superabundance of figurative flavor:
'Outshining the beauty of the moon.' // VjivC_2.55 //

children.text:
etadeva viśeṣaṇavakratvaṃ nāma prastutaucityānusāri sakalasatkāvyajīvitatvena lakṣyate, yasmādanenaiva rasaḥ parāṃ paripoṣapadavīmavatāryate /
yathā
children.translated_text: This very qualificative obliquity, conforming to propriety of subject, is recognized as the life-force of all excellent poetry, for it is precisely through this that <s>rasa</s> (aesthetic sentiment) is led to its supreme level of nourishment. For example:
'Nestled in the hollow of her hand' — and so forth. // VjivC_2.56 //
By whose own greatness are fashioned extraordinary splendors —
<s>rasa</s>, natural expression, and figuration — their instrument is the qualifier. // Vjiv_2.57 (interpolated verse) //
This is an interpolated verse. //

children.text: evaṃ viśeṣaṇavakratāṃ vicārya kramasamarpitāvasarāṃ saṃvṛtivakratāṃ vicārayati---
children.translated_text: Having thus examined qualificative obliquity, he examines concealment obliquity (<s>saṃvṛtivakratā</s>), whose occasion has been delivered in sequence:
Where a thing is concealed, with the intention of producing variety,
by pronouns and the like — that is called concealment obliquity (<s>saṃvṛtivakratā</s>). // Vjiv_2.16 //

children.text:
soktā saṃvṛtivakratā---yā kilaivaṃvidhā sā saṃvṛtivakratetyuktā kathitā /
saṃvṛtyā vakratā saṃvṛtipradhānā veti samāsaḥ /
yatra yasyāṃ vastu padārthalakṣaṇaṃ savriyate samācchādyate /
kena hetunā---vaicitryasya vivakṣayā vicitrabhāvasyābhidhānecchayā, yayā padārtho vicitrabhāvaṃ samāsādayatītyarthaḥ /
kena saṃvriyate---sarvanāmādibhiḥ kaiścit /
sarvasya nāma sarvanāma tadādiryeṣāṃ te tathoktāstaiḥ kaiścidapūrvairvācakairityarthaḥ /
atra bahavaḥ prakārāḥ saṃbhavanti /
yatra kimapi sātiśayaṃ vastu vaktuṃ śakyamapi sākṣādabhidhānādiyattāparicchinnatayā parimitaprāyaṃ mā pratibhāsatāmiti sāmānyavācinā sarvanāmnā samācchādya tatkāryābhidhāyinā tadatiśayābhidhānapareṇa vākyāntareṇa pratītigocaratāṃ nīyate /
yathā
children.translated_text: That 'is called concealment obliquity' — what is of such a kind is called, is designated, concealment obliquity. The compound [means either] 'obliquity through concealment' or 'obliquity predominantly characterized by concealment.' 'Where' — in which [expression] — 'a thing,' an entity of the nature of a referent, 'is concealed,' is covered over. For what reason? — 'With the intention of producing variety' (<s>vaicitryasya vivakṣayā</s>): with the desire to express an elaborate quality, by which the referent attains an elaborate character — this is the meaning. By what is it concealed? — 'By pronouns and the like' (<s>sarvanāmādibhiḥ kaiścit</s>): 'the name of all' is a pronoun (<s>sarvanāman</s>); that which begins with those — thus designated — by those, by some unprecedented expressions — this is the meaning. Here many types are possible. Where a certain superlative thing, though capable of being stated directly, is concealed by a generic pronoun lest through direct expression it appear limited, circumscribed to a finite extent, and is then brought into the domain of cognition through another sentence that expresses its effect and that conveys its superlative quality. For example:
Then, when that father was desirous of taking a wife, that noble one performed what was to be done,

children.text: puṣpacāpaśikharasthakapolo manmathaḥ kimapi yena nidadhyau // VjivC_2.58 //
children.translated_text: [and] <s>Manmatha</s> (the god of love), with the flower-bow's tip touching his cheek, pondered something. // VjivC_2.58 //

children.text:
atra sadācārapravaṇatayā gurubhaktibhāvitāntaḥ karaṇo lokottaraudāryaguṇayogādvividhaviṣayopabhogavitṛṣṇamanā nijendriyanigrahamasaṃbhāvanīyamapi śāntanavo vihitavānityabhidhātuṃ śakyamapi sāmānyābhidhāyinā sarvānāmnācchādyottarārdhena kāryāntarābhidhāyinā vākyāntareṇa pratītigocaratāmānīyamānaṃ kāmapi camatkārakāritāmāvahati /
ayamaparaḥ prakāro yatra svaparispandakāṣṭhādhirūḍheḥ sātiśayaṃ vastu vacasāmagocara iti prathayituṃ sarvānāmnā samācchādya tatkāryābhidhāyinā tadatiśayavācinā vākyāntareṇa samunmīlyate /
yathā
children.translated_text: Here, though it is possible to state directly that <s>Śāntanu's</s> son [<s>Bhīṣma</s>], whose inner faculty is imbued with devotion to his father through his inclination toward righteous conduct, who is of extraordinary generosity and therefore of a mind free from desire for the enjoyment of manifold objects, performed even the inconceivable act of self-restraint of his senses — yet by concealing it with a generic pronoun and then bringing it into the domain of cognition through another sentence in the latter half that expresses another effect, it produces a certain wonder. This is another type, where, in order to proclaim that a superlative thing, having ascended the summit of its own vibration, is beyond the reach of speech, it is concealed by a pronoun and then revealed through another sentence that expresses its effect and conveys its superlative quality. For example:

children.text: yāte dvāravatī tadā madhuripau taddattakampānatāṃ kālindījalakelivañjulalatāmālambaya sotkaṇṭhayā /
children.translated_text: When <s>Madhuripa</s> (<s>Kṛṣṇa</s>) had gone to <s>Dvāravatī</s>, then, with eager longing, grasping the <s>vañjula</s> creeper on the bank of the <s>Kālindī</s> waters — the one made to tremble by him —
<s>Rādhā</s> sang that song, with voice faltering with heavy tears and choked with emotion, so that even the aquatic creatures moving under water cried out in agitation. // VjivC_2.59 //

children.text:
atra sarvanāmnā saṃvṛtaṃ vastu tatkāryābhidhāyinā vākyāntareṇa samunmīlya sahṛdayahṛdayahāritāṃ prāpitam /
yathā vā
children.translated_text: Here, the thing concealed by the pronoun was revealed through another sentence expressing its effect, and thereby attained the quality of captivating the hearts of the connoisseurs. Or for example:
[Prakrit:] 'Then <s>Viśākhā</s> wept, O <s>Kaṇha</s> (<s>Kṛṣṇa</s>), with a voice choked with sobbing,

children.text: jaha kassa vi jammasae vi koi mā vallaho hou // VjivC_2.60 //
children.translated_text: [saying:] May no one become anyone's beloved, even in a hundred births!' // VjivC_2.60 //
[Sanskrit shadow:] 'Then <s>Viśākhā</s> wept, O <s>Kṛṣṇa</s>, with a voice choked with sobbing,

children.text: yathā kasyāpi janmaśate 'pi ko 'pi mā vallabho bhavatu //
children.translated_text: [saying:] May no one become anyone's beloved, even in a hundred births!'

children.text:
iti chāyā /
atra pūrvārdhe saṃvṛtaṃ vastu rodanalakṣaṇaṃ tadatiśayābhidhāyinā vākyāntareṇa kāmapi tadvidāhlādakāritāṃ nītam /
idamaparamatra prakārāntaraṃ yatra sātiśayasukumāraṃ vastu kāryātiśayābhidhānaṃ vinā saṃvṛtimātraramaṇīyatayā kāmapi kāṣṭhamadhiropyate /
yathā
children.translated_text: This is the <s>chāyā</s> (Sanskrit rendering). Here, in the first half, the thing concealed — characterized as weeping — is brought by another sentence that expresses its superlative quality to a certain capacity to delight the connoisseurs. This is yet another type here, where a superlatively delicate thing, without any expression of superlative effect, is raised to a certain pinnacle through the charm of concealment alone. For example:

children.text: darpaṇe ca paribhogadarśinī pṛṣṭhataḥ praṇayino niṣeduṣaḥ /
children.translated_text: In the mirror, gazing at the enjoyment to come, while the beloved was seated behind her,

children.text: vīkṣya bimbamanubimbamātmanaḥ kāni kāni na cakāra lajjayā // VjivC_2.61 //
children.translated_text: seeing the reflected image as a counterpart of herself — what all she did not do out of modesty! // VjivC_2.61 //

children.text:
ayamaparaḥ prakāro yatra svānubhasaṃvedanīyaṃ vastu vacasā vaktumaviṣaya iti khyāpayituṃ saṃvriyate /
yathā
children.translated_text: This is another type, where a thing that is cognizable only through one's own experience is concealed in order to proclaim that it is beyond the domain of speech. For example:
'Those syllables resound as something in the heart.' // VjivC_2.62 //
Thus.

children.text:
pūrvameva vyākhyātam /
idamapi prakārāntaraṃ saṃbhavati yatra parānubhasaṃvedyasya vastuno vakturagocaratāṃ pratipādayituṃ saṃvṛtiḥ kriyate /
yathā
children.translated_text: This was already explained earlier. This other type also is possible, where concealment is employed in order to convey that a thing cognizable only through another's experience is beyond the speaker's domain. For example:
'<s>Manmatha</s> pondered something.' // VjivC_2.63 //

children.text:
atra hi tribhuvanaprathitapratāmahimā tathāvidhaśaktivyāghātaviṣaṇṇacetāḥ kāmaḥ kimapi svānubhavasamucitamacintayaditi /
idamaparaṃ prakārāntaramatra vidyate ---yatra svabhāvena kavivivakṣayā vā kenacidaupahatyena yuktaṃ vastu mahāpātakamiva kīrtanīyatāṃ nārhatīti samarpayituṃ saṃvriyate /
yathā
children.translated_text: Here indeed, <s>Kāma</s> (the god of love), whose power and grandeur are renowned in the three worlds, with his mind despondent at the obstruction of such power, pondered something appropriate to his own experience. This is yet another type here — where a thing that, by nature or by the poet's intention, is accompanied by some offense, is concealed in order to convey that, like a great sin, it does not deserve to be uttered. For example:

children.text: durvacaṃ tadatha māsma bhūnmṛga- stvayyasau yadakariṣyadojasā /
children.translated_text: 'That unspeakable thing — may the deer not do to you by force what he was about to do,

children.text: nainamāśu yadi vāhinīpatiḥ pratyapatsyata śitena patriṇā // VjivC_2.64 //
children.translated_text: had not the commander of the army quickly dispatched him with a sharp arrow.' // VjivC_2.64 //
Or for example:
'Restrain this <s>vaṭu</s> (boy-ascetic) from something, O friend — he is about to speak again, his lower lip trembling!

children.text: na kevalaṃ yo mahato 'pabhāṣate śṛṇoti tasmādapi yaḥ sa pāpabhāk // VjivC_2.65 //
children.translated_text: Not only one who reviles the great is a partaker of sin, but also one who listens to it.' // VjivC_2.65 //

children.text:
atrārjunamāraṇaṃ bhagavadapabhāṣaṇaṃ ca na kīrtanoyatāmarhatīti saṃvaraṇena ramaṇīyatāṃ nītamiti /
vivakṣayo pahataṃ yathā
children.translated_text: Here, the killing of <s>Arjuna</s> and the reviling of the <s>Bhagavān</s> are brought to charm through concealment, as they do not deserve to be uttered. An example where the offense is produced by the poet's intention:

children.text: so 'yaṃ dambhadhṛtavrataḥ priyatame kartuṃ kimapyudyataḥ // VjivC_2.66 //
children.translated_text: 'This one, of hypocritical vows, is about to do something to the beloved.' // VjivC_2.66 //
Thus.

children.text:
prathamameva vyākhyātam /
eva saṃvṛtivakratāṃ vicārya pratyayavakratāyāḥ ko 'pi prakāraḥ padamadhyāntarbhūtatvādihaiva samucitāvasarastasmāttadvicāramācarati---
children.translated_text: This was already explained earlier. Having thus examined concealment obliquity, since a certain type of suffix obliquity (<s>pratyayavakratā</s>) is included within the middle of the word, its appropriate occasion is here — therefore he undertakes its examination:
The suffix, revealing the design of propriety to the subject
by its own greatness, within the middle of the word, causes another obliquity to shine forth. // Vjiv_2.17 //

children.text:
kaścit pratyayaḥ kṛdādiḥ padamadhyavṛttiranyāmapūrvāṃ vakratāmullāsayati vakrabhāvamuddīpayati /
kiṃ kurvan---prastutasya varṇyamānasya vastuno yadaucityamucitabhāvastasya vicchittimupaśobhāṃ vikāsayan samullāsayan /
kena---svamahimnā nijotkarṣeṇa /
yathā
children.translated_text: A certain suffix, such as a <s>kṛt</s> (primary) suffix and the like, operating within the middle of the word, causes another, unprecedented obliquity to shine forth, to kindle the oblique character. Doing what? — Revealing the design, the beauty, of the propriety to the subject, the matter being described — its state of being fitting — causing it to shine forth, to bloom. By what? — 'By its own greatness,' by its own excellence. For example:
'Clouds with swaying cranes.' // VjivC_2.67 //
Or for example:
'Eyes with affectionate sidelong glances.' // VjivC_2.68 //

children.text:
atra vartamānakālābhidhāyī śatṛpratyayaḥ kāmapyatītānāgatavibhramavirahitāṃ tātkālikaparispandasundarīṃ prastutaucityavicchittimullā sayan sahṛdayahṛdayahāriṇīṃ pratyayavakratāmāvahati /
idānīmetasyāḥ prakārāntaraṃ paryālocayati---
children.translated_text: Here the present-tense participial suffix (<s>śatṛ pratyaya</s>), denoting the present time, causing a certain design of propriety to the subject — beautiful through the vibration of the immediate moment, free from the confusion of past and future — to shine forth, produces a qualificative obliquity that captivates the hearts of the connoisseurs. Now he considers another type of this:
Beautiful through the vibration of grammatical derivation (<s>āgama</s>) and the like, [the suffix]
nourishes a certain supreme word-obliquity (<s>śabdavakratā</s>) that produces the flavor of compositional style. // Vjiv_2.18 //

children.text:
paro dvitīyaḥ pratyayaprakāraḥ kāmapyapūrvāṃ śabdavakratāmābadhnāti vācakavakratāṃ vidadhāti /
kīdṛk---āgamādiparispandasundaraḥ /
āgamo mumādirādiryasya sa tathoktaḥ, tasyāgamādeḥ parispandaḥ svavilasitaṃ tena sundaraḥ sukumāraḥ /
kīdṛśīṃ śabdavakratām---bandhacchāyāvidhāyinīṃ saṃniveśakāntikāriṇīmityarthaḥ /
yathā
children.translated_text: The second variety, that of the suffix, produces some unprecedented obliqueness of expression — an obliqueness of the signifier. Of what kind? — 'beautiful through the activity of augments and so forth.' That whose augment is the <s>mum</s>-augment and the like — such is its activity, its own display — beautiful by that, delicate. What kind of expression-obliqueness? — 'one that produces the lustre of composition' — meaning: one that creates a beauty of arrangement. For example —

children.text: jāne sakhyāstava mayi manaḥ saṃbhṛtasnehamasmā- ditthaṃbhūtāṃ prathamavirahe tāmahaṃ tarkayāmi /
children.translated_text: 'I know that in your friend's heart love toward me is gathered; I imagine her to be in such a state at this, the first separation.

children.text: vācālaṃ māṃ na khalu subhagaṃmanyabhāvaḥ karoti pratyakṣaṃ te nikhilamacirād bhrātaruktaṃ mayā yad // VjivC_2.69 //
children.translated_text: It is not the conviction of being favored that makes me talkative — for all that was said by me as your brother will soon be evident to you.' // VjivC_2.69 //
And also —
'The burning — water — a spreading-and-cooking' and so on // VjivC_2.70 //
And also —
'Drinking and drinking, the banana-leaf curled up in a spiral' // VjivC_2.71 //
Thus.

children.text:
atra subhagaṃmanyabhāvaprabhṛtiṣu śabdeṣu mumādiparispandasundarāḥ saṃniveśacchāyāvidhāyinī vācakavakratāṃ pratyayāḥ puṣṇanti /
evaṃ prasaṅgasamucitāṃ padamadhyavartipratyayavakratāṃ vicārya samanantarasaṃbhavinīṃ vṛttivakratāṃ vicārayati---
children.translated_text: Here, in words like '<s>subhagaṃmanyabhāva</s>' (the conviction of being favored) and so forth, the suffixes, beautiful through the activity of the <s>mum</s>-augment and the like, nourish an expression-obliqueness that produces the lustre of arrangement. Having thus examined the obliqueness of the suffix that occupies the middle of the word — appropriate to the occasion — he now examines the obliqueness of compositional modes (<s>vṛtti</s>), which follows immediately —
The beauty of compositional modes (<s>vṛtti</s>), chief among which is the <s>avyayībhāva</s> compound —
where that shines forth, that should be understood as the obliqueness of the variety of compositional modes. // Vjiv_2.19 //

children.text:
sā vṛttivaicitryavakratā jñeyā boddhavyā /
vṛttīnāṃ vaicitryaṃ vicitrabhāvaḥ sajātīyāpekṣayā saukumāryotkarṣastena vakratā vakrabhāvavicchittiḥ /
kīdṛśī---ramaṇīyatā yatrollasati /
rāmaṇīyakaṃ yasyāmudbhidyate /
kasya---vṛttīnām /
kāsām---avyayībhāvamukyānām /
avyayībhāvaḥ samāsaḥ mukhyaḥ pradhānabhūto yāsaṃ tāstathoktāstāsāṃ samāsataddhitasubdhātuvṛttīnāṃ vaiyākaraṇaprasiddhānām /
tadayamatrārthaḥ---yatra svaparispandasaundaryametāsāṃ samucitabhittibhāgopanibandhādabhivyaktimāsādayati /
yathā
children.translated_text: That obliqueness of the variety of compositional modes should be understood, should be known. The variety of compositional modes — the varied character — is the surpassing delicacy compared to those of the same class; the obliqueness through that is the charm of oblique quality. Of what kind? — 'the beauty that shines forth.' Where the loveliness springs up. Of what? — of the compositional modes. Which ones? — 'chief among which is the <s>avyayībhāva</s>.' Those in which the <s>avyayībhāva</s> (indeclinable) compound is the chief, i.e., primary — of such compound, secondary derivative (<s>taddhita</s>), primary derivative (<s>subdhātu</s>) modes, well-known in grammar. The meaning here is this: where the beauty of the inherent activity of these [modes] achieves manifest expression through connection with a fitting surface [of context]. For example —

children.text: abhivyaktiṃ tāvad bahiralabhamānaḥ kathamapi sphurannantaḥ svatmanyadhikatarasaṃmūrchitataraḥ /
children.translated_text: 'Not yet obtaining outward manifestation, somehow flickering within the self, growing ever more intensely concentrated,

children.text: manojñāmudvṛttasmaraparimala spandasubhagā- maho datte śobhāmadhimadhu latānāṃ navarasaḥ // VjivC_2.72 //
children.translated_text: the new sap of the creepers gives forth, wondrous in the season of spring, a charming beauty, delightful with the movement of the fragrance of risen <s>Smara</s> (love).' // VjivC_2.72 //

children.text:
atra "adhimadhu'-śabde vibhaktyarthavihitaḥ samāsaḥ samayābhidhāyyapi viṣayasaptamīpratītimutpādayan "navarasa'-śabdasya śloṣacchāyācchuraṇavaicitryamunmīlayati /
etadvṛttivirahite vinyāsāntare vastupratītau satyāmapi na tādṛktadvidāhlādakāritvam /
udvṛtta-parimalaspanda-subhaga-śabdanāmupacāravakratvaṃ parisphuradvibhāvyate /
yathā ca
children.translated_text: Here, in the word '<s>adhimadhu</s>' (in the season of spring), the compound formed with the sense of a case-ending, even though designating a season, by producing the cognition of a locative case, reveals the variety-flash of a <s>śleṣa</s> (paronomasia) lustre for the word '<s>navarasa</s>' (new sap / nine <s>rasas</s>). In a different arrangement devoid of this compositional mode, even though the understanding of the subject matter would be present, it would not produce such delight in the knowledgeable. The figurative obliqueness of the words '<s>udvṛtta</s>' (risen), '<s>parimala</s>' (fragrance), '<s>spanda</s>' (movement), and '<s>subhaga</s>' (charming) is manifestly discernible. And also —

children.text: ā svarlokāduraganagaraṃ nūtanālokalakṣmīṃ- vyātanvadbhiḥ kimiva sitatāṃ ceṣṭitaiste na nītam /
children.translated_text: 'By those whose actions extended from the world of the gods to the city of serpents the beauty of new appearance —

children.text: apyetāsāṃ dayitavirahe vidviṣatsundarīṇāṃ yairānītā nakhapadamayī maṇḍanā pāṇḍimānam // VjivC_2.73 //
children.translated_text: to what did they not bring whiteness? Yet of these women hostile in the separation from their beloved, by whom their ornament of nail-marks was brought to pallor.' // VjivC_2.73 //

children.text:
atra pāṇḍutva-pāṇḍutā-pāṇḍubhāva-śabdebhyaḥ pāṇḍima-śabdasya kimapi vṛttivaicitryavakratvaṃ vidyate /
yathā ca
children.translated_text: Here, as compared to the words '<s>pāṇḍutva</s>,' '<s>pāṇḍutā</s>,' and '<s>pāṇḍubhāva</s>,' the word '<s>pāṇḍima</s>' (pallor) possesses a certain obliqueness through the variety of compositional modes. And also —
'The moon — with the bathing-draughts from the cascades of the nectar of loveliness, flowing from the powder-anointing that delights the lustre of <s>Siṃhalī</s> (Sinhalese) women's faces,
by which the moon is made a single parasol over the drinking-festival rivalries of the mind-born god [<s>Kāma</s>], victorious over the lord of the thirty gods [<s>Indra</s>].' // VjivC_2.74 //

children.text:
atra subdhātuvṛtteḥ samāsavṛtteśca kimapi vakratāvaicitryaṃ parisphurati /
evaṃ vṛttivakratāṃ vicārya padapūrvārdhabhāvinīmucitāvasarāṃ bhāvavakratāṃ vicārayati---
children.translated_text: Here, a certain variety-obliqueness of the primary derivative (<s>subdhātu</s>) mode and the compound mode shines forth. Having thus examined the obliqueness of compositional modes, he now examines the obliqueness of verbal meaning (<s>bhāvavakratā</s>), which belongs to the first half of the word and arises at the appropriate occasion —
Where a state of being is expressed as completed, disregarding its being-in-process —
that is the obliqueness of the variety of verbal meaning (<s>bhāvavaicitryavakratā</s>). // Vjiv_2.20 //

children.text:
eṣā varṇitasvarūpā bhāvavaicitryavakratā bhavatyasti /
bhāvo dhātvartharūpastasyai vaicitryaṃ vicitrabhāvaḥ prakārāntarābhidhānavyatireki rāmaṇīyakaṃ tena vakratā vakratvavicchittiḥ /
kīdṛśī---yatra yasyāṃ bhāvaḥ siddhatvena pariniṣpannatvenābhidhīyate bhaṇyate /
kiṃ kṛtvā---sādhyatāmapyanādṛtya niṣpādyamānatāṃ prasiddhāmapyavadhīrya /
tadidamatra tātparyam---yat sādhyatvenābhidhānādapariniṣpatteḥ prastutasyārthasya durbalaḥ paripoṣaḥ tasmāt siddhatvenābhidhānaṃ pariniṣpannatvātparyāptaṃ prakṛtārthaparipoṣamāvahati /
yathā
children.translated_text: This, of the nature described, is the obliqueness of the variety of verbal meaning. The verbal meaning (<s>bhāva</s>) — in the form of the meaning of the verbal root — its variety is its varied character, a beauty that is different from expression in another mode; the obliqueness through that is the charm of oblique quality. Of what kind? — 'where' — in which [expression] — 'the state of being is expressed as completed' — as being finished, accomplished. Doing what? — 'disregarding its being-in-process' — rejecting, overlooking the well-known state of being-in-the-process-of-being-accomplished. The purport here is this: because from being expressed as in process, the subject matter would be weakly nourished due to its incompleteness — therefore expression as completed, being sufficient due to its completeness, brings about an adequate nourishment of the subject matter at hand. For example —

children.text: śvāsāyāsamalīmasādhararucerdeḥ kandalītānavāt keyūrāyitamaṅgadaiḥ pariṇataṃ pāṇḍimni gaṇḍatviṣā /
children.translated_text: 'Of her whose bodily lustre is dimmed and soiled by the labored sighing, whose armlets have become bracelets as the pallor of her cheeks has matured,

children.text: asyāḥ kiṃ ca vilocanotpalayugenātyantamaśrustrutā tāraṃ tādṛgapāṅgayoraruṇitaṃ yenotpratāpaḥ smaraḥ // VjivC_2.75 //
children.translated_text: and moreover — from this one's pair of lotus-eyes, dripping excessively with tears, such a reddening of the side-glances has been produced that <s>Smara</s> (the god of love) feels his authority threatened.' // VjivC_2.75 //

children.text:
atra bhāvasya siddhatvenābhidhānamatīva camatkārakāri /
evaṃ bhāvavakratāṃ vicārya prātipadikāntarvartinīṃ liṅgavakratāṃ vicārayati---
children.translated_text: Here, the expression of the verbal meaning as completed is exceedingly productive of wonder. Having thus examined the obliqueness of verbal meaning, he now examines the obliqueness of grammatical gender (<s>liṅgavakratā</s>), which resides within the nominal stem —
In which, through the co-referentiality of two different genders,
some beauty arises — that is the obliqueness of the variety of gender. // Vjiv_2.21 //

children.text:
eṣā kathitasvarūpā liṅgavaicitryavakratā stṣādivicitrabhāvavakratāvicchittiḥ /
bhavatīti saṃbandhaḥ, kriyāntarābhāvāt kīdṛśī---yasyāṃ yatra bhinnayorvibhaktasvarūpayorliṅgayordvayoḥ sāmānādhikaraṇyatastulyāśrayatvādekadravyavṛttitvāt kāpyapūrvā śobhābhyudeti kāntirullasati /
yathā
children.translated_text: This, of the stated nature, is the obliqueness of the variety of gender — the charm of obliqueness through the varied character of the feminine gender and the like. 'It is' — this is the syntactic connection, there being no other verb. Of what kind? — 'in which' — where — of two genders of distinct nature, through their co-referentiality, i.e., through their having a common substrate, through their applying to a single substance, some unprecedented beauty arises, some lustre shines forth. For example —
'By the mere task of stringing whose [bow], many have been made to abandon their vow of heroism — the lordly bow must be feathered with arrows by these arms of mine.

children.text: strīratnaṃ tadagarbhasaṃbhavamito labhyaṃ ca līlāyitā tenaiṣā mama phullapaṅkajavanaṃ jātā dṛśāṃ viṃśatiḥ // VjivC_2.76 //
children.translated_text: And that jewel among women, of unprecedented birth, is to be won from here, and the [whole] is a sport — therefore this is for my eyes a feast of twenty [sights, like] a field of blooming lotuses.' // VjivC_2.76 //
Or for example —
'On whose broad chest, the wishing-creeper made to dance by the wind,

children.text: uraḥ sthale 'kīryata dakṣiṇena sarvāspadaṃ saurabhamaṅgarāgaḥ // VjivC_2.77 //
children.translated_text: with a young coral fan, was scattered as a body-unguent — the all-pervading fragrance, by the southern [breeze].' // VjivC_2.77 //
'Fashioning a garland carefully prepared by the seasons, on the surface of his arm,

children.text: karāravindaṃ makarandabindu- syandi śriyā vibhramakarṇapūraḥ // VjivC_2.78 //
children.translated_text: her lotus-hand, dripping with drops of nectar — in beauty, became an ear-ornament of playfulness.' // VjivC_2.78 //
And this is another kind of gender-variety obliqueness —

children.text: sati liṅgāntare yatra strīliṅgaṃ ca prayujyate /
children.translated_text: Where, when another gender exists, the feminine gender is employed
for the purpose of producing beauty, because the very name 'woman' is charming. // Vjiv_2.22 //

children.text:
yatra yasyāṃ liṅgāntare satyanyasmin saṃbhavatyapi liṅge strīliṅgaṃ prayujyate nibadhyate /
anekaliṅgatve 'pi padārthasya strīliṅgaviṣayaḥ prayogaḥ kriyate /
kimartham---śobhāniṣpattaye kāntisampattaye /
kasmāt kāraṇāt---yasmānnāmaiva strīti peśalam /
strītyabhidhānameva hṛdayahāri /
vicchityantareṇa rasādiprayojana yogyatvāt /
udāharaṇaṃ
children.translated_text: 'Where' — in which [expression] — 'when another gender exists,' even when another gender is possible, 'the feminine gender is employed,' is bound. Even when the object has multiple genders, the usage is made in the domain of the feminine gender. For what purpose? — 'for the purpose of producing beauty,' for the attainment of loveliness. For what reason? — 'because the very name "woman" is charming.' The designation 'woman' itself is captivating to the heart — because, through another mode of charm, it has fitness for the purpose of <s>rasa</s> and the like. An example —
'Just as this bank (<s>taṭī</s>, feminine), with its intermingled summer heat, with its pale fissures, its withered creeper-shoots trembling in the breeze that issues from [her] mouth —

children.text: taṭī tāraṃ tāmyatyatiśaśiyaśāḥ ko 'pi jalada- stathā manye bhāvī bhuvanavalayākrāntisubhagā // VjivC_2.79 //
children.translated_text: pines away, exceedingly pale in [her] lunar radiance — so too, I imagine, shall be the coming [cloud], the one beautiful in [his] invasion of the circle of the world.' // VjivC_2.79 //

children.text: atra triliṅgatve satyapi "taṭa'-śabdasya, saukumāryāt strīliṅgameva prayuktam /
children.translated_text: Here, although the word '<s>taṭa</s>' (bank) has all three genders, the feminine alone has been employed, owing to its delicacy.

children.text: tena vicchintyantareṇa bhāvī nāyakavyavahāraḥ kaścidāsūtrita ityatīva ramaṇīyatvādvakratāmāvahati //
children.translated_text: Thereby, through another mode of charm, some coming conduct of a hero is suggested — and because this is exceedingly delightful, it produces obliqueness.
He now defines yet another subvariety of this [gender obliqueness] —
Where a particular gender is employed, even though another exists,
for the purpose of distinctive charm — that is another [kind], in conformity with the propriety of the subject. // Vjiv_2.23 //

children.text:
sā coktasvarūpā anyā aparā liṅgavakratā vidyate /
yatra yasyāṃ viśiṣṭaṃ yojyate liṅgatrayāṇāmekatamaṃ kimapi kavivivakṣayā nibadhyate /
katham---anyasmin saṃbhavatyapi, liṅgāntare vidyamāne 'pi /
kimartham---vicchittaye śobhāyai /
kasmāt kāraṇāt---vācyaucityānusārataḥ /
vācyasya varṇyamānasya vastuno yadaucityamucitabhāvastasyānusaraṇamanusārastasmāt /
padārthaucityamanusṛtyetyarthaḥ /
yathā
children.translated_text: That, of the stated nature — another, a different gender-obliqueness exists. 'Where' — in which [expression] — 'a particular [gender] is employed' — of the three genders, some one is bound at the poet's will. How? — 'even though another exists' — even though another gender is available. For what purpose? — 'for the purpose of distinctive charm,' for beauty. For what reason? — 'in conformity with the propriety of the subject.' The propriety, the fitness, of the subject being described — following that, conforming to it. Meaning: following the propriety of the object. For example —

children.text: tvaṃ rakṣasā bhīru yato 'panītā taṃ mārgametāḥ kṛpayā latā me /
children.translated_text: 'Since you, O timid one, were abducted by the <s>rākṣasa</s> on this path — these creepers of mine (<s>latā</s>, feminine),
out of compassion, showed me that path, being unable to speak — with branches whose shoots were bent downward.' // VjivC_2.80 //

children.text:
atra sītayā saha rāmaḥ puṣpakenāvataraṃstasyāḥ svayameva tadvirahavaidhuryamāvedayati---tattvaṃ rāvaṇena tathāvidhatvarāparatantracetasā mārge yasminnapanītā tatra tadupamardavaśāttathāvidhasaṃsthānayuktatvaṃ latānāmunmukhatvaṃ mama tvanmārgānumānasya nimittatāmāpannamiti vastu vicchittyantareṇa rāmeṇa yojyate /
yathā---he bhīru svābhāvikasaukumāryakātarāntaḥ karaṇe, rāvaṇena tathāvidhakrūrakarmakāriṇā yasminmārge tvamapanītā tametāḥ sākṣātkāraparidṛśyamānamūrtayo latāḥ kila mamādarśa yanniti /
tanmārgapradarśanaṃ paramārthatastāsāṃ niścetanatayā na saṃbhāvyata iti pratīyamānavṛttirutprekṣālaṅkāraḥ kaverabhimataḥ /
yathā---tava bhīrutvaṃ rāvaṇasya krauryaṃ mamāpi tvatparitrāṇaprayatnaparatāṃ paryālocya strīsvabhāvādārdrahṛdayatvena samucitasvaviṣayapakṣapātamāhātmyādetāḥ kṛpayaiva mama mārgapradarśanamakurvanniti /
kena karaṇabhūtena---śākhābhirāvarjitapallavābhiḥ /
yasmādvāgindriyavarjitatvādvaktumaśaknuvantyaḥ /
yatkila ye kecidajalpanto mārgapradarśanaṃ prakurvanti te tadunmukhībhūtahastapallavairbāhubhirityetadatīva yuktiyuktam /
tathā cātraiva vākyāntaramapi vidyate
children.translated_text: Here, <s>Rāma</s>, descending in the <s>Puṣpaka</s> [chariot] with <s>Sītā</s>, himself conveys to her the distress of separation from her: 'On the path by which you were abducted by <s>Rāvaṇa</s> — he whose mind was enslaved by such depravity — there, due to the destruction caused by him, the creepers' being in such a configuration, their directedness, became the occasion for my inference of your route' — thus the subject matter is joined by <s>Rāma</s> through another mode of charm. Namely: 'O timid one — one whose inner faculty is apprehensive from natural delicacy — on the path on which you were abducted by <s>Rāvaṇa</s>, the doer of such cruel deeds, these creepers, whose forms are directly visible, showed it to me, apparently.' The showing of the path, being in reality impossible due to the creepers' unconsciousness, is cognized [figuratively] — the figure <s>utprekṣā</s> (poetic fancy) is what the poet intends. Namely: 'Reflecting upon your timidity, <s>Rāvaṇa's</s> cruelty, and my own eagerness to rescue you — out of the tender-heartedness natural to the feminine, and through the greatness of the partiality befitting their own domain — these [creepers], out of compassion alone, showed me the path.' By what means? — 'with branches whose shoots were bent downward.' Since, being devoid of the organ of speech, they were unable to speak. For indeed, those who, being speechless, show the path — they do so with their arm-shoots directed toward it — and this is exceedingly appropriate. And here there is also another sentence in the same passage —
'And the female deer, disregarding the shoots of <s>darbha</s> grass, informed me, who knew of your arrival,

children.text: vyāpārayantyo dikhi dakṣiṇasyā- mutpakṣmarājīni vilocanāni // VjivC_2.81 //
children.translated_text: directing toward the southern quarter their eyes with upraised rows of lashes.' // VjivC_2.81 //

children.text:
hariṇyaśca māṃ samabodhayan /
kīdṛśam---tavāgatijñam, latāpradarśitamārgamajānantam /
tatastāḥ mamyagabodhayanniti, yatastāstadapekṣayā kiñcitprabuddhā iti /
tāśca kīdṛśyaḥ---tathāvidhavaiśasasaṃdarśanavaśād duḥkhitatvena parityaktatṛṇagrāsāḥ /
kiṃ kurvāṇāḥ---tasyāṃ diśi nayanāni samarpayantyaḥ /
kīdṛśāni---ūrdhvokṛtapakṣmapaṅktīni /
tadevaṃ tathāvidhasthānakayuktatvena dakṣiṇāṃ diśamantarikṣeṇa nīteti saṃjñayā nivedayantyaḥ /
atra vṛkṣamṛgādiṣu liṅgāntareṣu saṃbhavatsvapi strīliṅgameva padārthaucityānusāreṇa cetanacamatkārakāritayā kaverabhipretam /
tasmāt kāmapi vakratāmāvahati /
evaṃ prātipadikalakṣaṇasya subantasaṃbhavinaḥ padapūrvārdhasya yathāsaṃbhavaṃ vakrabhāvaṃ vicāryedānīmubhayorapi suptiṅantayordhātusvarūpaḥ pūrvabhāgo yaḥ saṃbhavati tasya vakratāṃ vicārayati /
tasya ca kriyāvaicitryanibandhanageva vakratvaṃ vidyate /
tasmāt kriyāvaicitryasyaiva kīdṛśāḥ kiyantaśca prakārāḥ saṃbhavantīti tatsvarūpanirūpaṇārthamāha---
children.translated_text: And the deer-does awakened me. How? — [They awakened] one ignorant of your departure, one who did not know the path indicated by the creepers. Then they partially awakened me, because they, in relation to that [departure], were somewhat aroused. And what were they like? — Having abandoned grazing on grass due to being distressed by witnessing such a slaughter. What were they doing? — Directing their eyes in that direction. What kind [of eyes]? — With rows of eyelashes lifted upward. Thus, by being endowed with such a posture, they were indicating through signs that [she] had been carried away through the sky in the southern direction. Here, although other grammatical genders are possible with respect to trees, deer, and so forth, the poet intentionally chose the feminine gender alone, in accordance with the propriety of meaning, because it produces <s>camatkāra</s> (aesthetic wonder) through [the attribution of] consciousness. Therefore it brings about a certain <s>vakratā</s> (obliqueness). Having thus examined, as appropriate, the oblique nature of the first half of the word — the nominal stem that belongs to the <s>subanta</s> (nominal inflection) — he now examines the obliqueness of the first part, which is the verbal root, belonging to the latter half of both <s>subanta</s> (nominal) and <s>tiṅanta</s> (verbal) [words]. And its obliqueness exists as grounded in <s>kriyāvaicitrya</s> (obliqueness of action). Therefore, to determine the nature of <s>kriyāvaicitrya</s> — what kinds and how many varieties are possible — he says:
Extreme intimacy of the agent, variegation through another agent,
variegation through one's own qualifier, charm of figurative usage, // Vjiv_2.24 //
concealment of the object and so forth — these five, which are graceful through propriety to the subject at hand,
are declared to be the varieties of obliqueness arising from <s>kriyāvaicitrya</s> (obliqueness of action). // Vjiv_2.25 //

children.text:
kriyāvaicitryavakratvaprikārā dhātvarthavicitrabhāvavakratāprabhedāsta ime smṛtā varṇyamānasvarūpāḥ kīrtitāḥ /
kiyantaḥ pañca pañcasaṃkhyāviśiṣṭāḥ /
kīdṛśāḥ---prastutaucityacāravaḥ /
prastutaṃ varṇyamānaṃ vastu tasya yadaucityamucitabhāvastena cāravo ramaṇīyāḥ /
tatra prathamastāvat prakāro yat---karturatyantaraṅgatvaṃ nāma /
kartuḥ svatantratayā mukhyabhūtasya kārakasya kriyāṃ prati nirvartayituryadatyantaraṅgatvam atyantamāntaratamyam /
yathā
children.translated_text: The varieties of obliqueness arising from <s>kriyāvaicitrya</s> (obliqueness of action) — that is, the subdivisions of obliqueness consisting in the variegated nature of the meaning of the verbal root — these are declared, that is, described as having the nature now being expounded. How many? Five, distinguished by the number five. What are they like? — <s>prastutaucityacāravaḥ</s> (graceful through propriety to the subject): <s>prastuta</s> is the subject being described; its <s>aucitya</s> (propriety) is its fitness; by that, they are <s>cāru</s> (charming), that is, beautiful. Among these, the first variety is: <s>karturatyantaraṅgatva</s> (extreme intimacy of the agent). The extreme intimacy — the utmost closeness — of the agent, who is the principal <s>kāraka</s> (case-relation) as the independent executor of the action with respect to the <s>kriyā</s> (action). For example:
He whose neck bends upward under the unbearable burden of the world resting upon his crest-jewel — let this head of the blessed <s>Śeṣa</s> assume an extraordinary boldness;

children.text: svairaṃ saṃspṛśatīṣadapyavanatiṃ yasmin luṭhantyakramaṃ śūnye nūnamiyanti nāma bhuvanānyuddāmakampottaram // VjivC_2.82 //
children.translated_text: Upon whom, when he touches even a slight inclination freely, the worlds, now in the void, surely roll about in disorder and go tumbling after the unrestrained trembling. // VjivC_2.82 //

children.text:
atroddhuratā dhāraṇalakṣaṇakriyā kartuḥ phaṇīśvaramastakasya prastutaucityamāhātmyādantarbhāvaṃ yathā bhajate tathā nānyā kāciditi kriyāvaicitryavakratāmāvahati /
yathā vā
children.translated_text: Here, the boldness — the action characterized as bearing — through the greatness of propriety to the subject, merges into the head of the lord of serpents as agent in such a way that no other [action] could, and thus it brings about the obliqueness of <s>kriyāvaicitrya</s> (obliqueness of action). Or for example:

children.text: kiṃ śobhitāhamanayeti pinākapāṇeḥ pṛṣṭasya pātu paricumbanamuttara vaḥ // VjivC_2.83 //
children.translated_text: "Have I been made beautiful by this one?" — may the kiss that is the answer of the bearer of the <s>Pināka</s> (Śiva), when asked thus, protect you! // VjivC_2.83 //

children.text:
atra cumbanavyatirekeṇa bhagavatā tathāvidhalokottaragaurī śobhātiśayābhidhānaṃ na kenacit kriyāntareṇa kartuṃ pāryata iti kriyāvaicitryanibandhanaṃ vakrabhāvamāvahati /
yathā ca
children.translated_text: Here, the declaration of the surpassing beauty of <s>Gaurī</s>, who is of such extraordinary, transcendent loveliness — which the blessed Lord could not accomplish by any other action except kissing — brings about obliqueness grounded in <s>kriyāvaicitrya</s> (obliqueness of action). And for example:
[Prakrit:] The third eye of <s>Rudra</s>, kissed by <s>Pārvatī</s>, is triumphant! // VjivC_2.84 //
The third eye of <s>Rudra</s>, kissed by <s>Pārvatī</s>, is triumphant!
Thus the Sanskrit rendering (<s>chāyā</s>).

children.text: yathā vā siḍhiliacāo jaai maaraddhao // VjivC_2.85 //
children.translated_text: [Prakrit:] Or for example: He whose bow is loosened — the banner of <s>Makara</s> (Kāmadeva) — is triumphant! // VjivC_2.85 //
He whose bow is loosened, <s>Makaradhvaja</s> (Kāmadeva, the god of love), is triumphant!
Thus the Sanskrit rendering (<s>chāyā</s>).

children.text:
etayorvaicitryaṃ pūrvameva vyākhyātam /
ayamaparaḥ kriyāvaicitryavakratāyāḥ prakāraḥ---kartrantaravicitratā /
anyaḥ kartā kartrantaraṃ tasmādvicitratā vaicitryam /
prastutatvāt sajātīyatvācca kartureva /
etadeva ca tasya vaicitryaṃ yad kriyāmeva kartrantarāpekṣayā vicitrasvarūpāṃ saṃpādayati /
yathā
children.translated_text: The obliqueness of these two has already been explained. Here is another variety of the obliqueness of <s>kriyāvaicitrya</s> — <s>kartrantaravicitratā</s> (variegation through another agent). Another agent is <s>kartrantara</s>; the variegation, that is, the variety arising from that, is <s>vicitratā</s>. It is of the agent alone, because [that agent] is the subject and of the same class. And this itself is its variegation: that it renders the action itself variegated in nature through dependence on another agent. For example:

children.text: naikatra śaktiviratiḥ kvacidasti sarve bhāvāḥ svabhāvapariniṣṭhitatāratamyāḥ /
children.translated_text: The power of no single entity has a limit anywhere; all things have degrees of excellence firmly established by nature.
<s>Agastya</s> drank up the ocean — which was being consumed by the submarine fire (<s>aurvadahana</s>) throughout the aeon — with a single sip! // VjivC_2.86 //

children.text:
atraikaculakenāmbhodhipānaṃ satatādhyavasāyābhāyāsakāṣṭhādhirūḍhiprauḍhatvādvāḍavāgneḥ kimapi kriyāvaicitryamudvahat vakratāmunmīlayati /
yathā vā
children.translated_text: Here, the drinking of the ocean with a single sip, by virtue of its robust boldness — having ascended to the highest pitch of effortless, unceasing determination — surpassing even the submarine fire in some inexplicable way, unfolds an obliqueness of <s>kriyāvaicitrya</s> (obliqueness of action). Or for example:
Nails that cut away the suffering of those who seek refuge. // VjivC_2.87 //
Or for example:

children.text: sa dahatu duritaṃ śāmbhavo vaḥ śarāgniḥ // VjivC_2.88 //
children.translated_text: May the arrow-fire of <s>Śambhu</s> (Śiva) burn away your sins! // VjivC_2.88 //

children.text:
etayorvaicitryaṃ pūrvameva pradarśitam /
ayamanyaḥ kriyāvaicitryavakrātāyāḥ prabhedaḥ---svaviśeṣaṇavaicitryam /
mukhyatayā prastutatvāt kriyāyāḥ svasyātmano yad viśeṣaṇaṃ bhedakaṃ tena vaicitryaṃ vicitrabhāvaḥ /
yathā---
children.translated_text: The obliqueness of these two has already been demonstrated. Here is another subdivision of the obliqueness of <s>kriyāvaicitrya</s> — <s>svaviśeṣaṇavaicitrya</s> (variegation through one's own qualifier). Since the action is principal as the subject, its own qualifier — that which differentiates it — produces the variegation, the state of being variegated. For example:
When the moon thus rose, by women whose eyes and minds were absorbed in the sweet conversation conveyed by the messenger of tender beauty,
the act of ornamentation was taken up, while their friends laughed at the reversed arrangement of ornaments. // VjivC_2.89 //

children.text:
atra maṇḍanavidhigrahaṇalakṣaṇāyāḥ kriyāyā viparītabhūṣāvinyāsahāsitasakhījanamiti viśeṣaṇena kimapi saukumāryamunmīlitam /
yasmāttathāvidhādaroparacitaṃ prasādhanaṃ yasya vyañjakatvenopāttaṃ mukhyatayā varṇyamānavṛttervallabhānurāgasya so 'pyanena sutarāṃ samuttejitaḥ /
yathā vā
children.translated_text: Here, through the qualifier "whose friends laughed at the reversed arrangement of ornaments" applied to the action characterized as undertaking ornamentation, a certain exquisite delicacy is revealed. Because the toilette arranged in such a confused state, which is adopted as suggestive of the love for the beloved — the principal subject being described — that [love] too is thereby all the more intensified. Or for example:
Attached to me, the three-quarter glance that steals [the beauty of] the eyes of a startled doe... // VjivC_2.90 //

children.text:
asya vaicitryaṃ pūrvamevoditam /
etacca kriyāviśeṣaṇaṃ dvayorapi kriyākārakayorvakratvamullāsayati /
yasmādvicitrakriyākāritvameva kārakavaicitryam /
idamaparaṃ kriyāvaicitryavakratāyāḥ prakārāntaram---upacāramanojñatā /
upacāraḥ sādṛśyādisamanvayaṃ samāśritya dharmāntarādhyāropastena manojñatā vakratvam /
yathā
children.translated_text: The obliqueness of this has already been stated. And this qualifier of the action illuminates the obliqueness of both action and <s>kāraka</s> (case-relation), since producing variegated action is itself the variegation of the case-relation. Here is yet another variety of the obliqueness of <s>kriyāvaicitrya</s> — <s>upacāramanojñatā</s> (charm of figurative usage). <s>Upacāra</s> (figurative usage) is the superimposition of another property based on similarity and the like; the charm, that is, the obliqueness produced by it. For example:

children.text: tarantīvāṅgāni skhaladamalalāvaṇyajaladhau prathimnaḥ prāgalbhyaṃ stanajaghanamunmudrayati ca /
children.translated_text: Her limbs seem to be swimming across a sea of spotless beauty; the fullness of her bosom and hips unseals the boldness of her amplitude;

children.text: dṛśorlolārambhāḥ sphuṭamapavadante saralatāmaho sāraṅgākṣyāstaruṇimani gāḍhaḥ paricayaḥ // VjivC_2.91 //
children.translated_text: The playful beginnings of her glances openly belie simplicity — ah, in the youth of the doe-eyed one, there is a deep familiarity! // VjivC_2.91 //

children.text:
atra skhaladamalalāvaṇyajaladhau samullasadvimalasaundaryasaṃbhārasindhau parisphuraparispandatayā plavamānatvena lakṣyamāṇāni pāraprāptimāsādayituṃ vyavasyantīveti cetanapadārthasaṃbhavisādṛśyopacārāttāruṇyataralataruṇīgātrāṇāṃ taraṇamutprekṣitam /
utprekṣāyāścopacāra eva bhūyasā jīvitatvena parisphuratītyutprekṣāvasara eva vicārayiṣyate /
prathimnaḥ prāgalbhyaṃ stanajaghanamunmudrayati ca (iti)-atra stanajaghanaṃ kartṛ prathimnaḥ prāgalbhyaṃ mahattvasya prauḍhimunmudrayatyunmīlayati /
yathā kaściccetanaḥ kimapi rakṣaṇīyaṃ vastu mudrayitvā kamapi samayamavasthāpya samucitopayogāvasare svayamunmudrayatyuddhāṭayati, tadevaṃ tatkāritvasāmyāt stanajaghanasyonmudraṇamuparitam /
tadidamuktaṃ bhavati yad tadeva śaiśavadaśāyāṃ śaktyātmanā vimīlitasvarūpamanavasthitamāsīt, tasya prathimnaḥ prāgalbhyasya prathamataratāruṇyāvatārāvasarasamucitaṃ prathanaprasaraṃ samarpayati /
dṛśorlolārambhāḥ sphuṭamapavadante saralatām (iti)---atra śaiśavapratiṣṭhitāṃ spaṣṭatāṃ prakaṭamevāpasārya dṛśorvilāsollāsāḥ kamapi navayauvanasamucitaṃ vibhramamadhiropayanti /
yathā keciccetanāḥ kutracidviṣaye kamapi vyavahāraṃ samāsāditaprasaramapasārya kimapi svābhiprāyābhimataṃ parispandāntaraṃ pratiṣṭhāpayantīti tatkāritvasādṛśyāllīlāvatīlocanavilāsollāsānāṃ saralatvāpavadanamupacaritam /
tadevaṃvidhenopacāreṇaitāstistro 'pi vakratāprakārāḥ pratipadaṃ saṃbhavantītyavasarāntare vicāryante /
idamaparaṃ kriyāvaicitryavakratāyāḥ prakārāntaram--karmādisaṃvṛtiḥ /
karmaprabhṛtīnāṃ kārakāṇāṃ saṃvṛtiḥ saṃvaraṇam, prastutaucityānusāreṇa sātiśayapratītaye samācchādyābhidhā /
sā ca kriyāvaicitryakāritvāt prakāratvenābhidhīyate /
kāraṇe kāryopacārād yathā---
children.translated_text: Here, in the ocean of spotless beauty that brims with resplendent, pure, and abundant loveliness, the limbs of the young woman trembling with youth are figuratively described as swimming — as though they were observed floating with pulsating motion and striving to reach the far shore — through the figurative usage of similarity applicable to conscious entities, the act of crossing is poetically fancied (<s>utprekṣā</s>). And since <s>upacāra</s> (figurative usage) constitutes the very life-force of <s>utprekṣā</s> (poetic fancy) for the most part, this will be examined in the context of <s>utprekṣā</s>. "The fullness of her bosom and hips unseals the boldness of her amplitude" — here the bosom and hips are the agent; they unseal, that is, reveal the boldness, the maturity of amplitude. Just as some conscious being, having sealed some precious object and kept it for a certain time, himself unseals it at the appropriate occasion for use — in the same way, the unsealing by the bosom and hips is figuratively described through similarity of agency. What is meant is this: that very same [amplitude] which during childhood existed in a latent form, with its nature concealed as potential — its boldness of amplitude is now given its proper expansion and spread at the fitting occasion of the first descent of youth. "The playful beginnings of her glances openly belie simplicity" — here, the sportive flashes of her glances openly remove, that is, push aside the straightforwardness established in childhood, and superimpose upon [the eyes] a certain coquetry befitting new youth. Just as certain conscious beings, having established a certain practice in some domain, push it aside and install some other activity that accords with their own intention — through similarity of such agency, the belying of simplicity by the sportive flashes of the charming woman's glances is figuratively described. Thus through such figurative usage, all these three varieties of obliqueness arise at every word, and will be examined on another occasion. Here is yet another variety of the obliqueness of <s>kriyāvaicitrya</s> — <s>karmādisaṃvṛti</s> (concealment of the object and so forth). The concealment, that is, the covering up of the <s>kāraka</s>s (case-relations) beginning with the object — the expression through concealment for the sake of intensified apprehension, following the propriety of the subject. And this is called a variety because it produces <s>kriyāvaicitrya</s> (obliqueness of action). Through figurative transfer of the effect onto the cause, for example:

children.text: netrāntare madhuramarpayatīva kiñcit karṇāntike kathayatīva kimapyapūrvam /
children.translated_text: She seems to place something sweet within the corner of the eye, she seems to whisper something unprecedented near the ear,

children.text: antaḥ samullikhati kiñcidivāsitākṣyā rāgālase manasi ramyapadārthalakṣmīḥ // VjivC_2.92 //
children.translated_text: she seems to inscribe something within the mind — the splendor of beautiful things upon a heart languid with passion, [conveyed] through the glance of the doe-eyed one. // VjivC_2.92 //

children.text:
atra tadanubhavaikagocaratvādanākhyeyatvena kimapi sātiśayaṃ pratipadaṃ karma saṃpādayantyaḥ kriyāḥ svātmani kamapi vakrabhāvamudbhāvayanti /
upacāramanojñatāpyatra vidyate /
yasmādarpaṇakathanollekhanānyupacāranibandhanānyeva cetanapadārthadharmatvāt /
yathā ca---
children.translated_text: Here, the actions — which at every word produce a certain intensified object that is inexpressible because it is accessible only to direct experience — bring about within themselves a certain obliqueness. The charm of figurative usage (<s>upacāramanojñatā</s>) is also present here, since the placing, telling, and inscribing are grounded in figurative usage alone, being properties of conscious entities. And for example:

children.text: nṛttārambhādviratarabhasastiṣṭha tāvanmuhūrtaṃ yāvanmaulau ślathamacalatāṃ bhūṣaṇaṃ te nayāmi /
children.translated_text: "Cease the impetuousness of [your] dance and stand still for a moment, until I fix the ornament that has loosened on [your] crown" —

children.text: ityākhyāya praṇayamadhuraṃ kāntayā yojyamāne cūḍācandre jayati sukhinaḥ ko 'pi śarvasya garvaḥ // VjivC_2.93 //
children.translated_text: When the crescent moon on his crest was being affixed by his beloved who spoke thus with loving sweetness, there triumphs some indescribable pride of the blessed <s>Śarva</s> (Śiva)! // VjivC_2.93 //

children.text:
atra "ko 'pi' ityanena sarvanāmapadena tadanubhavaikagocaratvādavyapadeśyatvena sātiśayaḥ śarvasya garva iti kartṛsaṃvṛtiḥ /
jayati sarvotkarṣeṇa vartate iti kriyāvaicitryanibandhanam /
children.translated_text: Here, by the pronoun "some" (<s>ko 'pi</s>), the pride of <s>Śarva</s> (Śiva), being intensified through inexpressibility since it is accessible only to direct experience, constitutes <s>kartṛsaṃvṛti</s> (concealment of the agent). "Is triumphant" means "exists with supreme excellence" — this is grounded in <s>kriyāvaicitrya</s> (obliqueness of action).
Thus this obliqueness of the first half of the word is established.
Only the barest indication of it [has been given]; the rest is to be ascertained in actual poetic instances. // VjivC_2.94 //

children.text:
iti saṃgrahaślokaḥ /
tadevaṃ suptiṅantayordvayorapi padapūrvārdhasya prātipadikasya dhātośca yathāyukti vakratāṃ vicāryedānīṃ tayoreva yathāsvamaparārdhasya pratyayalakṣaṇasya vakratāṃ vicārayati /
tatra kriyāvaicitryavakrātāyāḥ samanantarasaṃbhavinaḥ kramasamanvitatvāt kālasya vakratvaṃ paryālocyate, kriyāparicchedakatvāttasya /
children.translated_text: Thus the summary verse. Having thus examined, as appropriate, the obliqueness of the first half of both <s>subanta</s> (nominal) and <s>tiṅanta</s> (verbal) words — that is, of the nominal stem and the verbal root — he now examines the obliqueness of the latter half of each, namely the suffix. In that regard, since <s>kāla</s> (time) immediately follows the obliqueness of <s>kriyāvaicitrya</s> and is sequentially connected, the obliqueness of time is considered, because it delimits action.
Where the occasion attains beauty through the utmost propriety,
there exists this <s>kālavaicitryavakratā</s> (obliqueness of temporal variegation). // Vjiv_2.26 //

children.text:
eṣā prakrāntasvarūpā bhavatyasti kālavaicitryavakratā /
kālo vaiyākaraṇādiprasiddho vartamānādirlaṭprabhṛtipratyayavācyo yaḥ padārthānāmudayatirodhānavidhāyī, tasya vaicitryaṃ vicitrabhāvastathāvidhatvenopanibandhastena vakratā vakratvavicchittiḥ /
kīdṛśī---yatra yasyāṃ samayaḥkālākhyo ramaṇīyatāṃ yāti rāmaṇīyakaṃ gacchati /
kena hetunā--aucityāntaratamyena /
prastutatvātprastāvādhikṛtasya vastuno yadaucityamucitabhāvastasyāntaratamyenāntaraṅgatvena, tadatiśayotpādakatvenetyarthaḥ /
yathā
children.translated_text: This, whose nature is being set forth, is <s>kālavaicitryavakratā</s> (obliqueness of temporal variegation). <s>Kāla</s> (time) — well known to grammarians and others as the present tense and so forth, expressed by suffixes such as <s>laṭ</s> — which governs the arising and disappearance of things: its variegation, that is, its variegated nature, the arrangement in such a manner, produces <s>vakratā</s> (obliqueness), that is, the charm of obliqueness. Of what kind? — Where the occasion, called <s>kāla</s> (time), attains beauty, that is, reaches loveliness. By what cause? — Through the utmost propriety: the <s>aucitya</s> (propriety), that is, the fitness of the subject under discussion because it is the topic at hand; through its intimacy, that is, through its capacity to produce an intensification of that [propriety] — this is the meaning. For example:
[Prakrit:] With uniform and varied [distribution of] jewels, moving gently and slowly from all sides —

children.text: airā hohinti pahā maṇorahāṇaṃ pi dullaṅghā // VjivC_2.95 //
children.translated_text: Soon the paths, level and uneven without distinction, [becoming] slow-moving on every side, will become impassable even for desires. (Prākrit) // <s>Vjīv</s>C 2.95 //
Level and uneven without distinction, slow-moving on every side,
soon the paths will become impassable even for desires.
Thus the <s>chāyā</s> (Sanskrit rendering).

children.text:
atra vallabhāvirahavaidhuryakātarāntaḥ karaṇena bhāvinaḥ samayasya saṃbhāvanānumānamahātmyamutprekṣya uddīpanavibhāvatvavibhavavilasitaṃ tatparispandasaundaryasandarśanāsahiṣṇunā kimapi bhayavisaṃṣṭhulatvamanubhūya śaṅkākulatvena kenacidetadabhidhīyate---yadacirād bhaviṣyanti panthāno manorathānāmapyalaṅaghanīyā iti bhaviṣyatkālābhidhāyī pratyayaḥ kāmapi parārdhavakratāṃ vikāsayati /
yathā vā
children.translated_text: Here, someone whose inner faculty is distressed by the torment of separation from his beloved, having imagined through probable inference the greatness of the coming season, having experienced a certain terror from the inability to endure the sight of the beauty of the activity [of that season] as it flashes forth in the splendor of its role as a stimulant-factor (<s>uddīpanavibhāva</s>) — says this with an agitation of apprehension: 'Soon the paths will become impassable even for desires' — here the suffix denoting the future tense unfolds a certain second-half-of-word obliqueness. Or as —

children.text: yāvatkiñcidapūrvamārdramanasāmāvedayanto navāḥ saubhāgyātiśayasya kāmapi daśāṃ gantuṃ vyavasyantyamī /
children.translated_text: Just as these new [feelings], announcing to the tender-hearted something hitherto unknown, are about to attain some state of extraordinary felicity;

children.text: bhāvāstāvadananyajasya vidhuraḥ ko 'pyudyamo jṛmbhate paryāpte madhuvibhrame tu kimayaṃ karteti kampāmahe // VjivC_2.96 //
children.translated_text: just then, a certain agitation — self-born and distressed — begins to stir; but when the intoxication of spring is full, what will this one do? — We tremble [at the thought]. // <s>Vjīv</s>C 2.96 //

children.text:
atra vyavasyanti jṛmbhate kartā kampāmahe ceti pratyayāḥ pratyekaṃ pratiniyatakālābhidhāyinaḥ kāmapi padaparārdhavakratāṃ prakhyāpayanti /
tathā ca--prathamatarāvatīrṇamadhusamayasaukumāryasamullasitasundarapadāthrasārthasamunmeṣasamuddīpitasahajavibhavavilasitatvena makaraketormanāṅmātramādhavasāmarthya samullasitātulaśakteḥ sarasahṛdayavidhuratāvidhāyī ko 'pi saṃrambhaḥ samujjṛmbhate /
tasmādanenānumānena punaḥ paraṃ paripoṣamadhirohati /
kusumākaravibhavavibhrame māninīmānadalanadurlalitasamuditasahajasaukumāryasaṃpatsaṃjanitasamucitajigīṣāvasaraḥ kimasau vidhāsyatīti vikalpayantastatkusumaśaranikaranipātakātarāntaḥ karaṇāḥ kimapi kampāmahe cakitacetasaḥ saṃpadyāmaha iti priyatamāvirahavidhuracetasaḥ sarasahṛdayasya kasyacidetadabhidhānam /
evaṃ kālavakratāṃ vicārya kramasamucitāvasarāṃ kārakavakratāṃ vicārayati---
children.translated_text: Here, the suffixes in 'vyavasyanti' (are about to), 'jṛmbhate' (begins to stir), 'kartā' (will do), and 'kampāmahe' (we tremble) — each denoting a specifically delimited time — proclaim a certain second-half-of-word obliqueness. And thus: by the flash of the natural splendor stimulated by the beautiful procession of objects revealed at the first descent of the delicacy of the spring season, a certain tumult — producing the distress of the sensitive heart — of the flower-bannered Love-god, whose incomparable power has been brought to slight efflorescence by the onset of spring's potency, surges forth. Therefore, by this inference, the [tumult] will again ascend to greater fullness. When the full intoxication of the flower-season arrives — seized by the opportunity of a just conquest, generated by the wealth of natural delicacy that arises from the playful and haughty conduct that breaks the pride of proud women — 'what will he do?' — thus deliberating, those whose inner faculties are distressed by the fear of the shower of flower-arrows — 'we tremble' — 'we become alarmed' — this is the utterance of some sensitive-hearted person whose mind is distressed by separation from his beloved. Having thus analyzed tense-obliqueness, [the author] analyzes case-obliqueness (<s>kārakavakratā</s>), which comes at the appropriate point in the sequence —
Where the generality of a case-relation is principally composed,
through the superimposition of reality, expressing the [new] role as the principal quality; // <s>Vjīv</s> 2.27 //
in order to nourish a certain beauty of the charm of expression,
the transposition of case-relations — that is called case-obliqueness (<s>kārakavakratā</s>). // <s>Vjīv</s> 2.28 //

children.text:
soktā kārakavakratā sā kārakavakratvavicchittirabhihitā /
kīdṛśī---yatra yasyāṃ kārakāṇāṃ viparyāsaḥ sādhanānāṃ viparivartanam, gauṇamukhyayoritaretaratvāpattiḥ /
katham---yat kārakasāmānyaṃ mukhyāpekṣayā karaṇādi tat prādhānyena nibadhyate mukhyabhāvena prayujyate /
kayā yuktyā tattvādhyāropaṇāt /
taditi mukhyaparāmarśaḥ, tasya bhāvastattvaṃ tadadhyāropaṇāt mukhyaguṇabhāvābhidhānataḥ /
mukhyasya yo guṇabhāvastadabhidhānādamukhyatvenopanibandhādityarthaḥ /
kimartham---paripoṣayituṃ kāñcid bhaṅgībhaṇitiramyatām /
kāñcidapūrvāṃ vicchityuktiramaṇīyatāmullāsayitum /
tadevamacetanasyāpi cetanasabhavisvātantryasamarpaṇādamukhyasya karaṇādervā kartṛtvādhyāropaṇādyatra kārakaviparyāsaścamatkārakārī saṃpadyate /
yathā
children.translated_text: 'That is called case-obliqueness' — that charm of case-obliqueness has been described. Of what kind? — 'Where' — in which — there is the transposition of case-relations — a reversal of the agent, instrument, and so forth. For what purpose? — In order to nourish a certain beauty of the charm of expression — for the enrichment of a particular attractiveness of the mode of expression. How? — Through the superimposition of reality, expressing the [new] role as the principal quality — through the ontological superimposition of one case-relation upon another, expressing the exchange of the principal and subsidiary. For example —

children.text: yāñcāṃ dainyaparigrahapraṇayinīṃ nekṣvākavaḥ śikṣitāḥ sevāsaṃvalitaḥ kadā raghukule maulau nibaddho 'ñjaliḥ /
children.translated_text: 'The <s>Ikṣvāku</s> descendants have not been taught entreaty, that friend of abasement; when has the garland been bound on the head in the <s>Raghu</s> clan, accompanied by servitude?'

children.text: sarvaṃ tadvihitaṃ tathāpyudadhinā naivoparodhaḥ kṛtaḥ pāṇiḥ saṃprati me haṭhāt kimaparaṃ spraṣṭuṃ dhanurdhāvati // VjivC_2.97 //
children.translated_text: 'All that has been done by him; nevertheless the ocean made no obstruction — does my hand now forcibly wish to grasp the bow, something else [than begging]?' // <s>Vjīv</s>C 2.97 //

children.text:
atra pāṇinā dhanurgrahītumicchāmīti vaktavye pāṇeḥ karaṇabhūtasya kartṛtvādhyāropaḥ kāmapi kārakavakratāṃ pratipadyate /
yathā vā
children.translated_text: Here, instead of saying 'I wish to grasp the bow with [my] hand,' the hand, which is an instrument, has been superimposed with agency — this fosters a certain case-obliqueness. For [through this superimposition] the suggestion of the inherent, independent power of the hand to act — setting aside the speaker — becomes the cause of a certain extraordinary beauty —
'stanadvandvam' (the pair of breasts) — and so forth, the beginning. // <s>Vjīv</s>C 2.98 //
Or as —
With ten left hands, simultaneously falling upon [the bow], with deftly placed, beautifully savored, mutually contending fingertips, held was the bow <s>Kārmuka</s> —

children.text: savyānāṃ punaraprathīyasi vidhāvasmin guṇāropaṇe matsevāviduṣāmahaṃprathamikā kāpyambare vartate // VjivC_2.99 //
children.translated_text: but as for the left [hands], you are not yet renowned, O <s>Vidhātṛ</s> (Creator), in this attribution of qualities — there is a certain 'I-first' attitude among those unskilled in serving me, up in the sky! // <s>Vjīv</s>C 2.99 //

children.text:
atra pūrvaṃvadeva kartṛtvādhyāropanibandhanaṃ kārakavakratvam /
yathā vā
children.translated_text: Here, as before, there is case-obliqueness based on the superimposition of agency. Or as —
'baddhasparddha' (having rivaled) — thus. // <s>Vjīv</s>C 2.100 //

children.text: evaṃ kārakavakratāṃ vicārya kramasamanvitāṃ saṃkhyāvakratāṃ vicārayati, tatparicchedakatvāt saṃkhyāyāḥ---
children.translated_text: Having thus analyzed case-obliqueness, [the author] analyzes number-obliqueness (<s>saṃkhyāvakratā</s>), which comes in due sequence — because number is a delimiter of case-relations —
Where poets, governed by the desire for poetic variety,

children.text: yatra saṃkhyāviparyāsaṃ tāṃ saṃkhyāvakratāṃ viduḥ // Vjiv_2.29 //
children.translated_text: produce a transposition of number — that is known as number-obliqueness (<s>saṃkhyāvakratā</s>). // <s>Vjīv</s> 2.29 //

children.text:
yatra yasyāṃ kavayaḥ kāvyavaicitryavivakṣāparatantritāḥ svakarmavicitrabhāvābhidhitsāparavaśāḥ saṃkhyāviparyāsaṃ vacanaviparivartanaṃ kurvanti vidadhate tāṃ saṃkhyāvakratāṃ viduḥ tadvacanavakratvaṃ jānanti tadvidaḥ /
tadayamatrārthaḥ---yadekavacane dvivacane prayoktavye vaicitryārthaṃ vacanāntaraṃ yatra prayujyate, bhinnavacanayorvā yatra sāmānādhikaraṇyaṃ vidhīyate /
yathā
children.translated_text: 'Where' — in which — poets, governed by the desire for poetic variety, being under the sway of the wish to express the varied nature of their own creation, [produce] a transposition of number —

children.text: kapole patrālī karatalanirodhena mṛditā nipīto niśvāsairayamamṛtahṛdyo 'dhararasaḥ /
children.translated_text: The leaf-ornament on the cheek is crushed by the pressing of the palm; this lip-nectar, heart-delighting as ambrosia, is drunk up by the sighs;

children.text: muhuḥ kaṇṭhe lagnastaralayati bāṣpaḥ stanataṭīṃ priyo manyurjātastava niranurodhe na tu vayam // VjivC_2.101 //
children.translated_text: the tears, clinging again and again to the throat, make the breast-slope tremble — your anger, O beloved, has arisen against one who is not indifferent, not against us. // <s>Vjīv</s>C 2.101 //

children.text:
atra "na tvaham' iti vaktavye, "na tu vayam' ityanantaraṅgatvapratipādanārthaṃ tāṭasthyapratītaye bahuvacanaṃ prayuktam /
yathā vā
children.translated_text: Here, instead of saying 'not I,' 'not we' is said — for the purpose of conveying extreme intimacy, in order to produce the perception of detachment, the plural number has been composed. [One might object:] but 'us' is fitting because, with the inclusion of [his] friends, 'we, the circle of friends, are all devoted to you' — to this: no; because only the speaker is in the position of being offended — thus the number-obliqueness. For example —

children.text: vayaṃ tattvānveṣānmadhukara hatāstvaṃ khalu kṛtī // VjivC_2.102 //
children.translated_text: 'We are undone by the pursuit of truth, O bee; you indeed are the fortunate one.' // <s>Vjīv</s>C 2.102 //
Here too, as before, the perception of detachment [through the plural]. Or as —
'The eyes are gardens of blooming blue lotuses; the hands are lotus-pools.' // <s>Vjīv</s>C 2.103 //

children.text:
atra dvivacanabahuvacanayoḥ sāmānādhikaraṇyalakṣaṇaḥ saṃkhyāviparyāsaḥ sahṛdayahṛdayahāritāmāvahati /
yathā vā
children.translated_text: Here, the co-referentiality of dual and plural numbers — the number-transposition characterized by co-reference — brings about the capacity to captivate the hearts of connoisseurs. For example —
'The scriptures are a fresh eye.' // <s>Vjīv</s>C 2.104 //

children.text:
atra pūrvavadevaikavacanabahuvacanayoḥ sāmānādhikaraṇyaṃ vaicitryavidhāyi /
evaṃ saṃkhyāvakratāṃ vicārya tadviṣayatvāt puruṣāṇāṃ kramasamarpitāvasarāṃ puruṣavakratāṃ vicārayati---
children.translated_text: Here, as before, the co-referentiality of singular and plural is productive of variety. Having thus analyzed number-obliqueness, [the author] analyzes person-obliqueness (<s>puruṣavakratā</s>), which comes in due order —
The first person and the third person are conjoined by transposition

children.text: yatra vicchittaye saiṣā jñeyā puruṣavakratā // Vjiv_2.30 //
children.translated_text: where [this is done] for charm — that should be known as person-obliqueness (<s>puruṣavakratā</s>). // <s>Vjīv</s> 2.30 //

children.text:
yatra yasyāṃ pratyaktā nijātmabhāvaḥ parabhāvaśca anyatvamubhyamapyetadviparyāsena yojyate viparivartanena nibadhyate /
kimartham---vicchittaye vaicitryāya /
saiṣā varṇitasvarūpā jñeyā jñātavyā puruṣavakratā puruṣavakratvavicchittiḥ /
tadayamatrārthaḥ---yadanyasminnuttame madhyame vā puruṣe prayoktavye vaicitryāyānyaḥ kadācit prathamaḥ prayujyate /
tasmācca puruṣaikayogakṣematvādasmādādeḥ prātipadikamātrasya ca viparyāsaḥ paryavasyati /
yathā
children.translated_text: 'Where' — in which — the first person, one's own self, and the third person, otherness — both of these are conjoined by transposition, by interchange —

children.text: kauśāmbīṃ paribhūya naḥ kṛpaṇakairvidveṣibhiḥ svīkṛtāṃ jānāmyeva tathā pramādaparatāṃ patyurnayadveṣiṇaḥ /
children.translated_text: 'Having humiliated <s>Kauśāmbī</s>, which was seized by our wretched enemies — I know well the negligence of the husband who hates wise counsel —

children.text: strīṇāṃ ca priyaviprayogavidhuraṃ cetaḥ sadaivātra me vaktuṃ notsahate manaḥ paramato jānātu devī svayam // VjivC_2.105 //
children.translated_text: 'and the heart of women, ever distressed by separation from their beloved — here my mind does not dare to speak further. Let the <s>Devī</s> know for herself.' // <s>Vjīv</s>C 2.105 //

children.text:
atra "jānātu devī svayam' iti yuṣmadi madhyamapuruṣe prayoktavye prātipadikamātraprayogeṇa vaktustadaśakyānuṣṭhānatāṃ manyamānasyaudāsīnyapratītiḥ /
tasyāśca prabhutvāt svātantryeṇa hitāhitavicārapūrvakaṃ svayameva kartavyārthapratipattiḥ kamapi vākyavakrabhāvamāvahati /
yasmādetadevāsya vākyasya jīvitatvena parisphurati /
evaṃ puruṣavakratāṃ vicārya puruṣāśrayatvādātmanepadaparasmaipadayorucitāvasarāṃ vakratāṃ vicārayati /
dhātūnāṃ lakṣaṇānusāreṇa niyatapadāśrayaḥ prayogaḥ pūrvācāryāṇām "upagraha'-śabdābhidheyatayā prasiddhaḥ /
tasmāttadabhidhānenaiva vyavaharati---
children.translated_text: Here, 'let the Devī know for herself' — where the second person, the middle person, should be employed — by using merely the nominal stem [instead of a pronoun], it becomes impossible for the speaker to express [the matter directly] because of the intervening gravity of the content — and thus person-obliqueness nourishes a certain beauty.
Of two words, one is aptly employed
for the beauty of [expression] where [the two combine] — they call that incorporation-obliqueness (<s>upagrahavakratā</s>). // <s>Vjīv</s> 2.31 //

children.text:
tāmuktasvarūpāmupagrahavakratāmupagrahavakratvavicchittiṃ jalpanti kavayaḥ kathayanti /
kīdṛśī---yatra yasyāṃ padayorubhayormadhyādevakamātmanepadaṃ parasmaipadaṃ vā viniyujyate vinibadhyate niyamena /
kasmātkāraṇāt---aucityāt /
varṇyamānasya vastuno yadaucityamucitabhāvastasmāt, taṃ samāśrityetyarthaḥ /
kimartham---śobhāyai vicchittaye /
yathā
children.translated_text: That, described as having the nature stated above, is incorporation-obliqueness — the charm of incorporation-obliqueness — so poets say, declare. Of what kind? — Where, of two words, one is aptly employed for the beauty of the other —

children.text: tasyāpareṣvapi mṛgeṣu śarānmumukṣoḥ karṇāntametya bibhide nibiḍo 'pi muṣṭiḥ /
children.translated_text: As he was about to release arrows at the other deer, his fist, though tightly clenched, split apart at the ear [from drawing the bow] —
when [the eyes of the deer], trembling with excessive fright, caused him to remember the playful eye-movements of his mature beloved. // <s>Vjīv</s>C 2.106 //

children.text:
atra rājñaḥ sulalitavilāsavatīlocanavilāseṣu smaraṇagocaramavataratsu tatparāyattacittavṛtterāṅgikaprayatnaparispandavinivartamāno muṣṭirbibhide bhidyate sma /
svayameveti karmakartṛnibandhanamātmane padamatīva camatkārakāriṇīṃ kāmapi vākyavakratāmāvahati /
evamupagrahavakratāṃ vicārya tadanusaṃbhavinīṃ pratyayāntaravakratāṃ vicārayati---
children.translated_text: Here, when the graceful coquettish eye-movements of the beautiful woman descend into the domain of recollection for the king — since his mental activity becomes dependent upon that, the principal [sentiment] —
Where a suffix other than the expected one is employed and

children.text: yatra kāmapi puṣṇāti sānyā pratyayavakratā // Vjiv_2.32 //
children.translated_text: nourishes a certain beauty — that is another: suffix-obliqueness (<s>pratyayavakratā</s>). // <s>Vjīv</s> 2.32 //

children.text:
sānyā pratyayavakratā sā samāmnātarūpādanyāparā kācit pratyayavakratvavicchittiḥ /
astīti saṃbandhaḥ /
yatra yasyāṃ pratyayaḥ kāmapyapūrvāṃ kamanīyatāṃ ramyatāṃ puṣṇāti puṣyati /
kīdṛśaḥ---pratyayāt tiṅādervihitaḥ padatvena vinirmito 'nyaḥ kaściditi /
yathā
