children.translated_text: 'That is another — suffix-obliqueness' — that is yet another, different from what has been enumerated before, a certain charm of suffix-obliqueness. 'Exists' — is the syntactical connection. For example —

children.text: līnaṃ vastuni yena sūkṣmasubhagaṃ tattvaṃ girā kṛṣyate nirmātuṃ prabhavenmanoharamidaṃ vācaiva yo vā bahiḥ /
children.translated_text: By whom the subtle, beautiful reality hidden in a subject is drawn out through speech; who is able to fashion this captivating [work] through words alone, or —

children.text: vande dvāvapi tāvahaṃ kavivarau vandetarāṃ taṃ punar- yo vijñātapariśramo 'yamanayorbhārāvatārakṣamaḥ // VjivC_2.107 //
children.translated_text: I salute those two supreme poets both; but yet more I salute that one whose recognized labor — capable of bearing the burden of [reconciling] these two — // <s>Vjīv</s>C 2.107 //

children.text:
"vandetarām' ityatra kāpi pratyayavakratā kaveścetasi parisphurati /
tataeva "punaḥ'-śabdaḥ pūrvasmādviśeṣābhidhāyitvena prayuktaḥ /
evaṃ nāmākhyātasvarūpayoḥ padayoḥ pratyekaṃ prakṛtyādyavayavavibhāgadvāreṇa yathāsaṃbhavaṃ vakrabhāvaṃ vicāryedānīmupasarganipātayoravyutpannatvādasaṃbhavadvibhaktikatvācca nirastāvayavatve satyavibhaktayoḥ sākalyena vakratāṃ vicārayati---
children.translated_text: In 'vandetarām' (I salute even more), a certain suffix-obliqueness shines forth in the poet's mind. Precisely for that reason, the word 'punaḥ' (again, yet more) — [distinguishing this] from the former —
In which there is the illumination of <s>rasa</s> and the like through prefixes and particles,
by being the sole life of the sentence—that is the other word-obliquity. (Vjiv 2.33)

children.text:
sāparā padavakratā---sā samarpitasvarūpāparā pūrvoktavyatiriktā padavakatvavicchittiḥ /
astīti saṃbandhaḥ /
kīdṛśī---yasyāṃ vakratāyāmupasarganipātayorvaiyākaraṇaprasiddhābhidhānayoḥ rasādidyotanaṃ śṛṅgāraprabhṛtiprakāśanam /
katham---vākyaikajīvitatvena /
vākyasya ślokāderekajīvitaṃ vākyaikajīvitaṃ tasya bhāvastattvaṃ tena /
tadidamuktaṃ bhavati---yadvākyasyaikasphuritabhāvena parisphurati yo rasādistatprakāśanenetyarthaḥ /
yathā
children.translated_text: That other word-obliquity—that is the other, the one different from those previously stated, whose essential nature has been [partly] presented; the strikingness of word-obliquity. 'Exists' is the connection. Of what kind?—in which obliquity there is the illumination of <s>rasa</s> and the like—the manifestation of <s>śṛṅgāra</s> (the erotic) and other [aesthetic sentiments]—through prefixes and particles, those designations well-known in grammar. How?—by being the sole life of the sentence. The sole life of a sentence, a verse and so forth—the essence of being that; by means of that. What is being said is: that <s>rasa</s> and the like which flash forth through the single unified manifestation of the sentence—by the illumination of those—this is the meaning. For example:

children.text: vaidehī tu kathaṃ bhaviṣyati hahā hā devi dhīrā bhava // VjivC_2.108 //
children.translated_text: 'But how will <s>Vaidehī</s> fare? Alas! Ah, O <s>Devī</s>, be steadfast!' (Vjiv 2.108)

children.text:
atra raghupatestatkālajvalitoddīpanavibhāvasaṃpatsamullāsitaḥ saṃbhramo niścitajanitajānakīvipattisaṃbhāvanastatparitrāṇakaraṇotsāhakāraṇatāṃ pratipadyamānastedekāgratollikhitasākṣātkārastadākāratayā vismṛtaviprakarṣaḥ pratyagrarasaparispandasundaro nipātaparaṃparāpratipādyamānavṛttirvākyaikajīvitatvena pratibhāsamānaḥ kāmapi vākyavakratāṃ samunmīlayati /
tu-śabdasya ca vakrabhāvaḥ pūrvameva vyākhyātaḥ /
yathā vā
children.translated_text: Here, the agitation of the Lord of the <s>Raghus</s>, brought to light by the wealth of the <s>vibhāva</s> (determinant) of excitation blazing at that moment, as it takes on the character of being the cause of the eagerness to rescue [<s>Sītā</s>], whose misfortune he is certain to have imagined—[that agitation], sketched with single-pointed vividness, having forgotten distance through taking on the form of [her immediate] presence, beautiful through the fresh vibration of <s>rasa</s>, expressed through the succession of particles, appearing as the sole life of the sentence, brings to light a certain sentence-obliquity. The oblique nature of the particle 'tu' (but) was explained earlier. Or for example:

children.text: ayamekapade tayā viyogaḥ priyayā copanataḥ suduḥsaho me /
children.translated_text: At one and the same time, this separation from my beloved has descended upon me, most difficult to bear,
and there must be [endured] the days [made] beautiful by the shelterlessness [caused by] the rising of fresh rain-clouds. (Vjiv 2.109)

children.text:
atra dvayoḥ parasparaṃ suduḥsahatvoddīpanasāmarthyasametayoḥ priyāvirahavarṣākālayostulyakālatvapratipādanaparaṃ "ca'-śabdadvitayaṃ samasamayasamullasitavahnidāhadakṣadakṣiṇavātavyajanasamānatāṃ samarthayat kāmapi vākyavakratāṃ samuddīpayati /
"su' -"duḥ'-śabdābhyāṃ ca priyāvirahasyāśakyapratīkāratā pratīyate /
yathā ca
children.translated_text: Here, of the two—separation from the beloved and the rainy season—both possessing the capacity to kindle mutual unbearableness, the pair of 'ca' (and) particles, intent upon conveying their simultaneity, suggesting a likeness to a southern breeze-fan capable of kindling a fire blazing at the same moment, ignites a certain sentence-obliquity. And by the words 'su' (very) and 'duḥ' (un-), the impossibility of counteracting the separation from the beloved is perceived. And for example:
Her face, with lower lip repeatedly covered by her finger, charmingly flustered by the syllables of prohibition,

children.text: mukhamaṃsavivarti pakṣmalākṣyāḥ kathamapyunnamitaṃ na cumbitaṃ tu // VjivC_2.110 //
children.translated_text: the face of the long-lashed one, turning away from the shoulder—somehow raised up but not kissed. (Vjiv 2.110)

children.text:
atra nāyakasya prathamābhilāṣavivaśavṛtteranubhavasmṛtisamullikhitatatkālasamucitatadvadanendusaundaryasya pūrvamaparicumbana skhalitasamuddīpitapaścāttāpadaśāveśa dyotanaparaḥ "tu'-śabdaḥ kāmapi vākyavakratāmuttejayati /
etaduttaratra pratyayavakratvamevaṃvidhapratyayāntaravakrabhāvāntarbhūtatvāt pṛthaktvena noktamiti svayamevotprekṣaṇīyam /
yathā
children.translated_text: Here the particle 'tu' (but), intent upon illuminating the state of subsequent remorse kindled by the earlier failure to kiss—of the hero whose conduct was helplessly overcome by the first onset of desire, whose beauty of her moon-like face at that time was sketched by the memory of experience—stirs up a certain sentence-obliquity. It should be understood by oneself that suffix-obliquity, being subsumed within the oblique nature of other such suffixes, is not stated separately after this [section]. For example:

children.text: yena śyāmaṃ vapuratitarāṃ kāntimāpatsyate te barheṇeva sphuritarucinā gopaveṣasya viṣaṇoḥ // VjivC_2.111 //
children.translated_text: 'By which your dark body will acquire radiance all the more, like [<s>Kṛṣṇa</s>] in his cowherd disguise, resplendent with the peacock [feather].' (Vjiv 2.111)

children.text:
atra "atitarām' ityatīva camatkārakāri /
evamanyeṣāmapi sajātīyalakṣaṇadvāreṇa lakṣaṇaniṣpattiḥ svayamanusartavyā /
tadevamiyamanekākārā vakratvavicchittiścaturvidhapadaviṣayā vāvayaikadeśajīvitatvenāpi parisphurantī sakalavākyavaicitryanibandhanatāmupayāti /
children.translated_text: Here 'atitarām' (all the more) is exceedingly productive of wonder. Thus the derivation of definitions for other [types] too, through the gateway of cognate definitions, should be followed by oneself. Thus this multiform strikingness of obliquity, pertaining to four types of words, even when flashing forth as the life of merely a part of the sentence, attains the status of being the ground for the strikingness of the entire sentence.
Even a single type among the varieties of obliquity, in the work of a poet,
attains the status of being the cause of delight for the knowledgeable. (Vjiv 2.112)

children.text:
ityantaraślokaḥ /
yadyevamekasyāpi vakratāprakārasya yadevaṃvidho mahimā, tadete bahavaḥ saṃpatitāḥ santaḥ kiṃ saṃpādayantītyāha---
children.translated_text: Thus ends the intervening verse. If even a single type of obliquity has such greatness, then what do these many [types] accomplish when they converge together?—to this he says:
Many types, having fallen together somewhere, for the beauty of each other,
generate this [vakratā] that is captivating through its variegated shading. (Vjiv 2.34)

children.text:
kvacidekasmin padamātre vākye vā vakratāprakārā vakratvaprabhedā bahavaḥ prabhūtāḥ patitāḥ kavipratibhāmāhātmyasamullasitāḥ /
kimartham---parasparasya śobhāyai, anyonyasya vicchittaye /
etāmeva citracchāyāmanoharāmanekākārakāntiramaṇīyāṃ vakratāṃ janayantyutpādayanti /
yathā
children.translated_text: Somewhere—in a single word-unit or sentence—the types of obliquity, the varieties of obliqueness, being many, abundant, having fallen [together], having been brought to light by the greatness of the poet's creative power—for what purpose?—for the beauty of each other, for the mutual strikingness. They generate, produce this very obliquity that is captivating through its variegated shading, delightful through its beauty of manifold forms. For example:
'As if crossing...' and so forth. (Vjiv 2.113)

children.text:
atra kriyāpadānāṃ trayāṇāmapi pratyekaṃ triprakāraṃ vaicitryaṃ parisphurati---kriyāvaicitryaṃ kārakavaicitryaṃ kālavaicitryaṃ ca /
prathimastana-jaghana-taruṇimnāṃ trayāṇāmapi vṛttivaicitryam /
lāvaṇyajaladhi-pragalbhya-saralatā-paricaya-śabdānāmupacāravaicitryam /
tadevamete bahavo vakratāprakārā ekasmin pade vākye vā saṃpatitāścitracchāyāmanoharāmetāmeva cetanacamatkārakāriṇīṃ vākyavakratāmāvahanti /
evaṃ nāmākhyāto pasarganipātalakṣaṇasya caturvidhasyāpi padasya yathāsaṃbhavaṃ vakratāprakārān vicāryedānīṃ prakaraṇamupasaṃhṛtyānyadavatārayati---
children.translated_text: Here, in each of the three verbal words, a threefold variety shines forth: variety of action, variety of case-relation, and variety of tense. Of the three [words denoting] fullness of breasts, hips, and youthfulness—variety of <s>vṛtti</s> (style/function). Of the words '<s>lāvaṇyajaladhi</s>' (ocean of charm), '<s>prāgalbhya</s>' (boldness), '<s>saralatā</s>' (simplicity), '<s>paricaya</s>' (familiarity)—variety of figurative usage. Thus these many types of obliquity, having converged in a single word-unit or sentence, produce this very sentence-obliquity that is captivating through its variegated shading and productive of wonder in consciousness. Having thus examined the types of obliquity pertaining to the fourfold word characterized by noun, verb, prefix, and particle—and now concluding the chapter and introducing another [topic]—

children.text: vāgvallyāḥ padapallavāspadatayā yā vakratodbhāsinī vicchittiḥ sarasatvasaṃpaducitā kāpyujjvalā jṛmbhate /
children.translated_text: That strikingness of the vine of speech, shining forth with obliquity, resting on the tender shoots of words, endowed with a certain brilliant richness of juiciness,

children.text: tāmālocya vidagdhaṣaṭpadagaṇairvākyaprasūnāśrayaṃ sphārāmodamanoharaṃ madhu navotkaṇṭhākulaṃ pīyatām // Vjiv_2.35 //
children.translated_text: having contemplated that, let the honey—whose abode is the flowers of the sentence, captivating through its pervading fragrance, newly agitated with eagerness—be drunk by the swarms of discriminating bees! (Vjiv 2.35)

children.text:
vāgeva vallī vāṇīlatā tasyāḥ kāpyalaukikī vicchittirjṛsbhate śobhā samallasati /
katham---padapallavāspadatayā /
padānyeva pallavāni suptiṅantānyeva patrāṇi tadāspadatayā tadāśrayatvena /
kīdṛśī vicchittiḥ---sarasatvasaṃpaducitā, rasavattvātiśayopapannā /
kiṃviśiṣṭā ca---vakratayā vakrabhāvenodbhāsate bhrājate yā sā tathoktā /
kīdṛśī---ujjvalā, chāyātiśayaramaṇīyā /
tāmevaṃvidhāmālocya vicārya vidagdhaṣaṭpadagaṇairvibudhaṣaṭcaraṇacakrairmadhu pīyatāṃ makaranda āsvādyatām /
kīdṛśam---vākyaprasūnāśrayam /
vākyānyeva padasamudāyarūpāṇi prasūnāni puṣpāṇyāśrayaḥ sthānaṃ yasya tattathoktam /
anyacca kīdṛśam---sphārāmodamanoharam /
sphāraḥ sphīto yo 'sāvāmodastaddharmaviśeṣastena manoharaṃ hṛdayahāri /
kathamāsvādyatām--navotkaṇṭhākulaṃ nūtanotkalikāvyagram /
madhukarasamūhāḥ khalu vallyāḥ prathamollasitapallavollekhamālocya pratitacetasaḥsamanantarodbhinnavastu sukumārakusumamakarandapānamahotsavamanubhavanti /
tadvadeva sahṛdayāḥ padāspadaṃ kāmapi vakratāvicchittimālocya navotkalikākalitacetaso vākyāśrayaṃ kimapi vakratājīvitasarvasvaṃ vicārayantviti tātparyārthaḥ /
atraikatra sarasatvaṃ svasamayasaṃbhavi rasārdratvam, anyatra śṛṅgārādivyañjakatvam /
vakrataikatra bālendusundarasaṃsthānayuktatvam, itaratra rūḍhyādivaicitryam /
vicchittirekatra suvibhaktapatratvam, anyatra kavikauśalakamanīyatā /
ujjvalatvamekatra parṇacchāyātiśaya yuktatvam aparatra saṃniveśasaundaryasamudayaḥ /
āmodaḥ puṣpeṣusaurabham, vākyeṣu tadvidāhlādakāritā /
madhu kusumeṣu makarandaḥ, vākyeṣu sakalakāvyakāraṇakalāpa saṃpatsamudaya iti /
iti śrīrājānakakuntakaviracite vakroktijīvite kāvyālaṅkāre dvitīya unmeṣaḥ /
children.translated_text: Speech itself is the vine, the creeper of language; of that, a certain extraordinary strikingness shines forth, beauty blossoms. How?—resting on the tender shoots of words. The words are the tender shoots, the inflected forms are the leaves; by resting on them, by having them as their support. Of what kind is the strikingness?—endowed with a richness of juiciness, possessing a superabundance of relishability. And distinguished by what?—that which shines forth, blazes, through obliquity, through the oblique mode—it is so described. Of what kind?—brilliant, delightful through the superabundance of its shade. Having contemplated, having examined that [strikingness] of such a kind, let the honey, the nectar, be drunk, be savored, by the swarms of discriminating bees, by the assemblies of the six-footed wise ones. Of what kind [is the honey]?—whose abode is the flowers of the sentence. The sentences, being in the form of collections of words, are the flowers, the blossoms; the abode, the place of that [honey]—it is so described. And what else [characterizes it]?—captivating through its pervading fragrance. The pervading, the abundant fragrance—through the quality specific to that—it is captivating, stealing the heart. How should it be savored?—'newly agitated with eagerness,' brimming with fresh longing. Just as swarms of bees, having observed the first delineation of newly unfurled tender shoots of a vine, with minds now set upon [them], experience the great festival of drinking the nectar of the delicate flowers that bloom immediately after—just so, the connoisseurs, having contemplated a certain strikingness of obliquity resting on words, their minds stirred with fresh longing, should examine the totality of the life of obliquity whose abode is the sentence—this is the purport. Here, 'juiciness' (<s>sarasatva</s>) in one context is the moisture of relishability proper to its own occasion; in another, it is the capacity to suggest <s>śṛṅgāra</s> (the erotic) and other [sentiments]. 'Obliquity' in one context is the possession of a beautifully curved form like a young crescent moon; in the other, the variety of <s>rūḍhi</s> (conventional usage) and the like. 'Strikingness' in one context is the quality of having well-separated leaves; in the other, the beauty of the poet's skill. 'Brilliance' in one context is the possession of an excess of foliage-shade; in the other, the aggregate of the beauty of arrangement. 'Fragrance' in flowers is their sweet scent; in sentences, the quality of being delightful to the knowledgeable. 'Honey' in flowers is the nectar; in sentences, the aggregate of the complete collection of all causes of poetry. Thus ends the Second <s>Unmeṣa</s> (Chapter) in the <s>Vakroktijīvita</s>, a treatise on poetic ornamentation, composed by the venerable <s>Rājānaka Kuntaka</s>.

children.text:
vakroktijīvitam tṛtīyonmeṣaḥ evaṃ pūrvasmin prakaraṇe vākyāvayavānāṃ padānāṃ yathāsaṃbhava vakrabhāvaṃ vicārayan vācakavakratāvicchittiprakāraṇāṃ dikpradarśanaṃ vihitavān /
idānīṃ vākyavakratāvaicitryamāsūtrayirtu vācyasya varṇanīyatayā prastāvādhikṛtasya vastuno vakrātāsvarūpaṃ nirūpayati, padārthāvabodhapūrvakatvād vākyārthāvasiteḥ---
children.translated_text: VAKROKTIJĪVITAM — THIRD UNMEṢA. Having thus, in the preceding chapter, examined as far as possible the oblique nature of words that are the components of a sentence, and having provided an indication of the direction of the types of expressor-obliquity (<s>vācakavakratā</s>), he now, in order to thread out the variety of sentence-obliquity, determines the essential nature of the obliquity of the expressed object—the thing brought under discussion by virtue of being described—since the ascertainment of sentence-meaning presupposes the understanding of word-meanings:
The description of an object through the beauty of its own noble vibration,
as being within the scope of oblique expression alone—that is [its] obliquity. (Vjiv 3.1)

children.text:
vastuno varṇanīyatayā prastāvitasya padārthasya, yadevaṃvidhatvena varṇanaṃ sā tasya vakratā vakratvavicchittiḥ /
kiṃvidhatvenetyāha---udārasvaparispandasundaratvena /
udāraḥ sotkarṣaḥ sarvātiśāyī yaḥ svaparispandaḥ svabhāvamahimā tasya sundaratvaṃ saukumāryātiśayastena, atyantaramaṇīyasvābhāvikadharmayuktatvena /
varṇanaṃ pratipādanam /
katham---vakraśabdaikagocaratvena /
vakro yo 'sau nānāvidhavakratāviśiṣṭaḥ śabdaḥ kaścideva vācakaviśeṣo vivakṣitārthasamarpaṇa samarthastasyaivaikasya kevalasya gocaratvena pratipādyatayā viṣayatvena /
vācyatveneti noktam, vyaṅgyatvenāpi pratipādanasaṃbhavāt /
tadidamuktaṃ bhavati---yadevaṃvidhe bhāvasvabhāvasausumāryavarṇanaprastāve bhūyasāṃ na vācyālaṅkārāṇāmupamādīnāmupayogayogyatā saṃbhavati, svabhāvasaukumāryātiśayamlānatāprasaṅgāt /
nanu ca saiṣā sahṛdayāhlādakāriṇī svabhāvoktiralaṅkāratayā samāmnāt, tasmāt kiṃ taddaṣaṇadurvyasanaprayāsena ? yatasteṣāṃ sāmānyavastudharmamātramalaṅkāryam, sātiśayasvabhāvasaundaryaparipoṣaṇamalaṅkāraḥ pratibhāsate /
tena svabhāvokteralaṅkāratvameva yuktiyuktamiti ye manyante tān prati samādhīyate---tadetannāticaturastram /
yasmādagatikagatinyāyena kāvyakaraṇaṃ na yathākathañcidanuṣṭheyatāmarhati, tadvidāhlādakārikāvyalakṣaṇaprastāvāt /
kiñca---anutkṛṣṭadharmayuktasya varṇanīyasyālaṅkaraṇamapyasamucitabhittibhāgollikhitālekhyavanna śobhātiśayakāritāmāvahati /
yasmādatyantaramaṇīyasvābhāvikadharmayuktaṃvarṇanīyavastu parigrahaṇīyam /
tathāvidhasya tasya yathāyogamaucityānusāreṇa rūpakādyalaṅkārayojanayā bhavitavyam /
etāvāṃstu viśeṣo yat svābhāvikasaukumāryaprādhānyena vivakṣitasya na bhūyasā rūpakādyalaṅkāraupakārāya kalpate, vastusvabhāvasaukumāryasya rasādiparipoṣaṇasya vā samācchādanaprasaṅgāt /
tathā caitasmin viṣaye sarvākāramalaṅkāryaṃ vilāsavatīva snānasamaya-virahavrataparigraha-suratāvasānādau nātyantamalaṅkaraṇasahatāṃ pratipadyate, svābhāvikasaukumāryasyaiva rasikahṛdayāhlādakāritvāt /
yathā
children.translated_text: Of an object—of a word-meaning brought under discussion by virtue of being described—description of such a kind constitutes its obliquity, its strikingness of obliqueness. Through what kind [of description]?—he says: through the beauty of its own noble vibration. 'Noble' means surpassing all else; 'its own vibration' is its natural greatness; 'beauty' thereof is the superabundance of delicacy; through that—through being endowed with exceedingly beautiful natural qualities. 'Description' is presentation. How?—as being within the scope of oblique expression alone. An oblique [expression]—one distinguished by manifold types of obliquity—some particular expressor capable of conveying the intended meaning—of that alone, of that single one, by being within the scope, by being the object of presentation. It is not said 'as the expressed,' since presentation through suggestion too is possible. What is being said is this: in such an occasion of describing the beauty of the nature of an emotional state, there is for the most part no fitness for the employment of expressed figures such as <s>upamā</s> (simile) and the like, since the superabundance of the delicacy of nature would be impaired. But then, this <s>svabhāvokti</s> (natural description), which delights the hearts of connoisseurs, has been transmitted as an ornament; so what is the point of this labor of obsession with another definition? For them, the mere general property of the object is the thing to be ornamented; the nourishment of the superabundance of natural beauty appears to them as the ornament. Thus they who think that the status of <s>svabhāvokti</s> as an ornament is indeed logically justified—to them it is replied: this is not very shrewd. For poetic composition does not deserve to be practiced in a makeshift manner according to the principle of 'any port in a storm,' since the occasion of defining poetry as that which delights the knowledgeable [has already been stated]. Moreover, the ornamentation of an object to be described that is endowed with non-excellent qualities does not produce a superabundance of beauty—like a painting sketched on an unsuitable wall-surface. Since the object to be described must be one endowed with exceedingly beautiful natural qualities. Of such an object, there should be, as appropriate, a yoking of ornaments such as <s>rūpaka</s> (metaphor) and the like, in conformity with propriety. But this is the distinction: for that which is intended [to be described] with the predominance of natural delicacy, ornamentation with <s>rūpaka</s> and other figures is for the most part not conducive—since it would occasion the concealment of the natural delicacy of the object or of the nourishment of <s>rasa</s> and the like. And thus, in this domain, the thing to be ornamented, like a coquettish woman at the occasion of bathing, the vow-of-separation, or the end of lovemaking, does not excessively tolerate being ornamented—since it is the natural delicacy alone that delights the hearts of the aesthetes. For example:

children.text: tāṃ prāṅmukhīṃ tatra niveśya tanvīṃ kṣaṇaṃ vyalambanta puro niṣaṇṇāḥ /
children.translated_text: Seating that slender one there facing east, the women—seated before her—lingered a moment,
their eyes being drawn away by the beauty of the real [unadorned form], even though the toilette was at hand. (Vjiv 3.1)

children.text:
atra tathāvidhasvabhāvikasaukumāryamanoharaḥ śobhātiśayaḥ kaveḥ pratipādayitumabhipretaḥ /
asyā alaṅkaraṇakalāpakalanaṃ sahajacchāyātirodhānaśaṅkāspadatvena saṃbhāvitam /
yasmāt svābhāvikasaukumāryaprādhānyena varṇyamānasyodārasvaparispandamahimnaḥ sahajacchāyātirodhānavidhāyi pratītyantarāpekṣamalaṅkaraṇakalpanaṃ nopakāritāṃ pratipadyate /
viśeṣatastu---rasaparipoṣapeśalāyāḥ pratītervibhāvānubhāvavyabhicāryaucityavyatirekeṇa prakārāntareṇa pratipattiḥ prastutaśobhāparihārakāritāmāvahati /
tathā ca prathamatarataruṇītāruṇyāvatāraprabhṛtayaḥ padārthāḥ sukumāravasantādisamayasamunmeṣaparipoṣaparisamāptiprabhṛtayaśca svapratipādakavākyavakratāvyatirekeṇa bhūyasā na kasyacidalaṅkaraṇāntarasya kavibhiralaṅkaraṇīyatāmupanīyamānāḥ paridṛśyante /
yathā
children.translated_text: Here, a superabundance of beauty that is charming through such natural delicacy is what the poet intends to convey. The application of an ornamental complex to it is regarded as a ground for the apprehension of concealing its innate lustre. For when the subject is being described with the predominance of natural delicacy, the fabrication of ornamentation that requires the cognition of something else and that conceals the innate lustre does not attain the status of being helpful — [it works against] the greatness of the subject's own noble vibration. In particular, the apprehension of the cognition that is delicate with the nourishment of <s>rasa</s>, through some other mode apart from the propriety of <s>vibhāvas</s> (determinants), <s>anubhāvas</s> (consequents), and <s>vyabhicārins</s> (transitory emotions), brings about the impairment of the beauty of the subject at hand. And thus, referents such as the first dawning of fresh youth and so forth, and the budding, nourishment, and completion of the delicate spring season and so forth, are generally observed by poets not to be subjected extensively to any other ornamentation beyond the obliquity of the sentence that conveys them. For example:

children.text: smitaṃ kiñcinmugdhaṃ taralamadhuro dṛṣṭivibhavaḥ parispando vācāmabhinavavilāsoktisarasaḥ /
children.translated_text: A slightly innocent smile, the wealth of a glance sweetly tremulous, a vibration of words fresh with the fragrance of new, playful speech,

children.text: gatānāmārambhaḥ kisalayitalīlāparimalaḥ spṛśantyāstāruṇyaṃ kimiva hi na ramyaṃ mṛgadṛśaḥ // VjivC_3.2 //
children.translated_text: the beginning of movements perfumed with the playfulness of tender sprouts — for a doe-eyed woman entering youth, what indeed is not charming? // VjivC_3.2 //
Or for example:

children.text: avyutpannamanobhavā madhurimasparśollasanmānasā bhinnāntaḥ karaṇaṃ dṛśau mukulayantyāghrātabhūtodbhramāḥ /
children.translated_text: Inexperienced in the ways of love, their minds delighting at the touch of sweetness, their inner faculties breaking open, closing their eyes, bewildered by the fragrance of the awakened [spring],

children.text: rāgecchāṃ na samāpayanti manasaḥ khedaṃ vinaivālasā vṛttāntaṃ na vidanti yānti ca vaśaṃ kanyā manojanmanaḥ // VjivC_3.3 //
children.translated_text: they do not fulfill the desire for passion in their minds, yet without weariness they are languid; they do not know what is happening, yet the maidens fall under the power of the Mind-Born [<s>Kāma</s>]. // VjivC_3.3 //
And also:
'Up to the root of the trees' and so forth. // VjivC_3.4 //
Or for example:

children.text: garbhagranthiṣu vīrudhāṃ sumanaso madhye 'ṅkuraṃ pallavā vāñchāmātraparigrahaḥ pikavadhūkaṇṭhodare pañcamaḥ /
children.translated_text: Among the seed-knots of creepers — flowers; amid [flowers] — a sprout; among sprouts — the fifth [note], grasped by mere desire, in the throat of the cuckoo's mate;

children.text: kiṃ ca trīṇi jaganti jiṣṇu divasairdvitrairmanojanmano devasyāpi cirojjhitaṃ yadi bhavedabhyāsavaśyaṃ dhanuḥ // VjivC_3.5 //
children.translated_text: moreover, in two or three days, [the bow] conquers the three worlds — of the god <s>Manmatha</s> (Love), even if the bow, long-abandoned, were to become obedient through practice. // VjivC_3.5 //
Or for example:
'In the calls of the swans' and so forth. // VjivC_3.6 //
And also:

children.text: sajjehi surahimāso ṇa dāva appei juaijaṇalakkhasahe /
children.translated_text: [Prakrit:] 'The fragrant [spring] month is making ready — it does not yet drive forth, able to withstand the target of young women,
the arrows of <s>Anaṅga</s> (the bodiless Love), whose faces are fresh mango blossoms, whose blades are new sprouts.' // VjivC_3.7 //
[Sanskrit shadow:] 'The fragrant [spring] month is making ready — it does not yet drive forth, able to withstand the target of young women,
the arrows of <s>Anaṅga</s>, whose faces are fresh mango blossoms, whose blades are new sprouts.'
This is the <s>chāyā</s> (Sanskrit rendering). //

children.text:
evaṃvidhaviṣaye svābhāvikasaukumāryaprādhānyena varṇyamānasya vastunastadācchādanabhayādeva na bhūyasā tatkavibhiralaṅkaraṇamupanibadhyate /
yadi vā kadācidupanibadhyate tattadeva svābhāvikaṃ saukumāryaṃ sutarāṃ samunmīlayitum, na punaralaṅkāravaicitryopapattaye /
yathā
children.translated_text: In a subject of this kind, when the thing is being described with the predominance of natural delicacy, out of fear of concealing that [delicacy], poets do not extensively bind ornamentation to it. Or if they ever do bind it, it is only to cause that very natural delicacy to shine forth all the more, not to establish the variety of ornamentation. For example:

children.text: dhautāñjane ca nayane sphaṭikācchakāntir- gaṇḍasthalī vigatakṛtrimarāgamoṣṭham /
children.translated_text: Eyes washed of collyrium, cheek-surfaces of crystal-clear radiance, lips free of artificial color,

children.text: aṅgāni dantiśiśudantavinirmalāni kiṃ yanna sundaramabhuttaruṇījanasya // VjivC_3.8 //
children.translated_text: limbs immaculate as the teeth of a young elephant — what is there of the body of young women that is not beautiful? // VjivC_3.8 //

children.text:
atra "dantiśiśudantavinirmalāni" ityupamayā svābhāvikameva saundaryamunmīlitam /
yathā vā
children.translated_text: Here, by the simile 'immaculate as the teeth of a young elephant,' the natural beauty itself is made to shine forth. Or for example:
'Rivaling the tusk-buds of a tender she-elephant' and so forth. // VjivC_3.9 //

children.text:
etadevātīva yuktayuktam /
yasmānmahākavīnāṃ prastutaucityānurodhena kadācit svābhāvikameva saundaryamaikarājyena vijṛmbhayitumabhipretaṃ bhavati, kadācid vividhāracanāvaicitryuktamiti /
atra pūrvasmin pakṣe, rūpakāderalaṅkāraṇakalāpasya nātyādṛtatvam /
aparasmin punaḥ sa evasutarāṃ samujjṛmbhate /
tasmādanena nyāyena sarvātiśāyinaḥ svābhāvikasaundaryalakṣaṇasya padārthaparispandasyālaṅkāryatvameva yuktiyuktatāmālambate, na punaralaṅkāraṇatvam /
sātiśayatvaśūnyadharmayuktasya vastuno vibhūṣitasyāpi piśācāderiva tadvidāhlādakāritvavirahādanupādeyatvamevetyalamatiprasaṅgena /
yadi vā prastutaucityamāhātmyānmukyatayā bhāvasvabhāvaḥ sātiśayatvena varṇyamānaḥ svamahimnā bhūṣaṇāntarāsahiṣṇuḥ svayameva śobhātiśayaśālitvādalaṅkāryo 'pyalaṅkaraṇamityabhidhīyate tadayamāsmākīnaeva pakṣaḥ /
tadatiriktavṛtteralaṅkārāntarasya tiraskāratātparyeṇābhidhānānnātra vayaṃ vivadāmahe /
evameṣaiva varṇyamānasya vastuno vakratetyutānyā kācidastītyāha--
children.translated_text: This very [principle] is exceedingly well-reasoned. For great poets, in accordance with the propriety of the subject, sometimes intend to cause natural beauty alone to flourish in sole sovereignty, and sometimes [intend it to be] endowed with the variety of manifold composition. In the former case, the ornamental complex of <s>rūpaka</s> (metaphor) and so forth is not much valued. In the latter, however, it flourishes all the more. Therefore, by this principle, it is well-reasoned that the vibration of the subject matter — characterized by natural beauty that surpasses everything — holds the status of the 'ornamentable' (<s>alaṅkārya</s>), not of the 'ornament' (<s>alaṅkaraṇa</s>). A thing endowed with properties devoid of superlative quality, even when adorned, like a <s>piśāca</s> (ghoul) and the like, is not to be accepted, because of the absence of the capacity to delight the connoisseurs — but enough of this digression. Alternatively, if, through the greatness of propriety to the subject, the emotional nature, being described with superlative quality as the primary concern, is by its own greatness intolerant of other adornment — and since it itself possesses superabundant beauty, though it is the 'ornamentable,' it is called the 'ornament' — then this is precisely our own position. Since we do not dispute that the other ornament, whose operation goes beyond that, is spoken of with the purpose of eclipsing [it]. Thus, is this the only obliquity of the subject being described, or is there another? He says:
Another [obliquity] is the creation (<s>nirmiti</s>), adorned by the poet's skill both innate and acquired,
whose domain is an unprecedented depiction that transcends the mundane. // Vjiv_3.2 //

children.text:
aparā dvitīyā varṇyamānavṛtteḥ padārthasya nirmitiḥ sṛṣṭiḥ /
vakrateti saṃbandhaḥ /
kīdṛśī---sahajāhāryakavikauśalaśālinī /
sahajaṃ svābhāvikamāhāryaṃ śikṣābhāyāsasamullāsitaṃ ca śaktivyutpattiparipākaprauḍhaṃ yat kavikauśalaṃ nirmātṛnaipuṇaṃ tena śālate ślāghyate yā sā tathoktā /
anyacca kīdṛśī---nūtanollekhalokātikrāntagocarā /
nūtanastatprathamo yo 'sāvullikhyata ityullekhastatkālamullikhyamānātiśayaḥ, tena lokātikrāntaḥ prasiddhavyāpārātītaḥ ko 'pi sarvātiśāyī gocaro viṣayo yasyāḥ sā tathokteti vigrahaḥ /
nirmitistena rūpeṇa vihitirityarthaḥ /
tadidamatra tātparyam--- yanna varṇyamānasvarūpāḥ padārthāḥ kavibhirabhūtāḥ santaḥ kriyante, kevalaṃ sattāmātreṇaiva parisphuratāṃ teṣāṃ tathāvidhaḥ ko 'pyatiśayaḥ purādhīyate, yena kāmapi sahṛdayahṛdayahāriṇīṃ ramaṇīyatāmadhiropyante /
tadidamuktam
children.translated_text: The other, the second, is the creation (<s>nirmiti</s>), the fashioning, of the subject matter whose character is being described — [this is] its obliquity — this is the syntactic connection. Of what kind? — 'Adorned by the poet's skill both innate and acquired' (<s>sahajāhāryakavikauśalaśālinī</s>): the poet's skill, the maker's expertise, which is innate, natural, and acquired, brought forth through the effort of learning — ripened through the maturation of creative power and erudition — by that [skill] it is adorned, praised — thus it is called. And what else [characterizes it]? — 'Whose domain is an unprecedented depiction that transcends the mundane' (<s>nūtanollekhalokātikrāntagocarā</s>): 'new' — the depiction that is first sketched, the superabundance being sketched at that very moment — by that, 'transcending the mundane,' going beyond well-known activity — some all-surpassing domain, subject — she whose [domain] is such is so called. 'Creation' means fashioning in that form — this is the meaning. The purport here is this: that the referents whose nature is being described are not made non-existent by poets — merely upon those that flash forth by their existence alone, some such unprecedented superabundance is bestowed, by which they are raised to a certain charm that captivates the hearts of the connoisseurs. This is what was said:
'Latent in the thing...' // VjivC_3.10 //

children.text:
ityādi /
tadevaṃ sattāmātreṇaiva parisphurataḥ padārthasya ko 'pyalaukikaḥ śobhātiśayavidhāyī vicchittiviśeṣo 'bhidhīyate, yena nūtanacchāyāmano hāriṇā vāstavasthititirodhānapravaṇena nijāvabhāsodbhāsitasvarūpeṇa tatkālollikhita iva varṇanīyapadārthaparispandamahimā pratibhāsate, yena vidhātṛvyapadeśapātratāṃ pratipadyante kavayaḥ /
tadidamuktam
children.translated_text: and so forth. Thus, of the subject matter that flashes forth merely through its existence, a certain extraordinary, beauty-superabundance-producing, special design is being described — by which the greatness of the vibration of the subject being described appears as if being sketched for the first time, with a charm of fresh lustre that captivates the mind, with a nature inclined toward concealing the actual state of affairs, with its essential nature illuminated by its own radiance — and by which poets attain the fitness for being called 'creators.' This is what was said:
In the boundless world of poetry, the poet alone is the creator (<s>Prajāpati</s>);

children.text: yathāsmai rocate viśvaṃ tathedaṃ parivartate // VjivC_3.11 //
children.translated_text: as he fancies, so this universe revolves. // VjivC_3.11 //

children.text:
saiṣā sahajāryabhedabhinnā varṇanīyasya vastuno dviprakārā vakratā /
tadevamāhāryā yeyaṃ sā prastutavicchittividhāpyalaṅkāravyatirekeṇa nānyā kācidupapadyate /
tasmād bahuvidhatatprakāraprabhedadvāreṇātyantavitatavyavahārāḥ paridṛśyante /
yathā
children.translated_text: This very [obliquity], divided by the distinction of innate and acquired, is the twofold obliquity of the subject being described. Thus, this acquired [obliquity] cannot possibly be anything other than the fashioning of the design of the subject at hand without the aid of figuration. Therefore, through the door of the manifold sub-types of such [figuration], its applications are observed to be exceedingly extensive. For example:

children.text: asyāḥ sargavidhau prajapatirabhūccandro nu kāntadyutiḥ śṛṅgāraikarasaḥ svayaṃ nu madano māso nu puṣpākaraḥ /
children.translated_text: Was the Moon (<s>Candra</s>) of beautiful radiance the creator (<s>Prajāpati</s>) for her creation, or was it <s>Madana</s> (the god of love), whose sole <s>rasa</s> is <s>śṛṅgāra</s> (erotic sentiment), or was it the month of flowers (<s>Puṣpākara</s>, i.e. spring)?

children.text: vedābhyāsajaḍaḥ kathaṃ nu viṣayavyāvṛttakautūhalo nirmātuṃ prabhavenmanoharamidaṃ rūpaṃ purāṇo muniḥ // VjivC_3.12 //
children.translated_text: How could the ancient sage [<s>Brahmā</s>], dull from the study of the <s>Vedas</s>, with his curiosity turned away from worldly objects, have the power to create this enchanting form? // VjivC_3.12 //

children.text:
atra kāntāyāḥ kimapi kāntimattvamasamavilāsasaṃpadāṃ padaṃ ca rasavattvamasāmānyasauṣṭhavaṃ ca saukumāryaṃ pratipādayituṃ pratyekaṃ tatparispandaprādhānyasamucitasaṃbhāvanānumānamāhātmyāt pṛthak pṛthagapūrvameva nirmāṇamutprekṣitam /
tathā ca kāraṇatritayasyāpyetasya sarveṣāṃ viśeṣaṇānāṃ svayam iti saṃbadhyamānametadeva sutarāṃ samuddīpayati /
yaḥ kila svayameva kāntadyutistasya saujanyasamucitādarocakitvāt kāntikatkāryakaraṇakauśalamevopapannam /
yaśca svayameva śṛṅgāraikarasastasya rasikatvāde rasavadvastuvidhānavaidagdhyamaucityaṃ bhajate /
yaśca svayameva puṣpākarastasyābhijātyādeva tathāvidhaḥ sukumāra eva sargaḥ samucitaḥ /
tathā cottarārdhe vyatirekamukhena trayasyāpyetasya kāntimattvāderviśeṣaṇairanyathānupapattirupapāditā /
yasmād vedābhyāsajaḍatvāt kāntimadvastuvidhānānabhijñatvam, viṣayavyāvṛttakautukatvād rasavatpadārthe vihitavaimukhyam, purāṇatvāt saukumāryasarasabhāvaviracanavairasyaṃ prajāpateḥ pratīyate /
tadevamutprekṣālakṣaṇo 'yamalaṅkāraḥ kavinā varṇanīyasya vastunaḥ kamapyalaukikollekhavilakṣaṇamatiśayamādhātuma nibaddhaḥ /
sa ca svabhāvasaundaryamahimnā svayameva tatsahāyasaṃpadā mahārghamahanīyatāmīhamānaḥ sandehasaṃsargamaṅgīkarotīti tenopabṛṃhitaḥ /
tasmāllokottaranirmātṛnirmitatvaṃ nāma nūtanaḥ ko 'pyatiśayaḥ padārthasya varṇayamānavṛtternāyikāsvarūpasaundaryalakṣaṇasyātra nirmitaḥ kavinā, yena tadeva tatprathamamutpāditamiva pratibhāti /
yatrāpyutpādyaṃ vastu prabandhārthavadapūrvatayā vākyārthastatkālamullikhyate kavibhiḥ, tasmin svasattāsamanvayena svayameva parisphuratāṃ padārthānāṃ tathāvidhaparasparānvayalakṣaṇasaṃbandhopanibandhanaṃ nāma navīnamatiśayamātrameva nirmitiviṣayatāṃ nīyate, na punaḥ svarūpam /
yathā
children.translated_text: Here, in order to convey a certain ineffable radiance of the beloved, her being a receptacle of unparalleled graces, her being imbued with <s>rasa</s>, and her unprecedented delicacy — through the greatness of inference based on conjecture appropriate to the predominance of each vibration individually — a separate, unprecedented creation is imagined for each. And thus, of this threefold cause as well, the fact that the word 'himself' (<s>svayam</s>) is syntactically connected with all the qualifiers fully kindles this very [obliquity]. For the one who is himself of beautiful radiance — due to the attractiveness fitting his noble nature, his skill in producing the effect of radiance is established. The one who is himself whose sole <s>rasa</s> is <s>śṛṅgāra</s> — due to his being a connoisseur, his expertise in fashioning a <s>rasa</s>-ful thing befits propriety. The one who is himself the month of flowers — due to his noble birth alone, such a delicate creation is fitting for him. And thus in the latter half, through the mode of contrast (<s>vyatireka</s>), the impossibility otherwise of all three — radiance and so forth — is established through qualifiers. For due to dullness from <s>Vedic</s> study, ignorance of fashioning a radiant thing; due to curiosity turned away from objects, an aversion established toward <s>rasa</s>-ful subjects; due to being ancient, an unfitness for composing something flowing with delicacy — these are cognized regarding <s>Prajāpati</s> (<s>Brahmā</s>). Thus this figure called <s>utprekṣā</s> (poetic fancy) is composed by the poet to bestow upon the subject being described some extraordinary superabundance distinguished by unprecedented depiction. And that [superabundance], wishing through its own greatness of natural beauty to attain preciousness and worthiness through the wealth of an appropriate ally, accepts the association with conjecture. Therefore, the being-created-by-an-extraordinary-creator is a certain unprecedented superabundance of the subject matter — of the nature of the heroine's beauty being described — here created by the poet, by which that very [beauty] appears as if being produced for the first time. And even where the thing to be produced is a sentence-meaning being sketched by poets at that very moment, with an unprecedented quality like the meaning of a composition, there too — merely the new superabundance characterized by the relation of mutual connection among the referents that flash forth through their own existence — only that is brought into the domain of creation, not their essential nature. For example:

children.text: kastvaṃ bho divi māliko 'hamiha kiṃ puṣpārthamabhyāgataḥ kiṃ tenāstu mahān krayo yadi mahaccitraṃ tadākarṇyatām /
children.translated_text: 'Who are you, sir?' 'I am a garland-maker.' 'Why have you come here?' 'For flowers.' 'What of it?' 'There is a great trade.' 'If great — then hear this wonder!

children.text: saṃgrāmeṣvalabhābhidhānanṛpatau divyāṅganābhaiḥ strajaḥ projjhantībhiravidyamānakusumaṃ yasmātkṛtaṃ nandanam // VjivC_3.13 //
children.translated_text: In the battles of the king named <s>Alabhā</s> (Unobtainable), the heavenly women, discarding their garlands, have rendered <s>Nandana</s> (the paradise garden) devoid of flowers.' // VjivC_3.13 //

children.text:
tadevaṃvidhe viṣaye varṇanīyavastuviśiṣṭātiśayavidhāyī vibhūṣaṇavinyāso vidheyatāṃ pratipadyate /
tathā ca---prakṛtamidamudāharaṇamalaṅkaraṇakalpanaṃ vinā samyaṅ na kathañcidapi vākyārthasaṅgati bhajate /
yasmāt pratyakṣādipramāṇopapattiniścayābhāvāt svābhāvikaṃ vastu dharmitayā vyavasthāpanaṃna sahate, tasmādvidagdhakavipratibhollikhitālaṅkaraṇagocaratvenaiva sahṛdayahṛdayāhlādamādadhāti /
tathā ca, duḥsahasamarasamayasamucitaśauryātiśayaślāghayā prastutanaranāthaviṣaye vallabhalābharabhasollasitasurasundarīsamūhasamarpyamāṇamandārādikusumadāmasahastrasaṃbhāvanānumānanandanodyānapādapaprasūnasamṛddhipradhvaṃsabhāvasiddhiḥ sutprekṣitā /
yasmādutprekṣāviṣayaṃ vastu kavayastadiveti tadeveti vā dvividhamupanabadhnantītyeta (tta)llakṣaṇāvasara eva vicārayiṣyāmaḥ /
tadevamiyamutprekṣā pūrvārdhavihitāprastutapraśaṃsopanibandhabandhurā prakṛtapārthivapratāpātiśayaparipoṣapravaṇatayā sutarāṃ samudbhāsamānā tadvidāvarjanaṃ janayatīti sātiśayatvam /
children.translated_text: In a subject of this kind, the arrangement of ornamentation that produces a distinctive superabundance of the subject being described attains the status of being the instrument. And thus, this present example, without the fabrication of ornamentation, does not in any way achieve coherence of sentence-meaning. For since, due to the absence of certainty from the evidence of perception and the like, the natural thing does not tolerate being established as the property-bearer — therefore, only through being the domain of ornamentation sketched by the creative intuition of the skilled poet, does it bestow delight on the hearts of the connoisseurs. And thus, through the praise of the superabundant valor appropriate to the present king in the context of fierce battle, the destruction of the abundance of flowers in the trees of the <s>Nandana</s> garden is imagined as established through the inference of the conjecture that a multitude of garlands of <s>mandāra</s> and other flowers are offered by the throng of celestial beauties delighting in the eager attainment of the beloved. Since poets compose the subject of <s>utprekṣā</s> in two ways — as 'as if that' and 'as if this very thing' — we shall examine this at the appropriate occasion of [defining] its characteristic. Thus this <s>utprekṣā</s>, made beautiful by the composition of the <s>aprastutapraśaṃsā</s> (indirect praise) fashioned in the first half, shining forth all the more through its inclination toward nourishing the superabundance of the valor of the king at hand, generates captivation of the connoisseurs — and this is its superlative quality.
'endowed with a surpassing poetic fancy (<s>utprekṣā</s>)' // VjivC_3.14 //
— of this [figure]; and the entry into the essential nature [of every figure], i.e., of hyperbole (<s>atiśayokti</s>) —
'what ornamentation exists without this?' // VjivC_3.15 //

children.text:
iti sakalālaṅkaraṇānugrāhakatvam /
tasmāt pṛthagatiśayoktireveyaṃ mukhyatayetyucyamāne 'pi na kiñcidatiricyate /
kavipratibhotprekṣitatvena cātyantamasaṃbhāvyamapyupanibadhyamānamanayaiva yuktyā samañjasatāṃ gāhate, na tapunaḥ svatantryeṇa /
yadvā kāraṇato lokātikrāntagocaratvena vacasaḥ saiveyamityastu, tathāpi prastutātiśayavidhānavyatirekeṇa na kiñcidapūrvamatrāsti /
tadevamabhidhānasya pūrvamabhidheyasya ceha vakratāmabhidhāyedānīṃ vākyasya vakratvamabhidhātumupakramate---
children.translated_text: — [shows] its being a supporter of all ornamentation. Therefore, even when it is said that this [hyperbole] is indeed a separate [figure] in its primary sense, nothing further is added. And because what is absolutely inconceivable too, when represented through the poet's intuitive fancy, attains propriety precisely by this device — not independently. Or alternatively, even granting that this very thing [hyperbole] is [a separate figure] because the scope of speech transcends the mundane in respect of its cause — still, apart from the production of the relevant surpassing quality, there is nothing unprecedented here. Having thus previously described the obliqueness of both expression and expressed, he now undertakes to describe the obliqueness of the sentence —
Apart from the excellences of oblique word and meaning, quality and ornamentation, belonging to the literary style —
the sentence has another obliqueness, whose life is a certain mode of expression. // Vjiv_3.3 //
Just as — apart from the beauties of the lustre of the charming tablet, the drawing, and the coloring —

children.text: citrasyeva manohāri kartuḥ kimapi kauśalam // Vjiv_3.4 //
children.translated_text: there is some other ineffable skill of the painter of a picture that is captivating. // Vjiv_3.4 //

children.text:
anyadvākyasya vakratvam---vākyasya parasparānvitavṛtteḥ padasamudāyasyānyadapūrvaṃ vyatiriktameva vakratvaṃ vakrabhāvaḥ /
bhavatīti saṃbandhaḥ, kriyāntarābhāvāt /
kutaḥ---mārgasthavakraśabdārthaguṇālaṅkārasaṃpadaḥ /
mārgāḥ sukumārādayastatrasthāḥ kecideva vakrāḥ prasiddhavyavahāravyatirekiṇo ye śabdārthaguṇālaṅkārāsteṣāṃ saṃpat kāpyupaśobhā tasyāḥ pṛthagbhūtaṃ kimapi vakratvāntarameva /
kīdṛśam---tathābhihitajīvitam /
tathā tena prakāreṇa kenāpyavyapadeśyena yābihitiḥ kāpyapūrvaivābhidhā saiva jīvitaṃ sarvasvaṃ yasya tattathoktam /
kisvarūpamityāha---kartuḥ kimapi kauśalam /
karturvidhātuḥ kimapyalaukikaṃ yatkauśalaṃ naipuṇaṃ tadeva vākyasya vakratvamityarthaḥ /
kathañcid citrasyeva, ālekhyasya yathā, manohāri hṛdayarañjakaṃ prakṛtopakaraṇavyatireki kartureva kauśalaṃ kimapi pṛthagbhūtaṃ vyatiriktam /
kuta ityāha---manojñaphalakollekhavarṇacchāyāśriyaḥ /
manojñāḥ kāścideva hṛdayahāriṇyo yāḥ phalakollekhavarṇacchāyāstāsāṃ śrīrupasobhā tasyāḥ /
pṛthagrūpaṃ kimapi tattvāntaramevetyarthaḥ /
phalakamālekhyādhārabhūtā bhittiḥ, ullekhaścitrasūtrapramāṇopapannaṃ rekhāvinyasanamātram, varṇā rañjakadravyaviśeṣāḥ, chāyā kāntiḥ /
tadidamatra tātparyam---yathā citrasya kimapi phalakādyupakaraṇakalāpavyatireki sakalaprakṛtapadārthajīvitāyamānaṃ citrakarakauśalaṃ pṛthakatvena mukhyatayodbhāsate, tathaiva vākyasya mārgādiprakṛtapadārthasārthavyatireki kavikauśalalakṣaṇaṃ kimapi sahṛdayahṛdayasaṃvedyaṃ sakalaprastutapadārthasphuritabhūtaṃ vakratvamujjṛmbate /
tathā ca, bhāvasvabhāvasaukumāryavarṇane śṛṅgārādirasasvarūpasamunmīlane vā vividhavibhūṣaṇavinyāsavicchittiviracane ca yaḥ paraḥ paripoṣātiśayastadvidāhlādakāritāyāḥ kāraṇam /
padavākyaikadeśavṛttirvā yaḥ kaścidvakratāprakārastasya kavikauśalameva nibandhanatayā vyavatiṣṭhate /
yasmādākalpānāmeva tāvanmātrasvarūpaniyataniṣṭhatayā vyavasthitānāṃ rasasvabhāvālaṅkaraṇavakratāprakārāṇāṃ navanavollekhavilakṣaṇaṃ cetanacamatkārakāri kimapi svarūpāntarametasmādeva samujjṛmbhate /
yenedamabhidhīyate---
children.translated_text: 'Another obliqueness of the sentence' — the sentence, being a collection of words whose functions are mutually connected, has 'another,' unprecedented, distinct obliqueness, oblique quality. 'It is' — this is the syntactic connection, there being no other verb. From what [is it distinct]? — 'from the excellences of oblique word and meaning, quality and ornamentation, belonging to the literary style.' The literary styles are the delicate (<s>sukumāra</s>) and so forth; belonging to those are certain oblique word-ornaments and meaning-ornaments, qualities and ornamentations that depart from common usage — the excellence of these, some supplementary beauty; distinct from that, some other form of obliqueness entirely. Of what kind? — 'whose life is a certain mode of expression.' A mode of expression (<s>abhihiti</s>) — some unprecedented designation — that is 'in such a way,' in some manner that cannot be described; that which has that as its life-force, its very essence, is thus described. What is its nature? — he says: 'some skill of the painter.' Of the painter, the creator — some extraordinary skill, expertise — that very thing is the obliqueness of the sentence, this is the meaning. Like what? — 'of a picture,' of a painting — 'captivating,' delighting the heart — a skill of the painter himself that is distinct from the [ordinary] materials at hand, something separate. From what? — he says: 'from the beauties of the lustre of the charming tablet, the drawing, and the coloring.' The beauties of certain captivating tablets, drawings, colors, and lustres — from them, there is some other reality entirely. The tablet is the surface that supports the painting; the drawing is merely the arrangement of outlines conforming to the proportions of the painting-guide; the colors are the particular pigment-substances; the lustre is the radiance. The purport here is this: just as, distinct from the entire set of implements such as the tablet and so forth, some skill of the painter — which animates the life of all the subject-matter at hand — shines forth as separate and primary, so too the obliqueness of the sentence — characterized as the skill of the poet — which is distinct from the subject-matter such as literary style and the rest, perceptible to the hearts of the sensitive, constituting the manifestation of all the subject-matter at hand — blazes forth. And so, in the description of the natural delicacy of the nature of things, in the unfolding of the essential nature of <s>śṛṅgāra</s> (erotic) and other <s>rasas</s>, and in the fashioning of the charm of the arrangement of various ornaments — whatever surpassing degree of nourishment there is, that is the cause of producing delight in the knowledgeable. And whatever variety of obliqueness operates as a part of word or sentence — the poet's skill alone stands as its foundation. Because from the beginningless [line of poets], the ever-fresh and unique character of the <s>rasa</s>, natural description, and ornamentation varieties — which are established as fixed in their essential nature to just that extent — some other essential nature, productive of wonder in the sentient, blazes forth from this very [skill]. Hence it is said —
[Prakrit:] 'Since the beginning of creation, though its essence has been grasped daily by the bulls among poets,

children.text: ajjavi abhinnamuddo vva jaai vāāṃ paripphando // VjivC_3.16 //
children.translated_text: even today, as if with its seal unbroken, the activity of speech triumphs.' // VjivC_3.16 //
[Sanskrit shadow:] 'Since the beginning of creation, though its essence has been grasped daily by the bulls among poets,
even today, as if with its seal unbroken, the activity of speech triumphs.'
This is the <s>chāyā</s> (Sanskrit rendering).

children.text:
atra sargārambhāt prabhṛti kavipradhānaiḥ prātisvikapratibhāparispandamāhātmyāt pratidivasagṛhītasarvasvo 'pyadyāpi navanavapratibhāsānantyavijṛmbhaṇādanuddhāṭitaprāya iva yo vākyaparispandaḥ sa jayati sarvotkarṣeṇa vartate ityevamasmin susaṅgate 'pi vākyārthe kavikauśalasya vilasitaṃ kimapyalaukikameva parisphurati /
yasmāt svābhimānadhvaniprādhānyena tenaitadabhihitam yathā---āsaṃsāraṃ kavipuṅgavaiḥ pratidivasaṃ gṛhītasāro 'pyadyāpyabhinnamudra ivāyam /
evamaparijñātatattvatayā na kenacita kimapyetasmād gṛhītamiti matpratibhoddhāṭitaparamārthasyedānīmeva mudrābandhodbhedo bhaviṣyatīti lokottarasvaparispandasāphalyāpattervākyaparispando jayatītisaṃbandhaḥ /
yadyapi rasasvabhāvālaṅkārāṇāṃ sarveṣāṃ kavikauśalameva jīvitam, tathāpyalaṅkārasya viśeṣatastadanugrahaṃ vinā varṇanāviṣayavastuno bhūṣaṇābhidhāyitvenābhimatasya svarūpamātreṇa parisphurato yathārthatvena nibadhyamānasya tadvidāhlādanidhānānupapattermanāṅmātramapi na vaicitryamutprekṣāmahe, pracurapravāhapatitetarapadārthasāmānyena pratibhāsanāt /
yathā
children.translated_text: Here, although from the commencement of creation, by the foremost among poets, through the greatness of the activity of their respective intuitive powers, all its essence has been grasped daily — yet even today, because of the infinite unfolding of ever-fresh appearances, the activity of the sentence, which remains as if largely unopened, triumphs — prevails with supreme excellence. Thus, even though the sentence-meaning is perfectly coherent, some extraordinary display of the poet's skill shines forth. Since with the predominance of the tone of self-regard, [the poet] has stated this as follows: 'Since the beginning of creation, though its essence has been grasped daily by the bulls among poets, even today this [activity of speech] is as if with its seal unbroken' — [meaning:] thus, because its truth has not been recognized by anyone, nothing has been taken from it by anyone; the ultimate truth, opened by my intuition, will now for the first time have its seal-bond broken — the activity of speech triumphs, due to the attainment of the fruitfulness of its own extraordinary activity: this is the syntactic connection. Although the poet's skill is indeed the life-force of <s>rasa</s>, natural description, and ornamentation — all of them — nevertheless, specifically for ornamentation, without that [skill's] favor, the object of description, which is merely manifested in its bare essential nature as something meant to be an ornament and is bound simply with verisimilitude — we do not imagine the slightest variety in it, since it appears as generality with the other objects in an abundant stream. For example —

children.text: dūrvākāṇḍamiva śyāmā tanvī śyāmālatā yathā // VjivC_3.17 //
children.translated_text: 'Dark as a shoot of <s>dūrvā</s> grass, slender as a dark creeper.' // VjivC_3.17 //

children.text:
iti ca nūtanollekhamanohāriṇaḥ puretasya lokottaravinyasanavicchittiviśeṣitaśobhātiśayasya kimapi tadvidāhlādakāritvamudbhidyate /
yathā
children.translated_text: and so on — here, of this [comparison], captivating with a fresh delineation, distinguished by an extraordinary beauty characterized by the charm of an unprecedented arrangement, some capacity to delight the knowledgeable arises. For example —
'Of her, in the creation of [her] form' // VjivC_3.18 //
and so on. Also —
'What, of the tree of youth?' // VjivC_3.19 //

children.text:
iti /
tadevaṃ pṛthagbhāvenāpi bhavato 'sya kavikauśalāyattavṛttitvalakṣaṇavākyavakratāntarbhāva eva yuktiyuktatāmavagāhate /
tadidamuktam
children.translated_text: and so on. Thus, even though existing separately, its inclusion within sentence-obliqueness — whose defining characteristic is dependence on the poet's skill — is what possesses logical fitness. This is what was stated —
'The oblique quality of the sentence, which is something different, is divided into a thousand [varieties],
in which that entire class of ornaments will be included.' // VjivC_3.20 //
An example of natural description (<s>svabhāva</s>) —

children.text: teṣāṃ gopavadhūvilāsasuhṛdāṃ rādhārahaḥ sākṣiṇāṃ kṣemaṃ bhadra kalindaśailatanayātīre latāveśmānām /
children.translated_text: 'Of those bower-houses on the bank of the daughter of Mount <s>Kalinda</s> [the <s>Yamunā</s>] — companions of the amorous sports of the cowherd women, witnesses of <s>Rādhā's</s> love-secrets —

children.text: vicchinne smaratalpakalpanamṛducchedopayoge 'dhunā te jāne jaraṭhībhavanti vigalannīlatviṣaḥ pallavāḥ // VjivC_3.21 //
children.translated_text: may it be well! Now that the use of their sprout-bedding, which served as cushions for the love-beds — fashioned by <s>Smara</s> (Love) — has been severed, I know that their shoots, losing their dark lustre, are growing old.' // VjivC_3.21 //

children.text:
atra yadyapi sahṛdayasaṃvedyaṃ vastusaṃbhavi svabhāvamātrameva varṇitam, tathāpyanuttānatayā vyavasthitasyāsya viralavidagdhahṛdayaikagocaraṃ kimapi nūtanollekhamanohāri padārthāntarlonavṛtti sūkṣmasubhagaṃ tādṛk svarūpamunmīlitaṃ yena vākyavakratātmanaḥ kavikauśalasya kācideva kāṣṭhādhirūḍhirupapadyate /
yasmāttadvyatiriktavṛttirarthātiśayo na kaścillabhyate /
rasodāharaṇaṃ yathā
children.translated_text: Here, although only the natural state of things — perceptible to the sensitive — has been described, nevertheless, because it is established in non-obviousness, some rare and delicate essential nature that is accessible only to the hearts of the few who are truly wise — captivating with a fresh delineation, operating within a separate domain of meaning, finely charming — has been revealed: whereby the poet's skill, which is the very self of sentence-obliqueness, attains a certain culmination. Because no surpassing of meaning of any other kind can be obtained without it. An example of <s>rasa</s> (aesthetic emotion) —

children.text: loko yādṛśamāha sāhasadhanaṃ taṃ kṣatriyāputrakaṃ syātsatyena sa tādṛgeva na bhavedvārtā visaṃvādinī /
children.translated_text: 'What the world says of that prince of <s>Kṣatriyas</s>, whose wealth is daring — if it be true, let him be exactly such; let the report not be deceiving.

children.text: ekāṃ kāmapi kālavipruṣamamī śauryoṣmakaṇḍūvyaya- vyagrāḥ syuściravismṛtāmaracamūḍimbāhavā bāhavaḥ // VjivC_3.22 //
children.translated_text: For these arms, eager to expend the itch of the heat of their valor — let them find some drop of time for the battle with the host of immortals, long forgotten.' // VjivC_3.22 //

children.text:
atrotsāhābhidhānaḥ sthāyibhāvaḥ samucitālambanavibhāvalakṣaṇaviṣayasaundaryātiśayaślāghāśraddhālutayā vijigīṣorvaidagdhyabhaṅgībhaṇitavaicitryeṇa parāṃ paripoṣapadavīmadhiropitaḥ san rasatāṃ nīyamānaḥ kimapi vākyavakrabhāvasvabhāvaṃ kavikauśalamāvedayati /
anyeṣāṃ pūrvaprakaraṇodāharaṇānāṃ pratyekantathābhihitijīvitalakṣaṇaṃ vākyavakratvaṃ svayameva sahṛdayairvicāraṇīyam /
children.translated_text: Here, the permanent mental state (<s>sthāyibhāva</s>) called enthusiasm (<s>utsāha</s>) — its <s>rasa</s>-quality being attained through the surpassing beauty of the appropriate substrate and <s>vibhāva</s> (determinant) characterized by the object, and through the earnest aspiration of respect and faith — having been elevated to the supreme stage of nourishment through the variety of the clever mode of utterance of one who desires conquest — reveals some skill of the poet, which is the very nature of sentence-obliqueness. The sentence-obliqueness characterized as 'whose life is a certain mode of expression,' pertaining to the other examples from the previous sections individually — that should be examined by the sensitive readers themselves.
'For the kinds of obliqueness that are endowed with the qualities of propriety,
this is sufficient stimulation — even for those great in their own activity.' // VjivC_3.23 //
'<s>Rasa</s>, natural description, and ornamentation, though they have existed since the beginning of creation,
by this [obliqueness], attain a novelty that produces delight in the knowledgeable.' // VjivC_3.24 //
These are intermediate verses.

children.text: evamabhidhānābhideyābhidhālakṣaṇasya kāvyopayoginastritayasya svarūpamullikhya varṇanīyasya vastuno viṣayavibhāgaṃ vidadhāti---
children.translated_text: Having thus outlined the essential nature of the triad — the expression, the expressed, and the mode of expression — which are useful in poetry, he now sets forth the division of domains of the subject matter to be described —
Of the entities to be described — whose beauty lies in the unfading propriety of their true nature —

children.text: cetanānāṃ jaḍānāṃ ca svarūpaṃ dvividhaṃ smṛtam // Vjiv_3.5 //
children.translated_text: the essential nature is known as twofold: of the sentient and of the insentient. // Vjiv_3.5 //

children.text:
bhāvānāṃ varṇyamānavṛttīnāṃ svarūpaṃ parispandaḥ /
kīdṛśam---dvividham /
dve vidhe prakārau yasya tattathoktam /
smṛtaṃ sūribhirāmnātam /
keṣāṃ bhāvānām---cetanānāṃ jaḍānāṃ ca /
cetanānāṃ saṃvidvatāṃ prāṇināmiti yāvat; jaḍānāṃ tadvyatirekiṇāṃ prāṇacaitanyaśūnyānām /
etadeva ca dharmidvaividhyaṃ dharmadvaividhyasya nibandhanam /
kīdṛksvarūpaṃ---aparimlānasvabhāvaucityasundaram /
aparimlānaḥ pratyagraparipoṣapeśalo yaḥ svabhāvaḥ pāramārthiko dharmastasya yadaucityamucitabhāvaḥ prastāvopayogyadoṣaduṣṭatva tena sundaraṃ sukumāraṃ tadvidāhlādakamityarthaḥ /
etadeva dvaividhyaṃ vibhajya vicārayati---
children.translated_text: The essential nature, i.e., the activity, of the entities (<s>bhāva</s>) to be described. Of what kind? — twofold. That which has two modes is thus described. 'Known' — traditionally cited by the wise. Of which entities? — 'of the sentient and of the insentient.' Of the sentient — those possessing consciousness, living beings; of the insentient — those that are different from them, devoid of life-consciousness. And this very twofold division of the property-bearer is the foundation of the twofold division of properties. What kind of essential nature? — 'whose beauty lies in the unfading propriety of their true nature.' 'Unfading' means charming with the delicacy of ever-fresh nourishment; the 'true nature' is the real property; its 'propriety' is its fitness — the state of being free from defects and suited to the occasion — beautiful, delicate, delightful to the knowledgeable through that. He now divides and examines this very twofold division —
Therein, the first is divided into just two categories,
through the connection with the primacy of gods and the like or of lions and the like, and the rest. // Vjiv_3.6 //

children.text:
tatra dvayoḥ svarūpayormadhyāt pūrvaṃ yatprathamaṃ cetanapadārthasaṃbandhi tad dvābhyāmeva rāśyantarābhāvāt prakārābhyāṃ vibhidyate bhedamāsādayati, dvividhameva saṃpadyate /
kasmāt---surādisiṃhaprabhṛtiprādhānyetarayogataḥ /
surādayaḥ tridaśaprabhṛtayo ye cetanāḥ surāsurasiddhavidyādharagandarvanaraprabhṛtayaḥ, ye cānye siṃhaprabhṛtayaḥ kesaripramukhāsteṣāṃ yatprādhānyaṃ mukhyatvamitaradaprādhānyaṃ ca tābhyāṃ yathāsaṃkhyena pratyekaṃ yo yogaḥ saṃbandhastasmāt kāraṇāt /
tadevaṃ surādīnāṃ mukhyacetanānāṃ svarūpamekaṃ kavīnāṃ varṇanāspadam /
siṃhādīnāmamukhyacetanānāṃ paśumṛgapakṣisarīsṛpāṇāṃ svarūpaṃ dvitīyamityetadeva viśeṣeṇonmīlayati---
children.translated_text: Therein, of the two essential natures, the first — that which relates to the sentient — is divided, attains subdivision, into just two categories, due to the absence of a third group. For what reason? — 'through the connection with the primacy of gods and the like or of lions and the like, and the rest.' The gods and the like — the celestials and so forth — those sentient beings such as gods, <s>asuras</s>, <s>siddhas</s>, <s>vidyādharas</s>, <s>gandharvas</s>, humans, and the like; and the others, the lions and the like — those headed by the lion — their primacy, i.e., being the principal, or the secondary status of the others; from the connection of each with these respectively, in due order. Thus, the essential nature of the gods and the like — the principal sentient beings — is one domain for poets' description. The essential nature of lions and the like — the non-principal sentient beings: animals, deer, birds, and reptiles — is the second. He now unfolds this very distinction further —
The principal [category] — captivating through the nourishment of unfabricated love (<s>rati</s>) and the like,
shining with the delineation of amorous play (<s>hevāka</s>) proper to its own class — and the other. // Vjiv_3.7 //

children.text:
mukhyaṃ yatpradhānaṃ cetanasurāsurādisaṃbandhi svarūpaṃ tadevaṃvidhaṃ sat kavīnāṃ varṇanāspadaṃ bhavati svavyāpāragocaratāṃ pratipadyate /
kīdṛśam---akliṣṭaratyādiparipoṣamanoharam /
akliṣṭaḥ kadarthanāvirahitaḥ pratyagratāmanoharo yo ratyādiḥ sthāyibhāvastasya paripoṣaḥ śṛṅgāraprabhṛtirasatvāpādanam, "sthāyyeva tu raso bhavedi' ti nyāyāt /
tena manoharaṃ hṛdayahāri /
atrodāharaṇāni vipralambhaśṛṅgāre caturthe 'ṅke vikramorvaśyāmunmattasya purūravasaḥ pralapitāni /
yathā
children.translated_text: The principal nature, which is connected with the primary conscious beings — gods, demons, and so forth — such being [its character], it becomes the object of description for poets, enters the domain of their creative activity. Of what kind? — Captivating through the undistorted nourishment of <s>rati</s> (love) and the other [permanent emotions]. 'Undistorted' — free from any marring — the nourishment of <s>rati</s> and the other permanent emotions (<s>sthāyibhāvas</s>), that is, their elevation to the status of <s>rasa</s> (aesthetic sentiment) such as <s>śṛṅgāra</s> (the erotic) and so forth — by the principle that 'the permanent [emotion] alone becomes <s>rasa</s>.' Captivating through that means delightful to the heart. Examples of this in <s>vipralambhaśṛṅgāra</s> (love-in-separation) are the ravings of the maddened <s>Purūravas</s> in the fourth act of the <s>Vikramorvaśīya</s>. For example —

children.text: tiṣṭhetkopavaśātprabhāvapihitā dīrghaṃ na sā kupyati svargāyotpatitā bhavenmayi punarbhāvārdramasyā manaḥ /
children.translated_text: 'Let her remain hidden through the power of anger — she does not stay angry long; if she has flown up to heaven, her mind is still tender toward me;'

children.text: tāṃ hartuṃ vibudhadviṣo 'pi na ca me śaktāḥ purovartinoṃ sā cātyantamagocaraṃ nayanayoryāteti ko 'yaṃ vidhiḥ // VjivC_3.25 //
children.translated_text: 'even the enemies of the gods are not able to seize her from before me — yet she has gone utterly beyond the range of my eyes. What is this fate?' // <s>Vjīv</s>C 3.25 //

children.text:
atra rājño vallabhāvirahavaidhuryadaśāveśavivaśavṛttestadasaṃprāptinimittamanadhi gacchataḥ prathamatarameva svābhāvikasaukumāryasaṃbhāvyamānamanantarocitavicārāpasāryamāṇopapatti kimapi tātkālikavikalpollikhyamānamanavalokanakāraṇamutprekṣamāṇasya tadāsādanasamanvayāsaṃbhavānnairāśyaniścayavimūḍhamānasatayā rasaḥ parāṃ paripoṣapadavīmadhairopitaḥ /
tathā caitadeva vākyāntarairuddīpitaṃ yathā
children.translated_text: Here, of the king, whose condition is overwhelmed by the state of distress from separation from his beloved, who cannot comprehend the cause of not obtaining her, and who first imagines possible causes consistent with her natural delicacy — each suitable consideration being successively dismissed as implausible — and then imagines, through transient fancies sketched in the moment, some reason for not seeing her — [and] since the impossibility of connecting [these reasons] with her attainment leads to the bewilderment of a mind fixed in the certainty of despair — the <s>rasa</s> has been elevated to the supreme stage of nourishment. And thus the same [idea] is stimulated by further sentences, as —

children.text: padbhyāṃ spṛśedvasumatīṃ yadi sā sugātrī meghābhivṛṣṭasikatāsu vanasthalīṣu /
children.translated_text: 'If that beautiful-limbed one should touch the earth with her feet, in the forest-grounds whose sands have been washed by the rain-clouds,

children.text: paścānnatā gurunitambatayā tato 'syā dṛśyeta cārupadapaṅktiralaktakāṅkā // VjivC_3.26 //
children.translated_text: 'then, because of the heaviness of her hips, she would lean backward, and her beautiful footprint-row, marked with lac, would be visible.' // <s>Vjīv</s>C 3.26 //

children.text:
atra padbhyāṃ vasumatīṃ kadācit spṛśedityāśaṃsayā tatprāptiḥ saṃbhāvyeta /
yasmājjaladharasalilasekasukumārasikatāsu vanasthalīṣu gurunitambatayā tasyāḥ paścānnatatvena nitarāṃ mudritasaṃsthānā rāgoparaktatayā ramaṇīyavṛttiścaraṇavinyāsaparaṃparā dṛśyeta, tasmānnairāśyaniścitirevasutarāṃ samujjṛmbhitā, yā taduttaravākyonmattavilapitānāṃ nimittatāmabhajat /
karuṇarasodāharaṇāni tāpasavatsarāje dvitīye 'ṅke vatsarājasya paridevitāni /
yathā
children.translated_text: Here, through the hope 'she might sometime touch the earth with her feet,' her obtainment is imagined. Because on the forest-grounds, whose sands are made delicate by the sprinkling of rain-cloud water, a series of footstep-impressions — deeply sealed in form because of her leaning backward due to the heaviness of her hips, and beautiful because of being tinged with lac-dye — would be visible. Therefore, the certainty of despair is all the more amplified — and that [despair] became the cause of the maddened ravings in the subsequent sentences. Examples for <s>karuṇarasa</s> (the pathetic sentiment) are the lamentations of <s>Vatsarāja</s> in the second act of the <s>Tāpasavatsarāja</s>. For example —

children.text: dhārāveśma vilokya dīnavadano bhrāntvā ca līlāgṛhā- nniśvasyāyatamāśu kesaralatāvīthīṣu kṛtvā dṛśaḥ /
children.translated_text: 'Having looked at the rain-pavilion with a sorrowful face, having wandered through the pleasure-houses, having sighed deeply, casting his gaze quickly upon the avenues of <s>kesara</s>-creepers —'

children.text: kiṃ me pārśvamupaiṣi putraka kṛtaiḥ kiṃ cāṭubhiḥ krūrayā mātrā tvaṃ parivarjitaḥ saha mayā yāntyātidīrghāṃ bhuvam // VjivC_3.27 //
children.translated_text: 'Why do you come to my side, little son? What use are your flatteries? You have been abandoned by your cruel mother — together with me you go to an exceedingly long land.' // <s>Vjīv</s>C 3.27 //

children.text:
atra rasaparipoṣanibandhanavibhāvādisaṃpatsamudayaḥ kavinā sutarāṃ samujjṛmbhitaḥ /
tathā cāsyaiva vākyasyāvatārakaṃ vidhūṣakavākyamevaṃvidhaṃ prayuktam---
children.translated_text: Here, the aggregate of the wealth of <s>vibhāvas</s> (determinants) and other [factors] that are the basis for the nourishment of <s>rasa</s> has been most fully amplified by the poet. And thus, the introductory sentence of the jester (<s>vidūṣaka</s>), serving as a lead-in to this very speech, has been composed thus —

children.text: pamādo eso kkhu devīe puttakidako dariṇapodo attabhavantaṃ aṇusaradi // VjivC_3.28 //
children.translated_text: 'Carelessness! Indeed the <s>Devī</s>'s pet fawn follows His Honor.' (Prākrit) // <s>Vjīv</s>C 3.28 //

children.text: pramādaḥ ! eṣa khalu devyāḥ putrakṛtako hariṇapoto 'trabhavantamanusarati //
children.translated_text: 'Carelessness! Indeed the <s>Devī</s>'s pet fawn follows His Honor.'

children.text:
iti chāyā /
etena karuṇarasoddīpanavibhāvatā hariṇapotakadhārāgṛhaprabhṛtīnāṃ sutarāṃ samutpadyate /
tathā ca "ayamaparaḥ kṣate kṣārāvakṣepaḥ" iti rumaṇvadvacanānantarametatparatvenaiva vākyāntaramupanibaddham, yathā
children.translated_text: Thus the <s>chāyā</s> (Sanskrit rendering). By this, the role of the fawn, the rain-pavilion, and so forth as stimulant-factors (<s>uddīpanavibhāvas</s>) for the <s>karuṇarasa</s> (pathetic sentiment) is all the more generated. And thus, immediately after the saying of <s>Rumaṇvat</s> — 'this is another sprinkling of salt upon a wound' — a further sentence was composed with precisely this purport, namely —

children.text: karṇāntasthitapadmarāgakalikāṃ bhūyaḥ samākarṣatā cañcvā dāḍimabījamityabhihatā pādena gaṇḍasthalī /
children.translated_text: 'Pulling with its beak at the ruby bud-earring at the ear-tip, thinking it a pomegranate seed, the cheek-surface was struck by its foot;'

children.text: yenāsau tava tasya narmasuhṛdaḥ khedānmuhuḥ krandato niḥśaṅkaṃna śukasya kiṃ prativaco devi tvayā dīyate // VjivC_3.29 //
children.translated_text: 'wherefore, to that playful friend of yours who cries out repeatedly in distress — to that parrot — O <s>Devī</s>, why is no answer fearlessly given by you?' // <s>Vjīv</s>C 3.29 //

children.text:
atra śukasyaivaṃvidhadurlalitayuktatvaṃ vāllabhyapratipādanaparatvenopāttam /
"asau' iti kapolasthālyāḥ svānubhavasvadamānasaukumāryotkarṣaparāmarśaḥ /
evaṃvidhoddīpanavibhāvaikajīvitatvena karuṇarasaḥ kāṣṭhādhirūḍhiramaṇīyatāmanīyata /
evaṃ vipralambhaśṛṅgārakaruṇayoḥ saukumāryādudāharaṇapradarśanaṃ vihitam /
rasāntarāṇāmapi svayamevotprekṣaṇīyam /
evaṃ dvitīyamapradhānacetanasihādisaṃbandhi yatsvarūpaṃ taditthaṃ kavīnāṃ varṇanāspadaṃ saṃpadyate /
kīdṛśam---svajātyucitadevākasamullekhojjvalam /
svā pratyekamātmīyā sāmānyalakṣaṇavastusvarūpā yā jātistasyāḥ samucito yo hevākaḥ svabhāvānusārī parispandastasya samullekhaḥsamyagullekhanaṃ vāstavena rūpeṇopanibandhastenojjvalaṃ bhrājiṣṇu, tadvidāhlādakārīti yāvat /
yathā
children.translated_text: Here, the parrot's being endowed with such playful mischief is taken up for the purpose of establishing intimacy [between the queen and the parrot]. 'Asau' (that one) — a reflection upon the supremely experienced delicacy of the cheek-surface. Through being exclusively animated by such stimulant-factors, the <s>karuṇarasa</s> has ascended to the extreme and is perceived as beautiful. Thus, examples from <s>vipralambhaśṛṅgāra</s> and <s>karuṇa</s> have been shown, due to their delicacy. The [examples] of the other <s>rasas</s> should be imagined by oneself. Thus, the second [type of] nature — that which is connected with non-principal conscious beings, lions and so forth — in this manner becomes the object of description for poets. Of what kind? — 'Brilliant through the complete delineation of the natural activity proper to its own species.' 'Own' means individual; the 'species' is the general nature of the class of objects; the 'natural activity' is the behavior conforming to nature that is proper to that [species]; the 'complete delineation' is the thorough depiction of that in its actual form, and the composition [that is] brilliant through that — radiant, meaning delightful to connoisseurs. For example —
'At some time, in a cave-chamber of the <s>Pāriyātra</s> [mountain], with eyes closed,
'sitting with two paws crossed, with tusk-tips touching the chin — [the lion] slept.' // <s>Vjīv</s>C 3.30 //

children.text:
atra giriguhāgehāntare nidrāmanubhavataḥ kaisariṇaḥ svajātisamucitaṃ sthānakamullikhitam /
yathā vā
children.translated_text: Here, the posture proper to the species of the lion sleeping inside the mountain cave-chamber has been delineated. Or as —

children.text: grīvābhaṅgābhirāmaṃ muhuranupatati syandane dattadṛṣṭiḥ paścārdhena praviṣṭaḥ śarapatanabhayād bhūyasā pūrvakāyam /
children.translated_text: 'Charming with the bending of its neck, [the deer] repeatedly follows the chariot, fixing its gaze; the hindquarters having entered [the thicket], the front body [projecting] further, out of fear of the arrow's fall;'

children.text: darbhairardhāvalīḍhaiḥ śramavivṛtamukhabhraṃśibhiḥ kīrṇavartmā paśyodagraplutatvādviyati bahutaraṃstokamurvyāṃ prayāti // VjivC_3.31 //
children.translated_text: 'with the path strewn by half-chewed <s>darbha</s> grasses falling from its mouth opened wide by fatigue — see: due to its forward leaps, it travels much more in the sky, and little upon the earth.' // <s>Vjīv</s>C 3.31 //
[The author] unfolds this very [principle] in another manner —
'Beautiful through the basis of the capacity to stimulate <s>rasa</s>,
'of non-principal conscious beings and also of inanimate things, for the most part.' // <s>Vjīv</s> 3.8 //

children.text:
cetanānāṃ prāṇināmamukhyānāmapradhānabhūtānāṃ yatsvarūpaṃ tadevaṃvidhaṃ sat, varṇanīyatāṃ pratipadyate prastutāṅgatayopayujyamānam /
kīdṛśamrasoddīpanasāmarthyavinibandhanabandhuram /
rasāḥ śṛṅgārādayasteṣāmuddīpanamullāsanaṃ paripoṣastasmin sāmarthyaṃ śaktistayā vinibandhanaṃniveśastena bandhuraṃ hṛdayahāri /
yathā
children.translated_text: The nature of non-principal conscious beings — beings that are not the main characters — such being [its character], it attains describability, being employed as a subsidiary component of the subject at hand. Of what kind? — 'Beautiful through the basis of the capacity to stimulate <s>rasa</s>.' The <s>rasas</s> are <s>śṛṅgāra</s> and the rest; their stimulation is their arousal, their nourishment; the capacity for that; the basis, the grounding, in that; beautiful, that is, captivating to the heart, through that. For example —
'The male cuckoo, whose throat is astringent from savoring the mango-sprout, sang sweetly;'

children.text: manasvinīmānavighātadakṣaṃ tadeva jātaṃ vacanaṃ smarasya // VjivC_3.32 //
children.translated_text: 'that very [song] became the word of <s>Smara</s> (the Love-god), skillful at destroying the pride of resolute women.' // <s>Vjīv</s>C 3.32 //

children.text:
jaḍānāṃ cāpi bhūyasā---jaḍānāmacetanānāṃ salilatarukusumasamayaprabhṛtīnāmevaṃvidhaṃ svarūpaṃ rasoddīpanasāmarthyavinibandhanabandhuraṃ varṇanīyatāmavagāhate /
yathā
children.translated_text: 'And also of inanimate things, for the most part' — of inanimate things — water, trees, flowers, seasons, and so forth — such a nature, beautiful through the basis of the capacity to stimulate <s>rasa</s>, enters the domain of describability. For example —

children.text: idamasulabhavastuprārthanādurnivāraṃ prathamamapi mano me pañcabāṇaḥ kṣiṇoti /
children.translated_text: 'This mind of mine, [already] consumed by the five-arrowed [Love-god] through the irresistible longing for an unattainable object, [is afflicted] even at first;'
'how much more so when the forest <s>sahakāra</s> (mango) trees, their pale leaves uprooted by the Malaya breeze, display their sprouts!' // <s>Vjīv</s>C 3.33 //
Or as —

children.text: udbhedābhimukhāṅkurāḥ kuravakāḥ śaivālajālākula-prāntaṃ bhānti sarāṃsi phenapaṭalaiḥ sīmantitāḥ sindhavaḥ /
children.translated_text: 'The <s>kuravaka</s> shrubs [have] sprouts straining toward blossoming; the pools shine with edges tangled in masses of <s>śaivāla</s> (moss); the rivers are parted with veils of foam;'

children.text: kiñcāsmin samaye kṛśāṅgi vilasatkandarpakodaṇḍika-krīḍābhāñji bhavanti santatalatākīrṇānyaraṇyānyapi // VjivC_3.34 //
children.translated_text: 'and moreover, at this season, O slender one, even the forests — continuously filled with creepers — become the play-bows of the radiant Love-god.' // <s>Vjīv</s>C 3.34 //
Having thus described the nature of objects grounded in their naturally beautiful activity, [the author] now concludes the same —
'This is the body of the [poetic] object, overflowing with beauty;'
'it should be known as that which is to be taken up — the object of description for poets.' // <s>Vjīv</s> 3.9 //

children.text:
arthasya varṇanīyasya vastunaḥ śarīramidam upādeyatayā jñeyaṃ grāhyatvena boddhavyam /
kīdṛśaṃ sat --- rāmaṇīyakanirbharam, saundaryaparipūrṇam,aupahatyarahitatvena tadvidāvarjakamiti yāvat /
kavīnāmetadeva yasmādvarṇanāspadamabhidhāvyāparāgocaram /
evaṃvidhasyāsya svarūpaśobhātiśayabhrājiṣṇorvibhūṣaṇānyupaśobhāntaramārabhante /
etadeva prakārāntareṇa vicārayati---
children.translated_text: This is the body of the object — of the subject to be described. 'To be known as that which is to be taken up' means to be understood as worthy of adoption. Of what kind? — 'Overflowing with beauty' — filled with loveliness — because it is free from the incidental, it is irresistible to connoisseurs. This is indeed the object of description for poets — the domain of their creative activity. Such a nature, resplendent with the superabundance of natural beauty, is what ornaments begin to adorn further. [The author] now examines this very [point] in another manner —
'Grounded in the activity of the means for accomplishing <s>dharma</s> (duty) and the rest,
