'and conforming to worldly practice — another [nature] also attains describability.' // <s>Vjīv</s> 3.10 //

children.text:
vyavahārocitaṃ cānyat /
aparaṃ padārthānāṃ cetanācetanānāṃ svarūpamevaṃvidhaṃ varṇanīyatāṃ labhate kavivyāpāraviṣayatāṃ pratipadyate /
kīdṛśam---vyavahārocitam, lokavṛttayogyam /
kīdṛśaṃ sat---dharmādisādhanopāyaparispandanibadhanam /
dharmādeścaturvargasya sādhane saṃpādane upāyabhūto yaḥ parispandaḥ svavilasitaṃ tadeva nibandhanaṃ yasya tattathoktam /
tadidamuktaṃ bhavati---yat kāvye varṇyamānavṛttayaḥ pradhānacetanaprabhṛtayaḥ sarve padārthāścaturvargasādhanopāyaparispandaprādhānyena varṇanīyāḥ, ye 'pyapradhānacetanasvarūpāḥ padārthāste 'pi dharmārthādyupāyabhūtasvavilāsaprādhānyena kavīnāṃ varṇanīyatāmavataranti /
tathā ca rājñāṃ śūdrakaprabhṛtīnāṃ mantriṇāṃ ca śukanāsamukhyānāṃ caturvargānuṣṭhānopadeśaparatvenaiva caritāni varṇyante /
apradhānacetanānāṃ hastihariṇaprabhṛtīnāṃ saṃgramamṛgayādyaṅgatayā parispandasundaraṃ svarūpaṃ lakṣye varṇyamānatayā paridṛśyate /
tasmādeva ca tathāvidhasvarūpollekhaprādhānyena kāvyakāvyopakaraṇakavīnāṃ citracitropakaraṇacitrakaraiḥ sāmyaṃ prathamameva pratipāditam /
tadevaṃvidhaṃ svabhāvaprādhānye rasaprādhānyena ca dviprakāraṃ sahajasaukumāryasarasaṃ svarūpaṃ varṇanāviṣayavastunaḥ śarīramevālaṅkāryatāmevārhati, na punaralaṅkāraṇatvam /
tatra svābhāvikaṃ padārthasvarūpamalaṅkaraṇaṃ yathā na bhavati tathā prathamameva pratipāditam /
idānīṃ rasātmanaḥ prādhānacetanaparispandavarṇyamānavṛtteralaṅkārakārāntarābhimatāmalaṅkāratāṃ nirākaroti---
children.translated_text: 'And another, conforming to worldly practice' — another nature of objects, both conscious and inanimate, of such a kind, attains describability, enters the domain of the poet's creative activity. Of what kind? — Conforming to worldly practice, suitable for the ways of the world. Of what kind? — Grounded in the activity of the means for accomplishing <s>dharma</s> and the rest — of the four aims of life (<s>caturvarga</s>), the activity that serves as the means for their accomplishment, that very own characteristic display — that which has this as its basis is so described. What has thus been stated is this: all the objects being depicted in poetry — beginning with the principal conscious characters — are to be described with the predominance of the activity that serves as the means for accomplishing the four aims of life; and even those objects that are non-principal conscious beings also enter the domain of describability for poets, with the predominance of their own characteristic display that serves as the means for <s>dharma</s>, <s>artha</s> (wealth), and the rest. And thus, the deeds of kings such as <s>Śūdraka</s> and the rest, and of ministers such as <s>Śukanāsa</s> and others, are described precisely with the purpose of instruction in the practice of the four aims of life. The nature of non-principal conscious beings — elephants, deer, and the rest — is seen as described in verse with the beautiful natural activity shown as a subsidiary component for battle, hunting, and so forth. And precisely for that reason — with the predominance of delineating such a nature — the likeness of poetry and its instruments to painters and their varied instruments of painting has been established at the very outset. Such a nature, resplendent with the predominance of natural [beauty] and in two kinds through the predominance of <s>rasa</s>, innately graceful and full of juice — is the body of the object of description — it alone deserves to be the thing adorned (<s>alaṅkārya</s>), not [to be] the ornament (<s>alaṅkāra</s>). That the natural form of objects is not an ornament — this has been established at the very outset. Now [the author] refutes the view, held by some other theorists, that the activity of the principal conscious characters, which is the thing depicted and has <s>rasa</s> as its soul, is an ornament —
<s>Rasa</s> is not an ornament (<s>alaṅkāra</s>), because what is beyond [the natural form] does not appear;
and because of the non-conjunction with word and meaning of that which is in excess of the natural form. // <s>Vjīv</s> 3.11 //

children.text:
alaṅkāro na rasavat /
rasavaditi yo 'yamutpāditapratītirnāmālaṅkārastasya vibhūṣaṇatvaṃ nopapadyate ityarthaḥ /
kasmāt kāraṇāt---svarūpādatiriktasya parasyāpratibhāsanāt /
varṇyamānasya vastuno yat svarūpamātmīyaḥ parispandastasmādatiriktasyābhyadhikasya parasya anyasya apratibhāsanādanavabodhanāt /
tadidamatra tātparyam---yat sarveṣāmeva satkavivākyānāmidamalaṅkāryamidamalaṅkaraṇam ityapoddhāravihito viviktabhāvaḥ sarvasya yasya kasyacit pramātuścetasi parisphurati /
rasavadalaṅkāravadityasmin vākye punaravahitacetaso 'pi na kiñcidetadeva budhyāmahe /
tathā ca---yadi śṛṅgārādireva prādhānyena varṇyamāno 'laṅkāryaḥ tatastadanyena kenacidalaṅkaraṇena bhavitavyam /
yadi vā tatsvarūpameva tadvidāhlādanibandhanatvādalaṅkaraṇamityucyate tathāpi tadvyatiriktamanyadalaṅkāryatayā prakāśanīyam /
tadevaṃvidho na kaścidapi vivekaścirantanālaṅkārakārābhimate rasavadalaṅkāralakṣaṇodāharaṇamārge manāgapi vibhāvyate /
tathā ca
children.translated_text: <s>Rasavat</s> (that which possesses rasa) is not an ornament. The ornament called <s>rasavat</s>—for which such a cognition has been produced—its status as an embellishment is not established. This is the meaning. For what reason?—because nothing beyond the inherent nature manifests as separate. Of the object being described, that which is its inherent nature, its own vibration—nothing beyond that, nothing separate, nothing other manifests, is apprehended. The purport here is this: in all the utterances of true poets, the discriminated state—'this is the thing to be ornamented, this is the ornamentation'—which is a distinction produced by abstraction, flashes forth in the mind of every perceiver. In a sentence like '<s>rasavad</s>, <s>alaṅkāravat</s>' (that which possesses rasa, that which possesses ornamentation), however, even with attentive mind, we cannot understand anything of this kind. And thus: if <s>śṛṅgāra</s> (the erotic) and the like are predominantly what is being described and are the thing to be ornamented, then there must be some other ornamentation besides them. Or, if their very nature is called ornamentation because it is the ground for delighting the knowledgeable, then even so, something else, distinct from it, must be shown as the thing to be ornamented. Such a discrimination of any kind is not perceived even slightly in the definition, example, and method [prescribed] for the <s>rasavad</s>-ornament as accepted by the ancient makers of ornamental figures. And thus:
'<s>Rasavat</s>: that in which <s>śṛṅgāra</s> and the like are clearly shown.' (Vjiv 3.35)

children.text:
iti rasavallakṣaṇam /
atra darśitāḥ spṛṣṭāḥ spaṣṭaṃ vā śṛṅgārādayo yatreti vyākhyāne kāvyavyatirikto na kaścidanyaḥ samāsārthabhūtaḥ saṃlakṣyate /
yo 'sāvalaṅkāraḥ kāvyameveti cet tadapi na suspaṣṭasauṣṭhavam /
yasmāt kāvyaikadeśayoḥ śabdārthayoḥ pṛthak pṛthagalaṅkārāḥ santītyupakramyedānīṃ kāvyamevālaṅkaraṇamityupakramopasaṃhāravaiṣamyaduṣṭatvamāyāti /
yadi vādarśitāḥ spaṣṭaṃ śṛṅgārādayo yeneti samāsaḥ, tathāpi vaktavyameva---ko 'sāviti /
pratipādanavaicitryameveti cet, tadapi na samyak samarthanārham /
yasmāt pratipādyamānādanyedeva tadupaśobhānibandhanaṃ pratipādanavaicitryam, na punaḥ pratipādyamānameva /
spaṣṭatayā darśitaṃ rasānāṃ pratipādanavaicitryaṃ yadyabhidhīyate, tadapi na supratīpādanam /
spaṣṭatayā darśane śṛṅgārādīnāṃ svarūpapariniṣpattireva paryavasyati /
kiñca rasavataḥ kāvyasyālaṅkāra iti tathāvidhasya satastasyāsāviti na kiñcidanena tasyābhidheyaṃ syāt /
athavā tenaivālaṅkāreṇa rasavattvaṃ tasyādhīyate, tadevaṃ tarhyasau na rasavato 'laṅkāraḥ pratyuta rasavānalaṅkāra ityāyāti, tanmāhātmyāt kāvyamapi rasavat saṃpadyate /
yadi vā tenaivāhitarasasambandhasya rasavataḥ kāvyasyālaṅkāra iti tatpaścādrasavalaṅkāravyavadeśamāsādayati---yathāgniṣṭomayājyasya putro bhavitetyucyate, tadapi na supratibaddhasamādhānam /
yasmād "agniṣṭomayāji'-śabdaḥ prathamaṃ bhūtalakṣaṇe viṣayāntare niṣpratipakṣatayā samāsāditaprasiddhiḥ paścād bhaviṣyati vākyārthasabandhalakṣaṇayogyatayā tamanubhavituṃ śaknoti /
na punaratraivaṃ prayujyate /
yasmādrasavataḥ kāvyasyālaṅkāra iti tatsaṃjñandhitayaivāsya svarūpabdhireva /
tatsaṃbandhinibandhanaṃ ca kāvyasya rasavattvamityevamitaretarāśrayalakṣaṇadoṣaḥ kenāpasāryate /
yadi vā raso vidyate yasyāsau tadvānalaṅkāra evāstu ityabhidhīyate, tathāpyalaṅkāraḥ kāvyaṃ vā nānyat tṛtīyaṃ kiñcidatrāsti /
tatpakṣadvitayamapi pratyuktam /
udāharaṇaṃ lakṣaṇaikayogakṣematvāt pṛthaṅ na vikalpyate /
children.translated_text: This is the definition of <s>rasavat</s>. Here, in the explanation 'that in which <s>śṛṅgāra</s> and the like are shown, touched, or [shown] clearly'—no compound-meaning other than poetry itself is apprehended. If it be said that this ornament is poetry itself—that too is not well-formed in its elegance. For having begun with 'the ornaments of the two parts of poetry, word and meaning, are separate'—to now say 'poetry itself is the ornamentation' incurs the fault of inconsistency between the introduction and the conclusion. Or, if the compound is analyzed as 'that by which <s>śṛṅgāra</s> and the like are clearly shown,' even then the question remains: what is that [thing]? If it be said it is the variety of presentation—that too does not deserve proper justification. For the variety of presentation is something other than what is being presented, being the ground for its embellishment—it is not the thing being presented itself. If it is said that the variety of presentation is [the means by which] <s>rasas</s> are 'clearly shown,' that too is not well established. For 'clearly showing' of <s>śṛṅgāra</s> and the like culminates merely in the complete realization of their own nature. Moreover: an ornament 'of poetry that possesses rasa'—of that which is such, it being that—this [definition] would not state anything [meaningful] about it. Or, if it is said that its rasa-possessing quality is conferred by that very ornament—then it comes to this: it is not an ornament of [poetry] that possesses rasa, but rather it is an ornament that possesses rasa—and by its greatness, poetry too becomes rasa-possessing. Or, if it is said that it is an ornament of poetry that possesses rasa [precisely because] the rasa-connection was established by it itself—and that afterwards it attains the designation 'rasavad-alaṅkāra'—like the statement 'a son will be born to the sacrificer of the <s>Agniṣṭoma</s>'—that too is not a well-grounded resolution. For the word '<s>agniṣṭomayājin</s>' (Agniṣṭoma-sacrificer), having first achieved its well-known status unopposed in another domain characterized by [present] reality, can afterwards experience the fitness characterized by sentence-meaning connection in the future [statement]. But it is not employed in the same way here. For 'an ornament of poetry that possesses rasa'—the very understanding of its nature depends on that connection [being already established]. And the rasa-possessing quality of poetry, which is the ground for that connection—thus the fault characterized as mutual dependence (<s>itaretarāśraya</s>) is not removed by anyone. Or if it is said: let there be an ornament that is <s>rasavat</s> (possessing rasa)—in which rasa exists; even so, [the question remains:] the ornament is either [equivalent to] poetry or nothing else—there is no third thing here. Both positions have been refuted. The example, having its destiny united with the definition, is not separately examined.

children.text: mṛteti pretya saṅgantuṃ yayā me maraṇaṃ smṛtam /
children.translated_text: 'She has died'—thinking thus, [I resolved on] death in order to unite with her in the next world;

children.text: saivāvantī mayā labdhā kathamatraiva janmani // VjivC_3.36 //
children.translated_text: that very <s>Avantī</s> [woman] has been found by me—how [can this be], in this very life? (Vjiv 3.36)

children.text:
atra ratiparipoṣalakṣaṇavarṇanīyaśarīrabhūtāyāścittavṛtteratiriktamanyadvibhaktaṃ vastu na kiñcidvibhāvyate /
tasmādalaṅkāryataiva yuktimatī /
yadapi kaiścit
children.translated_text: Here, beyond the mental state that constitutes the body of what is to be described, characterized by the fullness of love (<s>rati</s>), no other separate thing is perceived. Therefore, the status of being the thing-to-be-ornamented alone is logically justified. As for what some [have defined]—

'That which is the locus of <s>sthāyin</s> (permanent emotion), <s>sañcārin</s> (transitory emotions), <s>vibhāva</s> (determinants), and <s>abhinaya</s> (gestural representation), [each designated by] its own word.' (Vjiv 3.37)

children.text:
ityanena pūrvameva lakṣaṇaṃ viśeṣitam, tatra svaśabdāspadatvaṃ rasānāmaparigatapūrvamasmākam /
tatasta eva rasasarvasvasamāhitacetasastatparamārthavido vidvāṃsa evaṃ praṣṭavyāḥ---kiṃ svaśabdāspadatvaṃ rasānāmuta rasavata iti /
tatra pūrvasmin pakṣe---rasyantaiti rasāste svaśabdāspadāsteṣu tiṣṭhantaḥ śṛṅgārādiṣu vartamānāḥ santastajjñairāsvādyante /
tadidamuktaṃ bhavati---yat svaśabdairabhidhīyamānāḥ śrutipathamavatarantaścetanānāṃ carvaṇacamatkāraṃ kurvantītyanena nyāyena ghṛtapūraprabhūtayaḥ padārthāḥ svaśabdairabhidhīyamānāstadāsvādasaṃpadaṃ saṃpādayantītyevaṃ sarvasya kasyacidupayogasukhārthinastairudāracaritairayatnenaiva tadabhidhānamātrādeva trailokyarājyasaṃpatsaukhyasamṛddhiḥ pratipādyetaiti namastebhyaḥ /
rasavatastadāspadatvaṃ nopapadyate, rasasyaiva svavācyasyāpi tadāspadatvābhāvāt, kimutānyasyeti /
tadalaṅkāratvaṃ ca prathamameva pratiṣiddham /
śiṣṭaṃ sthāyyādi pūrvalakṣaṇaṃ vyākhyātameveti na punaḥ paryālocyate /
yadapi
children.translated_text: By this the definition was already qualified previously. Therein, the quality of rasas being designated by their own words has not been apprehended by us before. Therefore, from those very [scholars]—whose minds are absorbed in the totality of rasa, who are truly knowledgeable about its ultimate meaning—the learned should be asked: is the quality of being designated by one's own word a property of the rasas, or of that which possesses rasa? In the first alternative: 'rasas' [etymologically means] 'they are tasted'—they, being designated by their own words, standing in <s>śṛṅgāra</s> and the like, are savored by the connoisseurs. What is being said is this: that those designated by their own words, descending upon the path of hearing, produce the relishing wonder of sentient beings—by this reasoning, substances such as ghee-preparations and the like, when designated by their own words, accomplish the fullness of their savoring—thus for anyone desiring the pleasure of enjoyment, by those [words] of noble character, effortlessly, merely through their designation, the wealth of happiness equal to sovereignty over the three worlds would be established—our salutations to them! The quality of being the locus of that [designation] for [poetry] that possesses rasa is not established, since even for rasa itself, which is its own expressed meaning, the quality of being that locus is absent—how much less for something else. And its status as an ornament has already been refuted. The remaining [portion] of the definition—<s>sthāyin</s> and the rest—has already been explained and need not be reconsidered. As for [the definition]—
'<s>Rasavat</s>, because of its dependence upon rasa.' (Vjiv 3.38)

children.text:
iti kaiścillakṣaṇamakāri tadapi na samyak samādheyatāmadhitiṣṭhati /
tathā hi---rasaḥ saṃśrayo yasyāsau rasasaṃśrayaḥ, tasmāt kāraṇādayaṃ rasavadalaṅkāraḥ saṃpadyate /
tathāpi vaktavyameva---ko 'sau rasavyatiriktavṛttiḥ anyapadārthaḥ? kāvyameveti cet tadapi pūrvameva pratyuktam, tasyasvātmanikriyāvirodhādalaṅkāratvānupapatteḥ /
athavā rasasya saṃśrayo rasena saṃśriyate yastasmād /
rasasaṃśrayāditi /
tathāpi ko 'sāviti vyatiriktatvena vaktavyatāmevā (yāti) /
udāharaṇajātamapyasya lakṣaṇasya pūrveṇa samānayogakṣemaprāyamiti (na) pṛthak paryālocyate /
children.translated_text: This definition made by some also does not properly attain the status of being well-resolved. For: that which has rasa as its support is '<s>rasasaṃśraya</s>'; because of that, this becomes the <s>rasavat</s>-ornament. Even so, one must still say: what is that other entity whose function is distinct from rasa? If poetry itself—that too has already been refuted, since the status of being an ornament is not established due to the contradiction of action upon itself. Or [analyzing differently]: that which is supported by rasa, from which rasa provides support—'because of rasa-dependence.' Even so, the question 'what is it?' demands to be answered in terms of something distinct. The class of examples of this definition, being for the most part the same in outcome as the previous [definition], is not separately examined.
'<s>Rasapeśala</s> (charming through rasa).' (Vjiv 3.39)

children.text:
iti pāṭhe na kiñcidatrātiricyate /
atha (vastusvabhāvarasādi-) pratipādakavākyopārūḍhapadārthasārthasvarūpamalaṅkāryaṃ rasasvarūpānupraveśena vigalitasvaparispandānāṃ dravyāṇām iva kathamalaṅkaraṇaṃ bhavatītyetadapi cintyameva /
kiñca tathābhyupagame 'pi pradhānaguṇabhāvaviparyāsaḥ paryavasyatīti na kiñcidetat /
atraiva (dūṣaṇāntaramu) pakramate---śabdārthāsaṅgaterapi /
śabdārthāsaṅgaterapi /
śabdārthayorabhidhānābhidheyayorasamanvayācca rasavadalaṅkāropapattirnāsti /
atra ca raso vidyate (tiṣṭha) ti yasyeti matuppratyaye vihite tasyālaṅkāra iti ṣaṣṭhisamāsaḥ kriyate, rasavāṃścāsāvalaṅkāraśceti viśeṣaṇasamāso vā /
tatra pūrvasmin pakṣe---rasavyatiriktaṃ kimanyat padārthāntaraṃ vidyate yasyāsāvalaṅkāraḥ /

tadevamuktalakṣaṇe mārge rasavadalaṅkārasya śabdārthasaṅgatirna kācidasti /
yadi vā nidarśanāntaraviṣayatayā samāsadvitaye 'pi śabdārthasaṅgatiyojanā vidhīyate, yathā
children.translated_text: In this reading, nothing additional [is achieved]. Now, the expressed meaning ([consisting of] the nature of things, rasa, etc.)—the thing to be ornamented, whose nature is the aggregate of word-meanings mounted upon the presentational sentence—when the inherent vibrations of substances dissolve through the entry of the rasa-nature [into them], how can there be ornamentation? This too requires reflection. Moreover, even granting [that position], the result is a reversal of the principal and the subordinate—so this amounts to nothing. Here he commences another objection: 'even because of the incoherence of word and meaning.' Even because of the incoherence of word and meaning—because of the lack of syntactic coherence between the expressor and the expressed, the establishment of the <s>rasavat</s>-ornament is not possible. And here, when the possessive suffix '-vat' is applied—'rasa exists in which'—the genitive compound 'an ornament of that [which possesses rasa]' is formed; or the qualifying compound 'that which is rasavat and is an ornament.' In the first alternative: what other, rasa-distinct entity exists of which this is an ornament? If poetry itself—then too, what other entity distinct from it exists where the designation 'rasavat-ornament' finds scope? No entity beyond the particular is perceived that attains the determination 'that possesses rasa is an ornament.' Thus, on the path of the stated definition, there is no syntactic coherence of word and meaning for the <s>rasavat</s>-ornament. Or, if the syntactic coherence is arranged in both types of compound with respect to another domain of illustration—for example:

children.text: tanvī meghajalārdrapallavatayā dhautādharevāśrubhiḥ śūnyevābharaṇaiḥ svakālavirahād viśrāntapuṣpodgamā /
children.translated_text: Slender, with her lower lip washed by tears or by cloud-water-moistened foliage, as if empty of ornaments, with flower-buds resting from their efflorescence due to separation from their own season,

children.text: cintāmaunamivāsthitā madhukṛtāṃ śabdairvinā lakṣyate caṇḍī māmavadhūya pādapatitaṃ jātānutāpeva sā // VjivC_3.40 //
children.translated_text: she appears as if settled into the silence of brooding, without the sounds of bees—<s>Caṇḍī</s> [the creeper], as though feeling remorse, as though having spurned me who fell at her feet. (Vjiv 3.40)
Or for example:

children.text: taraṅgabhrūbhaṅgā (kṣubhita) vihagaśreṇiraśanā vikarṣantī phenaṃ vasanamiva saṃrambhaśithilam /
children.translated_text: With waves for frowning brows, with agitated bird-flocks for a girdle, dragging foam like a garment loosened in passion,

children.text: yathāviddhaṃ yāti skhalitamabhisaṃdhāya bahuśo nadībhāveneyaṃ dhruvamasahanā sā pariṇatā // VjivC_3.41 //
children.translated_text: she goes as though wounded, stumbling repeatedly, approaching purposefully—this river has surely transformed through the state of being an intolerant [beloved]. (Vjiv 3.41)

children.text:
atra rasavattvamalaṅkāraśca prakaṭaṃ pratibhāsete /
tasmānna kathañcidapi tadvivekasya duravadhānatā /
tena rasavato 'laṅkāra iti ṣaṣṭhīsamāsapakṣe śabdārthayorna kiñcidasaṅgatatvam, rasaparipoṣaparatvādalaṅkārasya tannibandhanameva rasavattvam /
rasavāṃścāsāvalaṅkāraśceti viśeṣaṇasamāsapakṣe 'pi na kiñcidasaṅgatvam /
tathā caitayorudāharaṇayorlatāyāḥ saritaścoddīpanavibhāvatvena vallabhābhāvitāntaḥ karaṇatayā nāyakasya tanmayatvena (niścetana?) meva padārthajātaṃ sakalamavalokayataḥ tatsāmyasamāropaṇaṃ taddharmādhyāropaṇaṃ cetyupamārūpakakāvyālaṅkārayojanaṃ vinā na kenacit prakāreṇa ghaṭate, tallakṣaṇavākyatvāt /
satyametat, kintu "alaṅkāra'-śabdābhidhānaṃ vinā viśeṣaṇasamā (sapa) kṣe kevalasya rasavāniti (asya) prayogaḥ prāpnoti /
rasavānalaṅkāra iti cet pratītirabhyupagamyate, tadapi yukti (yuktatāṃ nārhati), rūpakāderabhāvāt /
rasavato 'laṅkāra iti ṣaṣṭhīsamāsapakṣo 'pi na suspaṣṭasamanvayaḥ /
sarvasya kasyacit kāvyasya rasavattvameva /
yasmātsātiśayatvanibandhanaṃ tathāvidhaṃ tadvidāhlādakāri kāvyaṃ karaṇīyamiti tasyālaṅkāra ityāśrite sarveṣāmeva ca rūpakādīnāṃ rasavadalaṅkāratvameva nyāyopapannatāṃ pratipadyate /
alaṅkārasya ca yasyakasyacitsarvasya rasavattvād viśeṣaṇasamāsapakṣe 'pyeṣaiva vārttā /
kīñca tadabhyupagame 'pi pratyekamutskhalitalakṣaṇānāṃ prakṛtaparipoṣaparatayā labdhātmanāmalaṅkāraṇāṃ prātisvikalakṣaṇābhihitātiśayavyatiriktamanena na kiñcidādhikyamādhīyate /
tasmāttattalla(kṣaṇa) karaṇavaiyarthyamaprativāritaprasarameva parāpatati /
na caivaṃvidhaviṣaye rasavadalaṅkāravyavahārasyāvakāśaḥ, tajjñaistathānavagamāt, alaṅkārāntarāṇāṃ ca mukhyatayā vyavasthānāt /
athavā cetanapadārthagocaratayā rasavadalaṅkārasya, niścetanavastuviṣayatvena copamādīnāṃ viṣayavibhāgo vyavasthāpyate, tadapi na vidvajjanāvarjanaṃ vidadhāti /
yasmādacetanānāmapi rasoddīpanasāmarthyasamucitasatkavisamullikhitasaukumāryasarasātvādupamādīnāṃ praviralaviṣayatā nirviṣayatvaṃ vā syāditi śṛṅgarādirasanisyandasundarasya satkavipravāhasya ca nīrasatvaṃ prasajyata iti pratipāditameva pūrvasūribhiḥ /
yadi vā vaicitryāntaramanohāritayā rasavadalaṅkāraḥ pratipādyate, yathābhiyuktataraustairevābhyadhāyi---
children.translated_text: Here, the <s>rasa</s>-ful quality and the [presence of an] ornament are manifestly apparent. Therefore, the discernment of the two is in no way difficult. Thus, in the view that takes the compound '<s>rasavato 'laṅkāra</s>' as a genitive compound ('the ornament of the <s>rasa</s>-ful'), there is no inconsistency of word and meaning, since the ornament, being devoted to the nourishment of <s>rasa</s>, has its <s>rasa</s>-ful quality grounded precisely in that [relation]. In the view that takes it as a qualificative compound — 'it is both <s>rasa</s>-ful and an ornament' — there is likewise no inconsistency. And thus, in both these examples, the creeper and the river, functioning as stimulating determinants (<s>uddīpanavibhāva</s>), with the inner faculty of the hero being imbued by [the thought of] the beloved, with his identification [with those objects] — observing the entire class of referents, even the inanimate, as identical with [the beloved] — the superimposition of similarity to her and the superimposition of her properties — all this cannot be accomplished in any way without the employment of the poetic figures <s>upamā</s> (simile) and <s>rūpaka</s> (metaphor), since these are sentences whose very nature constitutes those [figures]. This is true; however, without the expression of the word 'ornament,' in the qualificative compound view, only the usage '<s>rasavān</s>' (the <s>rasa</s>-ful) would result. If the understanding '<s>rasavān alaṅkāra</s>' (a <s>rasa</s>-ful ornament) is accepted, that too does not attain logical validity, due to the absence of <s>rūpaka</s> and the like [as separate entities]. The genitive compound view '<s>rasavato 'laṅkāra</s>' (the ornament of the <s>rasa</s>-ful) also does not have a perfectly clear syntactic connection. For every piece of poetry whatsoever is <s>rasa</s>-ful. Since poetry is to be composed such that it delights the connoisseurs, being grounded in superlative quality — when one resorts to calling that its 'ornament,' it logically follows that all figures such as <s>rūpaka</s> and the rest are precisely <s>rasavad alaṅkāras</s>. And since every ornament whatsoever is <s>rasa</s>-ful, the same observation applies in the qualificative compound view. Moreover, even granting this, for ornaments whose individual definitions have been separately formulated and which have attained their identity through devotion to the nourishment of the subject at hand — this [designation] does not add any surplus beyond the superlative quality stated in their respective individual definitions. Therefore, the futility of formulating those respective definitions descends with unobstructed force. Nor is there scope for the usage '<s>rasavad alaṅkāra</s>' in a subject of this kind, since the experts do not understand it thus, and since the other ornaments are established as primary. Alternatively, if a division of domain is established such that the <s>rasavad alaṅkāra</s> pertains to sentient referents while <s>upamā</s> and so forth pertain to non-sentient subjects, even that does not produce conviction in the learned. For since even non-sentient objects — when sketched by excellent poets with a delicacy appropriate to their capacity for stimulating <s>rasa</s> — possess flowing charm, [the domain of] <s>upamā</s> and the like would become extremely narrow or entirely void of subject matter, and it would follow that the stream of excellent poetry, beautiful with the flowing of <s>śṛṅgāra</s> and other <s>rasas</s>, would become tasteless — as has been demonstrated by earlier authorities. Alternatively, if the <s>rasavad alaṅkāra</s> is presented through the charm of some other kind of variety, then, as the most competent among them have themselves stated:
'Where the sentence-meaning is some other primary [content], and <s>rasa</s> and the like are subordinate elements,

children.text: kāvye tasminnalaṅkāro rasādiriti me matiḥ // VjivC_3.42 //
children.translated_text: in such poetry, <s>rasa</s> and the like constitute the ornament — this is my view.' // VjivC_3.42 //

iti /
yatrānyo vākyārthaḥ prādhānyādalaṅkāryatayā vyavasthitastasmin tadaṅgatayā vinabadhyamānaḥ śṛṅgārādiralaṅkāratāṃ pratipadyate /

children.translated_text: Thus: where another sentence-meaning is established as the primary, as the ornamentable, and the <s>śṛṅgāra</s> and other [<s>rasas</s>], being bound subordinately to that, attain the status of ornament — since the quality, [being subordinate,] adorns the primary through the prior manifestation of the emotional state — therefore the discernment of the ornamentation is manifest. For example:

children.text: kṣipto hastāvalagnaḥ prasabhamabhihato 'pyādadānoṃ'śukāntaṃ gṛhṇan keśeṣvapāstaścaraṇanipatito nekṣitaḥ saṃbhrameṇa /
children.translated_text: [<s>Śiva</s>,] who, though pushed away while clinging to [her] hand, though struck forcefully while seizing the edge of [her] garment, though grasping [her] hair while being thrown aside, though falling at [her] feet while not being looked upon —

children.text: āliṅgan yo 'vadhūtastripurayuvatibhiḥ sāstranetrotpalābhiḥ kāmīvārdrāparādhaḥ sa dahatu duritaṃ śāmbhavo vaḥ śarāgniḥ // VjivC_3.43 //

children.text:
atra sāstranetrotpalādiśabdagmyavaiklavyasya śāmbhavaśarāgnidahyamānāsurasundarīṇāṃ, tripuraripuprabhāvaprakhyāpanaparasya prayojakatvena karuṇo rasaḥ aṅga, na punarīrṣyāvipralambhaśṛṅgāraḥ, tasyānanubhūyamānatvāt /
tadayamatra paramārthaḥ---kavipratibhāparipoṣitaprakarṣagamyamāna-karuṇarasopabṛṃhita-saundaryadhārādhirūḍho bhagavatprabhāvātiśayaḥ kāmapi sahṛdayahṛdayahāritāṃ pratipadyate /
na ca śabdavācyatvaṃ nāma samānaṃ kāmiśarāgnitejasoḥ saṃbhavatīti tāvataiva tayostathāvidhaviruddhadharmādhyāsādivaruddhasvabhāvacoraikyaṃ kathañcidapi vyavasthāpayituṃ pāryate, parameśvaraprayatnenāpi svabāvasyānyathākartumaśakyatvāt /
na ca tathāvidhaśabdāvācyatāmātrādevaṃ tadvidāṃ tadanubhavapratītirastiḥ guḍakhaṇḍādiśabdābhidhānādapi prītiviṣādādestadāsvādaprasaṅgāt /
tadanubhavapratītau satyāṃ rasadvayasamāveśadoṣo 'pyanivāryatāmācarati /
rasadvayasamāveśādoṣo 'pyatra guṇapradhānabhāvasya pra(yojaka iti vaktuṃ na pāryate) /
yadi vā bhagavatprabhāvasya mukhyatve dvayorapyetayoraṅgatvād bhūṣaṇatvamityucyate tadapi (na) samañjasam /
yasmāt karuṇasya vāstavatvādeka eva syāt nirmūlatvādeva tayorbhāvābhāvayoriva na kathañcidapi sāmyopapattirityalamanucitacarvaṇacāturyacāpalena /
yadi vā nidarśane 'sminnanāśvasantaḥ samāmnātalakṣaṇodāharaṇasaṅgatiṃ samyak samīhamānāḥ savimarṣaṇā udāharaṇāntaraṃ rasavadalaṅkārasya vyācakṣate, yathā
children.translated_text: Here, the distress apprehended through words like 'tear-filled lotus-eyes' and so forth — of the <s>asura</s> women being burned by the fire of <s>Śiva's</s> arrow — the compassionate <s>rasa</s> (<s>karuṇa</s>), as the instrumentality of proclaiming the power of the enemy of the three cities, is subordinate, not the <s>śṛṅgāra</s> (erotic sentiment) of jealous love-in-separation, since that is not actually experienced. The ultimate truth here is this: the superabundance of the <s>Bhagavān's</s> power, elevated upon a stream of beauty nourished by the <s>karuṇa rasa</s> whose intensity is apprehended through the cultivation by the poet's creative intuition, attains a certain captivation of the hearts of the connoisseurs. Nor can it be established that, merely because the words 'fire' and 'arrows of the god of love' share the property of being verbally expressible, an identity of contradictory natures — as if between locked enemies — can in any way be established between them, since even by the effort of the Supreme Lord, nature cannot be made otherwise. Nor does such a cognition of the experience of those [<s>rasas</s>] arise in the connoisseurs merely from verbal inexpressibility of that kind, since otherwise the relish of pleasure, sorrow, and the like would follow even from the utterance of words like 'candy' and 'sugar-lump.' If such experiential cognition exists, the fault of the conflation of two <s>rasas</s> also becomes unavoidable. [Nor can it be said that] the fault of conflation of two <s>rasas</s> is here overcome by the relation of subordinate and primary. Alternatively, if, with the <s>Bhagavān's</s> power being primary, the ornament-status of both these [<s>rasas</s>] is asserted due to their being subordinate, even that is not sound. For since the <s>karuṇa</s> is real, it alone would [qualify], and since the other two are rootless, no similarity between them — as between existence and non-existence — can in any way be established. Enough of this clumsy dexterity in inappropriate relishing! Alternatively, those who, not finding confidence in this example, properly seeking a coherent connection between the traditional definition and the example, judiciously explain another example for the <s>rasavad alaṅkāra</s>, as follows:

children.text: kiṃ hāsyena na me prayāsyasi punaḥ prāptaścirāddarśanaṃ keyaṃ niṣkaruṇa pravāsarucitā kenāsi dūrīkṛtaḥ /
children.translated_text: 'Will you not set forth with a laugh at me? I, who have long obtained your sight — what is this, O merciless one, this fondness for exile? By whom have you been driven away?

children.text: svapnānteṣviti te vadan priyatamavyāsaktakaṇṭhagraho buddhvā roditi riktabāhuvalayastāraṃ ripustrījanaḥ // VjivC_3.44 //
children.translated_text: Saying thus to you in dreams, with an embrace clasping the beloved's neck — then awakening, [the man], with empty arm-bracelets, weeps loudly' — so the women of the slain enemies [lament]. // VjivC_3.44 //

children.text:
"atra bhavadvinihatavallabho vairivilāsinīsamūhaḥ śokāveśāda(śara)ṇaḥ karuṇarasakāṣṭhādhirūḍhivihitamevaṃ vidhavaiśasamanubhavatī"ti tātparye sa eva prādhānyena vākyārthaḥ, tadaṅgatayā vinibadhyamānaḥ karuṇaḥ /
pravāsavipralambhaśṛṅgāraparatvamatra na paramārthaḥ /
parasparānvitapadārthasārthasamarpyamāṇavṛttirguṇabhāvenāvabhāsanādalaṃṅkaraṇamityucyate /
tasya ca nirviṣayatvābhāvād rasālambanavibhāvādisvakāraṇasāmagrīvirahavihitā lakṣaṇānupapattirna saṃbhavati /
rasadvayasamāveśaduṣṭatvamapi dūramapāstameva /
dvayorapi vāstavasvarūpasya vidyamānatvāttadanubhavapratītau satyāṃ nātmavirodhaḥ spardhitvābhāvāt /
tena tadapi tadvidāhlādavidhānasāmarthyasundaram, karuṇarasasya niścāyakapramāṇābhāvāt /
pravāsavipralambhasya svakāraṇabhūtavākyopārūḍhālambanavibhāvādisamarpyamāṇatvaṃ svapnāntasamaye, prabodhāvasare ca tathāvidhatvaṃ yuktyā saṃbhavatastasya karuṇasyetyubhayamupapannamiti prathamatarameva kathamasau samudbhavatīti caitadapi na samañjasaprāyam /
yasmāccāṭuviṣayamahāpuruṣapratāpākrānticakitacetasāmitastataḥ svavairiṇāṃ tatpreyasīnāṃ ca palāyanairapi pṛthagavasthānaṃ na yuktiprayuktatāmativartate /
karuṇarasasya satyapi niścaye, tasyaiva tathāvidhaparipoṣadaśādhārādhirūḍherekāgratāstimitamānasasya tathābhyastavyasanādhivāsitacetasā sucirātsamāsāditasvapnasamāgamaḥ pūrvānubhūtavṛttāntusamucitasamārabdhakāntasaṃlāpaḥ kathamapi saṃprabuddhaḥ prabodhasamanantarasamullasitapūrvāparānusaṃdhānavihitaprastutavastuvisaṃvādavidāritāntaḥ karaṇo bhavadvairivilāsinīsārtho roditīti karuṇasyaiva paripoṣapadavīsamadhirohaḥ tathāvidhavyabhicāryaucityacārutvaṃ tatsvarūpānupraveśoveti kutaḥ pravāsavipralambhasya pṛthagvyāpāre rasagandho 'pi ? yadi vā preyasaḥ prādhānye tadaṅgatvāt karuṇarasasyālaṅkaraṇatvamityabhidhīyate tadapi na niravadyam /
yasmād dvayorapyetayorudāharaṇayormukhyabhūto vākyārthaḥ karuṇātmanaiva vivartamānavṛttirupanibaddhaḥ /
paryāyoktānyāpadeśanyāyena vācyatāvyatiriktayoḥ pratīyamānatayā, na karuṇasya rasatvād vyaṅgyasya sato vācyatvamupapannam /
nāpi guṇībhūtavyaṅgyasya viṣayaḥ, vya(ṅgyasya prādhānyena ka)ruṇātmanaiva pratibhāsanāt /
na ca dvayorapi vyaṅgyatvam, aṅgāṅgibhāvasyānupapatteḥ /
etacca yathāsaṃbhavamasmābhirvikalpitam, na punasta(nnyāyamatra prayojakamityalaṃ vi) stareṇa /
kiñca "kāvye tasminnalaṅkāro rasādiḥ' iti rasa evālaṅkāraḥ kevalaḥ na tu rasavaditi matutpratyayasya jīvitam na kiñcidabhihitaṃ syāt /
evaṃ sadi śabdārthasaṅgaterabhāvādanavasthaiva tiṣṭhatītyetadapi na kiñcit /
evamalaṅkāratāṃ rasavataḥ pratyākhyāya varṇyamānārthaśarīratvāt tadekayogakṣemasya preyasaḥ saṃprati (tāṃ) vā (rayati):---na "preyastadviruddhaḥ syādapreyaḥ' iti---
children.translated_text: Here, with the purport being: 'the assemblage of enemy women whose beloved has been slain by you experiences such grief, their helplessness born of the overwhelming surge of sorrow having ascended the pinnacle of <s>karuṇa rasa</s>' — that alone is the primary sentence-meaning, and the <s>karuṇa</s>, being subordinately bound to that, [functions as ornament]. The intention of love-in-separation through exile is not the ultimate meaning here. The operation conveyed through the cluster of mutually connected referents, manifesting in the subordinate mode, is called ornamentation. And since its subject matter is not void — since there is no absence of its own causal complex of the <s>rasa's</s> substrate-determinants (<s>ālambana-vibhāva</s>) and so forth — the inapplicability of the definition does not arise. The fault of conflation of two <s>rasas</s> has also been thoroughly removed. Since the real nature of both exists, and since, given the existence of experiential cognition of them, there is no self-contradiction due to the absence of rivalry. Therefore, that too is beautiful with the capacity to produce delight in the connoisseurs, because there is no certain proof [for the primacy] of the <s>karuṇa rasa</s> alone. Since the love-in-separation through exile has its own substrate-determinants (<s>ālambana-vibhāva</s>) and so forth supplied through the sentence that is its own cause — at the time of the dream — and since at the moment of awakening such a character is logically possible for the <s>karuṇa</s> [as well] — both are established. [How?] Since for one whose intent gaze-absorbed mind has been perfumed by the disposition of long-practiced addiction [to the beloved], the dream-union attained after a long time, the loving conversation begun in a manner appropriate to the previously experienced events, the somehow-awakened [person] whose inner faculty is rent by the contradiction with the present reality realized through the connection of before and after illuminated immediately upon awakening — 'the assemblage of your enemy's women weeps' — this is the very ascent to the level of nourishment of the <s>karuṇa</s> [<s>rasa</s>], the charm of the propriety of the transitory emotions (<s>vyabhicārin</s>), the penetration into its essential nature. So whence even a trace of <s>rasa</s> for the love-in-separation through exile as a separate operation? Alternatively, if, with the <s>preyas</s> (the dear one) being primary, the <s>karuṇa rasa</s> is said to be an ornament due to its being subordinate, even that is not faultless. For in both these examples, the primary sentence-meaning is composed with its operation evolving as <s>karuṇa</s> in nature. By the principle of <s>paryāyokta</s> (circumlocution) and <s>anyāpadeśa</s> (allegory), through being suggested rather than directly expressed, the <s>karuṇa</s>, being a <s>rasa</s>, cannot properly have the status of the directly expressed when it is suggested. Nor is this a case of subordinated suggestion (<s>guṇībhūta-vyaṅgya</s>), since the <s>karuṇa</s> manifests as predominant in the form of the suggested. Nor is the suggested nature of both [possible], since the subordinate-primary relationship would be impossible. All this has been hypothesized by us as far as possible — but that reasoning is not the governing [principle] here, so enough of elaboration. Moreover, when it is said 'in such poetry, <s>rasa</s> and the like constitute the ornament' — <s>rasa</s> alone is the ornament, bare, not '<s>rasavat</s>' (the <s>rasa</s>-ful) — so the life of the possessive suffix <s>-matup</s> would have no [raison d'être] stated. If so, the absence of syntactic coherence of word and meaning would merely persist — and even this counts for nothing. Having thus rejected the ornament-status of the <s>rasavat</s>, he now wards off [the ornament-status] of <s>preyas</s> (the endearing), which shares the same fortune through being the body of the described meaning:
'The <s>preyas</s> (endearing) is not its opposite, the <s>apreyas</s> (unendearing), which would be an ornament;
they would belong among other ornaments, since they are not observed [as separate ornaments] elsewhere.' // Vjiv_3.12 //

children.text:
yaścirantanairalaṅkāraḥ samāmnātaḥ tasya na tadbhavāḥ saṃbhavati /
yasmāt kaiścit"preyaḥ priyatarākhyāna"miti lakṣaṇaṃ preyasaḥ samākhyātam /
kaiścittasyodāharaṇamātrameva lakṣaṇaṃ manyamānaistu(tā) vadeva pradarśitam /
yathā
children.translated_text: What has been traditionally transmitted by the ancients as an ornament — its being that [i.e. a separate ornament] is not possible. For some have declared the definition of <s>preyas</s> as 'a more endearing narration.' Others, considering merely the example itself as the definition, have shown just that much. For example:
<s>Vidura</s> said to <s>Kṛṣṇa</s> when he arrived at the house:
'In time, this joy would arise even from your coming alone.' // VjivC_3.45 //
Thus.
And this very example is accepted by the earlier [authorities].
And thus they have said:

children.text: adya yā mama govinda jātā tvayi gṛhāgate // VjivC_3.46 //
children.translated_text: 'Today, O <s>Govinda</s>, that [joy] which has arisen in me upon your arriving at the house...' // VjivC_3.46 //

children.text:
iti /
tadeva na kṣodakṣamatāmarhati /
tathā ca kālene (tyādino)cyate (yat) tadeva varṇyamānaviṣayatayā vastunaḥ svarūpaṃ, tadevālaṅkaraṇamityalaṅkāryaṃ na kiñcidavaśiṣyate /
tasyaivobhayamalaṅkāryatvamalaṅkaraṇatvaṃ cetyayuktiyuktam /
ekakriyāviṣayaṃ yugapadekasyaiva vastunaḥ karmakaraṇatvaṃ nopapadyate /
yadi dṛśyante tathāvidhāni vākyāni yeṣāmubhayamapi saṃbhavati---
children.translated_text: Thus. But even that does not deserve to withstand scrutiny. For when it is said 'in time' and so forth, that itself, as the subject being described, is the essential nature of the thing — and that very same [thing] is the ornamentation — so nothing is left over as the ornamentable. For the same thing to be both the ornamentable and the ornamentation is illogical. It is impossible for one and the same thing to be simultaneously the object and the instrument of a single action. If there are such sentences in which both are possible —
You know the Self by the Self, you create the Self by the Self,

children.text: ātmanā kṛtinā ca tvamātmanyeva pralīyase // VjivC_3.47 //
children.translated_text: and you, the accomplished one, by the Self dissolve into the Self alone. // VjivC_3.47 //

children.text:
ityabhidhīyate, tadapi niḥsamanvayaprāyameva /
yasmādatra vāstave 'pyabhede kālpanikamupacārasattānibandhanaṃ vibhāgamāśritya tadvyavahāraḥ pravartate /
kiṃ ca viśvamayatvāt parameśvarasya parameśvaramayatvādvā viśvasya, pāramārthike 'pyabhede māhātmyapratipādanārthaṃ prātisvikaparispandavicitrāṃ jagatprapañcaracanāṃ prati sakalapramātṛtāmasya saṃvedyamāno bhedāvabodhaḥ sphuṭāvakāśatāṃ na kadācidapyatikrāmati /
tasmādatra parameśvarasyaiva rūpasya kasyacittadāpyamānatvāt vedanādeḥ kriyāyāḥ karmatvaṃ kasyacitsādhakatamatvāt karaṇatvamiti na kiñcidasaṃgatam /
udāharaṇepunarapoddhārabuddhiparikalpanayāpi na kathañcidapi vibhāgo vibhāvyate /
tasmāt "svarūpādatiriktasya parasyāpratibhāsanāt" iti dūṣaṇatrāpi saṃbandhanīyam /
avibhāgapakṣe ca tadevālaṅkāryaṃ tadevālaṅkaraṇamiti preyaso rasavataśca svātmani kriyāvirodhāt "ātmaiva nātmanaḥ skandhaṃ kvacidapyadhirohati" iti sthitameva /
atha dūṣaṇāntaraṃ dadāti tadviruddhaḥ syāditi /
(anena nyāyena varṇyamānatvāttadviruddhasya preyasaḥ pratipakṣo 'pi apreyaḥ prasādādhikṛtaḥ ;tasmādalaṅkāro bhavet) /
tathāpi ko doṣaḥ syāditi cettadapi na samyak, taireva tathānabhyupagamāt /
anyacca laiṅkikamalaṅkāryālaṅkaraṇavyavahāraṃ paryālocya tathāvidhatvasāmānyamātraṃ samāśritya pūrvasūrayaḥ kāvye pravartitatadvyavahārāḥ saṃvṛttāḥ /
loke tribhuvanāntaravartipadārthajātamanantaṃ siddhavidyādharādyalaṅkāryam, alaṅkaraṇāni kaṭakakeyūrādīni katicideva, tadevameva kāvye varṇanāviṣayasya vastunaḥ śarīramaparyavasitamalaṅkāryam, tathaivālaṅkaraṇānyupamādīni katicideva /
varṇanīyasya prayeḥ prabhṛteralaṅkāratve varṇyamānādanyālaṅkaraṇānāmānantyaprasaṅgaḥ /
tataḥ parisamāptyabhāve saṃbhāvanāvadabhidhādīnāmanārambhaḥ /
tasmāllaukikavyavahārānyūnānatiriktamevālaṅkāryālaṅkāravyavahāraḥ kāvyaviṣaye 'pi vācyatāmarhati /
atraiva dūṣaṇāntaramupanyasyati---"alaṅkārāntare" iti /
saṃsṛṣṭisaṃkarau syātām /
prathamaḥ (maṃ) priyatarākhyānamātrasādhanasya varṇyamānatvādalaṅkāryasyāpyalaṅkaraṇatve sati, alaṅkārāntaraṃ rūpakādi yadā vidhīyate tadā tasmin vidhīyamāne preyasaḥ saṃsargasaṃkīrṇatānibandhane saṃsṛṣṭisaṅkarāvalaṅkāraviśeṣau syātām bhavetām /
preyobhaṇitayukteṣu vākyeṣu tajjñairna saṃsṛṣṭisakaravyavahāraḥ kadācidapi pravartitapūrvaḥ tathā pratibhāsābhāvāt /
yathā
children.translated_text: — it is said. But even that is almost devoid of coherent syntactic connection. Because here, even though in reality there is non-difference, the conventional usage operates by resorting to a division founded on figurative existence. Moreover, since the Supreme Lord (<s>Parameśvara</s>) is constituted of the universe, or since the universe is constituted of the Supreme Lord — even though in the ultimate sense there is non-difference — for the purpose of establishing his greatness, the cognition of difference, which is experienced with respect to his being the total cognizer in relation to the creation of the world-variety that is varied with the activity of each individual [being], never transcends the state of having clear scope. Therefore, herein, since some form of the Supreme Lord himself is that which is bestowed — feeling and the like [serve as] the object of action; since some [form] is the most effective instrument — [it serves as] the instrument. There is nothing incoherent in this. Furthermore, even through the fabrication of abstractive cognition, no division whatsoever can be discerned in the example. Therefore, the refutation 'because of the non-appearance of anything other than its own form' should be connected here as well. And in the position of non-difference, the very thing that is to be ornamented is the very thing that is ornamentation — hence, for both <s>preyas</s> (the endearing) and <s>rasavat</s> (the sentiment-laden), since there is a contradiction of action within oneself, the [principle] 'the self never climbs upon its own shoulder' stands firm. Now [the opponent] raises another refutation: 'it would be contradictory.' (By this reasoning, since the opposite of <s>preyas</s> — being described [as such] — would be <s>apreyas</s> [the non-endearing], and that falls under <s>prasāda</s>; therefore it would be an ornament.) Even so, what fault would there be? — even that is not sound, because they themselves have not accepted it in that way. Furthermore, having considered the worldly usage of 'thing-to-be-ornamented' and 'ornamentation,' the earlier masters, resorting merely to the similarity of that type, initiated that usage in poetry. In the world, the class of objects existing within the three worlds is infinite — the things to be ornamented: <s>siddhas</s>, <s>vidyādharas</s>, and so forth; the ornamentations — bangles, armlets, and the like — are only a few. Just so in poetry, the body of the subject matter to be described is unlimited — it is the thing to be ornamented; and likewise the ornamentations — simile and the like — are only a few. If the [entity] being described, such as <s>preyas</s>, were to be an ornament, then the absurd consequence follows that ornamentations other than what is being described would be infinite. And then, since there would be no completion, there would be no commencement of describing or defining them — just as with mere possibilities. Therefore, the usage of 'thing-to-be-ornamented' and 'ornamentation' in the domain of poetry too should be stated as neither less nor more than the worldly usage. At this very point he raises another refutation — 'in [the presence of] another ornament.' <s>Saṃsṛṣṭi</s> (combination) and <s>saṃkara</s> (confusion of figures) would result. The first [objection]: since <s>preyas</s> is being described as merely producing the effect of an endearing name, and since the thing being described — being to-be-ornamented — would also be an ornamentation, when another ornament such as <s>rūpaka</s> (metaphor) and the like is applied, then in that application, <s>saṃsṛṣṭi</s> and <s>saṃkara</s> — the specific ornamental varieties that depend on the intermixture of <s>preyas</s> — would result. But in sentences imbued with the expression of <s>preyas</s>, the experts have never instituted the usage of <s>saṃsṛṣṭi</s> or <s>saṃkara</s>, since there is no such appearance. For example —

children.text: indorlakṣma smaravijayinaḥ kāṇṭhamūlaṃ murāriḥ diṅnāgānāṃ madajalamaṣībhāñji gaṇḍasthalāni /
children.translated_text: 'The mark of the Moon, the root-necklace of the Conqueror of <s>Smara</s> [<s>Śiva</s>], <s>Murāri</s> [<s>Viṣṇu</s>'s] ink-paste and collyrium on the cheek-surfaces of the direction-elephants —

children.text: adyāpyurvovalayatilaka śyāmalimnānu(vi) liptā0 nyābhāsante vada dhavalitaṃ kiṃ yaśobhistvadīyaiḥ // VjivC_3.48 //
children.translated_text: even today, O tilaka-mark on the circle of the earth, anointed with dark pigment — tell me, is anything whitened by your glories?' // VjivC_3.48 //

children.text:
atra preyobhihitaralaṅkāryā, vyājastutiralaṅkaraṇam; na punarubhayoralaṅkārapratibhāso yena saṃsṛṣṭivyapadeśaḥ saṃkaravyapadeśo vā pravartate tṛtīyasyālaṅkāryatayā vastvantarasyāpratibhāsanāt /
etadeva prakārāntareṇa pratyākhyātumupakramate "anyatrādarśanādapi"(iti) /
"anyatra" anyasmin viṣaye preyobhaṇitivivikte varṇanīyāntare preyaso vibhūṣaṇatvāt(tve) upamāderivopanibandhaḥ prāpnoti /
na ca kvacidapi tathā dṛśyate, tasmādanyatrādarśanādapi na ca yuktiyuktamalaṅkāraṇatvaṃ, rasavato 'pi tadekayogakṣematvāt evameva vibhūṣaṇatvamanupapannam /
evaṃmalaṅkaraṇatāṃ preyasaḥ pratyādiśya varṇanīyaśarīra tvāttadekarūpāṇāmanyeṣāṃ pratyādiśati---
children.translated_text: Here, the expression of <s>preyas</s> is the thing to be ornamented; ironic praise (<s>vyājastuti</s>) is the ornamentation; but there is no appearance of both as ornaments such that the designation of <s>saṃsṛṣṭi</s> or the designation of <s>saṃkara</s> would apply — because no third entity as a thing-to-be-ornamented appears. He begins to reject this by another method — 'because it is not seen elsewhere either.' 'Elsewhere' — in another domain, in a different object of description separate from the expression of <s>preyas</s> — since <s>preyas</s> [would be] an ornament, its application would be expected as with simile and the like. But nowhere is such a thing seen; therefore, because it is not seen elsewhere either, its ornamentation-status is not logically sound. And since even <s>rasavat</s> is of the same fortune as it, its being an ornament is likewise unjustified. Having thus rejected the ornament-status of <s>preyas</s>, he rejects the ornament-status of the others too, which share the same nature as the body of what is being described —
Likewise, the ornament-status of <s>ūrjasvi</s> (the vigorous) and <s>udātta</s> (the exalted) does not exist;
and likewise of <s>samāhita</s> (the composed), which shines in two varieties. // Vjiv_3.13 //

children.text:
ūrjasvyudāttābhidhānayoḥ paurvāparyapraṇītayoraṃlakaraṇayoḥ "bhūṣaṇatvaṃ"-alaṅkaraṇatvaṃ "na vidyate"---na saṃbhavati /
kathaṃ "tadvat" /
tadvadityanantaroktarasavadādiparāmarśaḥ, tena tadvat tayoriva prathamapratiṣiddhavibhūṣaṇabhāva-rasādivadetayorvibhūṣaṇatvaṃ nāstītyarthaḥ /
(yadyapi) cirantanairlakṣaṇodāharaṇadarśanapūrvakametayoralaṅkaraṇatvamākhyātaṃ, tathāpyayuktiyuktatvāt (tat) nopapadyate---tathā ca kaiścit prathamasya lakṣaṇamudāharaṇaṃ ca darśitaṃ yathā
children.translated_text: The ornament-status — the status of being ornaments — of those called <s>ūrjasvi</s> and <s>udātta</s>, composed in the order [of the tradition], 'does not exist' — is not possible. How? — 'likewise' — like the <s>rasavat</s> and the others that were just refuted; by this word 'likewise,' the reference is to those. Therefore, just as those — whose ornament-status was first refuted — like <s>rasavat</s> and the rest, so too for these two, the ornament-status does not exist. Although by the ancients, their ornament-status was declared with the presentation of definitions and examples, nevertheless, being devoid of logical justification, it is not sustained. And thus, some have shown the definition and example of the first as follows —
'For <s>bhāvas</s> (emotions) and <s>rasas</s> that arise from causes such as desire and anger,

children.text: bhāvānāṃ ca rasānāṃ ca bandha ūrjasvi kathyate // VjivC_3.49 //
children.translated_text: proceeding in a manner lacking propriety — the composition [that presents them] is called <s>ūrjasvi</s> (the vigorous).' // VjivC_3.49 //

children.text: tathā kāmo 'sya vavṛdhe yathā himagireḥ sutām /
children.translated_text: 'His desire grew to such an extent that — to seize the daughter of the Himalaya —
he set forth by force, casting aside the righteous path.' // VjivC_3.50 //
Thus.

children.text:
kaiścidudāharaṇameva vaktavyatvāllakṣaṇaṃ manyamānaistadeva pradarśitam /
yathā vā
children.translated_text: Others, considering the example itself to be the definition — since [the term] needs to be expressed — have shown that very thing. Or for example —
'[It is] vigorous, [the passage where] <s>Karṇa</s>, having returned to [fight] <s>Pārtha</s> (<s>Arjuna</s>),

children.text: dviḥ sandadhāti kiṃ karṇaḥ śalyetyahirapākṛtaḥ // VjivC_3.51 //
children.translated_text: fits [his arrow] a second time — "Does <s>Karṇa</s> [really need to string his bow twice]? <s>Śalya</s>!" — thus the serpent was pushed aside.' // VjivC_3.51 //
Or for example —
'I am the one who will cut you down — let there be no fear in your heart!

children.text: vimukheṣu na me khaṅgaḥ prahartuṃ jātu vāñchati // VjivC_3.52 //
children.translated_text: My sword never desires to strike those who have turned their backs.' // VjivC_3.52 //
Thus.

children.text:
tatra prathamayorlakṣaṇodāharaṇayostāvadetat paryālocanīyam kiṃ tadanaucityaṃ nām, yena (tathā) pravṛttānāṃ rasādīnāmupanibandhanamalaṅkāraḥ saṃpadyate /
yasmādaucityapratiyoginā tena pratīyamānānāṃ teṣāṃ (na kevalaṃ) paripoṣaparihāṇiḥ, pratyuta saukumāryavirahaḥ sāvakāśatāṃ pratipadyate /
tadidamuktam---
children.translated_text: Therein, concerning the first definition and example — this is to be considered: what exactly is that impropriety, by virtue of the arising from which the representation of <s>rasas</s> and the like becomes an ornament? Since, when they are perceived as [arising from] the counterpart of propriety, the result for them is not merely the diminution of nourishment, but rather, the absence of delicacy comes to have scope. This is what was stated —
'There is no other cause for the destruction of <s>rasa</s> than impropriety.' // VjivC_3.53 //
Thus.

children.text:
yadi vā na pāramārthikamanaucityamatra vivakṣitamapi tu vibhāvānubhāvavyabhicāryau cityābhivyaṅgyaprastāvāntarāviṣayaniravadyarasāpekṣayā kimapi prastutānuguṇameva, tathā ca "kāmakrodhādikāraṇāt" iti yuktirupanyastetyucyate, tadapi na su sthitasamādhi /
yasmādaucityaparipoṣapuṣkalarasāpekṣayā kiñcidanaucityayuktarasabhāvopanibandhanaṃ parimitasattvaprāyaprāṇimātraviṣaye kāmādikāraṇāt karaṇīyatāmarhati na punarudāhṛte viṣaye /
(puṣka) lavibhāvādisamudayasamullāsitaḥ sahajakaviśaktikauśalasamudbhāsitasaukumāryasamarpitasvābhāvikarāmaṇīyakaḥ sarasamatimataḥ candrakāntakaumudīprakāśavadāścaryavilāsāpasāryamāṇopapatteḥ samucito 'pi rasaḥ paramasaundaryamāvahati /
tat kathamanaucityaparimlānaḥ kāmādikāraṇakalpanopasaṃhatavṛttiralaṅkāratāva bhāsatāṃ prayāsyati ? tathā ca tathāvidhe viṣaye varṇanīyāntarasamānatayā rasavattāṃ parikalpayantaḥ satkavayo nitāntaṃ (vi) rājante /
yathā
children.translated_text: Or if the impropriety intended here is not real but rather — some [appearance of impropriety] that is in fact appropriate to the context, as compared to the faultless <s>rasa</s> whose domain is the occasion other than one expressed through <s>vibhāva</s>, <s>anubhāva</s>, and <s>vyabhicārin</s> — and the reasoning is presented as 'from the cause of desire, anger, and the like' — even that is not well-established in its meditation. Because the representation of <s>rasa</s> endowed with some degree of impropriety — in contrast to <s>rasa</s> fully nourished by propriety — is appropriate only in the domain of beings of limited capacity, due to the cause of desire and the like, not in the illustrated domain. When [<s>rasa</s>] is illuminated by a full assemblage of <s>vibhāvas</s> and the like, made to shine with the delicacy imparted by the skill of the poet's natural creative power, endowed with the natural loveliness of propriety, savored by the most refined intellect — its appropriateness, like the radiance of moonstone gleaming under moonlight, is established through the marvelous display that opens before us — even then, <s>rasa</s> brings about the supreme beauty. Then how could [<s>ūrjasvi</s>], faded by impropriety, its operation constrained by the fabrication of desire and the like as its cause, ever aspire to the status of an ornament? And thus, good poets who imagine the <s>rasavat</s> quality of another subject for description in such a domain supremely shine. For example —
'Even <s>Paśupati</s> (<s>Śiva</s>) passed those difficult days, eager for union with the mountain's daughter;

children.text: kamaparavaśaṃ na viprakuryuḥ vibhumapi taṃ yadamī spṛśanti bhāvāḥ // VjivC_3.54 //
children.translated_text: whom would those feelings not render subject to another's will — those that touch even that all-pervading one?' // VjivC_3.54 //

children.text:
tadetadavasarāpatitamasmābhiḥ paryālocitam /
nanu bhatanayanipuṇamānasānāṃ paramārthavidāṃ tatrabhavatāṃ (asminviṣaye) vayaṃ vivadāmahe, yo 'yamatrodāhṛtaḥ sa bhagavān rasābhāsaviṣayatayā varṇanīyatāmarhati na veti ? kimaucityānaucityaparikalpanena /
sarvathā yathā tatrabhavadbhyaḥ pratibhāsate tattathaivāstām /
tathāpi tathāvidhastadīyaścittavṛttiviśeṣaḥ prādhānyena varṇyamānatvāt alaṅkāryatāṃ nātikrāmati /
"dviḥ sandadhāti" ityādau vīrasya vakturlokottarapauruṣābhidhānavyasaninaḥ sahajotsāhotsiktacittavṛttyatiśayavyatirekeṇa na kiñcidanyanmukyatayā vākyārthatāmupanītam /
tathāhi---sāyakasandhānakriyābhyāvṛttigaṇanamakasmādapi svaparispandatiraskārakāraṇaṃ manyamānaḥ kimityanena pariharati /
karṇa ityabhimānapratītiḥ (pradhānaṃ puruṣavakrabhāvopabṛṃhitaṃ) rūḍhivaicitryayoginaḥ śalyetyāmantraṇapadasyābhiprāyaḥ /
pārthāyeti sāmānyasya kasyacidākārāntaraśabda(ra?) pratīkārasya śatroḥ kṛte tatpratighātasamarthopādhyantaropakaraṇaṃ kadācitsaṃbhāvyetāpi iti prakaraṇāt pratīyate /
āgata iti tatpratiniya-tārthaṃ)manārthaṃ) prayatnenābhimānenānyo 'pi svayamāgataḥ san apākṛta ityabhimānotkarṣapratītiḥ prakaraṇādgamyate /

children.translated_text: The example itself is vigorous (<s>ūrjita</s>).

children.text: tadevamayaṃ pradhānacetanalakṣaṇopakṛtātiśayaviśiṣṭacittavṛttiviśeṣaḥ vastusvabhāva eva mukhyatayā varṇyamānatvātalaṅkāryo na punaralaṅkāraḥ /
children.translated_text: Thus, this particular state of mind — distinguished by the surpassing excellence aided by the characteristic of the principal sentient being — being primarily described as the very nature of the subject matter, is a thing-to-be-ornamented, not an ornament.
This is what was stated: 'The description [that consists in] the beauty of its own noble activity —
of the subject matter, being within the domain of oblique expression alone — that is the obliqueness.'

This very thing, having arisen at the opportune moment, has been considered by us. Surely we are disputing in this matter with those revered [authorities] who are skilled of mind in theatrical practice (<s>bhaṭanaya</s>) and who know the ultimate truth — whether the example cited here, being in the domain of the semblance of <s>rasa</s> (<s>rasābhāsa</s>), deserves to be described or not? What is the point of fabricating propriety and impropriety? In all respects, let it be just as it appears to those revered ones. Nevertheless, such a particular state of mind of his [i.e., <s>Śiva's</s>], being primarily described, does not transcend the status of being a thing-to-be-ornamented. In 'he fits [his arrow] a second time' and the like — apart from the surpassing excellence of the particular mental state that is naturally intoxicated with enthusiasm, belonging to the heroic speaker obsessed with declaring his extraordinary masculinity — nothing else has primarily been brought to sentence-meaning. Indeed: the counting of the repetition of the act of fitting the arrow, which [<s>Karṇa</s>] considers to be for some unknown reason the cause of eclipsing his own activity — he dismisses with 'why?' [i.e., 'does <s>Karṇa</s> really do this?']. '<s>Karṇa</s>' — the cognition of self-regard is predominant, nourished by the oblique quality of the person. The intent of the vocative word '<s>Śalya</s>' partakes of the obliqueness of conventional variety. 'For <s>Pārtha</s>' — from the context it is understood that for any enemy — a common counter-opponent of some kind — the aid of another instrument capable of countering him might sometimes be imagined. 'Having returned' — from the context one understands the cognition of the surpassing excellence of pride: that [the enemy], who was intended [to be defeated] by his effort alone, having himself come [back to the battle], was pushed aside.

children.text:
iti /
tasmādevaṃvidhasya cittavṛttiviśeṣatvāt rasabhāvatadābhāsānāṃ yathāyogamekatamasmin vivakṣāvaśādantarbhāvaḥ saṃbhavatītyalaṅkāryatvameva yuktam na tvalaṅkārabhāva iti /
tasmānna rasavadādyabhihitadūṣaṇapātratāmatikrāmati /
tadetaduktamatra sarvameva yojanīyam /
tadvad"apakartāhamasmi" ityaparamudāharaṇamanenaiva nyāyena samānayogakṣemaprāyamiti gatārthameva /
evamudāttasyobhayaprakārasyāpyalaṅkāryataiva yuktimatī na punaralaṅkaraṇatvaṃ, tatra prathamasya tāvallakṣaṇavākyameva duradhigamasamanvayam
children.translated_text: Therefore, since this kind of particular mental state — depending on the will [of the poet] — includes, as appropriate, any one among <s>rasa</s>, its <s>bhāva</s>, and its semblance (<s>ābhāsa</s>) — the status of being a thing-to-be-ornamented is alone justified, not the status of being an ornament. Therefore, [<s>ūrjasvi</s>] does not transcend being an object of the refutation stated regarding <s>rasavat</s> and the like. Everything stated here, then, should be applied in this manner. Likewise, the other example — 'I am the one who will cut you down' — by this very same reasoning, being of nearly equal fortune, is already understood. Thus, of <s>udātta</s> (the exalted) too, of both types — the status of being a thing-to-be-ornamented alone is logically justified, not the status of being an ornamentation. Therein, the definition-sentence of the first [type of <s>udātta</s>] is itself difficult to construe —
'The exalted is a subject matter endowed with prosperity' // VjivC_3.55a //
thus.

children.text:
atra yadvastu tadudāttam, alakaraṇaṃ kīdṛśamityākāṅkṣāyām ṛddhimadityanena yadi viśeṣyate tattadeva saṃpadupetaṃ vastu varṇyamānamalaṅkāryaṃ tadevālaṅkaraṇamiti svātmani kriyāvirodhalakṣaṇasya doṣasya durnivāratvāt svarūpādatiriktasya vastvantarasyāpratibhāsanāt ūrjasvivadudātte '(pi bhūṣa)ṇabhāvānupapattiḥ /
athavā ṛddhimadvastu yasmin yasyetyapi vyākhyānaṃ kriyate, tathāpi tadanyapadārthalakṣaṇaṃ vastu vaktavyameva yatsamāsārthopanītam /
tatkāvyameva tathāvidhaṃ bhaviṣyatīti cettadapi na kiñcideva, yasmāt kāvyasyālaṅkāra iti prasiddhirna punaḥ kāvyamevālaṅkaraṇamiti /
yadi vā ṛddhimadvastu yasmin yasya vā ityasāvalaṅkāraḥ (eva) samāsārthenopanīyate tathāpi varṇanīyādalaṅkaraṇamatiriktamalaṅkaraṇakalpamanyadatra (na kiṃ) cidevopalabhyate ityubhayathāpi śabdārthāsaṃgatilakṣaṇo doṣaḥ saṃprāptāvasaraḥ saṃpadyate /
kiṃ codāttasyālaṅkaraṇatve sati, alaṅkaraṇāntaravidhānāt tadapekṣānibandhanasya saṃsṛṣṭisaṃkaravyapadeśasyāprasiddheranyasmin viṣaye varṇanīyāntare rūpakādivat tadviruddhasya samṛddhirahitasya varṇanīyāntarasya cālaṅkāratvaprasaṃgāt udāttasya na kathañcidapi bhūṣaṇatvopapattirasti /
tathā dvitīyasyāpyudāttaprakārasyālaṅkāryatvamevopapannaṃ, na punaralaṅkārabhāvaḥ /
tathā caitasya lakṣaṇam---
children.translated_text: Here, what is the object? That is the <s>udātta</s> (sublime). [As for] what the ornamentation is like—when, in expectation [of an answer], it is qualified by 'endowed with splendor' (<s>ṛddhimat</s>), then that very same object endowed with wealth, being described, is the thing to be ornamented, and that very same thing is the ornamentation—since the fault characterized by the contradiction of action upon oneself is unavoidable, and since no other object beyond its own nature manifests, the status of being an embellishment is not established even for the <s>udātta</s>, just as for the <s>ūrjasvin</s> (vigorous). Or even if the interpretation 'that in which there is a splendid object, or of which [there is one]' is given, even then, some object characterized as another word-meaning, introduced through the compound-meaning, must be stated. If it be said that poetry itself will be of such a kind—that too amounts to nothing, since the well-known [usage] is 'an ornament of poetry,' not 'poetry itself is the ornamentation.' Or if this very ornament is introduced through the compound-meaning as 'that in which, or of which, there is a splendid object'—even then, nothing other than the thing to be described is apprehended here that would be an ornamentation or could serve as ornamentation beyond the described object—and thus in both ways the fault characterized by incoherence of word and meaning has its moment. Moreover: given that the <s>udātta</s> is an ornamentation, since another ornamentation is prescribed, and since the designation of <s>saṃsṛṣṭi</s> (combination) and <s>saṃkara</s> (confusion), grounded in mutual dependence, is not recognized; and since in another domain, another described object, like <s>rūpaka</s> and the rest—its opposite, one devoid of splendor, and another described object would absurdly become an ornament—the status of <s>udātta</s> as an embellishment is in no way established. Similarly, for the second type of <s>udātta</s> also, the status of being the thing-to-be-ornamented alone is justified, not the status of being an ornament. And thus, its definition is—
'...and the conduct of great souls,
attaining the status of characterization, having entered the mode of guidance (neti-vṛtta).' (Vjiv 3.55bcd)

children.text:
iti /
tatra vākyārthaparamārthavidbhirevaṃ paryālocyatām, yanmahānubhāvānāṃ vyavahārasya lakṣaṇamātravṛtteranvayaḥ prastute vākyārthe kaścicat vidyate na veti /
tatra pūrvasmin pakṣe tatra tadalīnatvāt pṛthagabhidheyasyāpi padārthāntaravat tadavayavatvenaiva vyapadeśonyāyyaḥ,pāṇyāderiva śarīre, na punarevālaṅkārabhāvo 'pi iti /
dvitīyasmin pakṣe tadanvayābhāvādeva vākyāntaravartipadārthavat tatra tasya sattaiva na saṃbhavati iti na punaralaṅkāracarcā /
nanu ca rūpakāderalaṅkārasyāpi tatrānvayo vidyate, tatastasyāpi tadanvitatvāt alaṅkāratā nivartate /
satyametat, kiṃ tu tadanvitasya dvaividhyaṃ vidyate, apakarṣāntaravat prastutatātparyāṅgabhāvena, vibhūṣaṇāntaravat tadupaśobhākāritvamātreṇaiva ca /
tatra pūrvasmin pakṣe yuktaruktaiva /
tadvicchattividhāyitvamātre mahāpuruṣacaritasya dūṣaṇānīti na duṣparihāraṇyeva /
tadviruddhavṛttervarṇanīyāntarasyālaṅkāratvaprasaṅgaḥ /
alaṅkārāntarasaṃnidhāne tadapekṣānibandhanasaṃsṛṣṭisaṃkaravyapadeśayogyatā, viṣayāntare 'pyalaṅkārāntaravat pravartanaṃ ceti /
yadapi samañjasodāharaṇabandhanavyasanitayā pūrvasūribhiratrādaraprathanapūrvakaṃ pratiṣṭhitam, tadapi prastutatātparyaparāyattavṛttitvādeva (sahṛdayabhāva) nāṃ prati manāgapi na pātratāṃ pratipadyate /
yathā
children.translated_text: Thus. Therein, let those who know the ultimate truth of sentence-meaning deliberate thus: whether some connection of the word-meaning characterized by the conduct of great personages—functioning merely as a definition—exists or not with the sentence-meaning under discussion. In the first alternative: since it is absorbed therein, even when stated separately, its designation as a component part [of the sentence-meaning] alone is proper, like a hand and so forth in [relation to] the body—but not its status as an ornament. In the second alternative: since there is precisely an absence of connection with it, like a word-meaning belonging to another sentence, its very existence there is not possible—so there is no occasion for deliberation about its being an ornament. But then, the connection of an ornament such as <s>rūpaka</s> and the like also exists there [in the sentence-meaning]; so, since it too is connected to it, its ornament-status would cease. True, but the connected [elements] are of two kinds: like another inferiority, by being subsidiary to the purport of the subject at hand; and like another embellishment, merely by producing enhancement of it. In the first alternative, what was said is indeed justified. The faults of the conduct of great personages as merely producing its strikingness [are the following:] the absurd consequence of ornament-status for another described object of contrary conduct; the fitness for the designation of <s>saṃsṛṣṭi</s> and <s>saṃkara</s> grounded in mutual dependence in the proximity of another ornament; and the operation like another ornament in another domain—these are not at all difficult to overcome. Moreover, whatever has been established by the earlier masters with reverent care, out of devotion to composing proper examples—that too, precisely because its operation depends on the purport of the subject at hand, does not at all attain the status of fitness for the state of connoisseurs. For example:
[garbled/corrupt text: nethā kunthapṛthak tarjarattā... ...masthāpatteḥ vicchitti...(?)] (Vjiv 3.56)

children.text: mahendrakandarakvaṇatkarṇeṣu ṭaṅkānvitāḥ te nīlā...śekharaśarakṣepaikavīthībhuvā... durgā avigāhitāḥ śaśirucā kīrtyā vasantyāstava (?) // VjivC_3.57 //
children.translated_text: [corrupt text: mahendrakandarakvaṇatkarṇeṣu ṭaṅkānvitāḥ te nīlā...śekharaśarakṣepaikavīthībhuvā... durgā avigāhitāḥ śaśirucā kīrtyā vasantyāstava (?)] (Vjiv 3.57)

children.text:
(atra pūrvāparavarṇitaḥ mahāpuruṣacaritalakṣaṇapadārtho (vyatirekopabṛṃhitaḥ?) prastatavākyārthatātparyameva vighaṭate, na punastadupaśobhāmātrameva /
tathācāyamatrābhiprāyo yadaskhalitaiḥ laikhamahāpuruṣapuruṣa (prabhṛtiḥ sakalasaṃcāritacaritāpasaraṇaṃ saṃraṃbhamātmasātkṛte ca kārye tadatiriktavṛttāntapuruṣāntaravyatirekeṇa na kasyacidanyasya niḥsāmānyavṛtterapi prakāśate /
tasmāttathāvidhamahāsattvāpadānamahamuditeṣvapi teṣu pradeśeṣu bhavataḥ paraṃ pratāpaḥ prathituṃ pragalbhata iti ?) evaṃ samāhitasyāpyalaṅkāryatvameva nyāyyam na punaralaṅkaraṇabhāvaḥ /
tadāha---"tathā samāhitasyāpi" /
"tathā"---tenaiva prakāreṇa pūrvoktenasamāhitābhidhānasya cālaṅkārasya "bhuṣaṇatvam" alaṅkaraṇatvaṃ na vidyate nāstītyarthaḥ /
tathāhi tasyedaṃ lakṣaṇam---
children.translated_text: (Here, the word-meaning characterized by the conduct of great personages, described in the preceding and following [portions], [strengthened by <s>vyatireka</s>?] disrupts the very purport of the sentence-meaning under discussion, and does not merely embellish it. And thus the purport here is: [the conduct of] the faultless worldly great personages... the withdrawal of all the transitory activities... in the task that has been appropriated through ardor—[such conduct's] distinction from other persons of different conduct is not manifest for anyone else of dissimilar conduct. Therefore, although in those very passages where the exploits of such great-souled ones are celebrated, your supreme prowess dares to spread forth...) Thus, even for [that which is] so established, the status of being the thing-to-be-ornamented alone is proper, not the status of being an ornament. Therefore he says: 'Similarly, even of the <s>samāhita</s>.' 'Similarly'—in that very manner, by the aforementioned reasoning—even of the <s>samāhita</s> (the harmonized)—the embellishment-status does not exist, is absent—this is the meaning. For its definition is—

'The subsidence of <s>rasa</s>, <s>bhāva</s> (emotion), and their semblances, whose sequence is unknown (?), whose form is devoid of other <s>anubhāvas</s> (consequent expressions)—that is the <s>samāhita</s> (harmonized).' (Vjiv 3.58)

children.text:
rasabhāvatadābhāsānāṃ praśamavyapadeśaviṣayo daśāviśeṣaḥ, tadanantararasāvatārataraṅgavarjito nijavyañjakavyāpāravirāmaviśrāntavibhramaḥ prathamaparispandaiḥ parisamāpteḥ uttarasamudāyādanabhivyakterasaṃvedyamānakramaḥ sandhyāsamayanibhasaṃniveśaviśeṣaḥ satkavibhirapi kathañcidunneyavṛtti (ra) nimittamanoharaḥ samāhitamalaṅkaraṇam /
tathā
children.translated_text: A particular state that is the domain of the designation 'subsidence' of <s>rasa</s>, <s>bhāva</s>, and their semblances—free from the waves of <s>rasa</s>'s subsequent descent, a charm resting in the cessation of the activity of its own suggestive factors, whose sequence is imperceptible due to the completion of the initial vibrations and the non-manifestation from the subsequent aggregate—a particular configuration resembling the twilight hour—whose operation is somehow barely inferable even by true poets, captivating without apparent cause—[that] is the <s>samāhita</s>-ornamentation. Thus:

children.text: akṣṇoḥ sphuṭāśrukaluṣo 'ruṇimā vilīnaḥ śāntaṃ ca sārdhamadharasphuraṇaṃ bhrukuṭyā /
children.translated_text: The reddish flush of the eyes, turbid with manifest tears, has dissolved; the quivering of the lower lip has subsided along with the frown;

children.text: bhāvāntarasya (tava) gaṇḍagato 'pi kopo nodgāḍhavāsanatayā prasaraṃ dadāti // VjivC_3.59 //
children.translated_text: the anger, stationed on your cheek, belonging to another emotional state, does not allow [itself] to spread, due to the deeply-rooted [residual] impression. (Vjiv 3.59)

children.text:
tadapi na saṃpat (samyak) samāhitam /
yasmādrasādiviśeṣasya satastasya svarūpalobhaḥ /
teṣāṃ ca cittavṛttiviśeṣatvāt bhūṣaṇatve nipiddhasyāpi tadekarūpatvāt kathaṃ tadupapadyate /
kiṃ ca pradhānacetanasvarūpatvāt varṇanīyasvabhāvabhūtasya (tadanyavidhasya) arthātmanaḥ sahajavyañjakāsahiṣṇoḥ vyatiriktapadārthāntarasaṃparkasahatvaṃ svacchasvabhāvatvādeva na kathañcidapi samañjasatāṃ samāsādayatītyevaṃ svarūpādatiriktapadārthāntarasyāpratibhāsanādityādi yathāsaṃbhavamanivāryam /
yadapi kaiścitprakārāntareṇa samāhitākhyamalakaraṇamākhyātaṃ tasyāpi tathaiva bhūṣaṇatvaṃ na vidyate, tadabhidhatte---
children.translated_text: That too is not properly established. For since that specific form of <s>rasa</s> and the like exists, there is the desire [to grasp] its essential nature. And since they are specific states of mental activity, and since even when posited as embellishment, they have a uniform nature with it—how can that [ornament-status] be established? Moreover, since the nature of the described object, being of the nature of the principal consciousness, has the character of meaning that is inherently incapable of tolerating its own natural suggestive factors—its tolerance for contact with a separate, extraneous word-meaning, precisely because of its transparent nature, cannot in any way attain propriety. Thus, 'because nothing beyond the inherent nature manifests as separate'—this and so forth is unavoidable as applicable. As for the ornament called <s>samāhita</s>, which has been expounded by some in another manner—its embellishment-status too likewise does not exist. He states this—
'Similarly, even of the <s>samāhita</s>, which is beautiful through two types.' (Vjiv 3.60)

children.text:
pūrvoktena prakāreṇa anena cāpareṇeti dvābhyāṃ prakārābhyāṃ śobhamānasya samāhitasyālaṅkaraṇatvaṃ na sabhavati /
tathācāsya lakṣaṇodāharaṇe---
children.translated_text: By the aforementioned manner and by this other—by both types—the embellishment-status of the <s>samāhita</s>, which is beautiful [through them], is not possible. And thus its definition and example—
When one undertakes some action, but again through the force of fate,
the convergence of the means for [accomplishing] that—what they call <s>samāhita</s> (the harmonized). (Vjiv 3.61)
Thus. This sentence has clear meaning.
Just as my feet are about to fall [in supplication] to remove her pride,
fortunately this thunderclap of clouds has risen up as an aid. (Vjiv 3.62)

children.text:
atra pūrvasya pūrvasya vastunaḥ pradhānaṃ samarthanamuttaratra samāhita (miti) yaducyate tadāstāṃ, samāhitaśabdavācyatve na kenacit (nivār)yate /
alaṅkaraṇatvaṃ punarddhayorapi sarasavṛttatvāt guṇapradhānabhāvasyābhāvānna kiñcidupapadyate /
dvayorapi vastudharmatayā varṇanīyatvameva samānaṃ (tadarthaṃ ghanagarjitamu)dīrṇamiveti pratītāvutprekṣā bhaviṣyati ityalamatiprasaṅgena /
tadevaṃ cetanācetanapadārthabhedabhinnaṃ svābhāvikasaukumāryamanoharaṃ vastunaḥ svarūpaṃ pratipāditam /
idānīṃ tadeva kavipratibhollikhitalokottarātiśayaśālitayā navanarmitaṃ manojñatāmupanīyamānamālocyate /
tathāvidhabhūṣaṇavinyāsavihitasaundaryātiśayavyatirekeṇa bhūṣyatvanimittabhūtaṃ na tadvidāhlādakāritāyāḥ kāraṇam /
children.translated_text: Here, the principal validation of the first object in the second [instance]—what is called <s>samāhita</s>—let that be; its being expressed by the word '<s>samāhita</s>' is not contested by anyone. But the status of being an ornamentation for both [types] is not at all established, since both have the character of a juicy event, and because there is no relation of principal and subordinate. For both alike, the quality of being describable, being a property of the subject-matter, is shared—and as for [the idea that] 'the thunderclap has risen as if for this purpose,' there will be an <s>utprekṣā</s> (poetic fancy) in that perception—enough of this digression. Thus, the essential nature of objects—differentiated by the distinction between conscious and inanimate entities, captivating through natural delicacy—has been established. Now, that very [nature], being brought to charm by being freshly crafted with transcendent excellence sketched by the poet's creative power, is contemplated. Without the superabundance of beauty produced by the arrangement of such embellishments, the mere quality of being the thing adorned is not the cause of delight for the knowledgeable.

children.text: prasiddho vastudharmo yo na vicchittyāśrayo bhavet /
children.translated_text: A well-known property of an object that does not become the ground of strikingness,
when it has entered the scope of description by the foremost poets, (Vjiv 3.63)
through qualities whose operation is touched by the delineation of transcendent excellence—
when [the object] shines through those, freshness becomes established. (Vjiv 3.64)

children.text:
ityantaraślokau /
tadevaṃ nūtanātiśayavidhāyinaḥ kāvyārthasvarūpasya alaṅkārāḥ /
tatastānevopakramate---
children.translated_text: Thus end the two intervening verses. Having thus [established the nature of] the essence of poetic meaning that produces fresh excellence—these are its ornaments. He now commences them—
There are two types of expression: one somehow makes it [the expressed object] manifest;
another, standing subordinately, illuminates the strikingness of poetry. (Vjiv 3.14)

children.text:
abhidhāyā ityādi /
rasavadalaṅkārādiḥ kaścidaṃśena vartamāno vibhūṣyasya śobhātiśayamāvahati /
kaścidaṅgato vyavasthitastasya mukhyatāṃ dyotayannātmano vibhūṣaṇabhāvamāviṣkarotīti codāhariṣyāmaḥ /
idānīmetadeva vibhajya vicārayati---
children.translated_text: 'Of expression' and so forth. Some [ornament], such as the <s>rasavat</s>-ornament and the like, existing partially, produces the superabundance of beauty of the thing adorned. Another, standing subordinately, illuminating its principal status—reveals its own embellishment-nature—this we shall illustrate. Now he examines this very [point] by dividing [it]—
Just as that which is called <s>rasavat</s>, [being] the life of all ornaments,
attains the status of the sole essence of poetry—how this [is so] is now examined. (Vjiv 3.15)

children.text:
yathetyādi /
"yathā sa rasavannāma"---ṭhayathā' yena prakāreṇa "saḥ'---pūrvaprakhyātavṛttiralaṅkāro (rasavannāma) rasavadabhidhānaḥ "kāvyaikasāratāṃ yāti" kavikarmaikasarvasvatāṃ pratipadyate /
"sarvālaṅkārajīvitaṃ"---sarveṣāmalaṅkārāṇāmupamādīnāṃ "jīvitaṃ" sphuritabhūtaṃ ca saṃpadyate, "tathā"---tenaprakāreṇa"idānīṃ" adhunā "vicāryate"---vivacyate, lakṣaṇodāharaṇabhedena vitanyate /
tameva rasavadalaṅkāraṃ lakṣayati---
children.translated_text: 'Just as' and so forth.
