'Just as that which is called rasavat'—'just as,' in the manner by which, 'that'—the ornament of previously-known function, 'called rasavat,' bearing the designation rasavat, 'attains the status of the sole essence of poetry,' attains the status of being the sole totality of the poet's art. 'The life of all ornaments'—it becomes the manifest being of all ornaments such as <s>upamā</s> and the rest. 'Thus'—in that manner, 'now,' at this point, 'it is examined'—it is discussed, it is elaborated through the distinction of definition and example. He now defines that very <s>rasavat</s>-ornament—
An ornament that functions on equal terms with <s>rasa</s>, through the operation of rasa-possessing quality,
is <s>rasavat</s>, since it produces delight for the knowledgeable. (Vjiv 3.16)

children.text:
rasenetyādi /
yo 'laṅkāraḥ sa rasavaditi /
yaḥ kilaivaṃsvarūpo rūpakādiḥ sa rasavadabhidhīyate /
kiṃsvabhāvaḥ? "rasena vartate tulyaṃ"---rasena śṛṅgārādinā tulyaṃ vartate samānamātiṣṭhati /
yathā brāhmaṇena tulyaṃ vartate brāhmaṇavat kṣatriyastathaivasau rasavadalaṅkāraḥ /
kasmāt ? "rasavattvavidhānataḥ"---raso 'syāsti iti rasavat kāvyaṃ, tasya bhāvastattvaṃ, tadvidhānataḥ---sarasatvasaṃpādanāt /
(kutaḥ?) "tadvidāhlādanirmiteḥ"---tat kāvyaṃ vidantīti tadvidaḥ tajñāḥ, teṣāmāhlādanirmiterānandaniṣpādanāt /
yathā rasaḥ kāvyasya rasavattāṃ tadvidāhlādaṃ ca vidadhātyevamupamādirapyubhyaṃ niṣpādayan rasavadalaṅkāraḥ saṃpadyate /

children.translated_text: For example:

children.text: upoḍharāgeṇa vilolatārakaṃ tathā gṛhītaṃ śaśinā niśāmukham /
children.translated_text: The face of night was so seized by the moon with its star-pupils rolling with passion intensified,

children.text: yathā samastaṃ timirāṃśukaṃ tayā puro 'pi rāgādgalitaṃ na lakṣitam // VjivC_3.65 //
children.translated_text: that the entire veil of darkness slipped off before her, unnoticed [by her] even in [her] passion. (Vjiv 3.65)

'With rasa' and so forth. 'That ornament which is rasavat'—whatever ornament of such a nature, being <s>rūpaka</s> and the like, is called <s>rasavat</s>. Of what nature?—'it functions on equal terms with <s>rasa</s>'—it functions, it operates on the same level as <s>rasa</s>, <s>śṛṅgāra</s> and the rest. Just as a <s>kṣatriya</s> functions on equal terms with a <s>brāhmaṇa</s>—he is <s>brāhmaṇavat</s> (brāhmaṇa-like)—just so is this <s>rasavat</s>-ornament. For what reason?—'through the operation of rasa-possessing quality.' <s>Rasavat</s> (possessing rasa) is poetry in which rasa exists; the nature of being that; through the operation of that—through accomplishing juiciness. (Why?) 'Since it produces delight for the knowledgeable.' Those who know that [poetry] are the knowledgeable; through producing delight, joy, for them. Just as <s>rasa</s> produces the rasa-quality of poetry and the delight of the knowledgeable, so too when <s>upamā</s> and the like also accomplish both, [the ornament] becomes the <s>rasavat</s>-ornament.

children.text:
atra svāvasarasamucitasukumārasvarūpayorniśāśaśinorvarṇanīyatvaṃ prādhānyena vākyārthaśarīram /
tatkāntikāritayā rūpakālaṅkāraḥ samāropitakāntavṛttāntaḥ kavinopanibaddhaḥ /
sa ca śleṣacchāyāmanojñaviśeṣaṇavakrabhāvāt viśiṣṭaliṅgasāmarthyācca sutarāṃ samudbhāsamānaḥ kāvyasya sarasatāṃ samullāsayan tadvidāmāhlādamādadhānaḥ svayameva rasavadalaṅkāratāṃ samāsāditavān /
yathā vilāsinīvallabhādiśabdābhidhāna(mantareṇāpi) tatsvarūpasamarpaṇasāmarthyarūpakasya sambhavati tathaikadeśavivartirūpakavicārāvasare sutarāṃ samunmīlayiṣyāmaḥ /
na cātra pūrvoktāni dūṣaṇāni (saṃsṛṣṭisaṃkarādīni) prabhavituṃ śaknuvanti /
"tathā cānyatra darśanāt" iti viṣayāntare paridṛśyamānatvādanenaivodāharaṇena (tat) parihṛtam /
"svarūpādatiriktasya parasyāpratibhāsanāt" ityalaṅkāryālaṅkaraṇayorapṛthagbhāvasya alaṅkāryatve svātmani kriyāvirodhāttasyaivālaṅkaraṇatvānupapattirudāharaṇāntaraiḥ parihṛtā /
yathā
children.translated_text: Here, the describability of the night and the moon — delicate in nature, appropriate to their own occasion — is principally the body of the sentence-meaning. On account of their producing beauty, the <s>rūpaka</s> (metaphor) figure, with the superimposed narrative of the beloved, has been composed by the poet. And that [metaphor], on account of the oblique character of charming qualifiers accompanied by the shade of <s>śleṣa</s> (double meaning), and on account of the power of a distinctive grammatical gender, shines forth all the more, stimulating the juiciness of poetry, bestowing delight on connoisseurs — [it] has itself attained the status of the <s>rasavadalaṅkāra</s> (ornament-of-rasa). Just as a <s>rūpaka</s> capable of conveying that [erotic] nature is possible even without the explicit mention of words like '<s>vilāsinī</s>' (coquettish woman) or '<s>vallabha</s>' (beloved), so [too] we shall make this more fully apparent at the occasion of examining the <s>ekadeśavivartirūpaka</s> (partial-transformation metaphor). Nor do the previously stated objections (such as conjunction-confusion and so forth) have any power here. The objection '[it would apply] because it is observed elsewhere too' is resolved by this very example, since it is observed in a different domain. The [objection] 'because what exceeds the natural form does not appear, there is no separation of adorned and adornment' — the impossibility of [rasa] being the ornament [itself] when the adorned and the adornment are not different, due to the contradiction of an action upon oneself — this has been resolved by other examples. For example —

children.text: calāpāṅgāṃ dṛṣṭiṃ spṛśasi bahuśo vepathumatīṃ rahasyākhyāyīva svanasi mṛdu karṇāntikaracaḥ /
children.translated_text: You touch her glance, which has trembling side-looks, again and again; you hum softly near her ear, as if telling a secret;

children.text: karaṃ vyādhunvatyāḥ pibasi ratisarvasvamadharaṃ vayaṃ tattvānveṣānmadhukara hatāstvaṃ khalu kṛtī // VjivC_3.66 //
children.translated_text: from her who waves her hand [to drive you away], you drink the lower lip — the totality of love's treasure. We are ruined by the pursuit of truth, O bee; you indeed are the fortunate one! // <s>Vjīv</s>C 3.66 //

children.text:
atra paramārthaḥ---pradhānavṛtteḥ śṛṅgārasya bhramarasamāropitakāntavṛttānto (rūpakaṃ) rasavadalaṅkāraḥ śobhātiśayamāhitavāt /
yathā vā
children.translated_text: Here the ultimate purport is: the <s>rūpaka</s> (metaphor), with the narrative of the beloved superimposed upon the bee, is the <s>rasavadalaṅkāra</s> (ornament-of-rasa) of <s>śṛṅgāra</s> (the erotic), which is the principal depiction — because it produces a superabundance of beauty. Or as —
'The leaf-ornament on the cheek —' // <s>Vjīv</s>C 3.67 //
and so forth. By this very reasoning,
'Thrown [into the water], he clings to the hand —' // <s>Vjīv</s>C 3.68 //

children.text:
ityatra rasavadalaṅkārapratyākhyānamayuktam /
satyametat, kituṃ vipralambhaśṛṅgāra (syāṅga) tā tatra nivāryate, śeṣasya punastattulyavṛttāntatayā rasavadalaṅkāratvamanivāryameva /
na cālaṅkārāntare sati rasavadapekṣānibandhanaḥ saṃsṛṣṭisaṃkaravyapadeśaprasaṅgaḥ pratyākhyeyatāṃ pratipadyate /
yathā
children.translated_text: here, the rejection of the <s>rasavadalaṅkāra</s> is unjustified. This is true; however, [what] is being denied there is its being a subsidiary component of <s>vipralambhaśṛṅgāra</s> (love-in-separation); but for the remainder, since it has an analogous narrative, its being a <s>rasavadalaṅkāra</s> is indeed undeniable. Nor does the threat of the designation 'conjunction-confusion' (<s>saṃsṛṣṭisaṃkara</s>), which depends on the need for a <s>rasavad</s> [when] another ornament is present, deserve rejection. For example —
Grasping the mass of darkness with its rays as if with fingers [grasping] a mass of hair,
the moon kisses, as it were, the face of night, whose lotus-eyes have been gently closed. // <s>Vjīv</s>C 3.69 //

children.text:
atra rasavadalaṅkārasya rūpakādīnāṃ ca saṃnipātaḥ sutarāṃ samudbhāsate /
tatra "cumbatīva rajanīmukhaṃ śaśī"ti utprekṣālakṣaṇasya rasavadalaṅkārasya prādhānyenopanibandhaḥ /
tadaṅgatvenopamādīnām /
kevalasya prastutatarasaparipoṣāpariniṣpatteḥ /
children.translated_text: Here, the convergence of the <s>rasavadalaṅkāra</s> with <s>rūpaka</s> and other [figures] shines forth abundantly. Therein, 'kisses as it were' —
<s>Indra</s>'s bow — resembling a fresh nail-scratch upon a pale cloud — autumn, bearing it,

children.text: prasādayantī sakalaṅkaminduṃ tāpaṃ raverabhyadhikaṃ cakāra // VjivC_3.70 //
children.translated_text: propitiating the blemished moon, intensified the heat of the sun. // <s>Vjīv</s>C 3.70 //

children.text:
iti /
atra samayasaṃbhavaḥ padārthasvabhāvaḥ tadvācakevādiśabdābhidhānaṃ vinā pratīyamānotprekṣālakṣaṇena rasavadalaṅkāraema kavinākāmapikamanīyatāmadhiropitaḥ ; pratītyantaramanohāriṇāṃ sakalaṅkādīnāṃ vācakānāmupanibandhāt, pāṇḍupayodhareṇārdranakhakṣatābhamaindraṃ dhanuḥ dadhāneti śleṣopamayośca tadānuguṇyena viniveśanāt (ca) /
evaṃ sakalaṅkamapi prasādayantī parasyābhyadhikaṃ tāpaṃ cakāretyevaṃrūpaḥ prakāro hi rūpakālaṅkāranibandhanaḥ prakaṭāṅganāvṛttāntasamāropa (ramaṇīyaḥ) sutarāṃ samanvayaṃ samāsāditavān /
atrāpi pratīyamānavṛtteḥ rasavadalaṅkārasya pradhānyaṃ, tadaṅgatvamupamādīnāmiti pūrvavadeva saṅgatiḥ /
yatrāpi prathamodbhedamanohararatyādivadācaraṇamalaṅkārāṇāṃ tatrāpyayameva samanvayaḥ sahṛdayaiḥ svayamanusandheyaḥ /
yathā
children.translated_text: Thus. Here, the natural character of objects arising from the season — without the explicit mention of words such as 'like' (<s>iva</s>) that denote it — the suggested excellence [takes the form of <s>rasavad</s>] —
Placing upon [its] face a <s>tilaka</s>-mark of the beauty of honey, variegated with the devotion of collyrium-like clinging bees,
[spring] adorned its lip of mango-shoots with a flush tender as the young dawn. // <s>Vjīv</s>C 3.71 //

children.text:
atra samāropitanāyikāvṛttāntasya śleṣacchāyāsahāyasya rūpa (kasya tadvadā) caraṇāt rasavadalaṅkāratvam /
yadapi nīrasaprāyaṃ padārthajātaṃ tadapi sarvamanenaiva sarasatāmupapadyate /
yathā
children.translated_text: Here, the <s>rūpaka</s> with the superimposed narrative of the heroine, assisted by the shade of <s>śleṣa</s> (double meaning), behaves like that [<s>rasavad</s>] — and thus the <s>rasavadalaṅkāra</s> —
'Curved like the young crescent moon —' // <s>Vjīv</s>C 3.72 //
Thus.

children.text: tadevamayaṃ sakalakāvyopaniṣadbhūtaḥ kāṣṭhakuḍyopamānāṃ padārthānāmalaṅkārāṇāṃ kimapi sphuritaṃ samarthayaṃścetanacamatkārakāritāyāḥ kāraṇatāṃ pratipadyate /
children.translated_text: In this way, this [<s>rasavadalaṅkāra</s>], being the secret doctrine (<s>upaniṣad</s>) of all poetry, [contrasted with] ordinary ornaments that are like posts and walls [of a building], shining forth somehow [above them all] —
This [figure] called <s>rasavat</s> (having <s>rasa</s>), the foremost of all ornaments,
shines like a crest-jewel, the sole cause of the excellence of the body [of poetry]. // <s>Vjīv</s>C 3.73 //
The entire treasure of the poet's skill has now been revealed directly;
it shall enter the domain of the deliberation of the learned. // <s>Vjīv</s>C 3.74 //
Thus the two intervening verses.

children.text:
evaṃ nīrasānāṃ padārthānāṃ sarasatāṃ samullāsayituṃ rasavadalaṅkāraṃ samāsāditavān /
idānīṃ svarūpamātreṇaivāvasthitānāṃ vastūnāṃ kamapyātiśayamuddīpayituṃ dīpakālaṅkāramupakramate /
tacca prācīnācāryairādidīpakaṃ madhyadīpakam antadīpakamiti dīpyamānapadāpekṣayā vākyasyādau madhye 'nte ca vyavasthitaṃ, dīpayatīti kriyāpadameva dīpakākhyamalaṅkaraṇamākhyātm /
yathā
children.translated_text: Thus [the author] has established the <s>rasavadalaṅkāra</s> to stimulate the juiciness of juiceless objects. Now —
Intoxication generates pleasure, and together with <s>Anaṅga</s> (the Love-god), pride that is fragile;

children.text: sa priyāsaṅgamotkaṇṭhāṃ sāsahyāṃ manasaḥ śucam // VjivC_3.75 //
children.translated_text: it [generates] the longing for union with the beloved, and unbearable grief of the mind. // <s>Vjīv</s>C 3.75 //
Spring adorns women who wear jasmine-garland garments;
and [it adorns] the cries of <s>hārīta</s> birds and parrots, and the foothills of mountains. // <s>Vjīv</s>C 3.76 //
The forests with <s>cīrī</s> (cricket)-sounds, the rivers whose waters are drying,

children.text: pravāsināṃ ca cetāṃsi śucirantaṃ ninīṣati // VjivC_3.77 //
children.translated_text: and the minds of those who are away from home — summer wishes to bring to an end. // <s>Vjīv</s>C 3.77 //

children.text:
atra kriyāpadānāṃ dīpakatvaṃ prakāśakatvam, yasyamāt kriyāpadaireva prakāśyante svasaṃbandhitayā khyāpyante /
tadevaṃ sarvasya kasyaciddīpakavyatirekiṇo 'pi kriyāpadasyaikarūpatvāt dīpakādvaitaṃ prasajyate /
kiṃ ca śobhātiśayakāritvasya yuktaśūnyatve alaṅkaraṇatvānupapattiḥ /
anyaccāstāṃ tāvatkriyā /
evaṃ yasya kasyacidvākyavartinaḥ kadasya saṃbandhitayā padāntaradyotanaṃ svabhāva eva /
parasparānvayasaṃbandhanibandhanatvāt vākyārthasvarūpasyeti punarapi dīpakavaiśvarūpyamāyātam /
ādau madhye cānte vā vyavasthitaṃ kriyāpadamatiśayamāsādayati yenālaṅkāratāṃ pratipadyate (iti cet) teṣāṃ ca vākyādīnāṃ parasparaṃ tathāvidhaḥ kaḥ svarūpātirekaḥ (viśeṣaḥ) saṃbhavati kriyāpadaprakārabhedanibandhanaṃ vākyasya yadādimadhyāntaṃ tadetadarthakavākyādiṣvapi saṃbhavatītyevamapi dīpakaprakārānantyaprasaṅgaḥ /
dīpakālaṅkāravihitavākyāntarvartinaḥ kriyāpadasya bhvādivyatiriktatvameva kāvyatvavyapadeśaḥ /
yadi vā samānavibhaktīnāṃ bahūnāṃ kārakāṇāmekaṃ kriyāpadaṃ prakāśakaṃ dīpakamityucyate, tatrāpi kāvyacchāyātiśayakāritāyāḥ kiṃ nibandhanamiti vaktavyameva /
prastutāprastutaviṣayasāmarthyasaṃprāptapratīyamānavṛttisāmyameva nānyatkiñcidityabhiyuktataraiḥ pratipāditameva /
yathā
children.translated_text: Here, the action-words have the function of illumination (<s>dīpakatva</s>), that is, of making manifest; because it is through the action-words alone that the related multiple subjects are illuminated —
Having as their domain the beginning, middle, and end; conjoining with the principal and the other [subordinate elements];
where the property of comparison is internally contained — that they know as <s>dīpaka</s> (illumination). // <s>Vjīv</s>C 3.78 //
And it has been exemplified in another text, as —
The lord-elephants wander about, their hearts stolen by the scent of the rut of the guardian-elephants of the directions; (Prākrit)

children.text: duḥkha baṇe ca kaiṇo bhaṇiivisamamahākaimagge // VjivC_3.79 //
children.translated_text: poets too [wander] with difficulty in the forest on the path of the great poet, with its uneven mode of expression. (Prākrit) // <s>Vjīv</s>C 3.79 //
The lord-elephants wander about, their hearts stolen by the scent of the rut of the guardian-elephants of the directions;
poets too [wander] with difficulty in the forest on the path of the great poet, with its uneven mode of expression.
Thus the <s>chāyā</s> (Sanskrit rendering).

children.text:
atra (prastutāprastutaviṣayasāmarthyasaṃprāpta) sāmyasamullasitaṃ sahṛdayahṛdayāhlādakāri kāvyarāmaṇīyakaṃ svarūpameva /
kriyāpadaṃ punarvākyāvinābhāvi vākyāntaravad vyavasthitam, atraiva padāntaravacca /
(ayama)tra vākyārthaḥ /
yathā dikkuñjaramadāmodasuhitamānasāḥ karīndrāḥ kānane kathamapi duḥkhaṃ caṅkramyante, tathā bhaṇitiviṣame vakroktivicitre mahākavimārge kavaya iti caśabdasyārthaḥ /
te hi sābhimānāḥ santaḥ tadatiriktaparispandatayā vartitumīhamānāḥ kṛcchreṇa samācakṣire ityabhiprāyaḥ /
tasmāt sāmyaikajīvitamalaṅkaraṇamidaṃ pratīyamānatvānmanohāri prakārāntaram /
(yatra) trividhaṃ hi pratīyamānavṛttisāmyaṃ samudbhāsate tatrāyameva nyāyo 'nusandheyaḥ /
śiṣṭaṃ punarvārtāmātrameva, yathā
children.translated_text: Here, the similarity — shining forth through the power of the relevant and irrelevant subjects — delighting the hearts of connoisseurs —
'The sun has set; the moon shines; the birds go to their resting-place.' // <s>Vjīv</s>C 3.80 //

children.text:
iti /
tadidānīṃ dīpakamalaṅkārāntarakaraṇaṃ kalayan kāmapi kāvyakamanīyatāṃ kalpayituṃ prakārāntareṇa prakramate---
children.translated_text: Thus. Now, considering <s>dīpaka</s> as producing another ornament [through interaction], and fashioning a certain poetic beauty through it —
Bearing propriety, unfading, the cause of delight for connoisseurs,
that which illuminates objects and their <s>dharma</s>s (properties) and meanings — that is the real <s>dīpaka</s> (illumination). // <s>Vjīv</s> 3.17 //

children.text:
aucityāvahamityādi /
"vastu dīpakaṃ" vastu siddharūpamalaṅkaraṇaṃ /
bhavatīti saṃbandhaḥ, kriyāntarāśravaṇāt /
tadevaṃ sarvasya kasyacidvastunaḥ sadbhāvāttadāpattirityāha---"dīpayat" prakāśayadalaṅkaraṇaṃ saṃpadyate /
kiṃ kasyetyabhidhatte---"dharmaṃ" = parispandaviśeṣam, "arthānāṃ" = varṇanīyānām /
kīdṛśaṃ---"aśaktam" = aprakaṭam, tenaiva prakāśamānatvāt /
kiṃsvarūpaṃ ca---"aucityāvahaṃ" = aucityamaudāryamāvahatiyaḥ taṃ tathoktam /
anyacca kiṃvidham---"amlānaṃ" = pratyagramanālīḍhamiti yāvat /
evaṃvidhasvarūpatvāt "tadvidāhlādakāraṇaṃ" = kāvyavidānandanimittam /
asyaiva prakārāntarān nirūpayati---
children.translated_text: 'Bearing propriety' and so forth. 'Vastu dīpakaṃ' — the illumination that is a natural, established ornament. 'Exists' is the syntactical connection —

children.text: ekaṃ prakāśakaṃ, santi bhūyāṃsi bhūyasāṃ kvacit /
children.translated_text: One [element] is the illuminator; there are many among many [subjects] in some [cases];

children.text: kevalaṃ paṅktisaṃsthaṃ vā dvividhaṃ paridṛśyate // Vjiv_3.18 //
children.translated_text: it is merely arranged in sequence, or [appears in] two varieties. // <s>Vjīv</s> 3.18 //

children.text:
ekamiti /
"dvividhaṃ paridṛśyate" = dviprakāramavalokyate lakṣye vibhāvyate /
kathaṃ ?"kevalaṃ" = asahāyaṃ, "paṅktisaṃsthaṃ vā " paṅktau vyavasthitaṃ tattulyakakṣāyāṃ sahāyāntaroparacitāyāṃ vartamānam /
katham ? "ekaṃ" (bhūyasā) bahūnāṃ padārthānāmekaṃ "prakāśakaṃ" dīpakaṃ kevalamityucyate /
yathā vā
children.translated_text: 'One' — thus. 'It is seen in two varieties' — it is observed in two forms, is to be discerned in examples. How? — 'Merely in sequence' —
'Worthless is <s>saṃsāra</s> —' // <s>Vjīv</s>C 3.81 //

children.text:
ityādi /
atra "vidhātuṃ vyavasitaḥ" kartā saṃsārādīnāmasāratvaprabhṛtīn dharmān udyotayan dīpakālaṅkāratāmavāptavān /
paṅktisaṃsthaṃ (?) "bhūyāṃsi" = bahūni vastūni dīpakāni "bhūyasāṃ" prabhūtānāṃ varṇanīyānāṃ "santi vā kvacit" bhavanti vā kasmiṃścidviṣaye /
yathā
children.translated_text: And so forth. Here, "determined to create" — the agent, illuminating qualities such as the essencelessness of <s>saṃsāra</s> (worldly existence) and the like, has attained the status of the figure <s>dīpaka</s> (illumination). In the sequential arrangement (?), "many" — many objects serve as <s>dīpaka</s>s (illuminators); "of many" — of the numerous things to be described — "exist sometimes" — they occur in some subject matter. For example:
[Prakrit:] The lion among poets, the chief jeweler of words and pearls,

children.text: ṭhāṇāṭhāṇa jāṇai kusumāṇa a jīṇamālāro // VjivC_3.82 //
children.translated_text: [Prakrit:] knows the proper and improper placement of flowers, like an aged garland-maker. // VjivC_3.82 //
The lion among poets, the chief jeweler of words and pearl-gems,
knows the proper and improper placement of flowers, like an aged garland-maker.
Thus is the <s>chāyā</s> (Sanskrit shadow translation).

children.text:
cirantanairetadevodāhṛtaṃ, taccāyuktamiti pūrvapakṣatāṃ prāpitamidānīṃ kimetasyāpyatiriktatvamāyāti, yena siddhāntasiddhamanupādeyatāmadhitiṣṭhati ? yuktamuktam /
kiṃ tu tairvākyaikadeśavṛtti kriyāpadaṃ kārakāṇi bahūni svasaṃbandhitayā prakāśayadekaṃ dīpakamityabhihitam, (vayaṃ)punastānyeva kārakāṇi varṇanīyānāṃ vastūnāṃ kamapyatiśayaṃ prakāśayanti bahūni dīpakānīti brūmaḥ /
tathā ca "sthānāsthānaṃ jānāti" ityasyāyamabhiprāyaḥ /
prastutavastuśobhātiśayāvahaṃ kamapyavakāśaviśeṣaṃ vettīti /
kimuktaṃ bhavati ? kavikesarī padānāmupanibandhavidagdhatayā kamapi chāyātiśayamutpādayati, mauktikaratnānāṃ cādivaikaṭikaḥ, kusumānāṃ ca jīrṇamālākāra iti /
yadyapi padānāṃ kesariprabhṛtīnāṃ ca sajātīyāpekṣayā parasparapratīyamānavṛttisāmyaṃ samudbhāsate, tathāpi prādhānyāddīpakaṃ tātparyaparyavasitam /
vākyārthena sāmyaṃ punaḥ nātra paribhāsate /
yathā vā
children.translated_text: This has indeed been cited by the ancients, and it was presented as the <s>pūrvapakṣa</s> (prima facie view) that it is inappropriate — now does this too attain any superiority, by which it would assume the status of being unacceptable as established by the <s>siddhānta</s> (final conclusion)? What was said is correct. However, those earlier teachers stated that a single <s>dīpaka</s> (illumination) is when a verbal predicate occurring in one part of a sentence illuminates many <s>kāraka</s>s (case-relations) as connected to itself; we, on the other hand, say that those very <s>kāraka</s>s, illuminating some extraordinary quality of the objects to be described, constitute many <s>dīpaka</s>s. And thus the meaning of "knows the proper and improper placement" is this: he knows some special scope that brings about an extraordinary degree of beauty to the subject matter at hand. What is being said? The lion among poets, through his skill in arranging words, produces some extraordinary luster; likewise the chief jeweler of pearl-gems, and the aged garland-maker of flowers. Although the similarity of function mutually suggested between words and lions and the rest of the same class shines forth, nevertheless, because of its predominance, the <s>dīpaka</s> (illumination) is what the purport ultimately rests upon. The similarity at the level of sentence-meaning, however, does not manifest here. Or for example:
[Prakrit:] Night with moonbeams, the lotus-pond with lotuses, the creeper with flower-clusters,

children.text: haṃsehiṃ sāraasohā kavvakahā sajjanehiṃ karai garuri // VjivC_3.83 //
children.translated_text: [Prakrit:] autumnal beauty with swans — poetic discourse, like these, is made weighty by good people. // VjivC_3.83 //
Night with moonbeams, the lotus-pond with lotuses, the creeper with flower-clusters,
autumnal beauty with swans — poetic discourse is made weighty by good people.
Thus is the <s>chāyā</s> (Sanskrit shadow translation).

children.text:
atra ai(ndava mayūkhādibhi) retāḥ sarvāḥ samullāsitaśobhātiśayāḥ saṃpadyanta iti kartṛpadānyeva bahūni dīpakāni /
śiṣṭaṃ pūrvavadeva sarvaṃ samādeyam /
children.translated_text: Here, all of these — through lunar rays and the like — attain a heightened degree of beauty; thus the agent-words themselves constitute the many <s>dīpaka</s>s (illuminators). The rest is to be understood entirely as before.
Moreover, the sequential <s>dīpaka</s> is of three kinds, and sometimes many illuminate abundantly;
one <s>dīpaka</s> illuminates another, and that illuminating one is considered yet another. // Vjiv_3.19 //

children.text:
tadaparaṃ paṅktisaṃsthaṃ nāma (avasthābheda) kāraṇāt "triprakāraṃ" trayaḥ prakārāḥ prabhedāḥ yasyeti vigrahaḥ /
tatra prathamastāvat anantarokto bhūyāṃsi bhūyasāṃ kvacidbhavantīti /
dvitīyo "dīpakaṃ dīpayatyanyattadanyat" iti (yada) nyasyātiśayotpādakatvena dīpakam /
yadvihitaṃ tatkarmabhūtamanyat kartṛbhūtam /
"dīpayati" = prakāśayati, "tadupyanyaddīpayati" iti /
dvitīyadīpakaprakāro yathā--- kṣoṇīmaṇḍalamaṇḍanaṃ nṛpatayasteṣāṃ śriyo bhūṣaṇaṃ tāḥ śobhāṃ gamayatyacāpalamidaṃ pragalbhyato rājate /
children.translated_text: That further type called 'sequential arrangement' is "of three kinds" — due to differences of condition — the analysis being: that which has three varieties or divisions. Of these, the first is as already stated in what immediately precedes — that many <s>dīpaka</s>s of many things sometimes occur. The second is "a <s>dīpaka</s> illuminates another, that other" — when one serves as the producer of an extraordinary quality in another, that is a <s>dīpaka</s>. That which was established becomes the object, and the other becomes the agent. "Illuminates" means "makes manifest"; "that in turn illuminates another." The second type of <s>dīpaka</s> is illustrated thus — "Kings are the ornament of the earth's surface; their glories are its adornment; this steadfastness brings them to splendor; it shines forth through boldness;"

children.text: tadbhūṣyaṃ nayavartmanā tadapi cet śauryakriyālaṅkṛtaṃ bibhrāṇaṃ yadiyattayā tribhuvanaṃ chettuṃ vyavasyedapi // VjivC_3.84 //
children.translated_text: "That is to be adorned through the path of wise conduct; and if that too is embellished by deeds of valor, bearing such magnitude, it could resolve to conquer the three worlds." // VjivC_3.84 //

children.text:
atrottarottarāṇi pūrvapūrvapadadīpakāni mālāyāṃ kavinopanibaddhāni /
yathā vā
children.translated_text: Here, each successive element has been composed by the poet as a <s>dīpaka</s> (illumination) of the preceding element, arranged in a chain. Or for example:

children.text: śuci bhūṣayati śrutaṃ vapuḥ praśamastasya bhavatyalaṅkriyā /
children.translated_text: Learning adorns a pure body; tranquility becomes its ornament;
valor is the ornament of tranquility; and that valor is adorned by accomplishments achieved through wise conduct. // VjivC_3.85 //
And also:
Beauty adorned their bodies; the union with fresh, full youth adorned that beauty;
the splendor of <s>Manmatha</s> (the god of love) in turn adorned that youth; and intoxication, adorned by union with the beloved, adorned that splendor. // VjivC_3.86 //

children.text:
tṛtīyaprakāro 'traiva ślokārdhe dīpakaśabdasthāne dīpitamiti pāṭhāntaraṃ vidhāya vyākhyeyaḥ /
tadayamatrārtho ya "ddīpitaṃ" yadanyena kenacidutpāditātiśayasaṃ (pannaṃ) vastu tatkartṛbhūtamanyat dīpayat uttejayat tadanyaditi /
yathā
children.translated_text: The third type should be explained by adopting the variant reading <s>dīpita</s> (illuminated) in place of the word <s>dīpaka</s> in this very half-verse. Thus the meaning here is: that which is "illuminated" — a thing endowed with an extraordinary quality produced by something else — that agent-thing illuminates, that is, stimulates, yet another thing. For example:
"Intoxication generates delight, which is full of passion and fragile with pride." // VjivC_3.87 //

children.text:
ityādi /
(nanupūrvācāryaiścaitadeva pūrvamudāhṛtaṃ, tadeva prathamaṃ pratyākhyāyedānīṃ samāhitamityasyābhiprāyo vyākhyātavyaḥ /
satyamuktam /
tadayaṃ vyākhyāyate---kriyāpadamekameva dīpakamiti teṣāṃ tātparyam, asmāka punaḥ kartṛpadāni dīpakāni bahūni saṃbhavanti iti) /
(atra) prītyādīnāṃ prāgabhāvāt, teṣāṃ satāmabhūtaprādurbhāvaṃ vidadhātīti nābhidhīyate, madādiniyatakāraṇatvābhāvāt /
api tu svasaṃvṛttānāṃ kamapyapūrvamatiśayamutpādayati /
janayatīti kriyāpadasyārthaḥ yauvanaṃ paramaṅganānāṃ lāvaṇyaṃ janayatīti /
athavā jvalayatīti pāṭhāntaraṃ parikalpyodāhāryam /
idānīmetadevopasaṃharati---
children.translated_text: And so forth. (Now, since the earlier masters have already cited this very thing, the intention of first rejecting it and now accepting it must be explained. True, it has been said. This is now explained — their purport was that a single verbal predicate alone constitutes a <s>dīpaka</s>; our view, however, is that the agent-words constitute many <s>dīpaka</s>s.) Here, since delight and the like did not exist previously, it is not said that he brings about the manifestation of what was previously non-existent among existing things, because there is no fixed causal relation with intoxication and the like. Rather, he produces some unprecedented extraordinary quality in things already present in their own nature. The meaning of the verbal predicate "generates" is: youth generates the charm of other women's limbs. Alternatively, one may adopt the variant reading "inflames" and provide an illustration accordingly. Now he concludes this very topic —
The verbal predicate appropriate to the context, harmonizing with the mind of the learned,

children.text: varṇanīyasya vicchitteḥ kāraṇaṃ vastu dīpakam // Vjiv_3.20 //
children.translated_text: the object that is the cause of the charm of the thing to be described — that is <s>dīpaka</s> (illumination). // Vjiv_3.20 //

children.text:
"yathāyogikriyāpadam" = yathā yena prakāreṇa yujyate iti yathāyogi, kriyāpadaṃ yasya tattathoktaṃ tena yathāsaṃbandhamanubhavituṃ śaknoti /
yathā dīpake kriyā, "tadvidāṃ" kāvyajñānāṃ ("manaḥsaṃvādi")manasi saṃvadati = cetasi pratiphalati yat (tadapi) tathoktam /
(evaṃ dīpakamabhidhāya) sāmyaprāyaṃ rūpakaṃ vivinakti---
children.translated_text: "Having its verbal predicate appropriate to the context" means: that which is fitting in the manner in which it is joined — thus described — so that one can experience the connection as it is. Just as in <s>dīpaka</s> the action is such, "of the learned" — of those who know poetry — "harmonizing with the mind" means it resonates in the mind, it reflects in the heart — that too is thus described. Having thus set forth <s>dīpaka</s> (illumination), he now distinguishes <s>rūpaka</s> (metaphor), which is principally based on similarity —
Where the entire essence is <s>upacāra</s> (figurative transfer), bearing that similarity,

children.text: yadarpayati rūpaṃ svaṃ vastu tadrupakaṃ viduḥ // Vjiv_3.21 //
children.translated_text: a thing that bestows its own form — the learned know that as <s>rūpaka</s> (metaphor). // Vjiv_3.21 //
The cause of the charm of the thing to be described is known to be of two kinds:
that which pertains to the entire object, and that which is a partial transformation. // Vjiv_3.22 //

children.text:
upacāretyādi /
"vastu tadrūpakaṃ viduḥ"---"tadvastu" = padārthasvarūpaṃ "rūpakaṃ" = rūpakākhyamalaṅkāraṃ vidurjanā iti /
kīdṛśaṃ---"yadarpayati" "yat" kartṛbhūtam "arpayati" vinyasyati /
kiṃ---"svaṃ" = ātmīyaṃ "rūpaṃ" vācyasya vācakātmakaṃ parispandam, alaṅkāraprastāvādalaṅkārasyaiva svasaṃbandhitvāt /
kiṃ kurvat---"sāmyamudvahat" = samatvandhārayat /
anyacca (kīdṛśaṃ sāmyaṃ) "varṇanīyasya vicchitteḥ kāraṇam" "varṇanīyasya" = prastāvājhikṛtasya padārthasya "vicchitteḥ" = upaśobhāyāḥ "kāraṇaṃ" = nimittabhūtam, na punarjanyatva prameyatvādisāmānyaṃ, yasmāttenaiva pūrvoktalakṣaṇasāmyena varṇanīyaṃ sahṛdayahṛdayāhlādakāritāmavatarati /
"upacāraikasarvasvaṃ" "upacāraḥ" = tattvādhyāropaḥ, tasyaikaṃ sarvasvaṃ kevalameva jīvitaṃ, tannibandhanatvāt rūpakapravṛtteḥ /
yasmādupacāravakratājīvitametadalaṅkaraṇamiti prathamameva samākhyātaṃ "yanmūlāsarasollekhā rūpakādiralaṅkṛtiḥ " iti /
tadeva pūrvasūribhirabhyadhāyi /
tadevaṃ mukhaminduriti rūpakamalaṅkaraṇam /
tatkimana (yoḥ) (viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyayoḥ) bhinnasvarūpayoḥ sāmānādhikaraṇyasya kāraṇam ? ucyate /
induśabdaḥ prathamamāñjasyena candramasi vartamānaḥ pratyāsattinibandhana (tvād) atikāntimattvādiguṇavṛttitāmavalambate /
tatastasmādetatsadṛśavaktṛgataguṇavṛttiḥ san vadanaviśeṣaṇatāṃ pratipadyamānaścetanacamatkāritāṃ pratipadyate /
(upameyaśabdaḥ) svābhidhe (yāvinā) bhūtavṛttitāṃ (upamāna)śabdasya niyamayatītyetasmādeva viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāvanibandhanāt mukhendurityatra samāsopapattiḥ /
tasmādeva ca sahṛdayahṛdayasaṃvādamāhātmyāt "mukhaminduḥ" ityādi na kevalaṃ rūpakaṃ, yāvat "kiṃ tāruṇyataroḥ" ityevamādyapi /
evaṃ rūpakasāmānyalakṣaṇasvarūpamullikhya prakāraparyālocanena tadevonmīlayati--- "samastavastuviṣayam" iti /
samastavastuviṣayo yasya tattathoktaṃ; tadayamatra vā (kyār)thaḥ---yad sarvāṇyeva prādhānyena vācyatayā sakalavākyopārūḍhānyabhidheyāni alaṅkāryatayā sundarasvaparispandasamarpaṇena gocaro yasyeti tat /
viśeṣaṇānāṃ viśeṣyāyattatvāt asvātantrayeṇa pṛthagalaṅkāryatvābhāvātteṣāmaviṣayatvāt /
yathā
children.translated_text: Beginning with "<s>upacāra</s>" (figurative transfer) and so forth. "That thing is <s>rūpaka</s>" — "that thing" means the essential nature of the object; "<s>rūpaka</s>" means the figure called <s>rūpaka</s> (metaphor) — people know it thus. Of what kind? — "Which bestows" — "which" being the agent, "bestows" means places or superimposes. What? — "Its own" — its own "form," the expressed movement consisting of the expressed and the expressive, since in the context of discussing figures, the figure itself is what is connected to it. Doing what? — "Bearing similarity" — sustaining equality. And further, of what kind is this similarity? — "The cause of the charm of the thing to be described" — "of the thing to be described" means of the object under discussion; "of the charm" means of the enhanced beauty; "the cause" means the instrumental ground — not the generic commonality such as producibility or knowability, because it is through that very similarity of the aforementioned kind that the thing to be described enters into the capacity to delight the hearts of <s>sahṛdaya</s>s (sensitive readers). "The entire essence being <s>upacāra</s>" — "<s>upacāra</s>" means the superimposition of identity; its sole essence, its very life, is that alone, since the operation of <s>rūpaka</s> is grounded in it. Because this ornamentation, whose life is the obliqueness of figurative transfer, was stated at the very outset: "The figure such as <s>rūpaka</s> and others, whose root is the delineation of essence." That very thing was declared by the earlier masters. Thus "the face is the moon" is the ornamental <s>rūpaka</s>. Then what is the cause of the grammatical co-reference of two things — the qualifier and the qualified — that are different in nature? It is explained thus: the word "moon" (<s>indu</s>), first operating in its primary sense with reference to the actual moon, on the ground of proximity, takes on a secondary figurative usage through qualities such as possessing extreme beauty. Then, functioning with respect to similar qualities residing in a face, it assumes the status of qualifying the face, and thereby attains the quality of producing aesthetic wonder (<s>camatkāra</s>) in consciousness. The word for the object of comparison, by constraining the word for the standard of comparison to operate in its actualized sense, thereby grounds the qualifier-qualified relationship — and from this very relationship comes the justification of the compound "moon-face" (<s>mukhendu</s>). And it is precisely because of the greatness of its resonance with the hearts of <s>sahṛdaya</s>s that "the face is the moon" and similar expressions are not merely <s>rūpaka</s> (metaphor), but also expressions like "what of the tree of youth" and so forth. Having thus outlined the general definition of <s>rūpaka</s>, he now unfolds it through consideration of its varieties — "pertaining to the entire object" and so forth. That whose scope is the entire object is thus described; the meaning here is this — all the referents that are primarily ascended upon by the entire sentence as things to be expressed, serving as objects of ornamentation, whose scope is the bestowal of a beautiful form of their own manifestation for each one — that is it. Since qualifiers are subordinate to the qualified, they do not independently constitute objects of ornamentation, and hence are not within its scope. For example:
The deep sound of the rain-clouds, girdled with lightning-bracelets,

children.text: payomucāṃ dhvanirdhoro dunoti mama tāṃ priyām // VjivC_3.88 //
children.translated_text: bearing garlands of cranes, pains my beloved. // VjivC_3.88 //

children.text:
iti /
atra vidyudvalayasya kakṣyātvena, balākānāṃ tanmālātvena rūpaṇaṃ vidyate; payomucāṃ punardantibhāvena nāstītyeka (deśa) vivartirūpakamalaṅkāraḥ /
tadatyarthaṃ yuktiyuktam /
yasmādalaṅkāraṇasyālaṅkāryaśobhātiśayotpādanameva prayojanaṃ nānyatkiñciditi /
taduktarūpakaprikārāpekṣayā kiñcidvilakṣaṇametena yadi saṃpādyate tadetasya rūpakaprakārāntaratvopapattiḥ syāt /
tadetadāstāṃ tāvat ;pratyuta kakṣyādirūpaṇocitamukhyavastuviṣaye vighaṭamānatvādalaṅkāradoṣatvaṃ durnivāratāmavambate /
tasmādanyathaivaitadasmābhiḥ samādhīyate /
rūpakālaṅkārasya paramārthastāvadayaṃ, yatprasiddhasaundaryātiśayapadārthasaukumāryanibandhanaṃ varṇanīyasya vastunaḥ sāmyasamullikhitaṃ svarūpasamarpaṇagrahaṇasāmarthyamavisaṃvādi /
tena mukhamindurityatra mukhamevenduḥsaṃpadyate tena rūpeṇa vivartate /
tadevamayamalaṅkāraḥ (padapūrvārdhavakratānibandhanaḥ pa) dārthamātravṛtti) "alaṅkāropasaṃskāra-"ityādinā paryāyavakrabhāvāntarbhāvāt vākyavakrabhāvavicārāvasare vaktavyatāmeva kadācinnādhigacchediti /
dvaividhyamasyopapādayati---(samastavastuviṣayaṃ ekadeśavivarti ceti) sarve vākyopayoginaḥ padārthāḥ (pratyekaṃ) vibhūṣyatayā viṣayā yasyeti pratyekaṃ yathāyogametasminnupanibadhyamāne samaste 'pi vartanterūpāntareṇāvatiṣṭhanti /
yathā
children.translated_text: Here, the lightning-streak is metaphorized as a girdle, and the cranes as its garland — such metaphorical transformation exists; but the rain-clouds are not metaphorized as elephants — hence this is the figure of <s>ekadeśavivartirūpaka</s> (partial-transformation metaphor). This is extremely well-reasoned, since the purpose of ornamentation is solely to produce a heightened beauty in the object to be ornamented, and nothing else. If something slightly distinctive is accomplished by this in relation to the stated type of <s>rūpaka</s>, then that would justify its being a separate variety of <s>rūpaka</s>. But let that be set aside for now; on the contrary, since it fails to apply to the principal object that is suited to the metaphorical transformation of girdle and the like, it inevitably takes on the character of a flaw in the figure. Therefore, we resolve this matter differently. The ultimate truth of the figure <s>rūpaka</s> is this: the capacity to receive the bestowal of its own form, delineated through similarity, of the object to be described — grounded in the delicacy of referents possessing well-known extraordinary beauty — must be non-deceptive. Thus in "the face is the moon," the face itself becomes the moon, it transforms into that form. In this way, this figure, grounded in the obliqueness of the first half of the word, operates only at the level of word-meaning; since it is subsumed under the category of oblique expression through the principle "ornamental refinement" and so forth, it may perhaps never attain the need to be discussed on the occasion of examining sentence-level obliqueness. He now establishes its twofold nature — (pertaining to the entire object, and partial transformation): all referents useful to the sentence, each serving as the object of embellishment, when this is applied to each as appropriate, all of them also abide in an altered form throughout the whole. For example:
Youth, that gentle tender creeper, with the beautiful face-moon as its bright fortnight,
the intoxication of the elephant of <s>Manmatha</s> (the god of love) — victorious indeed is the onset of youth! // VjivC_3.89 //

children.text:
atraiva prakārāntaraṃ vicārayati--- "ekadeśavivarti ca" iti /
atra pūrvācāryairvyākhyātam---yathā yadekadeśena vivartate vighaṭate viśeṣeṇa vā vartate tattathoktamiti /
ubhayathāpyetaduktaṃ bhavati---yadvākyasya kasmiṃścideva sthāne svaparispandasamarpaṇātmakaṃ rūpaṇamādadhāti /
kvacideveti tadekadeśavivartirūpakam /
yathā
children.translated_text: [The author] now examines another type of this same [figure] — 'ekadeśavivarti ca' (and the partial-transformation). Here, the earlier masters have explained: that which transforms, that is, changes, in one part, or which exists in a special manner — is so called. In both ways, what is said amounts to this: that which applies the fashioning — consisting of the conveyance of its own activity — at only some particular point in the sentence. 'At some particular point' — that is the <s>ekadeśavivartirūpaka</s> (partial-transformation metaphor). For example —
To him whose form is tightly embraced by the creeper that is the daughter of the <s>Himālaya</s>;
to the sole wish-fulfilling tree on the desert-path that is <s>saṃsāra</s> — salutation to you! // <s>Vjīv</s>C 3.90 //

children.text:
ekadeśavivarto yatra tattathoktam, ekadeśa eva vivartate yatra rūpāntareṇāvatiṣṭhate (vā tadekadeśavivarti) rityarthaḥ /
teṣāṃ viśeṣaṇasāmarthyanibandhanāyāḥ padārthaśobhāyāḥ (atra) rūpātiśayakārirūpakālaṅkāraniṣpatteḥ /
yathā "upoḍharāgeṇa" ityādau timirāṃśukamityatraikadeśavivarti(rūpaṇaṃ) vidyate /
śiṣṭaṃ punaḥ śaśinaḥ kāmukatvaṃ, niśāyāśca kāminītvaṃ rūpaṇīyamapi pratītyantaravidhāyi viśeṣaṇaviśiṣṭiliṅgasāmarthyamātrasamadhigamyaṃ śabdenābhi(dhīyamānaṃ) punaruktatā grāmyatā cādhirohati /
children.translated_text: 'Partial-transformation — where that [exists]' — 'where it transforms in one part alone, where it takes on another form' — this is the meaning. [This occurs] because the beauty of the content, based on the power of the qualifier, produces the <s>rūpaka</s> (metaphor) figure, which creates a superabundance of form. For example, in 'upoḍharāgeṇa' (with the hue just risen) and so forth, there is the partial-transformation [metaphor] in 'timirāṃśuka' (darkness-as-garment). But the remainder — the moon's being a lover, and the night's being a beloved woman — though requiring [metaphorical] fashioning, becomes productive of another perception [only] through the power of the gender of the distinguishing qualifier and can be inferred merely from the capacity of the word; if stated explicitly, [it] would incur redundancy and vulgarity.

children.text: tasmāt vācyaṃ sāmarthyalabhyaṃ ca pratītyā ca samarpitam /
children.translated_text: Therefore the expressed, what is obtainable through implication, and what is conveyed through suggestion —
those who know recognize the self of ornamental figures as threefold. // <s>Vjīv</s> 3.23 //

children.text:
tatra vācyaṃ samastavastuviṣayaṃ rūpakaṃ pūrvamevodāhṛtam /
sāmarthyalabhyaṃ tad (tu) ekadeśavivarti tadeva "upoḍharāgeṇe"tyādi /
pratīyamānaṃ yathā
children.translated_text: Therein, the <s>rūpaka</s> that encompasses the entire subject as expressed — has been exemplified already. That which is obtainable through implication — that is the partial-transformation [metaphor]; that same [verse] 'upoḍharāgeṇa' and so forth. The suggested [type] — for example:
On this smiling face of yours now, O one of trembling, elongated eyes, whose beauty fills the quarters of space with the radiance of grace —

children.text: kṣobhaṃ yadeti na manāgapi tena manye suvyaktameva jala (ḍa) rāśirayaṃ payodhiḥ // VjivC_3.91 //
children.translated_text: that the [ocean] is not even slightly disturbed — therefore I think this ocean is surely a mass of water. // <s>Vjīv</s>C 3.91 //

children.text:
atra tvanmukhaminduriti rūpakaṃ pratīyamānatayā kavinopanibaddham /
ekadeśavṛttitvamanekadeśavṛttitvaṃ ca rūpakasya dīpakatvameva samālakṣyamiti tadanantaramasyopanibandhanam /
tadeva vicchittyantareṇa viśinaṣṭi---
children.translated_text: Here, the <s>rūpaka</s> 'your face is the moon' has been composed by the poet in a suggested manner. The partial-occurrence and the non-partial-occurrence of the <s>rūpaka</s> are indeed [forms of] <s>dīpaka</s> (illumination) — this is to be noted — and hence the [rūpaka's] composition immediately after [dīpaka]. [The author] now distinguishes this very [figure] through another type of charm —
Poets bring the <s>rūpaka</s> to a certain mysterious depth of obliqueness,
aided by the trace of another ornamental figure, through the power of creative inspiration. // <s>Vjīv</s> 3.24 //

children.text:
etadeva rūpakākhyamalaṅkaraṇaṃ "kāñcit" = alaukikīṃ "vakrabhāvarahasyatāṃ" vakratvaparamārthatāṃ kavayo "nayanti" (prāpayanti) /
tatropanibandhanavakratāvicchittyantarādhirūḍhāyāḥ ramaṇīyatā(yāḥ) tadeva tattvaṃ paraṃ pratibhāsate /
kīdṛśam ?"alaṅkārāntarollekhasahāyam"---alaṅkārāntarasya" = anyasya sasandehotprekṣāprabhṛteḥ, "ullekhaḥ", samudbhedaḥ, (tatra)"sahayaḥ"kāvyaśobhotpādane sahakārī yasya (tattathoktam) /
kasmānnayanti---"pratibhāvaśāt"---svaśakterāyattatvāt /
tathāvidhe lokātikrāntakāntigocare viṣaye tasyopanibandho vidhīyate /
yatra tathāprasiddhyabhāvāt siddhavyavahārāvataraṇaṃ sāhasamivāvabhāsate /
vibhūṣaṇāntarasahāyasya punarullekhatvena vidhīyamānatvāt sahṛdayahṛdayasaṃvādasundarī parā prauḍhirutpadyate /
yathā
children.translated_text: This very ornament called <s>rūpaka</s> — poets 'bring' it to 'a certain' extraordinary 'mysterious depth of obliqueness' — the ultimate reality of <s>vakratva</s> (obliqueness). Therein, the beauty — which has ascended another kind of charm through compositional obliqueness — that very reality appears supreme. Of what kind? — 'Aided by the trace of another ornamental figure' — of another [ornament] such as <s>sasandehotprekṣā</s> (poetic fancy with doubt) and so forth, the 'trace' is the emergence; 'aided' therein means a collaborator in producing poetic beauty. Why do they 'bring'? — 'Through the power of creative inspiration' — because of being governed by its own power. In such a domain, which transcends worldly beauty, the composition [of the metaphor] is fashioned. Where, because such a [comparison] is not well-established, the descent into established usage appears as a kind of boldness. But because it is fashioned as the trace [of another ornament] aided by another adornment, a supreme maturity — beautiful in its harmony with the hearts of connoisseurs — arises. For example —
'Like the shedding of the slough of the serpent of the sky; like the playful <s>tilaka</s>-ornament of the court of heaven —' // <s>Vjīv</s>C 3.92 //

children.text:
iti /
atra kavipratibhāpratibhāsasyāyamabhiprāyaḥ---yat lokottarasaundaryātiśayaślāghitayā varṇanīyasya vastunaḥ prakārāntareṇābhidhātumaśakyatvam /
evaṃvidhayā rūpakālaṅkārarekhayāpi tathā prasiddhyabhāvādeva niṣkampatayā vyavahartuṃ na yujyate /
tasmādasmākamevaṃsvarūpamevedaṃ varṇanīyaṃvastu pratibhātītyalaṅkārāntaramutprekṣālakṣaṇamatra sahāyatvenollikhitam /
yathā vā
children.translated_text: Thus. Here, the purport of the poet's creative vision is this: that the subject to be described, being celebrated for its extraordinary beauty surpassing the world, cannot be expressed in any other manner. Even through the stroke of the <s>rūpaka</s> figure, one cannot proceed confidently, precisely because such [a comparison] is not well-established. Therefore — 'this very subject to be described appears to us as having such a nature' — another ornament, characterized as <s>utprekṣā</s> (poetic fancy), is here sketched as an assistant. Or as —
'kiṃ tāruṇyataroḥ' (What of the tree of youth) — // <s>Vjīv</s>C 3.93 //

children.text:
ityādi /
atrāpyayameva nyāyo 'nusandheyaḥ /
kevalamanena kavinā sarvātiśāyitayā varṇanīyasya prakārāntarasya prastutasaukumāryasamarpaṇasāmarthyāsaṃbhavādevaṃsvarūpasya rūpakasya mukhendurityādivadaprasiddheḥ /
kevalasyopanibandhe "cakitatvādevaṃvidhaṃ kimatadvastu syāditi sandihyate mama cetasā" iti vicchittyā sasandehālaṅkārasahāyametadevopanibaddhamiti cetasvināṃ svasaṃvedanamevātra pramāṇam /
rūpakarūpaṅka nāma---
children.translated_text: and so forth. Here too the same reasoning should be followed. Only, since the poet, [describing something] surpassing all [comparisons], because of the inability of any alternative mode to convey the delicacy of the subject at hand — and because such a form of <s>rūpaka</s> as 'the face is the moon' and such is not well-established — merely the composition by itself, with the charm of 'being startled, one doubts in one's mind whether such a thing could exist' — with the <s>sasandeha</s> (doubt) ornament as its aid — has been composed thus. The self-evidence of the discerning is the proof here. The <s>rūpakarūpaṅka</s> (metaphor-like-figure) named —
'The eyebrow-creeper is a dancer —' // <s>Vjīv</s>C 3.94 //

children.text:
ityādi lakṣaṇāntarasyāsaṃbhavāt udāharaṇamātrādeva pṛthaṅ nopapadyate, lakṣaṇānantyaprasaṅgāt, punarapi rūpakāntarāvatāropapatteścānavasthāpravartanāt /
evaṃ rūpakaṃ vicārya tatsadṛśasāmyanirvacanāmaprastutapraśaṃsāṃ prastauti---
children.translated_text: and so forth — because another definition [of it as a separate figure] is impossible, it cannot be established separately merely from the example, because of the absurdity of infinite definitions, and because of the infinite regress that would arise from the descent into yet another variety of <s>rūpaka</s>. Having thus examined <s>rūpaka</s>, [the author] introduces <s>aprastutapraśaṃsā</s> (praise of the irrelevant), which is similar to it in its use of resemblance —
Even an irrelevant object, causing the charm of the relevant to descend,

children.text: padārtho vātha vākyārthaḥ prāpyate varṇanīyatām // Vjiv_3.25 //
children.translated_text: whether a word-meaning or a sentence-meaning — attains describability. // <s>Vjīv</s> 3.25 //
Where, resorting to a resemblance to that, or to another kind of relation,
it is called <s>aprastutapraśaṃsā</s> (praise of the irrelevant) — that ornament. // <s>Vjīv</s> 3.26 //

children.text:
aprastutetyādi /
"aprastutapraśaṃseti (kathitāsāva) laṅkṛtiḥ" "aprastutapraśaṃseti" nāmnāsau kathitālaṅkāravidbhiralaṅkṛtiḥ /
kīdṛśī---"yatra'-yasyām"aprastuto 'pi'---avivakṣitaḥ (api) padārthaḥ "varṇanīyatām prāpyate"---varṇanāviṣayaḥ saṃpadyate /
kiṃ kurvan ?"prastutasya'-vivakṣitasyārthasya "vicchittim'-upaśobhām "avatārayan'-samullāsayan /
dvividho hi tattvabhūtaḥ padārthaḥ saṃbhavati /
vākyāntarbhūtapadamātrasiddhor'thaḥ sakalavākyavyāpakakāryo vividhasvaparispandātiśayatvaviśiṣṭaprādhānyena vartamānaśca /
tadubhayarūpamapi prastutaṃ pratīyamānatayā cetasi nidhāya padārthāntaramaprastutaṃ tadvicchittisaṃpattaye varṇanīyatāmasyāmalaṅkṛtau kavayaḥ prāpayanti /
kiṃ kṛtvā ? "tatsāmyamāśritāya"--"tat"---anantaroktaṃ rūpakālaṅkāropakāri "sāmyaṃ"---samatvaṃ, āśritya---nimittīkṛtya, "saṃbandhāntarameva vā " "saṃbandhāntaram"---aparaṃ vā (saṃbandhaṃ) nimittabhāvādi saṃśritya /
"vākyārthaḥ"---asatya (bhū) to vā parasparānvitapadasamudāyalakṣaṇavākyakāryabhūtaḥ /
sāmyaṃ saṃbandhāntaraṃ vā samāśrityāprastutaṃ prastutaśobhāyai varṇanīyatāṃ yatra nayantīti /
tatra sāmyasamāśrayaṇādvākyāntarbhūtāprastutapadārthapraśaṃsodāharaṇaṃ yathā
children.translated_text: 'Even an irrelevant' and so forth. '<s>Aprastutapraśaṃsā</s> is the name given to that ornament' — by those who know ornaments. Of what kind? — 'Where' — in which — 'even an irrelevant' — unintended — 'object attains describability' — becomes the subject of description. Doing what? — 'Causing the charm' — the superadded beauty — 'of the relevant' — of the intended meaning — 'to descend' — to bring about. For the real object can be of two kinds: the meaning established merely from a word that is part of a sentence, and the [meaning] functioning as principal with the prominence of the excellence of manifold activity pervading the entire sentence. And placing both forms of the relevant in the mind through suggestion, poets bring another object — the irrelevant — to describability in this ornament, for the enrichment of its charm. Doing what? — 'Resorting to a resemblance to that' — to the similarity, the likeness, to the aforesaid <s>rūpaka</s>-figure-serving [relevant], having made [it] the basis; 'or to another kind of relation' — or resorting to another relation, such as cause-and-effect, and so forth. 'A sentence-meaning' — or a non-actual [meaning] that is the product of a sentence characterized as a collection of mutually connected words. Resorting to resemblance or to another relation, leading the irrelevant to describability for the beauty of the relevant — that is [the figure]. Therein, an example of praise of an irrelevant word-meaning within a sentence, based on the resort to resemblance —

children.text: lāvaṇyasindhuraparaiva hi keyamatra yatrotpalāni śaśinā saha saṃplavante /
children.translated_text: 'What is this here if not another ocean of grace and beauty, where lotuses swim together with the moon,

children.text: unmajjati dviradakumbhataṭī ca yatra yatrāpare kadalikāṇḍamṛṇāladaṇaḍāḥ // VjivC_3.96 //
children.translated_text: 'where the surface of an elephant's frontal globe rises, and where other lotus-stalk and banana-stem sprouts [emerge]?' // <s>Vjīv</s>C 3.96 //
Thus.
Here, through the resort to resemblance, the principal word-meaning intended by the poet is suggested by means of the praise of the irrelevant contained within the sentence.

children.text: sakalavākyavyāpakāprastutārthapraśaṃsodāharaṇaṃ yathā--- chāyā nātmana eva yā kathamasāvanyasya niṣpragrahā grīṣmoṣmāpadi śītalastalakṣuvi sparśo 'nilādeḥ kutaḥ /
children.translated_text: An example of the praise of an irrelevant [meaning] pervading the entire sentence, based on the resort to resemblance: 'A shadow that belongs not even to oneself — how can it be serviceable to another? In the calamity of summer's heat, how can there be a cool touch from the breeze and such?'

children.text: vārtā varṣaśate gate kila phalaṃ bhāvīti vārteva sā drāghimṇā muṣitāḥ kiyacciramaho tālena bālā vayam // VjivC_3.96 //
children.translated_text: 'After a hundred years have passed, the rumor says, there will be fruit — that rumor too [seems like a deceit]; how long have we foolish ones been deceived by the great length of the palm tree, alas!' // <s>Vjīv</s>C 3.96 //
An example of praise of an irrelevant word-meaning within a sentence, based on the resort to another kind of relation —

children.text: indurlipta ivāñjanena jaḍitā dṛṣṭirmṛgīṇāmiva pramlānāruṇimeva vidrumalatā śyāmeva hemaprabhā /
children.translated_text: 'The moon is as if smeared with collyrium; the gaze of the deer is as if stunned; the coral-creeper is like a faded redness; the golden lustre is as if dark;'

children.text: kārkaśyaṃ kalayā ca kokilavadhūkaṇṭheṣviva prastutaṃ sītāyāḥ purataśca hanta śikhināṃ barhāḥ saharhā iva // VjivC_3.97 //
children.translated_text: 'a harshness as if with a [waning] digit has appeared in the throats of cuckoo-brides; and before <s>Sītā</s>, alas, the peacocks' plumes seem as if out of season!' // <s>Vjīv</s>C 3.97 //

children.text:
atra induprabhṛtīnāṃ nimittināṃ vicchāyatā nimittam /
sītāyāḥ saṃbandhī śobhātiśayasaukumāryamanoharo mukhādyavayavasamūhaḥ prakṛtāṅgabhūtabhūṣaṇāntaropanibandhasahāyaḥ prastutapraśaṃsāṃ samarpayan sotkarṣaḥ pratīyate /
evamasmādeva saṃbandhā (ntara) samāśrayaṇāt sakalavākya-vyāpakāprastutapraśaṃsodāharaṇam yathā---
children.translated_text: Here, the diminished beauty of the moon and the rest, as objects related by cause, is the cause [of description]. <s>Sītā</s>'s ensemble of limbs — face and so forth — related [to her], captivating through the delicacy of the superabundance of beauty, aided by the composition of other ornamental descriptions that are components of the subject at hand, conveying the praise of the relevant, is suggested with its excellence. In the same way, an example of praise of the irrelevant pervading the entire sentence, based on the resort to this same other kind of relation —

children.text: parāmṛśita sāyakaṃ kṣipati locanaṃ kārmuke vilokayati vallabhāsmitasudhārdravaktraṃ smaraḥ /
children.translated_text: 'Taking up the arrow that has been grasped, he casts his eye upon the bow; he gazes at the face of his beloved, moist with the nectar of her smile; <s>Smara</s> (the Love-god)'

children.text: madhoḥ kimapi bhāṣate bhuvananirjayāyāvaniṃ gato 'hamiti harṣitaḥ spṛśati gātralekhāmaho // VjivC_3.98 //
children.translated_text: 'says something to <s>Madhu</s> (Spring); elated, saying "I have gone to conquer the world," he touches the line of his body — oh!' // <s>Vjīv</s>C 3.98 //

Here, the descent of the youthful freshness of the young woman, which is beyond the scope of description in any other manner, is suggested through the resort to the relation of cause-and-effect, on account of its being the cause of such an excess of amorous activity of <s>Manmatha</s> (the Love-god). An example of the praise of the relevant through the purport of a sentence-meaning that is not actual [but imagined] —

children.text: taṇṇatthi kiṃpi paiṇo pakappiaṃ jaṃ ṇa ṇiai gharaṇīe /
children.translated_text: 'There is nothing whatsoever arranged for the husband — who is accustomed to incessant wandering — by fate-as-housewife, (Prākrit)'
'as provisions for the traveler of time.' (Prākrit) // <s>Vjīv</s>C 3.99 //

children.text: tannāsti kimapi patyuḥ prikalpitaṃ yanna niyatigehinyā /
children.translated_text: 'There is nothing whatsoever arranged for the husband — who is accustomed to incessant wandering — by fate-as-housewife,'
'as provisions for the traveler of time.'
(Sanskrit rendering)

children.text:
atra sāmyaṃ, nimittanimittibhāvaḥ, sāmānyaviśeṣabhāvaśceti tritayamapi antarbhāvayituṃ yujyate /
yasmāt prahastavadhe śrāvayitavye sākṣādabhidhānānucitatvāt vicchittyaivamabhidhīyate /
tadevamayamaprastutapraśaṃsāvyavahāraḥ kavīnāmativitataprapañcaḥ paridṛśyate /
tasmāt sahṛdayaiśca svayamevotprekṣaṇīyaḥ /
praśaṃsāśabdo 'trārthaprakāśādivat viparītalakṣaṇayā garhāyāmapi vartate /
varṇanā sāmānyamātravṛttirvā /
evamaprastutapraśaṃsāṃ vicārya vivakṣitārthapratipādanāya prakārāntarābhidhānatvādanayaiva samacchāyaprāyaṃ paryāyoktaṃ vicārayati---
children.translated_text: Here, resemblance, the cause-and-effect relation, and the general-particular relation — all three can be subsumed. Because, when the killing of <s>Prahasta</s> is what should be narrated, since direct statement is unsuitable, it is expressed thus through charm. In this manner, this usage of <s>aprastutapraśaṃsā</s> (praise of the irrelevant) is seen to have a very extensive range among poets. Therefore it should be imagined by connoisseurs themselves. The word 'praśaṃsā' (praise), like 'arthaprakāśa' (illumination of meaning), also applies to blame through the operation of inverted reference. Or it has the function of merely general description. Having thus examined <s>aprastutapraśaṃsā</s>, [the author] now examines <s>paryāyokta</s> (indirect expression), which is mostly of the same complexion — since it is another mode of conveying the intended meaning —
That which is to be said through one sentence but is conveyed by another —
for the achievement of superadded beauty — that is called <s>paryāyokta</s> (indirect expression). // <s>Vjīv</s> 3.27 //

children.text:
yadvākyāntaretyādi---"paryāyoktaṃ taducyate" = paryāyoktābhidhānamalaṅkaraṇaṃ tadabhidhīyate /
"yadvākyāntaravaktavyaṃ" = vastu vākyārthalakṣaṇaṃ padasamudāyāntarābhidheyaṃ "tadanyena" = vākyāntareṇa yena "samarpyate" = pratipādyate /
kimartham ?"upaśobhāniṣpattyai" = vicchitti (viśeṣa) saṃpattaye /
tatparyāyoktamityarthaḥ /
nanvevaṃ paryāyavakratvāt kimatrātiricyate ? paryāyavakratvasya padārthamātraṃ vācyatayā viṣayaḥ, paryāyoktasya punarvākyārtho 'pyaṅgatayeti tasmāt pṛthagabhidhīyate /
udāharaṇaṃ yathā---
children.translated_text: 'That which through one sentence' and so forth. 'That is called <s>paryāyokta</s>' — the ornament called <s>paryāyokta</s> is so designated. 'That which is to be said through one sentence' — the subject, characterized as a sentence-meaning, expressible by another collection of words — 'by another' — by another sentence — 'is conveyed' — is expressed. For what purpose? — 'For the achievement of superadded beauty' — for the enrichment of a particular charm. That is <s>paryāyokta</s> — this is the meaning. Now, 'how does this differ from <s>paryāyavakratva</s> (synonym-obliqueness)?' The domain of <s>paryāyavakratva</s> is merely a word-meaning in its expressed [form]; but the domain of <s>paryāyokta</s> is also the sentence-meaning, as a subsidiary — and therefore it is described separately. An example —
He who, by the very command given through the blow of the discus, [caused] the womenfolk of <s>Rāhu</s> —
'The love-festival, barren of the rapture of passionate embrace, with only kissing remaining,' and so forth. // VjivC_3.100 //
Thus:

children.text: yatra vācyatayā nindā vicchittyai prastutasya sā /
children.translated_text: Where censure is expressed directly, for the beauty of the subject at hand,
and praise is conveyed through suggestion — that is regarded as ironic praise (<s>vyājastuti</s>). // Vjiv_3.28 //

children.text:
"yatra' = yasyāṃ, "vācyatayā' = śabdābhidheyatvena "nindā' = garhā, "vyaṅgyatayā stutiḥ' = pratīyamānatvena praśaṃsā "prastutasya vicchittyai' = śobhāyai, tadevamasau dviprakārā "vyājastutiḥ' alaṅkṛtiḥ "matā' = smṛtā /
yathā
children.translated_text: 'Where' — in which [expression]; 'directly' — through the expressed meaning of the words; 'censure' — blame; 'through suggestion, praise' — commendation through what is cognized indirectly; 'for the beauty of the subject' — for its splendor. Thus this twofold figure is 'regarded' — known as — ironic praise (<s>vyājastuti</s>). For example:

children.text: bhūbhārodvahanāya śeṣaśirasāṃ sārthena saṃnahyate viśvasya sthitaye svayaṃ sa bhagavān jāgarti devo hariḥ /
children.translated_text: <s>Śeṣa</s> girds up with the host of his heads to bear the burden of the earth; the blessed <s>Lord Hari</s> himself remains awake for the stability of the universe;

children.text: adyāpyatra ca nābhimānamasamaṃ rājaṃstvayā tanvatā viśrāntiḥ kṣaṇamekameva na tayorjāteti ko 'yaṃ kramaḥ // VjivC_3.101 //
children.translated_text: yet even now, O king, while you extend your incomparable pride, not even a single moment of rest is born for those two — what kind of procedure is this? // VjivC_3.101 //
Or for example:
'The mark of the moon...' // VjivC_3.102 //
and so forth. In the reverse — [i.e., where praise is expressed and censure suggested] — this very figure is employed for the ornamentable. For example:
'O you who are conquered in play...' // VjivC_3.103 //
and so forth. Or for example:
'Even the name of the final tree...' // VjivC_3.104 //
Thus. Or for example:

children.text: dinamavasitaṃ viśrāntāḥ smastvayā marukūpa he paramupakṛtaṃ vaktuṃ roṣaṃ hriyā na vayaṃ kṣamāḥ /
children.translated_text: The day is over; we are rested. O desert well, you have rendered us the greatest service — out of modesty, we are unable to express our gratitude.

children.text: bhavatu sukṛtairadhvanyānāmaśoṣajalo bhavā- niyamapi punaśchāyābhūyā tavopataṭaṃ śamī // VjivC_3.105 //
children.translated_text: May you, by the merits of travelers, remain with water unexhausted! But for now, again may you be [at least] shade — O <s>śamī</s> tree near your bank! // VjivC_3.105 //

children.text:
atra stutiśabdaḥ pūrvavadviparītalakṣaṇayā nindāyāmapi vartate /
evaṃ vyājastutiṃ vyākhyāya prakramopasaṃhārānanyatvasāmānyāt anayopa(mā)samānakakṣyāṃ (utprekṣāṃ) vivakṣurāha---
children.translated_text: Here the word 'praise' also applies to censure by the reverse characteristic, as before. Having thus explained ironic praise (<s>vyājastuti</s>), intending to discuss <s>utprekṣā</s> (poetic fancy) — which belongs to the same class as the foregoing — due to its common property of the identity of commencement and conclusion, he says:
By conjectural inference, or by similarity, or by both —
with the desire to convey the superabundance of the quality being described, // Vjiv_3.29 //
by [words] such as 'as if' (<s>iva</s>) and the like, whose own meaning is extracted through the capacity of the expressed and the expression — or without such markers, // Vjiv_3.30 //
'as if that' or 'as that very thing' —
the yoking of a meaning different from the sentence-meaning being sketched
is <s>utprekṣā</s> (poetic fancy), and it is called an ornament by those who know the truth of poetry. // Vjiv_3.31 //

children.text:
saṃbhāvanetyādi /
"samullikhitavākyārthavyatiriktārthayojanamutprekṣā"---"samullikhitaḥ"---samyagullikhitaḥ, svābhāvikatvena samarpayituṃ prastāvitaḥ /
"vākyārthaḥ"---padasamudāyābhidheyaṃ vastu, tasmād "vyatiriktasyārthasya"--vākyāntaratātparyalakṣaṇasya, "yojanam"---upapādanam /
"utprekṣā"---utprekṣābhidhānamalaṅkaraṇam /
utprekṣaṇamutprekṣeti vigṛhyate /
(ke) na sādhanenetyāha---"saṃbhāvanānumānena" saṃbhāvanayā yadanumānaṃ, saṃbhāvyamānasyārthasya ūhanaṃ tena /
tadavaśyaṃ tasya vastvantaratvāpādanaṃ tatsamānakāryadarśanāditi bhāvaḥ /
prakārāntareṇāpyeṣā saṃbhavatītyāha---sādṛśyeneti /
"sādṛśyena"---sāmyenāpi hetunā "samullikhitavākyārthavyatiriktārthayojanam" utprekṣaiva /
dvividhaṃ sādṛśyaṃ saṃbhavati vāstavaṃ kālpanikaṃ ceti /
tatra vāstavamupamādiviṣayam, kālpanikamihāśrīyate, sātiśayatvena prastāvāt /
sādṛśyasyobhayāśrayatvāvinābhāvāt, prastutavyatiriktasya padārthāntarasyāsaṃbhavāt, tasya ca dharmatve sati parāśritatvāt kevalasya kalpya(tva) mevānupapannamiti tadāśrayaḥ kaścidaparaḥ kalpanīyaḥ /
so 'pi ko 'sāviti niyamāsiddhiḥ /
ekasya kasyāpi kalpane 'pyanavasthāprasaṅgāt, guṇasamanvayābhāvādapratipatteśca vāstavasādṛśyādhārabhūtadharmyantarasadṛśaḥ pāriśeṣyāt parikalpanīyatāmarhatīti sacetasaḥ pramāṇam /
tasmāttathāvidhadharmiṇaḥ sādṛśyeneti vyaktam /
kvacidavāstavenāpi prauḍhivādena uktavidhaprakārāntaramamaparamasyāḥ pratipādayati---"ubhayena vā" saṃbhāvanānumānasādṛśyalakṣaṇobhayena vā kāraṇadvitayena saṃvalivṛttinā prastutavyatiriktārthāntarayojanamutprekṣā /
prakārātritayasyāpyasya kenābhiprāyeṇopanibandhanamityāha---"nirvarṇyātiśayodrekapratipādanavāñchayā"---varṇanīyotkarṣakāṣṭhādhirūḍhisamarpaṇākāṅkṣayā /
katham ? "tadiveti tadeveti vā "dvābhyāṃ prakārābhyām /
"tadiva" aprastutamiva /
tadatiśayapratipādanāya (yā) prastutasādṛśyopanibandhaḥ /
"tadeveti"---aprastutameva prastutamiti /
(samāropita) svarūpaprasaraṇapūrvakamaprastutasvarūpasamāro(pasya) prastutotkarṣadhārādhirohapratipattaye tātparyāntarayojanam /
kaiḥ utprekṣā prakāśyata ityāha---"ivādibhiḥ"---ivaprabhṛtibhiḥ śabdaiḥ yathāyogaṃ prayujyamānairityarthaḥ /
"vācyā" iti /
pakṣāntaramabhidhatte---"vācyavācakasāmarthyākṣiptasvārthaiḥ " taireva prayujyamānaiḥ pratīyamānavṛttibhirvā /
tatra saṃbhāvanānumānodāharaṇaṃ yathā---
children.translated_text: 'By conjectural inference' and so forth. '<s>Utprekṣā</s> is the yoking of a meaning different from the sentence-meaning being sketched': 'being sketched' — thoroughly depicted, presented as natural. 'Sentence-meaning' — the thing expressed by the aggregate of words. 'Of a meaning different' from that — characterized by the purport of another sentence — 'the yoking' — the establishment. '<s>Utprekṣā</s>' — the ornament called <s>utprekṣā</s>. Analyzing: '<s>utprekṣaṇam</s> is <s>utprekṣā</s>' (imagining is imaginative fancy). By what means? He says: 'By conjectural inference' (<s>saṃbhāvanānumānena</s>) — by the inference that consists of conjecture, the reasoning about a meaning that is being conjectured. That necessarily amounts to making the thing [appear as] another thing — the purport being: from observing a similar effect. It also occurs through another mode, he says: 'or by similarity' (<s>sādṛśyena</s>) — through resemblance as well, as a cause, 'the yoking of a meaning different from the sentence-meaning being sketched' is <s>utprekṣā</s> itself. Similarity is of two kinds: real (<s>vāstava</s>) and imagined (<s>kālpanika</s>). Therein, the real pertains to the domain of <s>upamā</s> (simile) and the like; the imagined is relied upon here, since it is presented with superlative quality. Since similarity cannot avoid being grounded in both [terms of comparison], since a referent other than the subject at hand cannot exist [by itself], and since, being a property, it depends on another — the mere imagining of it alone is impossible, so some other substrate must be imagined. And what is that? — there is no established restriction. Even in imagining any single [substrate], the fault of infinite regress would follow; and since without the connection of [common] properties there is no cognition — by elimination, a [substrate] similar to the property-bearer that grounds the real similarity deserves to be imagined. Therefore, 'by similarity of such a property-bearer' — this is clear. In some cases, even through a non-real [similarity], through bold assertion (<s>prauḍhivāda</s>), he presents yet another mode of this: 'or by both' — by both causes, namely conjectural inference and similarity, operating in conjunction, 'the yoking of a meaning other than the subject at hand is <s>utprekṣā</s>.' With what intent is this threefold [mode] employed? He says: 'with the desire to convey the superabundance of the quality being described' — with the wish to deliver the ascent to the pinnacle of the excellence of the thing being described. How? — by two modes: 'as if that' and 'as that very thing.' 'As if that' — as if the irrelevant. The composition of the similarity of the subject at hand — for the purpose of conveying the excellence of that [irrelevant thing]. 'As that very thing' — 'the irrelevant is the subject itself.' The yoking of another purport — for the purpose of the cognition of the ascent upon the stream of the subject's excellence — preceded by the diffusion of the superimposed nature. By whom is <s>utprekṣā</s> manifested? He says: 'by [words] such as "as if" (<s>iva</s>) and the like' — by words beginning with <s>iva</s>, employed as appropriate — this is the meaning. He states the alternative: 'through the capacity of the expressed and the expression, their own meanings being extracted' — by those very [words] employed, or through operations that are cognized [indirectly]. Therein, an example of conjectural inference:
Approaching the ear out of greed for the forehead-ornament, with the buzzing of bees placed close [to the ear] as whispered sounds,
[the face appears] as if the banner-bearing god [<s>Kāma</s>] is being taught the spell of enchantment for kings. // VjivC_3.106 //
An example of imagined similarity:
'As if the laughter of the Three-Eyed [<s>Śiva</s>] has been heaped up day after day.' // VjivC_3.107 //
Or for example:
'As if the sky-serpent has shed its slough.' // VjivC_3.108 //
and so forth. An example of real similarity:
[Prakrit:] 'With hands [soft as] tender sprouts, reaching to the ear, and tremulous, agitated...' // VjivC_3.109 //

children.text: hindu alīlaṃ vasa sa cāla bhavādihi āsati // VjivC_3.109 //
children.translated_text: [Prakrit continuation]
(<s>Chāyā</s>?) An example of both [conjectural inference and similarity]:
[Prakrit:] 'Sharply red, there in the forest, born of passion, the enemy shines forth, violent...' // VjivC_3.110 //

children.text: antire ude aase avandilagga riurūḍhirale savva mahureuṇā // VjivC_3.110 //
children.translated_text: [Prakrit continuation]

children.text:
(chāyā ?) (tikkhāruṇaṃ tam iti /
ārāt dūrāt bheda eva bhedo drutireva vidāraṇaṃ tatretyarthaḥ /
loke hi tīkṣṇaḥ śarādipadārtho 'ṅgavidāraṇe lagnarudhiraleśo dṛśyate /
iti taddharmasādṛśye nayanayugagatatīkṣṇāruṇāttatvasya vidyamāne prastutavastudharmo 'prastutavastudharmatvena saṃbhāvita ityubhayasādhaneyamutprekṣā /
yathā vā---
children.translated_text: (<s>Chāyā</s>?) ('Sharply red' and so forth. 'From afar' — the split is a split indeed; the speed is the tearing — this is the meaning. For in the world, a sharp object like an arrow, when it tears the body, is seen with a trace of blood clinging to it. Thus, when the property of similar redness-sharpness exists in the pair of eyes — the property of the subject at hand is conjectured as the property of the irrelevant subject — hence this is an <s>utprekṣā</s> established by both means.) Or for example:
[Prakrit:] 'The sighs, fragrant, of the beloved women, in a moment's separation from him, throb forth,
as if drops of the nectar of the flower-arrow drawn [from their] hearts.' // VjivC_3.111 //
[Sanskrit shadow:] 'The fragrant sighs of the beloved women, in a moment's separation from him, throb forth,
as if drops of the nectar of the flower-arrow planted in [their] hearts.'
This is the <s>chāyā</s> (Sanskrit rendering).
Here, an example of real similarity:

children.text: utphullacārukusumastabakena namrā yeyaṃ dhutā ruciracūtalatā mṛgākṣyā /
children.translated_text: This lovely mango creeper, weighed down by a cluster of beautiful blossoming flowers, shaken by the doe-eyed woman,

children.text: śaṅke na vā virahiṇīmṛdumardanasya mārasya tarjitamidaṃ pratipuṣpacāpam // VjivC_3.112 //
children.translated_text: I suspect, is — or is it not — the counter-flower-bow threatening [shot] of <s>Māra</s> (the god of love), whose torment is [normally] gentle? // VjivC_3.112 //

children.text:
atrāsūtritārthavyatirekivastvantaravidhānādapahnutibhrāntirna vidhātavyā, yatastasyāḥ prathamodbhedajīvitamutprekṣā na punarapahnutiretasyāḥ /
tadevānantaraṃ vyaktimāyāsyati /
tadivetyatra vādibhirvinodāharaṇaṃ yathā---
children.translated_text: Here, no confusion with <s>apahṇuti</s> (denial) should be made on account of the fashioning of some other thing different from the meaning that has been delineated, because <s>utprekṣā</s> is the life of the initial emergence of that [figure], and not <s>apahṇuti</s> of this [figure]. That very [point] will become manifest immediately after. An example of 'as if that' without [the use of] markers such as <s>iva</s>:
Swooning from the wind of the breath of serpents clinging to sandalwood trees,
this <s>Malaya</s> breeze in spring causes travelers to faint. // VjivC_3.113 //
Or for example:
'O <s>Devī</s>, by the mud of your face...' // VjivC_3.114 //
and so forth. Or for example:
'You, O timid one, by the <s>rākṣasa</s>...' // VjivC_3.115 //
and so forth. An example of 'as that very thing' without a marker:
'Raising each petal one by one...' // VjivC_3.116 //
and so forth. He begins another type of this [<s>utprekṣā</s>]:
Through the perceiver's apprehension, appropriate to the greatness of [the object's] own vibration,
[there is] the attribution of agency in action even to an actionless thing. // Vjiv_3.32 //

children.text:
"pratibhāsādityādi" /
tadidamutprekṣāyāḥ prakārāntaraṃ paridṛśyate-"kriyāyām"---sādhyasvarūpāyāṃ, "kartṛtārpaṇam"---svatantratvasamāropaṇaṃ /
kasya ? "vastunaḥ"---padārthasya /
"niṣkriyasyāpi" kriyāvirahitasyāpi /
kīdṛśaṃ ? "svabhāvotkarṣaḥ, tasyocitamanurūpam /
kasmāt ? ("boddhuḥ tathā pratibhāsāt") "boddhuḥ"---anubhavituḥ "tathā"---tena prakāreṇa /
"pratibhāsāt"---avabodhanāt /
"nirvarṇyātiśayodrekapratipādanavāñchayā /
tadiveti tadeveti vādibhirvācakaṃ vinā" iti pūrvavadihāpi saṃbandhanīye /
udāharaṇaṃ yathā---
children.translated_text: 'Through the perceiver's apprehension' and so forth. This is observed as another type of <s>utprekṣā</s>: 'in action' — in something of the nature of what is to be accomplished; 'the attribution of agency' — the superimposition of independence. Of what? — 'of the thing,' the referent. 'Even of the actionless' — even of one devoid of action. Of what kind? — 'the excellence of nature — appropriate to it, fitting to it.' From what cause? — 'Through the perceiver's apprehension' (<s>boddhuḥ pratibhāsāt</s>): 'the perceiver' — the experiencer; 'in that manner' — by that mode; 'through apprehension' — through cognition. The [verses] 'with the desire to convey the superabundance of the quality being described / by "as if that" or "as that very thing" — with or without markers' should be syntactically connected here as before. An example:
'Darkness smears the limbs, as it were; the sky rains collyrium, as it were.' // VjivC_3.117 //
Or for example:
'The limbs seem to swim in an ocean of unblemished charm.' // VjivC_3.118 //
Or for example:

children.text: viyati visarpatīva kumudeṣu bahubhavatīva yoṣitām pratiphalatīva jaraṭhaśarakāṇḍapāṇḍuṣu gaṇḍabhittiṣu /
children.translated_text: In the sky it seems to spread; among night-lotuses it seems to multiply; upon the pale cheek-surfaces, ashen as old reed-stalks, it seems to be reflected;

children.text: ambhasi vikasatīva hasatīva sudhādhavaleṣu dhāmasu dhvajapaṭapallaveṣu lalatīva samīracaleṣu candrikā // VjivC_3.119 //
children.translated_text: in the water it seems to blossom; in the nectar-white rays it seems to laugh; in the wind-stirred flag-cloth petals it seems to play — the moonlight! // VjivC_3.119 //

children.text:
(utprekṣāvācakānāmi) vādīnāṃ parigaṇanamatra daṇḍinā vihitamiti na punarvidhīyate /
seyamutprekṣā varṇanīyasya svabhāvavisaṃvādasundaraṃ kamapyatiśayamullāsayati /
kavipratibhāsāparaparyāyaprāyāṇāmanyeṣāmapi bhūṣaṇānāṃ keṣāñcidiyaṃ sārasvarūpamāsūtrayantī prathamollekhakāraṇatāṃ svayameva samākrāmati, tannibandhanatvādvicchittiviśeṣānām /
children.translated_text: The enumeration of the markers of <s>utprekṣā</s> — '<s>iva</s>' and the like — has been done by <s>Daṇḍin</s>, so it is not repeated here. This <s>utprekṣā</s> causes a certain superabundance to shine forth — one that is beautiful through its contradiction of the natural state of the subject being described. Of certain other ornaments too, which are virtually synonymous with the poet's creative apprehension (<s>kavipratibhāsa</s>), this [<s>utprekṣā</s>], delineating their essential core, itself assumes the status of being the cause of their initial depiction, since the special designs are grounded in it.
'Appropriating the splendor of the superabundant beauty of ornaments,
<s>utprekṣā</s> flourishes as the life of the initial depiction.' // VjivC_3.120 //

children.text:
ityantaraślokaḥ /
evamutprekṣāṃ vyākhyāya sātiśayatvāsādṛśyasamullasitāvasarām atiśayoktiṃ prastauti /
children.translated_text: This is an interpolated verse. Having thus explained <s>utprekṣā</s>, he introduces <s>atiśayokti</s> (hyperbole), whose occasion has arisen from the emergence of superlative quality and dissimilarity:
That which is called <s>atiśayokti</s> (hyperbolic expression) is the life-force of all ornaments;
in which a certain superabundance is conveyed through artful design,
of the properties of the subject being described — those that produce delight in the connoisseurs. // Vjiv_3.33 //

children.text:
"ucyate 'tiśayoktiḥ sā"---atiśayoktiralaṅkṛtirabhidhīyate /
kīdṛśī? "yasyāmatiśayaḥ"---prakarṣakāṣṭhādhirūḍhaḥ ko 'pyatikrāntaprasiddhavyavahārasaraṇiḥ /
"vicchittyā pratipādyate"---vaidagdhyabhaṅgyā samarpyate /
kasya ? "varṇanīyasya dharmāṇāṃ"---prastāvādhikṛtasya vastunaḥ svabhāvānusaṃbandhināṃ parispandānām /
kīdṛśānāṃ ? "tadvidāhlādadāyināṃ"---kāvyavidānandakāriṇām /
yasyāt sahṛdayāhlādakārisvaspandasundaratvameva vākyārthaḥ, tatastadatiśayaparipoṣikāyām atiśayoktāvalaṅkārakṛtaḥ kṛtādarāḥ /
children.translated_text: 'That which is called <s>atiśayokti</s>' — the ornament called hyperbolic expression is being described. Of what kind? — 'In which a superabundance' — one that has ascended the pinnacle of excellence, one that has transcended the well-known course of usage — 'is conveyed through artful design' — is delivered through an ingenious turn. Of what? — 'Of the properties of the subject being described' — of the vibrations connected with the nature of the thing that is the subject of the occasion. Of what kind? — 'Those that produce delight in the connoisseurs' — those that produce joy in those who know poetry. Since the sentence-meaning is precisely the beauty through one's own vibration that delights the connoisseurs — therefore, in <s>atiśayokti</s>, which nourishes the superabundance of that, the ornament-makers have placed their regard.
Of such essential nature, with their beauty thus made to shine forth,
<s>rasa</s>, natural expression, and ornament nourish the supreme obliquity (<s>vakratā</s>). // Vjiv_3.34 //

children.text:
"evaṃvidhasvarūpāste yathollāsitakāntayaḥ" samuddīpitaśobhātiśayāstrayo 'pi" parāṃ vakratāṃ"---alaukikaṃ kāvyarahasyabhūtavakrabhāvaṃ "puṣṇanti" udbhāsayanti /
yathā
children.translated_text: 'Being of such essential nature, with their beauty so brought to light'—with their superabundance of beauty so kindled, all three 'nourish the supreme obliquity'—they bring to light an extraordinary oblique nature that constitutes the secret of poetry. For example:
In the moonstone mansion on a cloudy day (?), she [the female <s>sārasa</s> crane] follows a departing royal goose, crying out,

children.text: jyotsnayā janitasaṃśayā punaḥ vakradūtiriva rauti sārasī // VjivC_3.121 //
children.translated_text: then, made uncertain by the moonlight, she cries out again like a crooked-speaking female messenger. (Vjiv 3.121)
Or for example:
The <s>saptacchada</s> (seven-leaf) trees, hidden by the moonlight which roams like the hue of a sky-flower,
were tracked by the voice of the bee-swarm. (Vjiv 3.122)

children.text:
atra bhāvasvabhāvātiśayaḥ paraṃ paripoṣamadhiropitaḥ /
yathā vā---
