children.translated_text: Here, the superabundance of the nature of emotional states has been raised to its supreme fullness. Or for example:

children.text: yasya prajvalati pratāpatapane tejasvināmityalaṃ lokālokadharādhare 'pyatiśayaḥ śītāṃśubimbe vṛthā /
children.translated_text: In him whose blazing valor-sun scorches even the radiant—'enough!' [they cry]; even upon the <s>Lokāloka</s> mountain the effect is excessive; upon the disk of the cool-rayed [moon] it is futile;

children.text: trailokyaprathitāpadānamahite kṣoṇīśavaṃśodbhave sūryācandramasau svayaṃ kṛśataracchāyāṃ samārohataḥ // VjivC_3.123 //
children.translated_text: born in the lineage of earth-lords famed for exploits renowned through the three worlds—the sun and moon themselves assume a dimmer shade [before him]. (Vjiv 3.123)
And for example:
Of the grounds [flower-beds] whose immersion is accomplished with snow-water, made pure by the touch of the young morning sun,

children.text: sāvitrabhāsā vihatāṅgaraga- maṅgaṃ kimapyaṅkuritaṃ sthalīnām // VjivC_3.124 //
children.translated_text: their body-pigment removed by the <s>sāvitrī</s> [solar] radiance—some indescribable [beauty] has sprouted upon their limbs. (Vjiv 3.124)

children.text:
atra pūrvasmin rūpakālaṅkārātiśayaparipoṣaprakarṣaḥ /
tathā prathame 'parasmiṃśca rasavadalaṅkāraparipuṣṭiḥ /
tathā ca tuhinasalilakṣālanakṣapitakalaṅkitayā nūtanātapapihatāṃśukenābhivyaktavimalabhāvenāṃbhaḥ snānādisarasaramaṇīvyapārasamāropaṇena kimapi saukumāryamāropitam /
yatā ca--
children.translated_text: In the first of these [pairs], there is the fullest nourishment of the superabundance of the <s>rūpaka</s> (metaphor) ornament. In the other first and in the second, there is the nourishment of the <s>rasavad</s>-ornament. And thus, through the washing away of blemishes by the ablution in snow-water, and through the manifestation of a pure state by the concealment of radiance by the new sunshine, by the superimposition of the juicy amorous conduct of a beautiful woman [upon the flower-bed] through bathing and the like—some indescribable delicacy has been superimposed. And for example:
The rays of the newly risen lord of herbs [the moon]—soft as the tips of tender barley shoots—
can be cut by the cups of your fore-nails for the making of ear-ornaments. (Vjiv 3.125)

children.text:
atra rasaparispandasaundaryātiśayaḥ samudbhāsate /
tathā ca nūtanodayānāṃ darśitasaukumāryāṇāṃ śaśāṅkakiraṇānāmanyādṛśaḥ ko 'pyatiśayaḥ saṃprati samujjṛmbhate, yenātyarthaṃ kapolakarṇālakasaṃparkaślāghanīyāṃ karṇapūraracanāvicchittimarhatīti pārvatīpatiḥ priyāyāḥ pratipādayaṃstadvadanendusaundaryadarśanena tatkāloditaśaśāṅkakarāvalokanena ca rasoccalitacittavṛttiḥ pratīyate /
evamalaṅkāryasya vastunaḥ pradhānabhūtasyāṅgabhāvena vya (vasthi)-to 'pyalaṅkāravargaḥ kiñcidatiriktavṛttitayopanibadhyamānaḥ saṃniveśasaukumāryamāhātmyādudriktabhāvena parisphuran guṇabhūto 'pi mukhyatāmivāpadyamānaḥ nibandhanaprabhāvāttu prādhānyenāvabhāsamāno vyākhyātaḥ /
idānīṃ sāmyasamudbhāsino vibhūṣaṇavargasya vinyāsavicchittiṃ vicārayati---
children.translated_text: Here the superabundance of the beauty of the vibration of <s>rasa</s> shines forth. And thus, some extraordinary superabundance of the newly risen moon's rays, whose delicacy has been displayed, now blossoms forth, by which [the rays] deserve the strikingness of being fashioned into ear-ornaments exceedingly praiseworthy for contact with the cheeks, ears, and tresses—thus the Lord of <s>Pārvatī</s> (<s>Śiva</s>), while presenting [this] to his beloved, is perceived as having his mental state stirred by <s>rasa</s> through the sight of the beauty of her moon-like face and through the observation of the moon-rays rising at that moment. Thus the class of ornaments, though standing subordinately as components of the principal object to be described, when composed with a slightly transcendent function—through the greatness of the beauty of their arrangement, flashing forth with an elevated status, even though subsidiary [in role], seeming to attain principal status—has been explained as appearing predominantly through the power of the composition. Now he examines the strikingness of the arrangement of the class of embellishments that shine forth with equality [to the described object]—
For the accomplishment of the charm of the intended vibration
of an object, [its] likeness with something possessing an excellence in that—that is <s>upamā</s> (simile). (Vjiv 3.35)
It, whether in the statement of a common property or in the sentence-meaning—through the connection of that [property],

children.text: ivādirapi vicchittyā yatra vakti kriyāpadam // Vjiv_3.36 //
children.translated_text: where even 'iva' and the like express it with strikingness, as does the verbal word. (Vjiv 3.36)

children.text:
vivakṣitetyādi---"yatra"---yasyāṃ, "vastunaḥ"---prastāvādhikṛtasya, "kenacit"---aprastutena padārthāntareṇa, "sāmyam" sopamā---upamālaṅkṛtirityucyate /
kimarthamaprastutena sāmyamityāha---"vivakṣitaparispandamanohāritvasiddhaye" "vivakṣitaḥ"---vaktumabhipreto yo 'sau "parispandaḥ"---kaścideva dharmaviśeṣaḥ (tasya "manohāritvaṃ"---hṛdayāhlādakatvaṃ tasya "siddhiḥ"---niṣpattiḥ) tadartham /
kīdṛśena padārthāntareṇa---"tadutkarṣavatā"; taditi manohāritvaṃ parāmṛśyate, tasya "utkarṣaḥ" (atiśayaḥ) sa vidyate yasya sa tathoktaḥ, tena tadutkarṣavatā, manohāritvātiśayavatā /
tadidamatra tātparyam---varṇanīyasya vivakṣitadharmasaundaryasiddhyarthaṃ aprastutapadārthena dharmiṇā sāmyaṃ yuktiyuktatāmarhati /
dharmeṇeti noktaṃ, kevalasya tasyāsaṃbhavāt; tadevamayaṃ dharmadvārako dharmiṇorupamānopameyalakṣaṇayoḥ phalata; sāmyasamuccayaḥ paryavasyati /
evaṃvidhāmupamāṅkaḥ pratipādayatītyāha---kriyāpadamityādi /
"kriyā"---dhātvarthaḥ /
(kriyāpadaśabdena) vācakasāmānyamātramatrābhipretaṃ na punarākhyātapadameva /
yasmāt amukhyabhāvenāpi kriyā yatra vartate tadapyupamāvācakameva /
tathā ca pācakaḥ ityatra pākaśakteḥ prādhānyena tadantarlonavṛttiḥ prakṛtyartho vidyata eva, pacati iti pācaka iti /
tathā pacatītyatra kriyāyāḥ prādhānye 'pi kārakārtha api antarlonaḥ /
tadevamubhayarūpamapi kriyāpadaparispandaspandinī "tāṃ"---apamāṃ, "vakti"---abhidhatte /
kathaṃ ?"vicchittyā"---vaidagdhyabhahgyā /
vicchittiviraheṇābhidhānena tadvidāhlādakatvaṃ na saṃbhavatīti bhāvaḥ /
kriyāpadaṃ na kevalaṃ tāṃ vakti yāvad "ivādirapi"(ivṛ) prabhṛtirapi tatsamarpaṇasāmarthyasamanvito yaḥ kaścideva śabdaviśeṣaḥ, samāso bahubrīhayādiḥ, pratyayo 'pi vatyādiḥ vicchityā tāṃ vaktīti /
apiḥ samuccaye /
kasmin sati ?"sādhāraṇadharmoktau"---"sādhāraṇaḥ" samānaḥ yo (' sau) tayorupamānopameyayorubhayoranuyāyī dharmaḥ (taduktau) /
dharmānvayayoḥ kriyāyoḥ kartṛbhedena subantasyopamā /
kutra ? "vākyārthe vā "---parasparānvayasaṃbandhena padasamūho vākyaṃ, tadabhidheyaṃ vā vastu vibhūṣyatvena viṣayo gocaraḥ tasmin /
kathaṃ ? "tadanvayāt"---taditi padārthaparāmarśaḥ, teṣāṃ padārthānāṃ "samanvayāt" anyonyamabhisaṃbadhyamānatvāt /
vākye hi bahavaḥ padārthāḥ saṃbhavanti /
tatra parasparābhisaṃbandhamāhātmyāt kasyacidekena kenacideva sāmyanibandhana)mupamotprekṣayoḥ) /
tadevaṃ tulye 'smin vastusāmye sati, upamotprekṣāvastunoḥ kīdṛk pṛthaktvamityāha---
children.translated_text: 'For the accomplishment' and so forth. 'Where'—in which, 'of an object'—of one brought under the subject at hand, 'with something'—with another, unrelated word-meaning, 'likeness'—<s>upamā</s>—is called the <s>upamā</s>-ornament. For what purpose is there likeness with something unrelated?—he says: 'for the accomplishment of the charm of the intended vibration.' 'Intended'—what is desired to be expressed, that 'vibration'—some particular property; its 'charm'—the quality of delighting the heart; the 'accomplishment'—the production of that; for that purpose. With what kind of other word-meaning?—'possessing an excellence in that': 'that'—charm is referred to; its 'excellence'—superabundance—that in which this exists is so described; with such a one, one possessing a superabundance of charm. The purport here is: the likeness of the object to be described with an unrelated object possessing the [relevant] property deserves to be logically justified for the purpose of accomplishing the beauty of the intended property. 'Property' was not said [alone], since that alone is impossible [without its locus]; thus this [simile], being mediated by the property, culminates as, in effect, a conjunction of likeness between the property-bearers characterized as the object of comparison and the standard of comparison. He says what indicates such a simile: 'the verbal word' and so forth. 'Action' (<s>kriyā</s>)—the meaning of a verbal root. By the expression 'verbal word' (<s>kriyāpada</s>), only the general category of expressor is intended, not the finite verb alone. For even where the action is present in a non-primary form, that too is indeed an expressor of simile. And thus, in '<s>pācaka</s>' (one who cooks), although the cooking capacity is predominant, the root-meaning functioning within it is indeed present—'he cooks, hence the cooker.' Similarly in '<s>pacati</s>' (he cooks), even when the action is predominant, the case-meanings too are contained within. Thus, vibrating with the vibration of the verbal-word in both forms, 'it'—the simile—'expresses'—denotes. How?—'with strikingness'—with the mode of poetic skill. Without strikingness, the expression does not accomplish the quality of delighting the knowledgeable—this is the meaning. The verbal word does not alone express it, but 'even <s>iva</s> and the like'—[words] beginning with '<s>iva</s>' (like) and so forth, whatever specific word endowed with the capacity to convey that [simile], [and also] a compound such as <s>bahuvrīhi</s> and the like, and even a suffix such as '-vat' and the like—these express it with strikingness. The word '<s>api</s>' (also) indicates conjunction. Under what condition?—'in the statement of a common property': the 'common' (<s>sādhāraṇa</s>), the shared property that follows both—of the standard of comparison and the object of comparison—the statement of that. Where the dharma-connection [yields] two actions differentiated by agent, the simile is expressed through the nominal form [rather than a finite verb]. Where?—'or in the sentence-meaning': the aggregate of words whose mutual connection constitutes a sentence, the thing expressed by it, being the domain as the thing adorned—in that. How?—'through the connection of that': 'that' refers to the word-meanings; through their 'connection,' through their being mutually related. For in a sentence, many word-meanings are possible. Among them, through the greatness of their mutual relation, the ground of likeness [is established] between one and some other—this is [the basis of] <s>upamā</s> and <s>utprekṣā</s>. Given such an equal likeness of objects, what is the difference between <s>upamā</s> and <s>utprekṣā</s> (poetic fancy)?—he says:
Even in the case of identity of the object of <s>utprekṣā</s>, the domain is another purport. (Vjiv 3.37)

children.text:
utprekṣāyāḥ sāmyasaṃbandhe vidyamāne 'pi "tātparyaṃ" padārthavyatiriktavṛtti vākyārthajīvitabhūtaṃ vastvantarameva "gocaro" viṣayaḥ tadvidāmantaḥ pratibhāsaḥ yasya, tathā caivodāhṛtaḥ /
upamotprekṣāvastunoratra kevale karaṇe karmaṇi vā avartinorubhayorapi tulyatvenābhisaṃbadhyamānatvāt /
evamupamitirupameti bhāvamātre vyavatiṣṭhate /
tathā ca varṇyasya ni (tarām avarṇanīye) na sāmyaṃ yasyāmiti lakṣaṇatātparyam /
ubhayameva niścitaṃ pratipādayati /
amukhyakriyāpadapratipanna /
padārthānāmudāharaṇaṃ yathā---
children.translated_text: Even when the connection of likeness exists for <s>utprekṣā</s>, 'the purport'—another object, distinct from the word-meaning, constituting the life of the sentence-meaning—is the 'domain,' the subject, the inner flash for the knowledgeable—and it has been thus illustrated. Of the objects of both <s>upamā</s> and <s>utprekṣā</s>, when neither exists in the instrument or object [case-relation alone], both are equally connected [to each other]. Thus <s>upamiti</s> (simile-cognition) becomes <s>upamā</s> and rests in the bare [likeness] state. And thus the purport of the definition is: [simile is that] in which the likeness of the described object is with something beyond description. He establishes both [types] definitively. An example of simile expressed through non-primary verbal words [i.e. derived forms]:
Your face, O lotus-eyed one, harmonizes with the full moon
and nourishes the ambition to conquer the three worlds of the flower-bowed [<s>Kāma</s>]. (Vjiv 3.126)
An example of simile expressed through word-meanings conveyed by '<s>iva</s>' and the like:
'Its flower-clusters being sucked by bees...' (Vjiv 3.127)
and so forth. An example of simile expressed through word-meanings conveyed by finite verbs:
'Then, with a reddish vibration...' and so forth. (Vjiv 3.128)
An example of such a sentence-simile:
With her face pale as a <s>ketaka</s> (screw-pine) leaf, her slender body-stalk bearing modest ornaments,

children.text: sthitālpatārāṃ taruṇendumaṇḍalāṃ vibhātakalpāṃ rajanīṃ vyaḍambayat // VjivC_3.129 //
children.translated_text: she mimicked a night at twilight, [having] a dim crescent moon-circle with few remaining stars. (Vjiv 3.129)
An example of simile expressed through word-meanings conveyed by '<s>iva</s>' and the like:
Kissing the cheek of his beloved, bristling [with goosebumps], he whose eyes blossomed at the touch, gently closed [her eyes]—
like a day-lotus, when the moon appears sweet-sleeping and blooming, touched by the moon, the night-lotus of the lotus-pool is closed. (Vjiv 3.130)
An example of such a sentence-simile:
This <s>Pāṇḍya</s> [king], with long garlands placed upon his shoulders,
his body anointed with <s>haricandana</s> (yellow sandalwood),
shines like the king of mountains, its peaks reddened by the young sun,
with the outpouring of waterfalls. (Vjiv 3.131)

children.text:
etayordvayorapi vākyayoḥ yadyapyupameyenopamānaiḥ saha pratyekaṃ svasaṃbandhinaṃ prati paraspara (sāmya) samanvayalakṣaṇasaṃbandhinābhisaṃbandhaḥ, tathāpi pūrvasmin sāmyasamanvayāvasāyapūrvako vākyārthāvasāyaḥ, parasmin punaḥ vākyārthāvasitapūrvakasāmyasamanvayāvasitiḥ /
asmin vākye samāsādi /
viṣayapratyayāntaranirapekṣatvāt padārthāvabodhasamanantaratayā parasparasāmyasamanvayasyāpyudbhidyamānatvāt, padārthopamāvyapadeśaḥ pravartate /
nātra prathamārdhe eva vākyārthaparisamāptirveditavyā, kavivivakṣāviṣayārthaniṣpatterananubhūtatvāt /
tatra "sālaṅkārasya kāvyatā" iti ca nyāyaḥ /
aparasmin punaḥ parasparānvayalakṣaṇasaṃbandhanibandhanavākyārthāvadhāraṇapūrvakatvāt upamānopameyaparasparasāmyasamanvayāvagateḥ vākyopamāvyapadeśaḥ yuktatāṃ pratipadyate /
(kriyāpadapratipādyopamodāharaṇānāmupamāvārtādyuktamityalamatiprasaṅgena) /
ādigrahaṇādivādivyatiriktenāpi yathādinā śabdāntareṇopamāpratītirbhavatīti (uktameva) /
(samāse 'nuktau uktau) vādvayaṃ yathā---
children.translated_text: In both of these sentences, although the connection between the object of comparison and the standard of comparison is through the mutual likeness-connection [operating] individually toward each [respective] correlate, nevertheless, in the first, the ascertainment of the sentence-meaning is preceded by the ascertainment of the likeness-connection; in the second, however, the ascertainment of the likeness-connection is preceded by the ascertainment of the sentence-meaning. In this [second] sentence, [there are] compounds and such. Because there is no dependence on any other domain or cognition, and because the mutual likeness-connection springs up immediately upon the understanding of the word-meanings, the designation 'word-simile' (<s>padārthopamā</s>) applies. The completion of the sentence-meaning should not be understood [as occurring] in the first half alone here, since the meaning intended by the poet has not been experienced [until the full verse is heard]. And therein, the principle applies: 'poeticity belongs to the ornamented [whole].' In the second [example], however, because the cognition of the mutual likeness-connection between the standard and the object of comparison comes after the ascertainment of the sentence-meaning—grounded in the connection characterized by mutual syntactic relation—the designation 'sentence-simile' (<s>vākyopamā</s>) is logically justified. (The examples of simile expressed through verbal words—the simile-door and such have been mentioned; enough of this digression.) By the inclusion of 'and the like' (<s>ādi</s>), the cognition of simile also occurs through words other than '<s>iva</s>' (like), such as '<s>yathā</s>' (as)—this has already been stated. An example of the two types through compound and through non-explicit [form]:
One whose face has the beauty of the full moon, whose eyes are [like] blue lotuses. (Vjiv 3.132)
And for example:
Of her who goes, repeatedly turning her neck, bearing that face resembling a turned-around fully-bloomed hundred-petaled [lotus],

children.text: digdho 'mṛtena ca viṣeṇa ca pakṣmalākṣyā gāḍhaṃ nikhāta iva me hṛdaye kaṭākṣaḥ // VjivC_3.133 //
children.translated_text: her sidelong glance, anointed with both nectar and poison, of the long-lashed one—is driven deep into my heart as if implanted. (Vjiv 3.133)
An example of simile expressed through suffixes:

children.text: māñjiṣṭhīkṛtapadmasūtrasadṛśaḥ pādānayaṃ puñjayan yātyastācalacumbinīṃ pariṇatiṃ svairaṃ grahagrāmaṇīḥ /
children.translated_text: This leader of planets [the sun], heaping up a <s>māñjiṣṭhī</s>-dyed-lotus-fiber-like [reddish hue] upon his rays, freely approaches the setting-mountain-kissing [western] transformation;

children.text: vātyā cakravivartitāmbujarajacchatrāyamāṇaḥ kṣaṇaṃ kṣīṇajyotirito 'pyayaṃ sa bhagavānambhonidhau majjati // VjivC_3.134 //
children.translated_text: canopied for a moment by lotuses whirled about by the wind like parasols, even this lord, his light diminished, sinks into the ocean. (Vjiv 3.134)
Or for example:
Having heard the words of <s>Kālanemi</s>, a deep, irresistible roar... at his feet... the proclamation of his approach;

the anger of the lord of the great <s>Asuras</s> (demons), surging with the wild intoxication that bursts forth from the pillar of steadfastness, is freely beheld—like an elephant's [fury]. (Vjiv 3.135)
For example:
Having heard thus, [the heart of] the eager one who looked tremulously at the ascetic's daughter—
the heart of one whose face came and went [in agitation], at the time of the <s>atimuktā</s> (jasmine) flower-cluster blooming, was bewildered (?). (Vjiv 3.136)
Or for example:

children.text: rāmeṇa mugdhamanasā vṛṣabhadhvajasya yajjarjaraṃ dhanurabhāji mṛṇālabhañjam /
children.translated_text: The bow of the Bull-bannered one [<s>Śiva</s>], which was shattered by the artless-minded <s>Rāma</s> as easily as breaking a lotus stalk—

children.text: tenāmunā trijagadarpitakīrtibhāro rakṣaḥ patirnanu manāṅ na viḍambito 'būt // VjivC_3.137 //
children.translated_text: was not the lord of <s>rākṣasas</s> [<s>Rāvaṇa</s>], who bore the burden of fame bestowed upon the three worlds, [thereby] even slightly humiliated by that very [act]? (Vjiv 3.137)

In the example of the suggested simile (<s>pratīyamānopamā</s>), through the capacity of words designating both objects — whose connection with the other <s>rasa</s> is complete, neither deficient nor excessive, with the activity of both terms — the cognition of simile is established even from the action-word and the like that conveys [the comparison]. For example —

children.text: mahībhṛtaḥ putravato 'pi dṛṣṭi- stasminnapatye na jagāma tṛptim /
children.translated_text: The gaze of the king who had sons did not attain satisfaction upon that offspring;

children.text: anantapuṣpasya madhorhi cūte dvirephamālā saviśeṣasaṅgā // VjivC_3.138 //
children.translated_text: for upon the mango tree of the spring with endless blossoms, the garland of bees has a special attachment. // VjivC_3.138 //

children.text:
atra yasmāttathāvidhānantasāmagrīkasya madhorapi tatsamānopa (nītacūte pratītirupa) lapsyate iti nyāyyametayoḥ suvyaktameva sāmyamupagamayati, tathācāsaṃkhyakusumatvādidharmasaukumāryātirekāt sāmyasaṃpattyādirvivakṣitetyādyupamālakṣaṇatātparya (ma) vikalpamevātra samarpyate /
na cārthāntaranyāsabhrāntiratrodbhāvanīyā, tasya vākyārthatātparya (sāmya) lakṣaṇasāmānyamātraviṣayatvāt /
tasmādanena nyāyena samānavastunyāsopanibandhanā prativastūpamāpi na pṛthagvaktavyatāmarhati, pūrvodāharaṇenaiva samānayogakṣematvāt /
tathā ca lakṣaṇodāharaṇe tasyāḥ samānavastunyāsena prativastūpamā yathā---
children.translated_text: Here, since even for the spring — which possesses such an infinite assemblage of [flowers] — the cognition [of comparison] with the mango tree brought near [as analogous] will be obtained, therefore the equality of these two is made perfectly clear through propriety. And thus, due to the surpassing delicacy of properties such as possessing innumerable blossoms and the like, the purport of the definition of simile — such as the attainment of equality (<s>sāmyasaṃpatti</s>) — is presented here as simply a variety [of simile]. Nor should the confusion with <s>arthāntaranyāsa</s> (corroboration) be raised here, since that [figure] has as its domain merely the generality of the definition characterized by the purport of sentence-meaning [based on] equality. Therefore, by this reasoning, <s>prativastūpamā</s> (counter-subject simile) too, which is founded upon the juxtaposition of analogous subjects, does not deserve to be stated as separate, since it shares the same fortune as the preceding example. And thus, the definition and example of that [figure] — the <s>prativastūpamā</s> through the juxtaposition of analogous subjects — is as follows:
How many are there who possess virtues, whose beauty is shared with the good?
How many are the wayside trees, bent low with fruits ripened by their own [sweetness]? // VjivC_3.139 //

children.text:
atra samānavilasitānāmubhayeṣāmapi kavivikṣita (tā) viralatvalakṣaṇasāmyavyatireki (na) kiñcidanyanmanohāri jīvitamatiricyamānamupalabhyate /
tadevaṃ prativastūpamāyāḥ pratīyamānopamāyāmantarbhāvopapattau satyāmidānīmupameyopamāderupamāyāmantarbhāvo vicāryate /
children.translated_text: Here, of both [sets of subjects] whose play is analogous, apart from the equality characterized by the rarity that is intended by the poet, no other captivating life-force is found to be in excess. Thus, when the inclusion of <s>prativastūpamā</s> within <s>pratīyamānopamā</s> (the suggested simile) is established, now the inclusion of <s>upameyopamā</s> (reciprocal simile) and the like within simile is examined —
This <s>upameyopamā</s>, [involving] the compared and the standard of comparison,
is common [to simile]; because — due to the relevance [of both terms] and the non-otherness of the definition. // Vjiv_3.38 //

children.text:
upameyopametyādi---"upameyopamā nāma" = kācidalaṅkṛtiḥ "sāmānyā"---na vyatiriktā /
kutaḥ---prastutatvādupamāyāḥ /
kasmāt kāraṇāt ? "lakṣaṇānanyathāsthiteḥ"---tatsvarūpasya asādhāraṇamabhidhānaṃ lakṣaṇaṃ, tasya ananyathāsiddherapi = atiriktabhāvānavasthānāt /
tathā copameyamupamānaṃ yasyāmiti vigrahe (sva) yamupamānamupameyaṃ saṃpadyate, yadupamānaṃ tadupameyamuditam /
children.translated_text: '<s>Upameyopamā</s>' and so forth — 'the [figure] called <s>upameyopamā</s>' is a certain ornament, 'common' — not distinct [from simile]. Why? — because of the relevance (<s>prastutatva</s>) of the simile. For what reason? — 'because of the non-otherness of the definition' — the definition is the distinctive designation of its own essential nature; the non-otherness of that means the impossibility of its existing in a distinct state, i.e., the absence of an excess beyond [simile]. And in the analysis 'that in which the compared becomes the standard of comparison,' the compared becomes the standard, and what was the standard is declared to be the compared.

children.text: "prasuptamathāvā nidrā ca śokātmatāmāpannasya hṛdayahārīti raterāśvāsanābhūmayaḥ" // VjivC_3.140 //
children.translated_text: 'Fallen asleep, or rather — sleep, having assumed the nature of grief, steals the heart — these are the grounds of consolation for <s>rati</s> (love).' // VjivC_3.140 //
Whether from this point the status of being a variety of <s>tulyayogitā</s> (equal pairing) is established or not — he says:
That [figure] called <s>tulyayogitā</s> is not a separate ornament;
in this [simile], many or two objects that are equally paired // Vjiv_3.39 //
attain the status of varieties, due to the removal of primacy.

children.text: (vastu mukhyatayā varṇyaṃ, kiṃ syāt kasya bhūṣaṇam) // Vjiv_3.40 //
children.translated_text: (The subject described as principal — what would be the ornament of what?) // Vjiv_3.40 //

children.text:
yeyaṃ tulyayogitā nāma nāsāvalaṅkṛtiḥ yasmāt "etasyāṃ dvau bahavo vā padārthāḥ tulyayoginaḥ prakāratvamupapadyante, "varṇanīyatāṃ nīyante /
atra varṇyate mukhyatayā varṇanīyaṃ vastu (iti) kiṃ kasya vibhūṣaṇaṃ syāt alaṅkaraṇaṃ bhavet /
pratyekaṃ prādhānye niyamā niściteḥ na kiṃcit kasyacidityarthaḥ /
yadi vā sarvasya kasyacidbhūṣaṇatvaṃ syādityabhidhīyate, tatraitadapi nopapadyate /
kasmāt---"prādhānyasya" = parito mukhyabhāvasya "nivartanāt " /
yasmādbhūṣaṇatve sati parāṅgatvameva /
tena vastunaḥ prādhānyaṃ nivartate /
mukhyaṃ hi vastu yenaiva rūpeṇaprādhānyamanubhavati, na tenaiva parāṅgatvamanubhavitumarhati, rūpāntaraṃ vinā parasparāviruddhayorekatrānupapatteḥ /
yadi vā rājānucarādāvekasmin mukhyatvaṃ guṇabhāvaśca saṃbhavatītyabhidhīyate, tatra rūpadvayasya saṃbhāvta, tathā ca rājānucareṣu svāmyapekṣayā bhṛtyabhāvaḥ svabhṛtyāpekṣayā svāmibhāvaśceti dharmadvayaṃ viruddhavyapekṣādvitayalakṣaṇasya rūpadvayasya vidyamānatvādupapannameva /
tadevamihāpi svarūpāntarasadbhāve bhūṣaṇatvaṃ kena vāryate /
satyametatat /
bhūṣaṇatvaṃ na vāryate tulyayogitāprakāratvaṃ punarapasāryate ityāha---
children.translated_text: 'That called <s>tulyayogitā</s>' — this is not an ornament, because 'in this, two or many objects that are equally paired attain the status of varieties,' i.e., are brought to the state of being described. Here, the subject described as the principal thing to be described — 'what would be the ornament of what?' — what would be the ornamentation of what? Since there is a definite restriction of primacy for each individually, nothing [is the ornament] of anything — this is the meaning. Or if it be said that any one of all [the subjects] would have the status of being an ornament, even that is not tenable. Why? — 'due to the removal of primacy' — the removal of principal status everywhere. Since when ornament-status obtains, there is only subordination. Thereby the primacy of the subject is removed. For indeed, the principal subject, by that very form through which it experiences primacy, cannot experience subordination by that same form — because without a difference of form, the co-existence of mutually contradictory [properties] in one thing is impossible. Or if it be said that, as in the case of a king's retainer and the like, both mastership and servanthood are possible in one [person] — there, the existence of two forms is possible, and thus in [the case of] the king's retainers, servanthood in relation to their master and mastership in relation to their own servants — the twofold property is established because of the existence of two forms characterized by two mutually contradictory relations. Thus, even here, if another form of its own [nature] exists, who prevents it from having ornament-status? This is true. Ornament-status is not prevented; but the variety-status of <s>tulyayogitā</s> is removed — he says:
Or, the describability of these — if the equality is in excess,

children.text: eteṣāṃ prastutānāṃ sā bhavatyupamitiḥ sphuṭam // Vjiv_3.41 //
children.translated_text: then of these relevant [subjects], that clearly becomes a simile (<s>upamiti</s>). // Vjiv_3.41 //

children.text:
varṇyatvamityādi = "athavā" ityanena prakārāntarasyopapatteḥ /
avarṇyatve 'pi varṇanīyabhāve bhavatyapyeteṣāṃ prastutānāṃ padārthānāṃ yadi "sāmyaṃ" = sādṛśyaṃ kadācitatiricyate = varṇyamānatvādadhikatāṃ pratipadyate /
tataḥ kiṃ syādityatrāha---"sā bhavatyupamitiḥ sphuṭam" prakaṭā cāsāvalaṅkṛtiḥ sāmyasamanvayādisaṃvādādupamaiva nānyā kācidityarthaḥ /
tathā samuccitopamāyāṃ---samuccitena varṇyamānatayār'thenābhisaṃbadhyamāne sati samuccitā upamā yasyāṃ sā tathoktā samuccitopamā, tadvattayā tulyaṃ vartate /
upamābhidhānamatropamāne vartate na samuccitopamāyām /
upamānaṃ prastutatvāt varṇanīyaṃ sāmyasamanvayātirekāt alaṅkaraṇāya kalpate yathā---
children.translated_text: 'Describability' and so forth — by 'or' (<s>athavā</s>), the establishment of another alternative [is indicated]. Even when there is no describability, yet if for these relevant objects the 'equality,' i.e., similarity, sometimes 'is in excess,' i.e., attains a greater degree than [what is inherent in] being described — then what would result? — to this he says: 'that clearly becomes a simile.' And that is a manifest ornament; through the correspondence of equality and connection, it is simile alone, nothing else — this is the meaning. Likewise, regarding <s>samuccitopamā</s> (accumulated simile) — [the term] 'accumulated' [means that] when a subject being described is connected with an accumulated [set of comparisons], the simile that is accumulated is thus called <s>samuccitopamā</s>; it operates in the same manner. The word 'simile' (<s>upamā</s>) here applies to the standard of comparison, not to the accumulated simile [as a separate figure]. The standard of comparison, being relevant and described, is fitted to serve as ornamentation through the excess of equality-connection. For example —

children.text: pararaimattaa amahe puṇo ssaṇo dei dāri aar pasaṇanu vinudi khilāsiṇio aṇo hucchaṇaṃ yadusadaṃ ca dappaṇo bahuṇi are (?) // VjivC_3.141 //
children.translated_text: [Prakrit:] 'The enemy's intoxication was appeased, and again [his own] valor returns; it gives a flood; moreover, the playful one drives away the [enemy] with arrows; another's entreaty — the [hero's] vaunting of the <s>Yadu</s> clan — and the mirror of pride — many [are the wonders], indeed!' // VjivC_3.141 //

children.text:
tadetadevamihāpi varṇyamānatve 'pi sāmyātirekādupamaiva bhavatumarhatīti bhāvaḥ /
yathā---
children.translated_text: Thus, this very [point holds] here too: even though being described, through the excess of equality, it deserves to become a simile alone — this is the purport. For example —
Both of those residents of <s>Sāketa</s> (<s>Ayodhyā</s>) were beings to be celebrated by the people:
the one [<s>Rāma</s>], free from desire for the treasure offered by the teacher, and the king [<s>Daśaratha</s>], more generous than the seekers' wishes. // VjivC_3.142 //

A standard of comparison fashioned in the domain of some other charming property — surpassing in its beautiful delicacy — shines forth for the attainment of the excellence of the intended compared-subject. For example —

children.text: ubhau yadi vyomni pṛthak-pravāhā- vākāśagaṅgāpayasaḥ patetām /
children.translated_text: If in the sky the waters of the celestial <s>Gaṅgā</s> were to fall in two separate streams,
by that [alone] could this chest of his be compared — dark as a <s>tamāla</s> tree, with released pearl-creepers. // VjivC_3.143 //

children.text:
(e) taddvayorapi nidarśanam /
tadevamananvaye 'pi varṇyamānasaukumāryamāhātmyāt kālpanikamapyumānaṃ nopapannamiti manyamānāḥ tatsvarūpasamāropitavyatirekāmupamāṃ tāṃ varṇyanti /
yathā---
children.translated_text: This is an illustration of both [types]. Thus, even in <s>ananvaya</s> (non-sequential [simile]), those who consider that, due to the greatness of the beauty of [what is] being described, even an imagined standard of comparison is not adequate — they describe that simile as one with <s>vyatireka</s> (contrast) superimposed upon its own essential nature. For example —

children.text: tatpūrvānubhave bhavanti laghavo bhāvāḥ śaśāṅkādayaḥ tadvaktropamite paraṃ pariṇamecceto rasāyāmbujāt /
children.translated_text: In the prior experience of that [face], the <s>bhāvas</s> (emotions) such as the moon and so forth become trivial; when [anything] is compared to that face, the mind would rather dissolve into the <s>rasa</s> of the lotus;

children.text: evaṃ niścinute manastava mukhaṃ saundaryasārāvadhi badhnāti vyavasāyametumupamotkarṣaṃ svakāntyā svayam // VjivC_3.144 //
children.translated_text: thus the mind determines: 'Your face is the ultimate essence of beauty' — and the standard of comparison itself, by its own radiance, abandons the enterprise of rising to [match] the excellence [of your face]. // VjivC_3.144 //
Thus, such is the manifold variety of the modes of descriptive expression — not of the distinctions of definitions.
The infinity of the modes of expression,
born of [poetic] intuition, cannot be stated explicitly — like the variety of the graceful play of a beautiful woman. // VjivC_3.145 //

children.text:
antaraślokaḥ /
tulyayogitāpyatraivāntarbhāvānnātiricyate /
tathā ca lakṣaṇaṃ nidarśanaṃ caitasyāḥ---
children.translated_text: This is an intermediate verse. <s>Tulyayogitā</s> too is included here [in simile] and does not stand apart. And the definition and illustration of this [figure] are:
Even of what is inferior, through the intention to express equality of qualities with what is superior,
by the conjunction of simultaneous action — thus is stated <s>tulyayogitā</s> (equal pairing). // VjivC_3.146 //

children.text:
iti /
taiḥ pratipāditā, yasmāt sāmyātiśayāt /
yathā---
children.translated_text: Thus. It was propounded by them [the earlier authorities], since [it arises] from the excess of equality. For example —

children.text: śeṣo himagiristvaṃ ca mahānto guravaḥ sthirāḥ /
children.translated_text: <s>Śeṣa</s> [the cosmic serpent], the snowy mountain, and you [the king] — [all three are] great, weighty, and steadfast;
never transgressing [your] bounds, you bear the earth as she trembles. // VjivC_3.147 //

children.text:
atra lakṣaṇe tāvadupamāntarbhāvaṃ tulyayogitāyāḥ pratipādayati-(asi)-dvātiśayasya vastunaḥ siddhātiśayena sādharmyasamanvayo nibandhanamupamāyāḥ; purarasyā guṇasāmyavivakṣayā tulyakālakriyāyogaḥ prastutāprastutasāmyavyatirekeṇa na kiñcidatra tātparyaṃ pratipādayati /
nidarśanamapyevaṃprāyameva /
varṇanāviṣayasya varṇyamānavṛttiśleṣādisāmyavyatirekeṇa atiriktatayā na kiñcidapi pratibhāsate /
tena caitadudāharaṇaṃ vivaktārthavṛttiśliṣṭatāpratibhāsamāhātmyāt na ca nidarśanāntaramiti yadabhiyuktataraiḥ tairevābhyadhāyita, na tadapi yuktiyuktam /
yathā---
children.translated_text: Here, regarding the definition, he demonstrates the inclusion of <s>tulyayogitā</s> within simile: the concordance (<s>sādharmyasamanvaya</s>) of an object whose excellence is to be established with one whose excellence is already established is the foundation of simile; the conjunction of simultaneous action through the intention of expressing equality of qualities for the other — apart from the distinction of equality between the relevant and irrelevant — presents no [distinct] purport here. The illustration too is of this very nature. Apart from the distinction of equality through <s>śleṣa</s> (paronomasia) and the like in the conduct of what is being described as the object of description, nothing at all appears as distinct. Therefore, [the claim] that was stated by those more learned [authorities] themselves — that this example, due to the greatness of the appearance of the paronomastic character of the conduct of the intended meaning, is not [merely] another illustration — even that is not well-reasoned. For example —

children.text: yairdṛṣṭā sā na vā dṛṣṭā muṣitāḥ samameva te /
children.translated_text: Those who have seen her and those who have not seen her — they are equally robbed:
of the former, the heart has been stolen; of the latter, the fruit of their eyes. // VjivC_3.148 //

children.text:
etadalaṅkāravārtāmātrānabhijñasya kasyacitpralapitamiti sacetasāṃ pratibhāsate /
yasmādvaidagdhyasya bhaṅgyā taruṇīlāvaṇyātiśayapratipādanapareyaṃ aprastutapraśaṃsā kavicetasi parisphurati /
yadi vā nidarśanāntaraviṣayatvena tulyayogitā saṃbhavati /
yathā---
children.translated_text: This strikes the sensitive as the prattle of someone who is not acquainted even with the rudiments of ornament-lore. Because what shines forth in the poet's mind is the <s>aprastutapraśaṃsā</s> (praise of the irrelevant [to praise the relevant]), aimed at conveying the surpassing loveliness of the young woman through the manner of cleverness. Or, [if one considers it] as being in the domain of another illustration, <s>tulyayogitā</s> is possible. For example —

children.text: yatkāvyārthanirūpaṇaṃ prayikathālāpā raho 'vasthitaṃ kaṇṭhāntaṃ mṛdugītamādṛtasuhṛdaduḥkhāntarāvedanam // VjivC_3.149 //
children.translated_text: 'The examination of poetic subject-matter, the conversations in a festive gathering, the intimate soft singing, the revelation of the inner grief of a dear friend who is honored —' // VjivC_3.149 //

children.text:
ananvayo 'pyupamāyāmevāntarbhavatīti vivecyate /
tathā cāsya lakṣaṇamudāharaṇaṃ ca---
children.translated_text: <s>Ananvaya</s> (non-sequential [simile]) too is included within simile itself — this is examined. And its definition and example are:
Where, by that very [thing] itself, there is the relation of standard-and-compared,
due to the intention of expressing incomparability — that they call <s>ananvaya</s>. // VjivC_3.150 //
Having a ring of <s>tāmbūla</s>-redness, with gleaming teeth-radiance,
with eyes beautiful as <s>indīvara</s> (blue lotus) — your face is [comparable only] to your own face. // VjivC_3.151 //

children.text:
etasya lakṣaṇānanyatvameva (vaṃ) (tatsahāya) mabhidhāvaicitryavidhāyakatvaṃ ceti dvitayamapyupamāntarbhāvameva sādhayati /
tatropamānopameyabhāvavyavasthiteḥ /
upamāntareṇa saha lakṣaṇānvitatvamananvayasya na saṃbhavatītyabhīdhīyate tadapi na samādhānaṃ, yasmātsamāropitarūpasya (dvitvasyābhyupagamādu) pamānopameyabhāvasaṃbandhanibandhanameva (sāmyaṃ) bhavatāmananvayalaśraṇasya pravṛttinimittam, asmākaṃ kevalenāpi sādhyate tadityāha---
children.translated_text: Two things establish the inclusion of this [<s>ananvaya</s>] within simile: the non-otherness of its definition [from simile's], and its being effected by the variety of descriptive expression, assisted by that [simile]. Therein, because of the established relation of standard-and-compared. [If it be said that] the <s>ananvaya</s> cannot share a definition with any other simile — even that is not a resolution, because for those [authorities], the very equality that is the foundation of the relation of standard-and-compared — [proceeding] from the acceptance of a superimposed duality of form — is the cause of the application of their definition of <s>ananvaya</s>; for us, even by [equality] alone it is established — thus he says:
Poets know <s>ananvaya</s> to be equal to <s>kalpitopamā</s> (imagined simile). // Vjiv_3.42 //

children.text:
"kalpitā"---ullikhitā (vā) "upamā" yasyāḥ sā tathoktā /
tathā kalpitopamayā "tulyaṃ" anyūnānatiriktamananvayamalaṅkaraṇaṃ "kavayaḥ"---tadvidaḥ "viduḥ"---jānanti /
tathā ca kalpitopamāyāṃ varṇanāviṣayasya vastunaḥ saundaryadhārādhirūḍhasvasāmya samanvayaḥ samudbhavati /
sātiśayatvasamarpaṇasāmarthyavirahāt sarveṣāṃ padārthānāṃ bhūtānāmasadbhataṃ kimapi kālpanikamupamānamullikhanto yathāruci rucirāśayāḥ kavayaḥ paridṛśyante /
(asadbhūtaṃ) samullikhitamiti ca punarapi parasparasāmyanibandhanastayorupamānopameyabhāvaḥ paryavasyāti, nānyatkiñcidatiriktaṃ manohāritāyāḥ kāraṇam /
tathā ca lakṣaṇamudāharaṇaṃ ca
children.translated_text: '<s>Kalpitā</s>' — 'imagined' or 'delineated'; the simile that has that [imagined quality] is thus called. Thus, <s>ananvaya</s> [is] 'equal' to <s>kalpitopamā</s> — neither less nor more — [this] ornament is [what] the 'poets,' the knowledgeable ones, 'know,' i.e., understand. And in <s>kalpitopamā</s>, the concordance of self-equality, mounted upon the stream of beauty of the subject being described, arises. Poets of charming disposition are seen delineating, according to their fancy, some imagined and unprecedented standard of comparison for all real objects — due to the absence of the capacity to convey a state of surpassing excellence. And since [what has been] delineated is 'as if [really] existent' — again the relation of standard-and-compared between the two terminates in their mutual equality as its foundation, and nothing else beyond that is the cause of their captivating quality. And thus the definition and example [follow]:

children.text: upameyopamāṃ nāma bruvate tāṃ yathoditām // VjivC_3.152 //
children.translated_text: They call it <s>upameyopamā</s> (reciprocal simile), as stated above. // <s>Vjīv</s>C 3.152 //
Fragrant, delighting the eyes, pinkish with the intoxication of wine,

children.text: ambhojamiva te vaktraṃ tvadāsyamiva paṅkajam // VjivC_3.153 //
children.translated_text: Your face is like a lotus, and the lotus is like your face. // <s>Vjīv</s>C 3.153 //

children.text:
nāpyatra lakṣaṇamupamālaṅkārādalaṅkārāntarasya kāraṇam /
pūrvoktayā nītyā tasya nirākṛtatvāt /
(upamānopameyabhāvaścātra paryāyato bhavet) /
(te) nopamānopameyabhāve (bheda) pratibhāso 'bhedapratibhāso 'pi sapra (māṇaḥ) /
na ca upamānāntaranirāsalakṣaṇatātparyādalaṅkārāntaratvam, mukhamindurityādau upamānetarasvabhāvagandhasyāpyavidyamānatvā (t) /
(pratibhā) pratibhāsi prauḍhipratipāditamabhidhāprakāravaicitryamātramevātra vijṛmbhate na punaralaṅkaraṇāntaratvam /
vācyāntareṣvapi vaicitryāntaradar (śanāt) /
yathā---
children.translated_text: Nor is the definition here a reason for [positing] a figure separate from the simile-figure. Because that [separate figure] has been refuted by the previously stated principle. (And here the relation of standard and object of comparison would be alternating.) The appearance of difference (or non-difference) in the relation of standard and object of comparison is not authoritative. Nor is it a separate figure due to the purport of negating another standard of comparison, because in 'the face is the moon' and the like, not even a trace of another standard's nature exists. The variety of modes of expression, established by the vigor of poetic intuition, alone manifests here -- not the status of a separate ornament. Because variety of a different kind is seen in other expressible contents as well. For example --

children.text: tadvalgunā yugapadunmiṣitena tāvat sadyaḥ parasparatulāmādhirohatāṃ dve //
children.translated_text: With that charming [glance] suddenly opened, at once let the two ascend to mutual comparison --

children.text: praspandamānaparuṣetaratāramantaḥ cakṣustava pracalitabhramaraṃ ca padmam // VjivC_3.154 //
children.translated_text: Your eye, with its restless, rough, other star within, and the lotus with its trembling bee. // <s>Vjīv</s>C 3.154 //
For example --
<s>Rāma</s> and <s>Lakṣmaṇa</s>, those two inhabitants of <s>Sāketa</s> (Ayodhyā), were both of commendable character.
The one (the prince) was more free from desire than the wealth given by the preceptor; and the king was more generous than those desirous of wealth. // <s>Vjīv</s>C 3.155 //

children.text:
atra dvayorapi prastutatvādvarṇanīyasāmyasadbhāvaḥ (na) punaralaṅkārabhāvaḥ /
yathā vā---
children.translated_text: Here, since both are being described, there is equality of things to be depicted, not a figure-relation. Or for example --
He who playfully broke <s>Hara</s>'s (<s>Śiva</s>'s) bow, he too who with playful steps gratified the crescent-moon-crested one (<s>Śiva</s>),

children.text: tasyaiva so 'sya ca....sakhya vā syāt ślāghyaṃ dvayorubhayathāpi tavādya teṣām // VjivC_3.156 //
children.translated_text: Between that one and this one... there could be friendship, or praiseworthy [comparison] -- for both, in both ways, [this belongs] to you today, among them. // <s>Vjīv</s>C 3.156 //

children.text:
atra pūrvoktamevānusandheyam /
yadyapyupamālakṣaṇāvasare bhāvamātramityubhayaniṣṭhamalaṅkaraṇa mākhyātam, tathāpi tatrāprastutatvādupamānasya parāṅgatvamupapannam /
iha punaḥ prastutasya mukhyatvam /
kathaṃ taditi vicāritameva /
parivṛttirapyanena nyāyena pṛthaṅ nāstīti nirūpyate /
tathā ca lakṣaṇaṃ parivṛtteḥ---
children.translated_text: Here, what was stated previously should be followed. Although at the occasion of defining simile, what was declared as ornament was called 'mere being' (<s>bhāvamātra</s>) resting on both [terms], nevertheless, since the standard of comparison is not the primary topic, its subordinate status is justified there. But here, the primacy of the primary subject [obtains]. How that is so has already been examined. <s>Parivṛtti</s> (exchange/reversal) too, by this same principle, is shown to not exist as a separate [figure]. And the definition of <s>parivṛtti</s> is --

children.text: "arthānāṃ yo vinamayaḥ parivṛttistu sā matā " // VjivC_3.157 //
children.translated_text: "The interchange of meanings -- that is considered <s>parivṛtti</s> (exchange)." // <s>Vjīv</s> 3.157 //

children.text:
iti /
parivartanaṃ ca sāvantarāvakāśe vastvantarasyāvasthānam /
asau parivṛttiralaṅkāro 'bhidhīyate /
sā ca bahuprakārā---ekasyaiva viṣayiṇā samucitaviṣayāvakāśe viṣayāntaraṃ parivartate /
yathā---
children.translated_text: Thus. And exchange is the placement of another entity in the available space of [the original entity]. That exchange is called a figure. And it is of many kinds -- [in one type,] a single perceiver's appropriate domain is exchanged for another domain. For example --

children.text: svalpaṃ jalpa bṛhaspate suraguro naiṣā sabhā vijriṇaḥ // VjivC_3.158 //
children.translated_text: "Speak briefly, O <s>Bṛhaspati</s>, teacher of the gods! This is not the assembly of the sinful one." // <s>Vjīv</s>C 3.158 //

children.text:
kvacidekasyaiva krameṇa samuccitadharmagocare dharmāntaraṃ parivartate /
yathā---
children.translated_text: Sometimes, for a single [entity], in sequence, one property is exchanged for another within the domain of the appropriate property. For example --
"Withdrawn from the lip that has shed its color, and from the ball reddened by the body-ointment of her breasts,
Her hand, its fingers scratched by picking <s>kuśa</s> grass, was made devoted to the rosary by her." // <s>Vjīv</s>C 3.159 //

children.text:
atra gauryāḥ karakalalakṣaṇo dharmaḥ parivartitaḥ kvacidekasyaiva dharmiṇaḥ sucitasvasaṃvādidharmāvakāśe dharmāntaraṃ parivartate /
yathā---
children.translated_text: Here, the property in the form of the activity of <s>Gaurī</s>'s hand has been exchanged. Sometimes, for a single possessor of properties, another property is exchanged within the domain of its own corresponding property. For example --
"Why, casting aside ornaments in youth,
Have you donned bark-garments, which befit old age?" // <s>Vjīv</s>C 3.160 //

children.text:
kvacidvahūnāmapi dharmiṇāṃ parispardhinā pūrvoktāḥ sarve 'pi parivartante /
tathā ca lakṣaṇakāreṇātraivodāharaṇaṃ darśitam /

children.translated_text: For example --
"By the arm of your king that dealt weapon-blows,

children.text: cirārjitaṃ hṛtaṃ teṣāṃ yaśaḥ kumudapāṇḍuram // VjivC_3.161 //
children.translated_text: Their long-earned fame, white as jasmine, was seized." // <s>Vjīv</s>C 3.161 //
Sometimes, all the previously stated [types] are exchanged even for many possessors of properties, in a rivalrous manner. And the author of the definition has shown an example right here.
Thus, [<s>Kuntaka</s>] states that the status of <s>parivṛtti</s> as a [separate] ornament is not appropriate --
"The withdrawal of one thing, which is [simultaneously] the occurrence of another --

children.text: tadalaṅkaraṇaṃ na syāt pūrvavat parivartanāt // Vjiv_3.43 //
children.translated_text: That is not an ornament, because of [being merely] an exchange, as before." // <s>Vjīv</s> 3.43 //

children.text:
vinivartanamityādi---"yadekasya" padārthasya "vinivartanaṃ" apākaraṇaṃ "tadanyasya" tadvyatiriktasya parasya, "vartanaṃ" tadupanibandhanaṃ tadalaṅkaraṇaṃ na bhavati /
kasmāt ubhayoḥ "parivartamānatvāt" mukhyenābhidhīyamānatvāt /
kathaṃ "pūrvavat" yathāpūrvaṃ pratyekaṃ prādhānyānniyamāniściteśca (yathā) na kiñcit kasyacidalaṅkaraṇaṃ, tadvadihāpi vicāritam /
na ca tāvanmātrarūpatayā tayoḥ parasparavibhūṣaṇa (vibhūṣya) bhāvaḥ, (tathā sati) prādhānyanivartanaprasaṅgāt /
rūpāntarānirodheṣu punaḥ sāmyasadbhāve bhavatyupamitireṣā cālaṅkṛtiḥ samuccitopamāvat pūrvavadeva /
yathā---
children.translated_text: 'Withdrawal' etc. -- 'The withdrawal' -- the removal -- 'of one' object, [which is simultaneously] 'the occurrence' -- the establishment -- 'of another,' i.e. of a different, subsequent [thing] -- that is not an ornament. Why? Because of 'exchange' -- because both are expressed as primary. How? 'As before' -- just as previously, since neither is established as the ornament of the other because each individually has primacy, so too here it has been examined. Nor do those two have the relation of ornament and ornamented merely by having that much form, since that would entail the abandonment of primacy. But when there is no obstruction of other forms and similarity exists, there arises simile -- and this is an ornament, just like an appropriate simile, as before. For example --
"Compassionately did the great-armed one embrace, [thinking] 'she might suddenly flee in alarm' --

children.text: aciropanatāṃ sa medinīṃ navapāṇigrahaṇāṃ vadhūmiva // VjivC_3.162 //
children.translated_text: The recently acquired earth, like a bride at the moment of taking her hand." // <s>Vjīv</s>C 3.162 //

children.text:
atra samatayā (dhriyamāṇaḥ) sānurāgaḥ pṛthivī (vadhūbhoga) yatnaḥ pārthivasya pratīyate, dvayorapi varṇyamānatvāt, tathā parivṛttāvapi sāmyapratiterupamaiva /
yathā---
children.translated_text: Here, the king's effort -- maintained with equality [of treatment], affectionate -- in [governing] the earth (and enjoying his bride) is perceived, since both are being described. Similarly, even in <s>parivṛtti</s> (exchange), when similarity is perceived, it is simile alone. For example --
"This battle that ends the lives of spies delighted [them], and the soldiers of the king also [delighted];

children.text: iha vrato śaktiśirobhirādarāt navāsidhārā na khalūtpalastrajaḥ // VjivC_3.163 //
children.translated_text: Here the vow [is fulfilled] with heads [mounted on] spears attentively -- [these are] indeed not lotus-garlands but new sword-edges!" // <s>Vjīv</s>C 3.163 //

children.text:
sāmyapratibhāsamātraṃ (atra) manohāritāyāḥ kāraṇamityalaṅkaraṇam /
yasmādevaṃvidhe viṣaye vicchittividhānasya saṃniyata (sāmyaṃ) pratīyamānamalaṅkaraṇamupanibadhnanti, na punarabhidhīyamānameva /
pratīyamānatvaṃ parivṛtterapi dṛśyate /
yathā---
children.translated_text: The mere appearance of similarity here is the cause of charm, hence it is an ornament. Because in such a domain, those who establish the arrangement of charm tie [it to] the perceived similarity as the ornament, not [to] what is merely expressed. And the quality of being perceived [rather than expressed] is seen in <s>parivṛtti</s> too. For example --

children.text: nirdiṣṭāṃ kulapatinā sa parṇaśālā- madhyāsya prayataparigrahadvitīyaḥ /
children.translated_text: "In the leaf-hut assigned by the patriarch, accompanied by his ritually-received [wife],

children.text: tacchiṣyādhyayananiveditāvasānāṃ saṃviṣṭaḥ kuśaśayane niśāṃ nināya // VjivC_3.164 //
children.translated_text: He spent the night lying upon a bed of <s>kuśa</s> grass, [the night's] end announced by his disciples' recitation." // <s>Vjīv</s>C 3.164 //

children.text:
atra sarvāṇyapi padāni yathāsvamākṣiptaparivartanīyapadārthāntarāṇyupanibaddhāni, tataḥ pratīyamānatvāttadvidāhlādakāritvamapi ( na ca) saṃvādinī parivṛttiḥ katham amupapadyamānatvāt anyathā ? (satyaṃ) yuktametat /
na parivṛtteratyantābhāvo 'smābhirabhidhīyate, varṇanīyatvādalaṅkṛtirna bhavatītyasmākamabhiprāyaḥ /
na ca pratīyamānatāmātramalaṅkaraṇasādhanam, alaṅkāryavastumātre 'pi tasyāḥ saṃbhavāt /
tathācaitadevodāharaṇam /
na ca yatpratīyamānaṃ tadalaṅkaraṇaṃ tadvidāhlādakāritvāt iti yujyate vaktum /
alaṅkārye 'pi tadvidāhlādakāritvasya darśanāt /
vastumātramalaṅkāro rasādayaśceti bhedatritayānupapatteśca /
kiṃ ca parivṛtteralaṅkāratve tadupaśobhāyai bhūṣaṇāntaraṃ nopayujyate, "kimityapāsyābharaṇāni" ityādau /
yadi vā "vada pradoṣe sphuṭacandratārakā vibhāvarī yadyaruṇāya kalpate" iti /
yadi vā bhūṣaṇe 'pi vibhūṣaṇāntaramasantoṣādupanibadhnantītyabhidhīyate, tadapi na yuktiyuktam /
yasmādanyasmin vibhūṣye saṃbhavati yatra bhūṣaṇopanibandhaḥ, tatra bhūṣaṇāntaramasantoṣādupapadyate, na punaranyasmin /
neyaṃ pūrvoktayā nītyā pratyekameva parasparaṃ dvayorapi bhūṣaṇabhāve pratyārakhāte parivṛttervibhūṣā saṃbhavati, yatra bhūṣaṇatvamevāvaśiṣyate /
tasmādupaśobhārthamupamākhyamalaṅkaraṇamupanibaddham /
tathā cāyamatra vākyārthaḥ---yauvanodbhedasamayasamucitābharaṇāpasāraṇapūrvakaṃ vārdhakopapannacīraparidhānagrahaṇaṃ prakaṭaśaśāṅkatārakayā (vibhāvaryā pradoṣe 'ruṇasamāgamakalpamiti) kimapi kāvyasphuritabhūtaṃ tadvidāhlādakāritvamunmīlayati /
tadayamatra paramārthaḥ---lakṣaṇollikhitarekhayā vibhūṣaṇavinyāso vidhātavyaḥ /
pratibhāpratibhāsamānabhaṇitivakratāprakāravaicitryeṇāpi yathā---
children.translated_text: Here, all the words are so arranged that each implies another interchangeable meaning, and therefore, because of being perceived [rather than expressed], the delight it produces for the connoisseur [is real]. 'But how can <s>parivṛtti</s> (exchange) not apply, since it is consonant?' True, this is reasonable. We do not assert the complete non-existence of <s>parivṛtti</s>; our view is that because it is [merely] something to be described, it does not become an ornament. Nor is mere perceivability alone the means of establishing ornament-status, since that [perceivability] is possible even in the mere subject matter that is to be ornamented. And this is exactly such an example. Nor is it proper to say 'whatever is perceived is an ornament because it produces delight for the connoisseur,' since delight for the connoisseur is seen even in what is to be ornamented [itself]. Because the threefold division -- mere subject matter, ornament, and <s>rasa</s> etc. -- would become impossible. Moreover, if <s>parivṛtti</s> were an ornament, no other ornament would be needed to embellish it, as in 'why casting aside ornaments' etc. Or as in 'tell me, if a night radiant with clear moon and stars serves for the dawn.' Or if one says that even for an ornament, another ornament is tied [to it] out of dissatisfaction -- that too is not logically sound. For [another ornament] is possible in a different thing to be ornamented where the tying of an ornament [occurs]; there, another ornament out of dissatisfaction is justified, but not in another [context]. This [<s>parivṛtti</s>], by the previously stated principle -- since each individually adorns the other and vice versa -- the possibility of <s>parivṛtti</s> being an ornament remains only where ornament-status alone is left over. Therefore, the ornament called simile is tied [to it] for the purpose of embellishment. And thus the sentence-meaning here is: the casting aside of ornaments appropriate to the time of youthful bloom, followed by the donning of bark-garments proper to old age -- [compared to] a night of visible moon and stars [compared to] the arrival of dawn -- reveals a certain poetic truth that produces delight for the connoisseur. Thus the ultimate meaning here is: the arrangement of ornaments must be made according to the line sketched by the definition. Also through the variety of modes of obliqueness of expression, appearing as poetic intuition -- for example --
[Prakrit verse, partially corrupt:] ... // <s>Vjīv</s>C 3.165 //
"Because the distinguished meaning is shown by the action itself,
This should be known as <s>nidarśanā</s> (illustration) alone, without words like 'as if' and 'like'." // <s>Vjīv</s> 3.166 //
Thus, what has been identified as <s>nidarśanā</s> (illustration) is also just simile.
"This sun, of dim radiance, wishes to set toward the west,
Informing men that 'rising is [only] for falling' -- even for the glorious." // <s>Vjīv</s>C 3.167 //

children.text:
atra tathaiveti kavipratibhārpitatātparyāntaraniścayalakṣaṇasya vastunaḥ tadiveti tadeveti vā sādṛśyasya pratipādakaṃ vinā tatpratipādanapragalbhavākya prayogamāhātmyādutprekṣāyāḥ pratīyamānatvāt /
yathā--- pavāṇa cala vijju ca duliṃ rāiāsu khanaanti me aāso uvāṇa urulisavdayami hiḷiāsuka jillai virahae /
children.translated_text: Here, without [the use of] 'thus' -- which would convey similarity as 'like that' or 'that very [thing]' -- the determination of another purport ascribed by poetic imagination, which has the character of factual [statement], [is established]. Because <s>utprekṣā</s> (poetic fancy) is perceived due to the power of the sentence-usage that is bold enough to convey that without [explicit expression]. For example -- [Prakrit:] 'O wind, move! O lightning! In the nights, dig wells! My hopes, rise up! I roll about. O one departed in jealousy, in separation...'
[Prakrit verse, partially corrupt] // <s>Vjīv</s>C 3.168 //

children.text: atra garjitaśabdaṃ śrutvā mahilāsu kāsucit...calavidyudbhāvikā (la) rātriṣu meghān vilokayantīti....mahilānāmabhiprāyaniścayasyāgocaratvāt vākyārthasyānyathānupapatteśca pūrvoktamanusartavyam /
children.translated_text: Here, having heard the sound of thunder, among the women, some... the nature of flashing lightning -- on nights when they gaze at the clouds -- since the intention of the women is beyond the reach [of direct expression], and because the sentence-meaning cannot be understood otherwise, what was stated earlier should be followed.
He, [resembling] the beauty of the half-risen orb of the moon... even he...
Drew upon himself the beauty of the forehead-mark of <s>Kāmapāla</s> (the Protector of Love), surpassed by his dim radiance. // <s>Vjīv</s>C 3.169 //

children.text:
atrārdhoditendubimbaśobhāyāḥ sādṛśyollaṅghitakāmapālalalāṭapaṭṭaśriyaḥ.....tadapyatiriktavṛttidhamyarntareṇa camatkārakāraṇamanyathā na kiñcanāpi upapadyate /
nānārthamupamāyāḥ kriyāpadamevaṃvidhapratipādakatāṃ prāpnoti /
tataśca gatārthatvābhidhāyinaḥ śabdasyāprayogaḥ sākṣādvilocanarathavṛttirna bhavatītyupacārapāraṃparyeṇa tadviśeṣaṇatāṃ prāpyate /
tathā ca dharmadharmibhāvalakṣaṇāyāḥ pratyāsatteḥ prathamaṃ svābhidheyalakṣaṇalakṣaṇāyā guṇamātreṇaiva tataśca sādṛśyanibandhanāyāḥ pratyāsattereva tatsadṛśe vilocanacchāyātiśayavṛttimāsādayati /
tadviśeṣaṇatvādeva samāse 'smin nīlotpalaśabdasya pūrvanipātaḥ saptamīviśeṣaṇe bahuvrīhāviti /
indumukhītyatra induriva mukhaṃ yasyāḥ sā tathoktā /
sakalalokavilokyamānākhilamṛgāṅkamaṇḍalasaṃsthānasādṛśye nimittabhāve pūrvoktayaiva (nītyā) induśabdasyaiva viśeṣaṇatvamiti pūrvavadeva samāsopapattiḥ /
yadi vā indumukhamiva mukhaṃ yasyāḥ sā tathoktetyatra induśabdastadekadeśe mukhe viśeṣaṇam (bhavati) yathā grāmo dagdha iti /
śiṣṭaṃ pūrvoktamevānusandheyam /
"puruṣavyāghraḥ" ityatra sādhāraṇadharmo 'pi pratīyate /
saṃbandhaṃ vinopamānopameyabhāvasyānupapatteḥ; padābhisaṃbandhasāmarthyāttasyāvagatau gatārthatvāt sāmānyaśabdasyāprayogaḥ /
tadidamuktam "upamitaṃ vyāghrādibhiḥ sāmānyāprayoge" iti /
induriva kāntaṃ mukhaṃ yasyāḥ sā indukāntamukhītyatra sāmānyaśabdasya śrūyamāṇatayā yuktirabhidhīyate /
"induriva kāntamindukāntam" iti "upamānāni sāmānyavacanaiḥ" ityanena samāse vihite paścādindukāntaṃ mukhaṃ yasyāḥ sā tathokteti /
sāmānyaśabdasya vṛttivākyayordvayorapi upapadyamānatvānna kenacinnyāyena śrūyamāṇatā vicārayituṃ pāryate, yatastenaiva saha padāntaraṃ samasyate, na punaranyeneti kutastasya śrūyamāṇavṛtteḥ pratīyamānatā kalpeta ? /
tadevaṃ vivakṣāvaśāt kvacidgamyamānatā, kvacitprayujyamānatvam /
evamādīnāṃ sādṛśyanibandhanobhayaviṣaya (sāmānya) saṃbandhābhidhāyināṃ gamyamānatvāda prayujyamānatvam /
arthapratyāyanārthaṃ hi śabdasya prayogaḥ kriyate /
sa cet kavikauśalakalpitāt prākārāntarāt pratipannaḥ tataḥ kiṃ śabdaprayogeṇa ? /
tathāca yatra anyūnātiriktacchāyāviśeṣamarthataḥ śabdataścopamānopameyayoḥ sāmyasamarpaṇa sāmarthya subhagaprasādasundaramupanibandhabandhuraṃ vākyaṃ śrutisamanantarameva varṇānupūrvyāḥ pratibhāsavadarthapratipattipūrvakamalaṅkāra pratīti mutpādayati, tatra tadupapādakānāmivādīnāṃ gatārthatvādaprayuktiḥ /
yathā--
children.translated_text: Here, the beauty of the half-risen moon-disc, the splendor of <s>Kāmapāla</s>'s forehead-plate surpassed by the likeness... that too, without an additional property exceeding the ordinary, cannot serve as a cause of aesthetic charm — otherwise nothing at all would be justified. The action-word of simile attains such demonstrative capacity in various ways. Consequently, since a word denoting what is already understood would not be employed, the activity of the eye does not directly function as a chariot — rather, through a chain of figurative usage, that qualifying status is reached. And thus, due to the proximity of the property-property-bearer relation, first [comes] the characteristic of one's own denotation, then merely as a quality; and then, due to the proximity based on similarity, it reaches the activity of the excellence of the eye's glow in that which is similar. Because of being a qualification of that, in this compound the word '<s>nīlotpala</s>' (blue lotus) comes first, according to the rule of locative-qualifier <s>bahuvrīhi</s> compounds. In '<s>indumukhī</s>' (moon-faced), she whose face is like the moon — she is so called. When the resemblance to the form of the entire moon-disc beheld by all the world is the cause, by the very principle stated before, the word '<s>indu</s>' (moon) itself becomes the qualifier — thus the compound is justified as before. Or alternatively, she whose face is like a moon-face — in this case, the word '<s>indu</s>' qualifies a part of it, namely the face, just as in 'the village was burned.' The rest should be understood as stated before. In '<s>puruṣavyāghraḥ</s>' (man-tiger), even the common property is implied. For without a relation, the state of being the compared and the object of comparison would not be possible; and since through the capacity of the word-connection that [common property] is understood, the generic word is not employed because it would be redundant. This is what has been stated: '<s>upamitaṃ vyāghrādibhiḥ sāmānyāprayoge</s>' (compared with tiger etc., when the generic term is not used). In '<s>indukāntamukhī</s>' (she whose face is moon-lovely), where the face is lovely like the moon — here, since the generic word is heard [in the compound], the reasoning is stated: 'lovely like the moon — <s>indukānta</s>' — by the rule 'objects of comparison with words denoting the common property,' when the compound is formed, then afterwards 'she whose face is moon-lovely, she is so called.' Since the generic word is justified in both the compound and the sentence, its being heard cannot be questioned by any principle — for it is with that very [word] that another word is compounded, not with anything else — so how could the heard form be imagined as implied? Thus, depending on the speaker's intention, sometimes [the common property] is implied, sometimes it is expressed. Of such [expressions] where the generic relation denoting the common ground based on similarity between both [compared and object of comparison] is implied, there is non-employment [of the word]. For the employment of a word is for the purpose of conveying meaning. If that [meaning] is grasped through some other device contrived by the poet's skill, then what is the use of employing the word? And thus, where a sentence that is graceful with lovely clarity, endowed with the capacity to present the equality of the compared and the object of comparison in meaning and in word — with a beauty that is neither deficient nor excessive — immediately upon hearing, produces the cognition of the figure preceded by the comprehension of meaning as if a flash of the sequence of phonemes, there, the words 'iva' etc. that would establish [the simile] are not employed because they would be redundant. For example:
Of a mountain that has sons, too... [<s>Vakroktijīvita</s> Commentary 3.170]

children.text:
yatrāpyalaṅkārāntarabhedanibandhanamantareṇa padārthaparivartanādau kavikauśalollāsitātiriktasāmyasamanvaya māhātmyādupamānopameyabhāvāvagatirudbhidyate, tatrāpyabhidhānaprakāravaicitryavaśādalaṅkaraṇavicchittireva tadvidāṃ tatpratītikāriṇāñcamatkṛtikāritāmāvahatīti pratīyamānatvamalaṅkārasya /
tadabhidhāyināmivādīnāmaprayogo yathā---
children.translated_text: Where also, without being grounded in a distinction of another figure, from the interchange of word-meanings etc., due to the power of an excellent concordance of similarity enlivened by the poet's skill, the comprehension of the compared-and-object-of-comparison relation arises — there too, due to the variety of the mode of expression, the charm of ornamentation itself produces in the connoisseurs and in those who perceive it a sense of wonder — thus the figure is implied. And the words 'iva' etc. that would express it are not employed. For example:
The streams from the great [mountain] are surely not garlands of <s>utpala</s> (lotuses)... [<s>Vakroktijīvita</s> Commentary 3.171]
Thus.

children.text:
yatra punarvācyamalaṃ (karaṇaṃ), tatrevādikaṃ pratipādanavaicitryāt bahuprakāraṃ prayogamarhati /
tathāca padārthaviṣayāyāmupamāyāṃ vākyaikadeśavartinorupamānopameyayoḥ parasparasāmyavācke prayukte, tasminneva vākye stanāntaravartinorupamānopameyayoḥ sādṛśyasaṃbandhābhidhāyī punarivādiḥ prayujyate /
(yadyapi) pratiyugalamupamānopameyabhāvasya parisamāptiḥ, tathāpi vākyārthaniṣpattāvupamānopameyabhāvasya saṃbhave prathamābhihitaiva yuktiranusartavyā /
yathā---
children.translated_text: But where the ornament is expressible, the 'iva' etc. deserve employment in many ways due to the variety of presentation. And thus, in a simile of word-meanings, when for the compared and the object of comparison situated in one part of the sentence a word expressing mutual similarity is employed, in that same sentence, for the compared and object of comparison situated in another part, the word 'iva' etc. expressing the relation of similarity is again employed. Although the compared-object-of-comparison relation is completed for each pair, nevertheless, when in the completion of the sentence-meaning the compared-object-of-comparison relation is possible, the reasoning stated first should be followed. For example:
Then <s>Raghu</s> set forth toward the northern direction of <s>Kubera</s>, like the sun,
As if to extract the essences from the northerners with his sharp arrows. [<s>Vakroktijīvita</s> Commentary 3.172]

children.text:
kvacitpadārthopamāyāmeva vākyaikadeśavyavasthitayorupamānopameyayoḥ sādṛśyasamanvayaḥ vācikaḥ /
vācakayukte tasminneva vākye tayorekatarasya dharmyantareṇa saha dharmāntaraṃ (ra) sādṛśyanibandhanatvāt upamānopameyabhāvaḥ saṃbhavati /
pūrvoktayā nītyā tadabhidhāyī punarivādiḥ prayujyate /
yathā---
children.translated_text: Sometimes, in a simile of word-meanings itself, the concordance of similarity between the compared and the object of comparison situated in one part of the sentence is verbal [i.e., explicitly expressed]. In that same sentence where the verbal marker is used, when one of the two [compared or object] enters into a similarity-based compared-object-of-comparison relation with another property-bearer through another property, by the principle stated before, the word 'iva' etc. expressing that is again employed. For example:
Having emerged, the splendor lovely as the beginning of day — like the disc of the sun — from the face of the great sage,
Bright as sparks of fire, it reached the face of <s>Pārtha</s> (<s>Arjuna</s>) like a shining lotus. [<s>Vakroktijīvita</s> Commentary 3.173]

children.text:
kvacitpadārthopamāyāmupameyānāmupamānānāṃ ca samasaṃkhyākānāṃ sūhadvaye prathamaṃ vivakṣitasamūhasaṃkhyābhedasamāhi (ta) dvitvameva samāśritya parasparasāmyasamanvayādupamānopameyabhāvamabhidhātumekasmin vācake prayukte samudāyadharmāṇāṃ samudāyapūrvakatvāttu paścādeteṣāṃ pratyekaṃ svasaṃbandhinaṃ prati sādhāraṇadharmasaṃbandhasāmarthyādupamānopameyabhāvaḥ paryavasyati /
yathā---
children.translated_text: Sometimes, in a simile of word-meanings, when the objects of comparison and the compared are equal in number, in two groups, first relying on the duality assembled by the division of the intended group-number, in order to express the compared-object-of-comparison relation through mutual concordance of similarity, when one verbal marker is employed — since the properties of the aggregate presuppose the aggregate — afterwards, for each of these individually, through the capacity of the relation of the common property with its own correlate, the compared-object-of-comparison relation is concluded. For example:
"Kissing the cheek..." [<s>Vakroktijīvita</s> Commentary 3.174]

children.text:
ityādau /
atra sparśollasaditi kriyāviśeṣaṇaṃ ceti dvābhyāṃ prakārābhyāmubhayaniṣṭhatayānyonyaṃ (sādhāraṇadharmasaṃbandhādupamānopameyabhāvaḥ) /
kvacitpadārthopamāyām ekasya vastunaḥ bahuvidhapadārthaviśeṣaṇaviśiṣṭatayā mukhyabhāvena varṇyamānavṛtterupameyatve tāvanmātraviśeṣaṇaiḥ svairviśiṣṭaṃ padārthāntaramupamānatāṃ yadā prāpnoti, tadā tayorubhayorapi tathāvidhayaiva parasparasāmyadharmatayānvayāt upamānopameyabhāvaḥ /
tadabhidhānārthamivādireva priyujyamānatāmarhati /
tadviśeṣaṇānāṃ parasparasāmyasaṃbandhābhidhāne pūrvoktaiva yuktiranusandheyā /
yathā---
children.translated_text: Here, through two modes — 'sparkling at the touch' as a qualification of action, and 'ca' (and) — by pertaining to both, [there is] the compared-object-of-comparison relation through the connection of the common property with both. Sometimes, in a simile of word-meanings, when a single object, being described primarily as qualified by many kinds of word-meaning qualifications, has the status of the compared, and when another object qualified by those very qualifications attains the status of the object of comparison, then, since both are connected by the very similarity of such mutual properties, the compared-object-of-comparison relation obtains. For expressing that, the word 'iva' etc. deserves to be employed. For the expression of the mutual similarity-relation of their qualifications, the reasoning stated before should be followed. For example:
"This <s>Pāṇḍya</s>..." etc. [<s>Vakroktijīvita</s> Commentary 3.175]

children.text:
tadevaṃvi(dha)pakṣe abhidhāprikāravaicitryāt vācakaśaktivaicitryācca sarvametadupapadyate /
upamādoṣaṇāṃ tu lakṣaṇasyeva sughaṭitatvāt dūrotsāritatvena neyārthādivadaparigaṇanam /
children.translated_text: Thus, in such cases, all this is justified due to the variety of the mode of expression and the variety of the power of the verbal marker. But the defects of simile, like the definition itself, being well-formulated, are set far apart and are not enumerated, like figurative meaning etc.
When a property that is the object of intention and that captivates the heart is expressed,
then these defects become ones whose functions are set far apart. [<s>Vakroktijīvita</s> Commentary 3.176]

This is an interpolated verse. Having thus expounded the ornament called <s>upamā</s> (simile), whose life is the similarity between the expressed contextual and non-contextual, he now expounds <s>śleṣa</s> (double meaning), which is essentially the similarity of the verbal marker and is predominantly of similar character:
That expressibility by a single word is maintained for two meanings;
The figure called <s>śleṣa</s> (double meaning) — such is the relation of the verbal marker and the expressed. [<s>Vakroktijīvita</s> 3.44]

children.text:
tadekaśabdavācyatvamityādi tadityanena śleṣopanibadhyamānavṛttervācakasya parāmarśaḥ /
tena tasyaivoktasya śabdasya padātmano vācakatvam /
tena "vācyatvam" abhidheyatvam /
"arthayoḥ" = vastunorabhidhīyamānayoḥ dvayoḥ satyabhūtayoḥ vākyārthatātparyasvarūpayoḥ "dhāryate" yasmin sa śleṣābhidhāno 'laṅkāraḥ /
"tādṛgvācakavācyatā" = sa iva dṛśyate yaḥ sa tādṛgucyate, tādṛkcāsau vācakaśca sa tathoktaḥ, tena vācyatā vācyatvaṃ abhidheyatvam /
tādṛśārthavācakatvaṃ yatra yasmin so 'pi śleṣa ucyate /
yaḥ śrutisāmyāt sa ivānubhūyate 'sau tādṛgucyate /
punaḥ sa eva svarādidharmāṇāmudāttādīnāmanyatvād bhidyate /
atra parasparāpekṣatvameva dvayorapi sādṛśyam /
yādṛgeko 'sya vācakaḥ tādṛk evāsāviti samāśrito vāstavapadavṛrtirvā yatraikasmin kvacidvākyaikadeśe, tadekaśabdavācyatvaṃ dvayoḥ /
atha tayoḥ tādṛgvācakavācyatvāviśeṣe 'pi śleṣa eveti katham /
atastribhiḥ prakāraistrividhaiḥ padārthaireva tatpratīteḥ /
arthaśleṣaḥ śabdaśleṣaḥ ubhayaśleṣaḥ iti /
tadevaṃvidhasyāsya pratipādakaṃ kimityāhaḥ---
children.translated_text: 'That expressibility by a single word' etc. — 'that' refers to the verbal marker whose activity is being connected with <s>śleṣa</s>. By that, the very word mentioned — having the nature of a <s>pada</s> (word-unit) — has the status of being a verbal marker. By that, 'expressibility' means the state of being denoted. 'Of two meanings' — of two real objects being denoted, whose nature is the purport of the sentence-meaning — 'is maintained' — in which that [expressibility] is maintained, that is the figure called <s>śleṣa</s>. 'Such is the relation of verbal marker and expressed' — that which appears like it is called '<s>tādṛk</s>' (such); and being such, it is also a verbal marker — thus described; by that, 'expressibility' means the state of being expressed, the state of being denoted. The state of being a verbal marker of such meaning — where that [exists], that too is called <s>śleṣa</s>. That which, due to similarity of sound, is experienced as if it were the same — that is called '<s>tādṛk</s>.' Again, that very [word] is differentiated by the otherness of properties such as accent (<s>udātta</s>) etc. Here, the mutual dependence of the two itself constitutes the similarity. Just as one verbal marker of this [meaning] is, so too is the other — thus, whether one resorts to the actual word-function or [finds it] somewhere in one part of the sentence, that expressibility by a single word pertains to the two [meanings]. Now, even though there is no difference in the relation of such a verbal marker to the expressed, how is it specifically <s>śleṣa</s>? Because the cognition of it arises through three kinds of word-meanings in three ways: <s>arthaśleṣa</s> (meaning-based double meaning), <s>śabdaśleṣa</s> (word-based double meaning), and <s>ubhayaśleṣa</s> (both combined). What demonstrates this kind [of figure]? — he says:
Another word-meaning is its demonstrator, [say] the poets;
The capacity of the expressed [meaning] is the other [demonstrator] — 'iva' etc. they accept. [<s>Vakroktijīvita</s> 3.45]

children.text:
padārthāntaramityādi /
"padārthāntaraṃ" = śliṣṭapadavyatiriktaṃ "aparaṃ" tatsamarpaṇasāmarthyasametametasya śleṣālaṅkārasya pratipādakaṃ samarpakaṃ kavayastadvidaḥ"pratijānate" pratyavabuddhyanti /
vācakaviśeṣa "maparaṃ ivādi" ivaprabhṛti vā padārthāntarādivyatiriktaṃ vācyasāmarthyamevavā kevalaṃ vākyaṃ sakṛtpratipāditam /
tasya svarūpasāmarthyavivakṣitārtha samarpaṇaśaktiyuktārthaṃ pratijānate /
pratipādakamiti saṃbandhaḥ /
triṣvapyeteṣu prakāreṣu dvayorarthayoḥ prādhānyena ca varṇyamānatve tathāvidhaśabdavācyatvalakṣaṇasāmyasamanvayasvarūpaṃ śobhānimittaṃ vākyasāmarthyalabhyaṃ pratīyamānamalaṅkaraṇaṃ, vācakasadbhāve punaḥ vācyameva /
prastutāprastutayorarthayoḥ pradhānaguṇabhāve sati tathaiva tathāvidhaśabdavācyatvasāmyasamanvaya eva /
mukhyatayā varṇyamānasyāpyekatarasyopamānatve samuccitopamādyā(locanayānyasyopameyatvasamanvayo 'nu) sandheyaḥ /
children.translated_text: 'Another word-meaning' etc. — 'Another word-meaning' — distinct from the word with double meaning — 'another' [means] that which is endowed with the capacity to present it — the knowledgeable poets 'accept' — understand it — as the demonstrator, the presenter, of this figure of <s>śleṣa</s>. A particular verbal marker — 'another' [meaning] 'iva' and the like, or distinct from another word-meaning — 'the capacity of the expressed alone' — merely the sentence once presented, having the power to convey the intended meaning through its own essential capacity — they accept [this] as the demonstrator. This is the syntactical connection. In all three of these modes, when two meanings are being described with prominence, the beauty that is the concordance of similarity characterized by such expressibility-by-a-single-word — obtainable through the capacity of the sentence — is the implied ornament. But when the verbal marker is present, it is simply expressed. When among the contextual and non-contextual meanings there is a relation of principal and subordinate, then likewise the very concordance of similarity characterized by such expressibility-by-a-single-word [obtains]. Even when one of them, though being described primarily, has the status of the object of comparison, the concordance of the other as the compared should be understood through the lens of accumulated simile etc.
A word that evokes one of the two meanings — of the word and its meaning,
When both appear as one, similarity expands, since they are governed by a single principle. [<s>Vakroktijīvita</s> 3.46]
From the recollection of a similar word, a meaning different from that is cognized;
Since the word arises and perishes, recollection is everywhere verbal. [<s>Vakroktijīvita</s> 3.47]
Among these, an example of the first [type], as follows:
"Inclined toward presenting one's own intent, stamped with the seal of sweetness, inscribing something indescribable within the hearts of those of noble mind through its charm,

children.text: ārūḍhaṃ rasavāsanāpariṇateḥ kāṣṭhāṃ kavīnāṃ paraṃ kāntānāṃ ca vilokitaṃ vijayate vaidagdhyavakraṃ vacaḥ // VjivC_3.177 //
children.translated_text: Having ascended to the highest stage of the maturation of the impression of <s>rasa</s> (aesthetic sentiment) — the oblique speech of the beloved and of poets reigns supreme in its sophistication." [<s>Vakroktijīvita</s> Commentary 3.177]
Of the second [type], for example:

children.text: yena dhvastamanobhavena balijitkāyaḥ purāstrīkṛtaḥ yaścodvṛttabhujaṅgāharavalayo gaṅgāṃ ca yo 'dhārayat /
children.translated_text: "He by whom, having destroyed <s>Manobhava</s> (Kāma), the body of <s>Balijit</s> (<s>Indra</s>) was formerly made into a woman; who bore <s>Gaṅgā</s> while wearing <s>Bhujaṅga</s> (serpent) necklaces with raised hoods;

children.text: yasyāhuḥ śaśimacchirohara iti stutyaṃ ca nāmāmarāḥ pāyātsa svayamandhakakṣayakarastvāṃ sarvado-mādhavaḥ // VjivC_3.178 //
children.translated_text: Whose praiseworthy name the gods call '<s>Śaśimacchirohara</s>' (bearer of the moon on his head / slayer of enemies) — may that <s>Mādhava</s> (<s>Viṣṇu</s> / <s>Śiva</s>), the destroyer of <s>Andhaka</s>, himself protect you, the giver of all!" [<s>Vakroktijīvita</s> Commentary 3.178]
Of the third [type], for example:
Wearing a garland fashioned of blooming <s>utpala</s> (blue lotus) shoots, igniting <s>Smara</s> (Love) with a glance whose sidelong cast is enchanting,

children.text: kāñcīdāmanibaddhabhaṅgi dadhatī vyalambinā vāsasā mūrtiḥ kāmaripoḥ sitāmbaradharā pāyādapāyājjagat // VjivC_3.179 //
children.translated_text: displaying a graceful bend caused by the girdle-string, with a garment hanging low — may the white-robed form of the Enemy of <s>Kāma</s> (<s>Śiva</s>) protect the world from calamity! [<s>Vakroktijīvita</s> Commentary 3.179]
An example of <s>śleṣa</s> (double meaning) with non-real factual content is as follows:

children.text: dṛṣṭyā keśava goparāgahṛtayā kiñcinna dṛṣṭaṃ mayā tenaiva skhalitāsmi nātha patitāṃ kiṃ nāma nālambase /
children.translated_text: "O <s>Keśava</s>, nothing was seen by me with my gaze stolen by the redness of the cows; by that very [blindness] I stumbled — O Lord, will you not support me who have fallen?
